paragraphs.text:
1. The first book holds the son of Cronos, the light-bringing ravisher of a maiden,
and the vault of stars battered by the hands of Typhon.

Tell, goddess, of the lightning, the courier of the fiery blaze of the son of Cronos,
the breath of the thunderbolt that brought to birth with a bridal spark,
the flash that served as bridal-chamber for Semele; tell too of the begetting
of Bacchus, twice-born, whom Zeus drew dripping out of the fire,
a half-completed infant of a mother whom no midwife delivered,
and, scoring with cautious hands an incision in his thigh,
brought to birth in a male womb, at once father and lady mother,
well aware of another such birth, since once from his teeming head,
bearing in his pregnant temple an unsown, unbelievable burden,
he shot forth Athena flashing in her armour.

Bring me the fennel-wand, clash the cymbals, you Muses,
and put into my hand the thyrsus of Dionysus, the god I sing.
But near the neighbouring island of Pharos set before me, joining the dance,
shifting Proteus of many turns, that he may appear
wearing his shape of many forms, since I hammer out a hymn of many forms.
For if he should creep forward as a serpent coiling along its track,
I will sing the divine ordeal, how with the ivied thyrsus
the dreadful tribes of the snake-haired Giants were cut to pieces.
If as a lion he should bristle, shaking the mane upon his neck,
I will hail Bacchus with the cry "euoi" upon the arm of grim Rhea,
stealing the breast of the goddess who suckles lions.
If, lifted high on a stormy leap of his feet,
a leopard should dart, changing into a richly varied shape,
I will hymn the son of Zeus, how he destroyed the race of the Indians,
riding down their elephants upon his car of leopards.
If his body should match the figure of a boar, I will sing the son of Thyone
desiring boar-slaying Aura, fit for marriage,
the Cybelean mother of Bacchus, the third and late-born.
If he should become mimicking water, I will sing Dionysus
plunging into the lap of the sea as Lycurgus armed against him.
If as a plant he should quiver, stretching out a counterfeit whisper,
I will recall Icarius, how beside the frenzied wine-press
the cluster was crushed by the trampling rivalry of feet.

Bring me the fennel-wand, you Mimallones, and bind upon my breast
the dappled fawnskin torn from the kill in place of my accustomed tunic,
full of the fragrance of nectar-sweet Maronian wine; let the heavy
sealskin be kept in the deep for Eidothea and Homer and Menelaus.
Give me the wild rattles and the goatskin shields, but to another
hand over the double-voiced sweet-singing pipe, lest I anger
my own Phoebus; for he refuses the breathing echo of reeds,
ever since, convicting the god-defying pipe of Marsyas,
he hung up the skin of the flayed herdsman upon a tree,
bellying out in the breezes, stripping bare every limb.

But, goddess, begin with Cadmus, the wandering searcher.
Once upon the Sidonian shore Zeus, a high-horned bull,
counterfeited a lovely lowing from his disguised throat
and felt the sweet sting of desire; and as he carried off the woman,
little Eros, circling his hands about, lightened her round the waist
with a double bond, and near at hand the bull that crossed the water,
bending low his curved neck beneath the girl who rode him,
crouching slantwise and stretching out his slackened back,
lifted Europa up; and as the bull rushed onward
his swimming hoof scored the silent water of the passable sea
with sparing tracks. Over the deep the girl,
quivering with fear, voyaged upon the bull's back,
unshaken and unwetted; and seeing her one might well have said
she was either Thetis or Galatea or the bedfellow of the Earth-shaker,
or Aphrodite seated upon the crest of Triton.
The dark-haired Earth-shaker marvelled at that voyage on hooves,
and Triton, hearing the deceitful lowing of Zeus,
bellowed a song answering the son of Cronos upon his conch,
singing the wedding hymn; and Nereus,
mixing wonder with fear, pointed out to Doris the woman borne aloft,
seeing the strange horned sailor. Riding the bull
that floated keel-deep, the bull-decked bride sailed on,
and trembling at the high-leaping course of her watery passage
she gripped the horn as a rudder, and Desire became her sailor.
And crafty Boreas, sick with love, bellied out
the whole robe shaken by the bridal breeze, and against both,
stealing his jealous look, hissed at her unripe breast.

As when one of the Nereids, peering up out of the sea,
seated on a dolphin, breaks the smooth calm of the waters,
and as she rises her wet hand is set in motion,
the very image of one swimming, and bearing her unwetted by the brine
the moist traveller is borne half-seen through the water,
arching his back, while creeping over the deep
the forked tail of the fish writes its outermost path:
so the bull lifted his back; and as the bull strained on,
Eros the herdsman lashed his enslaved neck with the love-girdle,
and lifting the bow on his shoulder like a herdsman's staff,
he shepherded with the Cyprian crook the bridegroom of Hera,
driving him into the watery pasture of Poseidon. And in shame
motherless Pallas blushed her virgin cheek
as she watched the wife who drove the son of Cronos.

And as Zeus sped along the watery track of his course,
the sea did not quench his desire, since the heavenly furrow
made the water, big with child, give birth to a deep-dwelling Aphrodite;
and the girl was both the steersman of the surge-free bull's passage,
his freight and his sailor. And gazing on
the swift-kneed, sentient ship of the sea that mimicked one,
the Achaean sailor, faring about, cried out such words:

"My eyes, what is this marvel? From where, cleaving the waves with his feet,
does a field-roaming bull swim through the barren water?
Is the son of Cronos making the land navigable? Through the sea
is a wet wagon-track being scored across the brine-soaked water?
I scan along the wave this counterfeit voyage. Is it Selene
who, holding her unyoked bull, travels the sea after the heavens?
Or does deep-dwelling Thetis steer this watery course?
The sea-bull has not got a shape like the land-bull
—for it has a fishy body—; and instead of bare-backed,
a strange-seeming Nereis with trailing robe drives over the waters
an unbridled bull that walks on land, a creature unaccustomed.
If it is Demeter of the grain-rich hair, and with her water-faring
bull's hoof she splits the grey-green back of the sea,
then you too, Poseidon, after the surge of the deep, as a wanderer
go on foot, a ploughman, over the thirsty back of the land,
cutting Demeter's furrow with a ship of the sea,
making a passable voyage on dry land with landward winds.

Bull, you have strayed off course, an exile; Nereus is no
herdsman, Proteus no ploughman, Glaucus no field-hand,
there is no marsh, no meadows in the swell, but sailing upon
the barren sea they cut the unploughed harbour-water
with the rudder and do not split it with iron;
the servants of the Earth-shaker do not sow furrows,
but the plant of the sea is seaweed and its seed is water,
the sailor a field-roamer, the voyage its furrows, the ship its plough-handle.
But from where do you pursue some maiden? Is it that bulls themselves
also, maddened with love, carry off women?
Has deceitful Poseidon seized the girl,
wearing the horned shape of a river-bull?
Has he woven yet another trick after the bed of Tyro,
as he did but yesterday, when as a watery bedfellow
the false Enipeus murmured with imitating streams?"

Such words the Greek sailor uttered as he passed,
in amazement. And the girl divined her bull-wedding,
and tearing her tresses she broke into a wailing cry:

"Deaf water, voiceless breakers, tell the bull,
if bulls can hear: be merciless no longer, pitiless one—spare the girl.
Tell, you breakers, for me to my child-loving father:
Europa, leaving her fatherland, sits upon some bull,
a ravisher and a sailor and, as I think, a bedfellow.
Carry these locks of mine to my mother, you circling breezes.
Yes, I beseech you, Boreas, as you carried off the Attic bride,
take me up on your wings into the air. Stop, my voice,
lest after the bull I should think Boreas too maddened with love."
So she spoke as the girl was ferried on the bull's spine.

It was from there that Cadmus, faring about, walking from land to land,
followed the restless tracks of the bride-stealing bull.
He came even to the murderous cave of the Arimoi, at the time when the roving
hills were battering the gates of unbreakable Olympus,
when the winged gods, high above the storm-free Nile,
mimicked the unreachable journey of birds,
oaring their strange path through the airy breeze,
and the seven-zoned vault was scourged. For going to the bed
of Plouto, Zeus son of Cronos, borne thither to beget
Tantalus, the foolish thief of the cups of heaven,
had set the gear of the upper air hidden in a hollow of the rock
and concealed his lightning. And as the thunderbolts beneath the roof
belched smoke, the white crag was blackened,
and with the hidden spark of the fire-pointed shaft
the springs grew warm, and with the steam of its ravine-channels
the foaming Mygdonian gorge resounded.

And stretching out his hands at the nod of his mother Earth,
Cilician Typhoeus stole the snowy weapons of Zeus,
the weapons of fire; and spreading the rank of his heavy-thundering throats
he raised a clamour of every cry of beasts speaking with one voice:
serpents grown together darted upon the face
of leopards, and licked the grim manes of lions,
and they girdled the horns of bulls in coils
with their twisting tails, and mingled the venom hurled
from their long-tongued jaws with the foam of boars.
Setting the gear of the son of Cronos beneath the cavernous rock,
he stretched up to the air the harvest of his towering hands;
and with skilful array round the very ankle of Olympus,
gripping the Cynosurid Bear on this side and pressing on that
the mane of the Parrhasian Bear leaning on its axle, he hauled it back,
and seizing Bootes with another hand he checked him,
and with another dragged the Morning Star; and in vain beneath the circling turning-post
the early-rising sound of the heavenly lash hissed.
He dragged at the dawn-born star, and as the Bull was held back
the unfinished, untimely Hour of the chariot grew weary;
and with the shadowy locks of his viper-haired heads
the light was mingled with mist, and by day
Selene, rising together with the sun, shone bright.

Nor did the Giant cease: with a backward course
from the North to the South, leaving one pole he stood at the other;
and gripping the Charioteer with his long hand
he lashed the back of the hail-bringing Goat,
and dragging the twin Fishes from the sky toward the sea
he shook the Ram, the navel-star of mid-Olympus,
high above the neighbouring fiery spring-circle,
that balances the day in equal poise within its mist.
On his coiling feet Typhoeus was lifted up
close to the clouds; and spreading the wide-scattered nation of his palms
he covered the silvery radiance of the cloudless air,
shaking the crooked army of his snakes. Of these one
ran upright along the rim of the axled circle,
and leapt upon the spine of the heavenly Dragon,
hissing at Ares; another, close to the maiden daughter of Cepheus,
coiling with its starry hands a circle of equal yoke,
fettered the bound Andromeda with a second bond,
slanting beneath its coils; another, a horned serpent,
coiled around the matching horn-tip of the Bull,
maddened, writhing above the brow of the Bull
against the answering Hyades, the image of horned Selene,
with jaws gaping; and the venom-shooting bands of the interwoven serpents
girdled Bootes about.
And another, bold, sprang up, seeing another Serpent of Olympus,
leaping about the snaky arm of Ophiuchus,
and weaving another wreath round the wreath of Ariadne,
arching its neck, it writhed with the trailing of its belly.
And shaking the girdle of Zephyrus and the wing of opposing Eurus,
many-armed Typhoeus ranged about
toward both turning-posts, after the Morning Star dragging the Evening Star
and the crest of Atlas. And in the weed-grown gulf
often gripping the Poseidonian chariot of the sea
he dragged it from the depths to the land; and by the brine-soaked hair
he hauled up again the stalled horse from its submarine manger
and flung the wandering colt up to the heavenly rim,
hurling at Olympus; and as his car was lashed
the circling horses of the Sun neighed beneath the yoke;
and often, snatching up the bull of the field, ceased from the plough-pole,
bellowing, and brandishing it in his threatening arm,
he hurled down the very likeness of Selene's own,
and stayed its course; and pulling back with the bridle
the white yoke-straps of the goddess's bulls he made them whirl,
pouring out the deadly hiss of his venom-spitting viper.

Nor did Titanic Mene yield to the armed Giant:
fighting against the matching horned heads of the Giant
she scored the light-bringing circle of her bull's horn;
and the gleaming oxen of Selene lowed,
struck with awe at the gaping chasm of the Typhaonian throat.

The fearless Hours armed the starry battalions,
and the ranks of the heavenly Spirals flashed for battle
in their guiding circle; and the shifting army hissed with fire,
raving through the air—those who hold Boreas,
and the western back of Libos, and those who got the rim of Eurus,
and the southern corners; and in their common-zealed turmoil
the unshaken choir of the fixed stars was driven from its place,
and met the wandering ones across the way; and the upright axle,
pierced through the heavenly hollow and fixed at the middle,
roared with sound; and watching the nations of the beasts,
Orion, hunter and rouser of dogs, drew his sword,
and as the bearer was armed
the bright back of the Tanagraean blade flashed;
and shaking the flame of his fire-hot throat,
the thirsty starry Dog seethed in his throat,
sending forth a hot baying, and instead of his accustomed hare
he belched at the Typhaonian beasts the steam of his teeth.

And the vault thundered; and answering, the sky itself
with its seven zones, from throats equal in number
to the Pleiades, the seven-mouthed echo cried aloud,
and the wandering stars thundered back an equal din.

And seeing the terrible snaky shape of the Giant,
gleaming Ophiuchus shook from his evil-averting hands
the grey-green backs of his fire-nurtured serpents,
hurling his dappled crooked dart; and round the flame
whirlwinds hissed, and the slanting snaky arrows
were shot, raving through the air;
and bold Sagittarius, running the course with the fishy Goat,
sent his shaft; and in the wagon-circle
the Dragon, shown mid-sky and parted between the twin Bears,
whirled the gleaming track of his heavenly spine;
and neighbouring Erigone's driver, fellow-traveller of the Wain,
Bootes, brandished his crook with shining arm;
and at the knee of the Phantom and beside the near-faring Swan
the starry Lyre prophesied the victory of Zeus.

And Typhoeus, seizing the heads of Corycus, shook them,
and pressing the stream of the Cilician river with its dweller
he gathered Tarsus and Cydnus together in one fist;
and shooting at the ranks of the brine with rocky missiles
he removed them to the cliffs, lashing the sea after the air;
and as the Giant moved with the trailing of his brine-soaked foot
his loins were shown bare and unwetted through the water,
and round his middle thigh the heavy-roaring water boomed;
and the swimming serpents, hissing Ares from their sea-loud throats,
made war upon the sea,
spitting out venom; and as Typhon stood in the fishy deep
within his weed-grown hollow,
his feet were fixed in the depth, and his belly mingled with the air,
pressed by the clouds; and the sea-lion,
hearing the dreadful roar of the high-crested lions of the Giant's head,
hid himself in the muddy gulf;
and the whole battalion of sea-monsters was straitened in the sea,
for the earth-born one filled the whole brine, greater than the land,
with his flood-free flanks; and the seals lowed,
and the dolphins hid themselves in the deep sea;
and weaving its interwoven coil in crooked spirals,
the wily-minded octopus fixed itself to its accustomed rock,
and the ravine-formed shape became the image of his limbs.
No creature was without trembling: even she who came in pursuit,
the love-maddened moray, longing for the serpent's bed,
shuddered at the god-defying breath of the sea-faring serpents.

The sea was towered up and consorted with Olympus
in its towering floods; and on the air-faring stream
the bird of the air, unwetted, bathed in the neighbouring sea.

And Typhoeus, holding the likeness of the deep-sea trident,
cutting with his immeasurable hand in an earth-shaking heave
an island, a fragment torn from the brine-founded margin of the land,
hurled it back-whirling, rolling it whole into a ball;
and as the Giant fought in the air, the palms that border the stars,
shadowing the sun, were arrayed against Olympus,
the hurlers of the towering crag.

And after the depth's limit, after the kindly earth's seat,
the false Zeus armed his hand with the fire-pointed thunderbolt;
and lifting the gear of the son of Cronos with his unconquerable
hands—two hundred of them—the monster Typhoeus laboured
under its weight; yet the son of Cronos lightens it with a single palm.
And on the dry palms of the cloudless Giant
the thunder sent forth a dull song of soundless echo,
buzzing faintly, and scarcely, in the drought of the air,
a thirsty dew of dripless snow distilled upon him;
and the lightning dimmed, and like smoke-coloured fume
a thin fire shone with a downcast gleam;
and the thunderbolts, knowing the hands of their untried bearer,
holding their male fire, were unmanned,
and slipping often from his measureless hands
with leaps of their own; and the fires strayed away,
longing for the accustomed hand of their heavenly bearer.

As when some horseman, a stranger and untaught,
lashing an unruly colt that spits out the bit,
toiled often in vain, while the bold beast, with knowing spirit,
recognized the false hand of the unaccustomed driver,
and goaded leapt up, and rising high upright
fixed firm the unshaken hoof of its hind foot,
and lightened its jutting forelegs, brandishing its knees,
and lifted its crest, and on both its shoulders
the spreading mane was shaken loose, hanging from its neck:
so the Giant laboured, lifting with alternate hands
the sun-fleeing flash of the wandering thunderbolt.

While Cadmus the wanderer was faring among the Arimoi,
meanwhile, above the Dictaean shore, the water-faring bull
laid down its girl from its mane, unwetted.

And Hera, seeing the son of Cronos shaken with desire,
in jealous madness joined her voice with mocking spite:

"Phoebus, stand by your father, lest some ploughman
take Zeus and drag him to the earth-shaking plough-handle.
Would that he took and dragged him, so that I might shout this to Zeus:
'Endure the double goads, both of the field-hands and of the Loves.'
As Nomios, glorious archer, shepherd your sire,
lest the cattle-driving Selene should yoke the son of Cronos,
lest, hastening to look upon the bed of the herdsman Endymion,
she should brand the back of Zeus with her unsparing lash.
Lord Zeus, when Io was a horned heifer she failed,
in that she never saw you as such a mate, that she might bear
some bull of equal form to her horned bedfellow.
Beware of Hermes, the cattle-thief of accustomed craft,
lest taking you like a bull he steal his own father,
and grant the lyre once again to your son Phoebus,
an heirloom of the ravisher now ravished. But what shall I do?
Would that Argus, with his whole body shining with sleepless eyes,
were still alive, that, dragging Zeus into a pathless pasture,
the herdsman of Hera might strike his flank with the crook."

So she spoke; and the son of Cronos, leaving his bull-faced shape,
like a youth ran round the unyoked girl;
and he touched her limbs, and from the bride's breast
first he loosed the girdle that ran about her, and as though unwilling
he pressed the swollen circle of her unyielding breast,
and kissed the edge of her lip, and unfolding in silence
the sacred knot of her unwedded maidenhood, kept till then,
he plucked the unripe fruit of the Cyprian Loves.

And her belly, swelling with twin seed, grew big with the wave of birth;
and Zeus the husband left his bride, pregnant
with a divine birthing, to Asterion, her wealthy consort;
and rising beside the ankle of the Charioteer
the starry bridegroom, the Bull of Olympus, gleamed,
keeping his dew-loving back for the springtime Sun,
rising crouched and slanting; and half-dipped
he stretches his jutting right foot toward Orion
and appears, and treading the western rim more swiftly
he passes the Charioteer who rises beside him.

So the Bull was fixed in heaven. But Typhoeus
was not to keep his hold on the weapons of Zeus much longer; for with the archer
Eros, Zeus son of Cronos, leaving the whirling vault,
met the wandering Cadmus, the roving searcher, upon the mountain,
and contrived a shared and crafty plan,
stitching for Typhon the threads of the ill-spinning Fate.
And Pan the goatherd, fellow-traveller of all-ruling Zeus,
gave oxen and sheep and ranks of fair-horned goats;
and weaving a hut of reeds with a coiling bond
he fixed it over the ground, and in some unknown shape,
fastening a herdsman's dress upon the skin of Cadmus,
clothed the false herdsman in imitating garments;
and bearing a crafty pipe he gave to the knowing Cadmus
the steersman of Typhaon's destruction.

And calling the false herdsman and driver of his lineage,
winged Zeus shaped a single plan with him:

"Cadmus, dear friend, pipe, and the sky will be fair-weathered;
you delay, and Olympus is scourged; for with my heavenly
weapons Typhoeus is helmeted and armed.
The aegis alone is left to me; but what will my aegis
do, striving against the thunderbolt of Typhon?
I fear lest old Cronos should laugh, and I shrink
from the proud neck of my adversary, lordly Iapetus;
I fear story-breeding Hellas the more, lest some Achaean
should call Typhon the rain-giver and the high-ruling
or the supreme one, defiling my name. Become an oxherd
for a single dawn, and piping with mind-stealing music
rescue with your shepherd's pipe the shepherd of the universe,
lest I hear the sound of Typhoeus the cloud-gatherer,
lest I hear the thunder of another, a false Zeus, but that I may stop him
warring with lightnings and casting the thunderbolt.
And if you have got the blood of Zeus and the race of Inachian Io,
with the evil-averting song of your cunning pipe
charm the mind of Typhon. And I will give you gifts worthy of your toils,
a double gift: for I will make you the saviour
of the harmony of the universe, and the consort of Harmonia.
And you, first-sown beginning of marriage that brings offspring to fulfilment,
stretch, Eros, your bow, and the universe wanders no more.
If all things come from you, loving shepherd of life,
draw one more arrow, that you may save the whole:
since you are fiery, arm yourself against Typhon, and the fire-bearing
thunderbolts may return from him to my hand.
All-subduer, strike one alone with your fire, and let your charmed
arrow capture him whom the son of Cronos has not conquered;
and let him have the sting of Cadmus' heart-charming song
as much as I had longing for the wedding of Europa."

So speaking, he sped away, the very image of a horned bull,
from where the mountain Taurus took its name. And drawing out sharply
the deceitful echo of his harmonious reeds,
leaning his back beneath a neighbouring oak of the wild wood,
and wearing the country garb of a true herdsman,
Cadmus sent a guileful hymn to the ears of Typhaon,
sending a thin breath from his swollen cheek.

There the song-loving Giant, with the snaky trailing of his foot,
sprang up, listening to the cunning melody; and within the cave
leaving the flaming weapons of Zeus beside his mother Earth,
he sought out the neighbouring strain of the delightful pipe,
following the music; and seeing him near the thicket
Cadmus, as though afraid, hid beneath a cleft rock.
But the high-headed Typhoeus, marking him as he shrank away,
the monster called him with speechless nods,
and did not recognize the clear-voiced guile; and to the answering
herdsman he stretched out one right hand, not knowing
it was the net of his destruction; and with his middle blood-red face,
laughing with human voice, he broke into vainglorious speech:

"Goatherd, why do you tremble at me? Why do you cover your eyes with your hand?
A fine thing it is for me to pursue a mortal man after the son of Cronos,
a fine thing for me to lift a pipe along with my lightnings!
What has reeds in common with the smoky thunderbolt?
Keep your pipe to yourself, since Typhoeus has got another
Olympian instrument that sounds of itself; and seated
with soundless hands, bereft of his accustomed noise,
cloudless Zeus has need of your pipe.
But let him have the clatter of your few little reeds; for worthless
unplaited reeds I do not roll in rows with reeds,
but joining rolling clouds with clouds
I send a din yoked to the crashes of heaven.
I will set up, if you wish, a friendly contest: but you, singing,
send forth your reedy melody, while I hammer out the thunder;
for with breath you, holding your jutting cheek swollen,
blow with your mouths, while, lashed by the breath
of Boreas the blower, the thunderbolts roar for me.
Oxherd, you shall have a reward for your pipe; for when I,
sceptred in place of Zeus, drive the heavenly throne,
following me from earth to the upper air I will carry you too,
together with your very pipe and, if you wish, with your flock as well;
nor shall you be parted from your herd; for of matching form
I will fix your goats above the spine of Capricorn,
or near the Charioteer, who in Olympus stretches out
the Olenian shining She-Goat with his gleaming arm;
and I will set beside the broad neck of the rain-breeding Bull
your starry oxen, rising over Olympus,
or beside the dewy turning-post, where with life-warming throat
the oxen of Selene send forth their windy lowing.
Nor shall you have need of your little hut; but in place of the thicket
let your flock flash with the airy Kids in the sky.
And I will make the likeness of another manger, that it too,
of equal form, may shine beside the neighbouring Manger of the Asses.
Be starry too, after your oxherding, where Bootes
appears, and you too, stretching out a starry crook,
become the Arctic driver of the Lycaonian Wain.
Hearth-fellow of heavenly Typhon, blessed shepherd,
play today on earth, and tomorrow within Olympus.
And as gifts worthy of your music, beside the star-shining circle
I will fix your Olympian face, and your sweet-voiced
pipe I will join to the heavenly Harp.
To you, if you wish, I will grant the holy marriage of Athena;
and if the grey-eyed one does not please you, take Leto,
or a Grace, or Cytherea, or Artemis, or marriage with Hebe;
only do not seek the bed of my own Hera.
And if you have got a horse-driving brother skilled in the chariot,
let him receive the fiery four-yoked car of the Sun;
and if you long, as a goatherd, to brandish the aegis of Zeus,
I will give you this gift. And I will journey to Olympus,
caring nothing for the weaponless son of Cronos; for what
could Athena, being female, do to me with her armour?
But strike up, oxherd, the song of Typhon's victory,
hymning me as the true new sceptred lord of Olympus,
bearing the sceptre of Zeus and the lightning-flashing tunic."
He spoke, and Adrasteia recorded all his words.

But when Cadmus knew that the son of earth had been carried
willingly, by the thread of Fate, into the net of capture,
struck by the sweet sting of the delightful reeds,
unsmiling he uttered a cunning voice:

"You marvelled at the slight sound of my pipe when you heard it;
tell me, what would you do when I sing of your throne,
hammering out the victory-hymn of my seven-toned lyre?
For even with heavenly plectra I once strove
and outran Phoebus with my harp, and my
sweet-sounding strings the son of Cronos crushed to dust with the thunderbolt,
doing a favour to his defeated son; but if ever I find
my sinews swelling again, stretching a song with the plectra,
I will charm all the trees and the mountains and the minds of beasts;
and the self-coiling crown, yoke-fellow of the agemate earth,
the Ocean that hastens, ever back-whirling, I will hold
to drive its circling water round the same turning-post,
and the battalion of the fixed stars and the running wanderers
I will stay, and Phaethon and the plough-pole of Selene.
But striking the gods and Zeus with your fiery shaft,
leave only the glorious archer alone, so that round the dinner of the table,
while Typhon feasts, I and Phoebus may contend,
which of us, singing of great Typhon, shall conquer the other.
Do not kill the dancing Pierides, that they too,
when Phoebus leads the revel, or your own herdsman,
may weave a female song in concert with the male music."

He spoke; and Typhoeus nodded with his glaring brows,
and shook his locks; and from his belching hair
the hills were sprinkled with snaky venom.

And swiftly he hastened to his cave; and from there, lifting
the sinews of Zeus, he gave them as a guest-gift to crafty Cadmus,
the sinews that once fell to the earth in the Typhaonian combat.
And the deceitful shepherd praised the ambrosial gift;
and he handled them, and as a string
to be fitted to his harp he hid them in the hollow rock,
kept for Zeus the slayer of Giants. And with sparing
breath, sending a thin blast from his closed lips,
stealing the tone of the echo from the pressed reeds,
he uttered a sweeter melody; and stretching out his many ears
Typhon listened to the harmony, and did not understand.

And to the charmed Giant the false shepherd piped
a tune as if singing of the flight of the immortals on his pipe,
and made music of the coming neighbouring victory of Zeus,
singing the doom of Typhon to seated Typhon;
and he roused a greater frenzy. And as a young man with the sweet sting
of love, delicate and love-maddened, is charmed by a maiden of his age,
and now at the silvery circles of her graceful face,
now at the wandering cluster of her deep-curled hair,
he gazes, now at her rose-coloured hand, now at the rim
of her rosy breast bound tight by the girdle he watches,
peering at her bared neck, and round her form
he is charmed, casting his insatiate gaze now here, now there,
and never wishes to leave the maiden: so Typhoeus
gave his whole mind, charmed by the music, to Cadmus.

2. The second book holds the star-roving war of Typhon
and the lightning and the labours of Zeus and the revel of Olympus.

So he stayed there beside the ankles of the wild wood,
trailing his shifting lips along the high-pierced pipe,
Cadmus son of Agenor, the false goatherd; and unforeseen
Zeus son of Cronos, unapproached, creeping noiseless beneath the cave,
armed his hands a second time with his accustomed fire
and hid Cadmus in a cloud beside the unobserved rock,
lest, learning the deceiving trick and the theft of the thunderbolt,
late-witted Typhoeus should secretly kill
the shifting herdsman; but he, with the sweeter sting,
wished the more to listen to the heart-charming rhythm of the song.

As when one, hearing the deceitful hymn of a Siren,
is drawn, untimely, to a self-summoned doom, a sailor
charmed by the melody, no longer cleaving the wave,
no longer whitening the grey water with calm-borne oars,
but falling upon the net of clear-voiced Fate
he takes delight, forgetting his rudder, leaving the star
of the seven-pathed Pleiad and the rim of the circling Bear:
so Typhon, shaken by the breaths of the cunning song,
received the sweet shaft of the pipe, the escort of his destruction.

But as Cadmus was hidden in the shadowy girdle of clouds,
the breathing reed of the sweet-singing herdsman fell silent
and checked the harmony. And Typhoeus, the high-flier,
seized with the frenzy of war, ran down into the cave's recess,
and sought the wind-roving thunder with roaming madness
and the unattainable lightning, and with searching foot
he hunted the blazing flash of the stolen thunderbolt,
and found the cave empty. Learning too late the crafty
purposes of the son of Cronos and the shifting wiles of Cadmus,
brandishing his weapons against the cliffs he leapt up at Olympus.

And dragging the crooked track of his foot with snaky sole
he spat venom from his hurling throat;
and as the high-crested Giant rained down springs
from his viper hair, the ravines surged with flood;
and as he rushed on, the deep-set seat of the earth,
the floor of the unshaken plain, was set quaking, the Cilician base,
by his serpent feet, and in the much-crashing tumult
of the battered ridge of the crested mountain
the neighbouring Pamphylian banks danced for fear,
and the earth's caverns boomed, the topmost shores
trembled, the recesses shook, and the headlands slipped
as the sand was loosened beneath his feet in the earth-shaking heave.

There was no pasture then, nor were the beasts unharmed; for the raw-devouring
bears were carved up by the face of Typhaon
with bearlike jaws, and the grey limbs of the shaggy-chested lions
were gulped down by his lion heads
with matching gapings, and with his snaky throat
the cold backs of the earth-fed serpents were torn,
and he feasted on the birds of the air with his neighbouring throat,
flying through the trackless heaven, and the close-shown
eagle he ate the more, since it is called the bird of Zeus;
he ate the plough-ox, and felt no pity, marking
its bloodstained neck scored by the yoking bond.
And he dried up the rivers, drinking the after-dinner water,
and battered down the battalions of the Naiads of the streams;
and a deep-dwelling Naiad nymph, treading the passable flood
with foot-leaping over the water, stood with limbs unwetted,
shoeless, a water nymph of the watery way, and with rivalling foot,
as the girl quivered beside the thirsty margin of the streams,
her fixed knees were bound fast by the muddy bond.

And seeing the many-shaped face of the maddened Giant
the old shepherd in terror shook off his pipe,
and fled afar; and seeing the wide-scattered nation of palms
the goatherd left his unsteady pipe to the storm-winds;
the patient ploughman did not cover the seed in the soil,
sprinkling the fresh-scored earth with back-cast grain,
nor with the guiding heave of the Typhaonian hand
did he cut the cleaving furrow with the earth-shaking iron,
but let his oxen go, and by the Giant's missile
the flanks of the cloven earth were laid bare.
And he loosed a watery vein, and as the chasm opened
the nether channel welled up with fountain streams,
pouring the under-bosomed water of the unroofed floor;
and crags were flung; and falling from the air
into the ravine-streams they were hidden in the sea,
turning the waters to dry land; and from the earthy missiles
the self-fixed ankles of new-born islands took root.
And trees were uptorn root and all from the soil,
and the unripe fruit fell to the ground, and the fresh-blooming
garden was made void, and the rose-bed reduced to dust;
and Zephyrus was shaken with the rolling of the cypresses'
withered leaves; and with grief-loving songs
Phoebus sang the dirge for the slain hyacinths,
weaving a mournful hymn, and over the Amyclaean clusters
much more he lamented the neighbouring laurel, cut down;
and grieving, Pan set upright his own fallen pine;
and remembering Moria, the city-bearing Attic bride,
the Grey-eyed one moaned over the olive she was cutting;
and the Paphian wept for the dusted anemone,
and oft mourning the fragrant tress of the buds
she tore the delicate lock of the dusted rose-bed;
and Deo lamented the half-finished, perished grain,
no longer leading the harvest-revel; and the Hamadryad
nymphs, agemates, mourned for the trees that lost their shade.

And some Hamadryad of the same age, with garland unbound,
leapt up from a fair-shooted laurel as its cluster was split,
and another maiden, fleeing on running foot from a pine,
appeared near at hand and addressed the neighbouring wandering nymph:

"Bed-fleeing Hamadryad of the laurel, let there be one course
for us both: may you not see Phoebus, may I not behold Pan.
Woodcutters, pass by these trees, do not cut the plants of poor Daphne,
grieved and stricken; spare them, carpenter,
do not finish a ship by cutting the pinewood timbers,
lest they touch the surge of sea-born Aphrodite.
Yes, woodsman, grant me a last favour: instead of clusters
cut me with your axes, and through my breast
fix the chaste bronze of unwedded Athena,
that I may die before marriage and come a virgin to Hades,
still innocent of love, like Pitys, like Daphne."

So speaking she made a counterfeit girdle of leaves,
and with a green sash hid the circle of her breast
in shame, and pressed thigh fast to thigh;
and the other, looking on her, broke into downcast speech:

"I have the inborn fear of maidenhood, since I too,
sprung from Daphne, am pursued, like Daphne.
Where shall I flee? Shall I sink beneath the cliffs? But the hills
flung at Olympus the thunderbolts have burned to ash,
and I tremble at your love-sick Pan, who will trouble me
as he troubled Pitys, as he troubled Syrinx; and pursued myself
I too shall become another echoing, mountain-roving Echo.
No longer do I haunt these clusters, but I dwell, half-seen,
in the mountains, away from the trees, where Artemis herself
hunts, the lover of maidens; but the son of Cronos
won the bed of Callisto by changing his shape into Artemis.
I will come to the swell of the sea: what is marriage to me? But in the deep
the Earth-shaker, woman-mad, pursued Asteria.
Would that I had light wings: along the high-pathed way
I would travel a road shared with the airy winds;
but soon the course of wings is empty, since Typhoeus
with his towering hands touches the clouds.
And if he forces me to unjust marriage, I will change my shape,
mingle with the birds, and flying as a nightingale
or as a swallow, announcer of the rose and the flowery dew,
I will be the swallow dear to springtime Zephyrus,
a chattering bird uttering the melody of echo beneath the eaves,
circling my nest with winged dance.
Procne, you who suffered bitter things, you weep in mournful song
for your son, and I will lament my own bed.
Lord Zeus, do not make me a swallow, lest Tereus too,
winged and angered, pursue me, as Typhoeus does.
Air, mountains, the impassable sea! Within the earth
I hide; but from the snaky soles of the Giant
the venom-shooting water-snakes that lurk go down beneath the earth.
Would I were the common water of a settlement, like Comaetho
who mingled her fresh-flowing streams with her father Cydnus;
but I will not go against the tale, since I shall join in my streams
my maiden-loving water to a maiden's love-sick water.
Where shall I flee? Shall I mate with Typhon? But then I will bear
a strange-formed, many-shaped son, like his father.
Would I were another tree, and pass from oak to oak,
bearing the name of a chaste child; but instead of Daphne
let me not be called by Myrrha's unlawful name of a shoot.
Yes, I beseech you: beside the stream of mournful Eridanus
let me too be one of the Heliades, and oft I will send
amber from my eyelids, and with grief-loving clusters
spread the entwined leaves of a neighbouring poplar,
mourning my maidenhood with rich tears;
for I do not lament Phaethon. Be gracious, laurel,
I am ashamed to be another plant after the plant of the former wood.
I will be, like Niobe, a stone myself, that travellers too
may pity me weeping in stone, turned to marble;
but what shape have I of an evil-tongued woman? Be gracious, Leto;
away with the god-defying name of that grievous-bearing nymph."

So she spoke; and the Sun, leaving the whirling vault,
turned his car toward the west; and rising from the earth
like a high-stretched cone into the air, silent Night
cloaked the heaven with a starry tunic,
adorning the sky; and beside the cloudless Nile
the immortals wandered, and beside the brow-frowning Bull
Zeus son of Cronos awaited the strife-rousing light of Dawn.

It was night; and the guarding ranks of Olympus stood
about its seven zones, and as if high above towers
there was a nightly war-cry, and the discordant clamour of stars
was borne wide about, and the sound of the axle's din
the turning-post of the Moon received from the starting-line of Cronos.
And the warding Hours of the upper air, attendants
of Phaethon, fenced the heaven with crowning veils
of close-set clouds; and on the unplundered gates
the stars locked the Atlantean bar,
lest some ambush should enter the pole while the blessed were away;
and instead of the din of pipes and the accustomed flute
the breezes piped a melody on their nightly wings.

And fellow-traveller of the heavenly Dragon and the Arcadian Bear,
gazing aloft at the nightly assault of Typhon,
old Bootes kept watch with sleepless eyes,
the Morning Star watched the east, the Evening Star
the west, and leaving the southern gate to the archer with the bow,
Cepheus ranged about the rainy gates of Boreas.
And there were fires everywhere, since the fiery flames of the stars
and the nightly lamps of the sleepless Moon
shone like torches, and with stormy whirling,
darting often from the air to the height of Olympus,
the shooting stars scored the air with fire,
to the right of the son of Cronos, and with tumbling heave,
darting often through the scored clouds,
the lightning leapt, and with alternate flashes
the back-running, unsteady radiance was hidden and shone,
and twisting his locks of plaited fire in clusters
the comet roughened his light with hairy flame,
and the visiting meteors gleamed, and like long
beams the long-fired bolts stretched from the air,
warring alongside Zeus, and shining beneath the rays
of the opposing Sun, bending in step with the rain,
the curved circles of the rainbow wove their many-coloured track,
mixing green with darkening, white with rose-coloured.

And to Zeus, left alone, Victory came as comforter,
tracing the topmost paths of the air with her sandal,
having the form of Leto, and arming the father
with answering lips she cried this shifting speech:

"Lord Zeus, stand as champion of your children, and let me not see
unwedded Athena, untaught in marriage, joined with Typhon;
do not make a mother of the motherless, but fighting
lift the lightning, the shining spear of Olympus,
and gather the clouds a second time, rain-bringing Zeus;
for already the seats of the steadfast universe are shaken
by the Typhaonian hands, and the yoke-fellow elements
being loosed, the four of them, Deo has renounced her harvest;
Hebe left the cup, and Ares shook off his spear,
Hermes laid down his wand, and Apollo flung away his lyre,
and the winged one flew off, leaving his winged arrows,
in the form of a swan, and the world of the wedding-goddess
became seedless, wandering Aphrodite,
and the cables of the unbreakable harmony were loosed; for the bridal-tending,
all-subduing, unsubdued, bold Eros has flown into fear,
leaving his generative bow; and leaving accustomed Lemnos
your fiery Hephaestus, dragging his unruly knees,
alas, slowly holds an unsteady course. Ah, great marvel,
I pity your Hera even as she rages much against me.
Will your father come again into the choir of stars?
May that never come to pass; and though I am called a Titaness,
I do not wish to see the Titans ruling Olympus,
but you and your children. With your prevailing thunderbolt
fight as champion for chaste Artemis: am I to keep
the bride dowerless for a forced bedfellow?
Will the stewardess of birth see her own birth? Will she stretch
her hands to me? And what gracious Eileithyia shall I call upon
for the archer-goddess, when an Eileithyia herself is in travail?"

As she spoke thus, Sleep, twining his shadowy wing,
lulled all panting Nature to rest; but the son of Cronos
was then alone sleepless. And spreading himself out, Typhoeus
laid his sluggish back on the heavy ground-couches,
filling mother Earth; and as her bosom opened
the lurking beds were hollowed with gaping chasm
as the snaky heads sank into the ground.

And when the sun appeared, from his throats that spoke one tongue
many-armed Typhoeus bellowed to the war,
calling great Zeus; and his grim voice reached the place
where the root-fixed base of the back-faring Ocean
encircles the rim of the universe, cut in four,
girdling the whole earth with a circling crown-like band;
and as the Giant spoke, answering his ranks of voice,
the echo crashed of every kind, no single concordant sound;
and as he was armed in the many-formed shape of his nature
there rang the howling of wolves, the roaring of lions,
the snorting of boars, the lowing of oxen, the hissing of serpents,
the bold gaping of leopards, the jaw of armed bears,
the rage of dogs; and in his middle, with a man's shape,
the Giant uttered a voice threatening Zeus:

"My hands, batter the house of Zeus, shake the base
of the universe along with the blessed ones, and the self-coiling
divine bar of Olympus break, and as the heavenly
column is dragged to the earth let shaken Atlas flee,
let him cast off the star-roving rim of Olympus,
no longer fearing its spiral course—for I will not allow
the son of Earth, bowed beneath his pressed shoulders,
to heave aloft the back-whirling burden of the air—
but, leaving the unending load to the other gods,
let him fight against the blessed, and break the rocks
with rugged missiles, shooting at the star-vault
that he once bore aloft; and scourged by the hills
let the fearful, strengthless Hours flee from heaven,
the handmaids of the Sun; and, gripping me in your coils,
mingle earth with air, water with fire, sea with Olympus.
And I will impose servile compulsion on the four winds:
I lash Boreas, I drive Notos in rout, I scourge Eurus,
and I would strike Zephyrus, and mingle night with day
with one hand; and my brother Ocean, with many-fountained throat,
leading his uplifted water against Olympus,
borne high above his five parallel circles,
let him flood the stars, and let the thirsty Bear
wander in the water as the Wain's plough-pole sinks.

My bulls, shaking the equinoctial rim of the circles,
low to the air, and with scoring horns
break the horns of the matching fiery Bull;
and let the oxen change the watery paths of Selene
in fear of the heavy-roaring lowing of my heads;
and opening the great gape of her grim jaws
let my Typhaonian bear madden the Bear of Olympus;
and my lion, vying against the heavenly Lion,
let him drive him unwilling from the zodiac path;
and let my serpents make the Serpent of the Wain shudder . . .
helmeted with a few lightnings. But the waves
of the raging sea, the hills of the land, the glens of the islands
are swords to me, and shields are the hills,
and the crags unbreakable breastplates, the rocks spears,
and the rivers quenchers of the feeblest thunderbolt.

I keep the bonds of Iapetus for Poseidon,
and round the topmost Caucasus another well-winged, mightier
eagle shall make bloody the ever-renewed liver, tearing
that of fiery Hephaestus, since for fire's sake
the liver of self-grown, scored Prometheus suffers;
and giving my sons a form like that of Iphimedeia's,
I will hide the son of Maia, entangled in unbreakable bonds,
kept in a brazen jar, that some one may say:
'Loosing the bond of Ares, Hermes was hidden as a prisoner.'
And loosing the untouched seal of her maidenhood
let Artemis be the compulsory wife of Orion,
and let Leto spread her old robes for Tityos,
dragged into a forced marriage; and the murderer Ares,
stripping him bare of his torn shields and binding him,
I will plunder, the lord of battle, in place of a slayer
a gentle thing; and to late-wedding Ephialtes joining
captive Pallas I will give as a bride, that I may see
Ares in servitude and Athena in travail.
And lifting on his wretched shoulders the back-whirling
Atlantean heaven, let the son of Cronos lighten it,
standing upright, and let him hear the wedding-hymn of my marriage,
stealing his jealous look, when I am the bridegroom of Hera.
Nor do I lack torches: of itself
the firebrand of my chamber is the flash of lightning, and instead of pine
Phaethon himself, kindling fire from his own flame,
shall stretch a servile gleam for the bridegroom Typhoeus,
and quivering the wedding sparks over Olympus
let the stars flash, the lamps of my Loves,
the stars, the evening lights; and with well-wedded Aphrodite
the bedfellow of Endymion, my handmaid Selene,
shall spread the bed for me; and if there is need of baths,
I will bathe in the waters of the starry Eridanus;
but after the bed of Zeus, you circling Hours,
fix the bridal chamber of Eros for Typhoeus; and from Ocean you too,
Leto, Athena, the Paphian, the Grace, Artemis, Hebe,
carry kindred water for bridal-tending Typhon;
and with wedding plectra, beside the feast of my table,
let Apollo the servant make music of Typhoeus in place of Zeus.
I bear no longing for a foreign land; for my own
star-backed heaven, my brother, I will drive,
holding heaven, my mother's house, as a son of earth.
And dragging raw-eating Cronos a second time into the light,
my brother and fellow-labourer, from the earthy pit,
I will loose his forced bonds, and bring back
the Titans to the upper air, and carry under one roof
the earth-born Cyclopes to heaven, and I will make other
weapons of fire; for I have need of many thunderbolts,
since I fight with two hundred, not two,
hands, I, the very likeness of the son of Cronos; and answering them
I will forge mightier, later-born lightnings with a brighter, greater fire,
and broader still I will make above on high
an eighth heaven, another, higher up,
adorned with brighter stars; for this near-shown
vault cannot cover the whole of Typhon.
And after the female children and the male-born race
of the much-begetting son of Cronos, I will plant another wide-scattered
blood of new gods, a many-necked race; nor will I leave
the choir of stars idle and unwed, but I will join
the female to the male, that a winged maiden,
bedded beside Bootes, may bear servile children."

He spoke, threatening; and the son of Cronos laughed to hear.
And the strife thundered upon both; and Eris was the escort
of the tumult for Typhon, but Victory led Zeus
to the conflict. It was not for the sake of a herd of oxen, not over a flock
that the contest stood, no quarrel over the beauty of a bride,
no battle about a lesser city; but over the very
heaven the strife was set, and on the knees of Victory lay
the sceptre of Zeus and his throne as the prizes of the fray.

Zeus, hammering the thunder from the lashed clouds,
trumpeted the airy lowing as the war-song of Enyo,
and fastening the clouds in coils upon his breast
he held them as a shelter from the Giant's missiles; nor was Typhoeus
silent: his heads, sending forth the lowing of oxen,
as self-sounding trumpets crashed against Olympus,
and his mingled serpents hissed, the pipes of Ares.
And Typhoeus armed his ranks of towering limbs,
fencing crag against great crag, until close-set,
unbreakable cliffs were towered in rows,
and he set rock on rock, ridge upon ridge;
and it was the likeness of an army arming: for near at hand
crag pressed crag, hill hill, neck neck,
and high in cloud elbow pushed many-folded elbow;
and the rocky hills were helmets to Typhon
as his heads were covered by the high-crested peak.
And as the Giant fought, in his many-ridged shape
there was one body, but countless battalions—some of palms,
some the well-whetted points of lion jaws,
others, with snaky locks, riders upon the stars.
And trees were folded from the Typhaonian hands,
shaken against the son of Cronos, and others, the fair-leaved
shoots of earth, which with a heavy heave
Zeus, unwilling, reduced to dust with a single spark of the thunderbolt;
much elm was hurled with its agemate pine,
and the broad plane, and poplars were cast
straight at Zeus; and much of the earth's flank was rent.

And the whole four-sided rim of the universe was buffeted,
and the four winds, warring alongside the son of Cronos,
towered up the airy darkling dust,
arching the waves; and as the sea was lashed
Sicily was shaken, the Pelorian banks roared
and the Aetnaean ridges, and the Lilybaean rocks bellowed,
prophets of things to come, and the western shore
sounded beside the stream of Pachynus; and near the Bear,
about the Thracian glen the Athonian nymph cried out,
and on the Pierian ridge the Macedonian wood resounded;
and the foundations of the east were shaken, and the tree-clad
fragrant courts of Assyrian Libanus rang.

And many shafts of the unwearied thunderbolt of Zeus
were cast from the Typhaonian hands;
and some, darting beside the chariot of Selene,
scored the unmarked tracks of the unsteady bulls,
and others, whirled through the air with sharp whistle,
the winds fanned aside with opposing breaths;
and many that strayed from the untouched thunderbolt of Zeus
the joyful hand of Poseidon received,
not sparing the earth-cleaving point of his trident;
and the brine-dipped shafts beside the stream of the Cronian sea
old Nereus dedicated, bringing an offering to Zeus.

And arming the two grim sons of Enyalius,
the grandsire Zeus held Fear and Dread the attendant,
shield-bearers of the air, agemate companions, and on the lightning
he set Fear, and on the thunderbolt he fixed Dread,
bringing terror to Typhon; and Victory lifted her shield,
stretching it before Zeus, and Enyo cried in answer,
and Ares thundered. And rushing on with the storm-blasts
aegis-bearing Zeus was borne aloft from the air,
seated on the winged four-yoked car of Time;
and the horses of the son of Cronos were yoked winds.
And now with lightnings he was armed, now with the thunderbolt,
now he assailed with thunders, now pouring
the stony backs of frozen hail in showers
with rainy missiles; and against the Giant's
heads dense watery columns broke,
sharp-pointed, and the hands of Typhoeus, as with a knife,
were cut by the airy hailstone missile;
and one hand was covered with dust, and did not let go the hill,
but struck by the cut of the snow-cast hail
it fought even as it fell, and darting from the earth
the maddened hand leapt of itself with rolling springs,
as though wishing to hurl even still the circle of Olympus.

And the champion of the heavenly ones, brandishing his fiery shaft on high,
guiding the war's right horn from the left,
fought high-shown; and into the watery ravines
the many-armed Giant rose, and joining close-set
fingers in an interwoven self-made bond,
hollowing his capacious palms, with which lifting
the mountain-running water amid the wintry rivers,
sending the divided streams with his deep-cupped hands,
he flung it at the lightning; and on the ravine-stream
the airy flame, struck, gleamed through the water
with a fiercer spark, and the thirsty water boiled,
smoke-darkened, and the wet downpour was dried by the hot mass;
for the bold Giant longed to quench the heavenly fire,
the fool; nor did he understand that the fire-gleaming thunderbolts
and lightnings are born of rain-bearing clouds.

And again, seizing the straight-cut caverns of the streams,
he longed to strike the breast of Zeus, unwounded by iron,
and the crag was stretched out facing Zeus; but with the tip of his lip
Zeus blew a little, and the high-cliffed circling rock,
though lofty, his slight breath turned aside.

And striking with his hand the whirling island-ridge,
many-whirling Typhoeus was lifted up for the battle,
and hurled it down at the unbreakable face of Zeus;
but Zeus avoided the opposing marble point
by bending his head aside, and Typhoeus met the lightning
that turned its hot spiral course, and at once the rock,
foaming at its tip, blackened with witnessing smoke.
And he flung a third; but as it rushed on, the son of Cronos
with the guiding wrist of his open palm's middle,
striking it like a leaping ball with unwearied hand,
sent it back at Typhon; and turned about with much
airy whirling on its back-faring journey
the hill of its own accord shot at the one who shot it.
A fourth he hurled, higher; but touching
the topmost fringes of the aegis the rock was split.
And he let fly another; and the stormy rock,
half-burnt, gleamed, shot through by the thunderbolt.
The cliffs did not cleave the watery cloud, but struck
against the watery clouds the hills were broken.

And shared and balanced between both was Enyo,
both for Zeus and for Typhon; and with the much-roaring missile
the dancing thunderbolts of the air raved.
And the son of Cronos fought in arms; and in the tumult
he held thunder for a shield, and a cloud became his breastplate,
and he brandished the lightning as a spear, and the Zeus-cast thunderbolts
were sent from the air as fire-pointed arrows;
for already, faring about from the earthy flank,
the dry, high-flying vapour of the soil ran up,
and confined within the cloud with fiery throat
it was stifled, heating the pregnant cloud; and around the smoke
of the fire-nurtured clouds rubbed together with a din,
the pressed inner flame was borne, hard to escape,
seeking a middle path, since to go up on high
the fire may not; for the lightning leaping up is held back
by the moist air bathed with rainy drops,
having thickened the watery cloud above; and from below,
as the parched part opens, the leaping fire ran through.

As a stone, bringing to birth a fiery pang against a stone,
hurled forth a stony self-born, much-pressed fire,
when the fire-born female is struck against the male rock:
so the heavenly flame is kindled in the pressed
soot and clouds; and from the earthy smoke
that grew thin the winds were brought to birth.
And another wandering vapour of the earth, drawn from the waters,
the sun, milking it face to face with fiery rays,
drew up its moist heat into the track of the air;
and growing thick it brought to birth the veil of clouds,
and shaking its thickest body with thinner vapour,
loosing the soft cloud again into a flood of rain,
it passed back to its former native watery matter.
Such was the fiery nature of the clouds, with which
the matching thunderbolts were brought to birth alongside the lightnings.

And father Zeus fought; and against his adversary, sending
his accustomed fire, he hurled it, the shooter of lions,
striking the many-voiced rank of countless throats
with the heavenly hurricane-bolt; and of the Zeus-cast missile
one flash burned the boundless hands, one flash
turned to dust the numberless shoulders and the shifting tribes of serpents,
and the unending points of heaven's spears tore the heads,
and the spiral comet turned to dust the locks of Typhon,
casting a hairy fire with answering spark,
and the heads gleamed, and as the hair was kindled
silence sealed the hissing tresses
with the heavenly spark, and as the serpents withered
the venom-shooting drops of their jaws were dried;
and as the Giant fought his eyes were turned to ash
by the sooty smoke, and the cheeks of his snow-struck faces
were whitened with snowy streams.

And he was held in the four-yoked compulsion of the four winds:
for if he turned his unsteady eyes to the east,
he received the fiery battle of neighbouring Eurus;
if he gazed at the storm-vexed quarter of the Arcadian Bear,
he was struck by the chilling frost of the wintry hurricane;
fleeing the cold blast of snow-cast Boreas
he was shaken by both the watery and the sooty missile;
and looking to the west, facing grim Dawn,
he shuddered at the western, storm-blowing Enyo,
hearing the sound of the springtime lash of Zephyrus;
and Notos, about the southern ridge of Capricorn,
lashed the airy rims, a hot wind,
bringing fire to Typhon with the fire-gleaming vapour of its heat.
If again rain-bringing Zeus poured a streaming shower,
Typhoeus bathed his whole flesh in the toil-loosing streams,
cooling his hot limbs worn out by the thunderbolt.
And by the rocky missiles of the hailstorm
as the son was scourged, the nurturing mother was lashed;
and seeing on the Giant's flesh the witness of Fate,
the stony fixed missiles and the watery point,
she besought the Titan Sun with downcast voice,
begging one hottest beam, that with a hotter
fire he might loose the stony water of Zeus,
pouring kindred radiance on the snow-struck Typhon;
and she melted with him as he was scourged; and seeing
the fire-crowned nation of his towering palms burning
she besought the wintry, stormy breeze to come
for a single dawn, that with cold winds
it might quench the thirsty compulsion of Typhon.

And the son of Cronos tipped the balance of the matched battle.
And casting off with her hand her leafy veil,
mother Earth grieved, gazing at the smoke
of the Typhaonian heads; and as his faces withered
the earth-born one's knees were loosed; and foretelling victory
the trumpet of Zeus lowed with thundering crashes;
and drunk with the heavenly fiery missile he fell,
having a wound of war wrought without iron, Typhoeus
the high-stretched, and casting his back upon mother Earth
he lay, spreading his snaky limbs in the dust,
spewing forth fire. And the son of Cronos taunted him laughing,
pouring out such a speech from his mocking throat:

"A fine helper old Cronos has found, Typhoeus;
the earth scarcely brought forth a son, the great offspring of Iapetus;
sweet is the avenger of the Titans; as I see,
the thunderbolts of the son of Cronos have soon proved feeble.
How long do you delay to dwell in the impassable air,
false sceptre-bearer? The throne of Olympus awaits you;
take the sceptre of Zeus and the robes, god-defying Typhoeus,
and bring Astraeus to heaven; and if you wish,
let Eurynome too return to the upper air, and Ophion,
and Cronos, fellow-voyager with both; and as you go
let crafty Prometheus, fleeing his bonds, accompany you
to the dappled rim of the high-pathed stars,
having as escort of his road the bold heavenly bird,
the unsparing diner upon his young, growing liver.
What more did you wish, after the tumult, than to see
Zeus and the Earth-shaker as attendants of your thrones?
Zeus weak and no longer sceptred lord of Olympus,
stripped of thunder and clouds, and instead of lightning,
in place of the divine fire, and instead of the accustomed thunderbolt,
holding a firebrand beside the Typhaonian bridal chamber,
the bedroom-servant of your captive wife Hera,
with jealous eye envying your marriage;
and the Earth-shaker, your yoke-fellow, unyoked from the sea,
after the deep serving at your table,
bearing your cup with thirsty hand in place of his trident.
You have Ares as servant, Apollo is your attendant;
and send to the Titans the courier, the son of Maia,
announcing your power and your heavenly radiance;
but leave the craftsman Hephaestus to accustomed Lemnos,
that he may fashion for your newly-yoked bride
a many-coloured necklace fair-hued with gleaming work,
or the bright glitterings of foot-treading sandals,
in which your consort may delight, or make
another gold-shining throne of Olympus, that your
gold-throned Hera may laugh, holding a mightier seat;
and having the earthy Cyclopes as dwellers in Olympus
forge a new spark of a mightier thunderbolt.
But Eros, who charmed your mind with the deceit of hope of victory,
bind in gold beside golden Aphrodite;
and bind in bronze Ares, the steersman of iron.
The lightnings flee and do not abide Enyo;
how did you not escape the unwarlike fire of a little lightning?
Or how, hearing with your countless ears
the small thundering rainy echo, did you fear it?
Who made you so strengthless? Where are your spears?
Where the heads of your dogs? Where those gapings of lions
and the earthy lowing of your heavy-voiced throats?
Where the long-shadowing venom of your snaky hair?
No longer do you hiss with your snaky circling mane?
Where the lowings of your bull-mouths? Where your hands'
hurlers of the towering crag?
No longer do you scourge the spiral rims of the stars?
No longer do the jutting points of your boars whiten
your soaked throat with foaming drops?
Where, I ask, are the dreadful gaping jaws of your raging bear?
Yield to the heavenly ones, earth-fed one; for with one hand
I have conquered the rank of your two hundred hands.
But let three-headed Sicily, hemming you in with deep-cliffed hills,
receive the whole of Typhon,
pitiably maned with a hundred dusted heads.
Yet, if you had an overweening mind, if even upon
Olympus itself you leapt up with vain hopes,
I will make you, all-luckless one, a cenotaph, and as a last word
beside your empty tomb, reckless one, I will score this:
'This is the monument of earth-born Typhoeus, who once with rocks
scourged the air, and the heavenly fire burned him up.'"
He spoke, mocking the breathing corpse, the son of Earth.

And pouring forth a victory-echo to all-ruling Zeus
the Cilician Bull bellowed with stony trumpet,
and with watery feet whirling Cydnus danced,
hailing the victory of Zeus with watery roaring,
shown midway, pouring his native stream for his agemate Tarsus.

And Earth, rending her rocky tunic,
grieved as she lay, and instead of a mournful knife
she sheared her tree-tresses, cut by the winds,
clipping the lock from her wooded head
as in the leaf-shedding month, and tore her ravine cheeks,
and through her well-watered flanks the sounding
river-tears of mourning Earth ran down.

And from the Typhaonian limbs the whirlings of the storm
lashed the waves, and rushing on to cover
the ships they rode down the unbroken calm,
not visitors on the surge alone; but on land too
often the quivering, storm-blowing dust
flooded the upright young crop of the threshing-floor.
And the steward of the universe, Nature of the reborn matter,
fixed the gaping flank of the rent earth,
and the island ridges, cut off from the streams,
she sealed again with the bond of unbreakable harmony.

No longer was there tumult among the stars; for the Sun
set the maned Lion, that had darted aside,
beside the grain-bearing Maid in the zodiac path;
and the Moon, reining back the Crab that had leapt
upon the face of the heavenly Lion,
opposite the unwarmed Capricorn, fixed it in place again.

Nor had Zeus son of Cronos forgotten the minstrel Cadmus,
but calling him he uttered this great speech,
scattering the shadowy cloud of airy darkness:

"Cadmus, with your pipe you have crowned the gates of Olympus;
I too honour your marriage with the heavenly Harp;
I will make you a son-in-law of both Ares and Cytherea,
and have the gods as guests of your earthly banquet.
I will come to your house: what dearer thing will you devise
than the king of the blessed touching your table?
But if you wish to flee the shifting waves of fortune,
ferrying the course of a calm life,
ever beware lest Dircaean Ares should trouble you,
Ares angered apart from any ambush; and at night,
stretching your eyes opposite the heavenly Dragon,
sacrifice above the altar, taking a sweet-smelling snake-stone,
invoking Olympian Ophiuchus, burning in the fire
the many-pointed horn of the Illyrian deer,
that you may escape whatever bitter things, fated to your lot,
the spiral spindle of Fate's compulsion has spun,
if the threads of the Fates may be obeyed. But of your angered
father Agenor let the memory go, and for your wandering
brothers do not fear; for, severally judged,
all still live, since Cepheus settled the southern land
of the Cephenian Ethiopians, their helper,
and Thasos came to Thasos, and round the snow-clad ridge
of the high-crested Bull, Cilix rules the Cilicians,
and Phineus, hastening off, came to the Thracian shore;
him, rich in deep-veined metals, I lead
as a son-in-law to Oreithyia and Thracian Boreas,
the prophetic bridegroom of garland-loving Cleopatra.
And you too, by the equal-drawing thread of Fate for your brothers,
rule over the Cadmeans and leave your name to the citizens;
renounce the back-faring circles of your wandering road,
and reject the unsteady track of the heifer; for by the Cyprian
yoking law Asterion the Dictaean lord of Corybantian Ida
has wedded your sister.
And some things I myself will prophesy, others to Phoebus
I will leave; but you, Cadmus, treading the navel-axle,
go to the speaking glens of Delphic Pytho."

So speaking, Zeus son of Cronos sent off the wandering
son of Agenor; and swiftly to the rim of the airy stars
he turned his golden car, and Victory, mounting it,
drove the ancestral horse with heavenly lash.

And the god came to the pole a second time; and as he came
the high-necked Hours spread wide the heavenly gates,
and crowned the air; and in their back-changed form
the gods returned to Olympus with victorious Zeus,
and exchanged again the winged likeness of their faces.

And Athena came to heaven in soft robes, without iron,
holding Ares as her Revel, and Victory was her Song;
and Themis displayed the weapons of the dead Giant
to foolish Earth, the mother of the Giants,
as a terror of things to come,
hanging them high beside the forecourt of Olympus.
3. In the third book search for the much-wandering ship of Cadmus, and the halls of Electra, and the hospitality of her table.

The contest was loosed, when the storm had passed; and showing its tip,
its light-bringing back like a knife on a cloudless baldric,
Orion rose, and no longer in the circling pool
did the frosty tracks of the sunken Bull bathe;
no longer beside the slope of the rain-breeding, thirsty Bear
was the gleaming water travelled with unwetted footsteps;
no longer did the Massagetan, lashing his wandering house,
crossing the stream on a wooden circling wagon-track,
score the watery furrows of the frozen Ister;
for already the pregnant Hour, herald of Zephyrus,
with the splitting of the buds made the dewy breezes drunk,
and the shrill swallow, the springtime herald, fellow-dweller with mortals,
chattering and twittering robbed them of their morning sleep,
newly come to light, and from its fragrant veil
the flower bared and laughed, bathed in springtime
life-giving dews. And beside the saffron streams of the Cilicians,
leaving the horned headland of the high-crested Bull,
Cadmus went early, when Dawn had cleaved the darkness.

And it was the season for sailing; and as Cadmus hastened
the cables that hold the ships were heaved from the land;
and the high-headed mast, striking the upper air,
stood upright fixed, and gently lashing the sea
with morning breaths the light breeze buzzed,
holding an escorting sound; and arching the waves
shifting in the gusts it checked the watery dance
of the dolphin, the tumbler of the silent calm.
And the twisted ropes whistled with a sharp hiss,
and as the wind hastened the forestays groaned, and the straight-faring
sail was bellied out, forced and big with the breeze;
and the unsteady wave was split, back-falling, and the swelling water
foamed, and as the ship hastened through the sea
with the booming wave an echo cried about the keel;
and the rudder's tip, with the cleaving track through the brine,
scored the curved, foam-flecked back of the sea.

And after the tenth turning-post of the storm-free circling Dawn
Cadmus, borne on the waveless breezes of Zeus,
splitting the Trojan passage of water-roaming Helle,
was drawn by the ravisher wind through the bellowing strait
to Samos, opposite the strife-rousing Camandrus,
neighbour of Sithonia, where as a maiden still for Cadmus
Harmonia was kept; and the prophetic breezes
escorted the ship to the Thracian shore, to divine Rhea.

And seeing the flame of the sleepless Samian pine,
the sailors with limbs near the land joyfully furled the sails;
and ferrying the ship near the waveless harbour
they scored the windless water with the tips of their oars,
and put in under the shelter of the haven; and of the unbending
crags the pierced rocky nail received the ships' cables,
and through the deepening gulf of the wet sand
the curved-toothed anchors of the ship were fastened
as Phaethon sank; and on the beach the sailors
spread for themselves unspread ground-couches on the sand
after the evening meal; and on the men's heavy
eyes wandering Sleep set his noiseless tread.

But when, beside the wing of the purple, fiery Eurus,
peering over the topmost scored cleft of Teucrian Ida,
spitting forth the dawn, Dawn appeared, watcher of the harbour,
lighting the dark swell of the sea across the way,
then, so that Cypris might join Harmonia to a husband,
the unsailable back of the silent calm was stretched out, unsailed.

And already the morning bird cried, cleaving the air,
and the well-helmeted ranks of the desert-dwelling Corybantes
beat out the Cnossian, shield-brandishing leap of the dance
with measured steps; and as the loud-crashing bull's-hide
was struck in coils with the rivalling iron,
the double-voiced pipe sang, and urging on the dancers
it crashed out a concordant tune with leaping beat.
And the oaks whispered, and the rocks bellowed,
and the frenzied woods were shaken with a sentient quivering,
and the Dryads cried out; and the circling bears rushed thick
into the dance with answering leaps,
and the lions with roaring from their kindred throats
mimicked the war-cry of the mystery-tending Cabeiri,
a frenzy that held its wits; and as dog-loving Hecate
sang, the company's pipes thundered,
the unyoked pipes that the Cronian horn-carving art invented.

And at the loud-sounding din of the noise-loving Corybantes
Cadmus woke early, and entangled together likewise
the Sidonian sailors, hearing the morning's unsilent
bull's-hide, from their well-pebbled beds
left the sea-beaten back of the shore-couch.

And tracking the city the traveller Cadmus wandered,
leaving the ship and hastening off from his comrades; and as he came
to the house of Harmonia, the bridal-attendant Persuasion met him,
having the form of a mortal woman, and through her burdened bosom,
like a patient working woman, having drawn a draught from the spring,
she lifted on her arm the silver well-rounded pitcher,
a messenger of things to come, since by accustomed law a bridegroom
before the wedding is sprinkled with life-giving baths.

And he was near the city, where in hollow troughs
women, treading with much-leaping feet
the dirty rows of close-packed entangled robes,
with eager feet. And from her topmost soles
to her head, hidden in a dark cloud,
Persuasion led Cadmus through the unmarked city,
the searcher for the hall of the guest-receiving king,
escort of the road at the Paphian's nod; and there a bird,
seated under the grey, delicate shelter of an olive,
the prophetic crow, opening her greedy mouth,
reproached the youth, that toward Harmonia his bride
he went, a sluggish traveller with sparing bridal foot,
and shaking her wings cried out a mocking voice:

"Cadmus has become a fool, or has become a stranger to the Loves;
swift Eros knows no slow bridegroom; be gracious, Persuasion,
your Cadmus delays though Aphrodite hastens.
Hot Eros calls you: why, bridegroom, do you travel sluggishly?
Sweet are you, who became the neighbour of lovely Adonis,
sweet, dwelling in a fatherland that shares a furrow with the Byblian women.
I erred: you have not seen the stream of Adonis, you have not looked
on the land of Byblos, where is the house of the Graces, where dances
Assyrian Cytherea and not bed-fleeing Athena.
You have Persuasion as escort, delighting in marriages,
the nurse of the Loves, not Artemis; cease from your toils,
have the joy of Harmonia and leave Europa to the bull;
hasten, and Electra will receive you, from whose hands
yes indeed, take on the cargo of wedding Loves,
entrusting the merchandise of love to Aphrodite,
and the Cyprian daughter kept for your bridal chamber
receive as another Cypris; and you will praise the crow,
and call me the bridal prophetic bird of the Loves.
I erred: but Cypris breathed on me; for from the Paphian
I prophesy your bed, even if I am the bird of Athena."
So speaking she sealed her chattering mouth with witnessing silence.

But when, as he walked, the public circles of the road
showed from afar the king's all-receiving hall
raised on columns, then, stretching out toward Cadmus
her finger, the knowing witness of answering speech,
with a silent herald Persuasion pointed out the house
flashing many-coloured; and the deity sank into the air,
otherwise-seeming, darting away on her winged sandal.

And Cadmus surveyed the house with wandering eye,
the skilled work of Hephaestus, which once for the bride Electra
the toil-worker of Lemnos wrought with Myrinaean art,
bearing many cunning ornaments. Of the new-built hall
the bronze threshold was well-trodden; and on both sides
the doorposts of the much-carved gateways were drawn out long,
and the crest was rounded into a ball at its navelled top,
shown in the middle of the roof; and the back of the stone-paved wall
was fixed firm, set fast with white gypsum,
to the inner recess from the threshold. And near, an orchard of the court,
spreading wide, was weighed down with the dewy fruit of its plants,
four acres before the house; and spreading its male leaves
the palm pledged its desire to the female palm;
the pear with splendid fruit, grown together with its agemate pear,
whispered in the morning, and twining with its clusters
struck the neighbouring bush of the rich olive;
beside the laurel that refuses the springtime winds
the myrtle leaves were shaken, and the fragrant breeze
fanned the morning foliage of the fair-leaved cypress;
and from the sweet-bearing fig and the moist pomegranate
the reddening fruit grew ripe beside the wine-dark fruit
planted close by, and apple bloomed beside neighbouring apple;
and much was the foliage marked with Phoebus' wise letters,
the tree-borne writing of the weeping-loving hyacinths;
and as Zephyrus breathed through the plant-nourishing garden
Apollo, insatiate of his longings, stretched his unsteady eye,
and, seeing the youth's plant shaken by the breezes,
remembering the discus he quivered, lest perchance the breeze,
jealous, might envy the boy even in the leaves,
if truly Apollo, seeing that boy once writhing in the dust,
once wept with eyes that had not wept,
and the flowery form shaped the tears of Phoebus,
inscribing on the hyacinth a self-summoned dirge.

Such was the well-shaded orchard; and near was a spring
with two mouths, from one was drink for the dwellers, from the other the gardener
channelled from a conduit the much-divided, winding water
to plant after plant; and a stream, as if from Phoebus,
buzzed delicately about the root of the singing laurel.

And a great, well-made boy of gold stood,
propping his foot on a rock, facing the diners,
stretching the after-dinner radiance of an evening lamp;
and many ranks of figures, with their matched limbs in cunning silence,
through the made gapings of their grinning throats,
the wise ranks of false dogs near the doors
stood here and there, and a golden dog, neighbour
to the silver dog, barked along with it from its swelling throat,
fawning on the accustomed man; and as Cadmus passed by
it sent forth the stranger-saving Echo of a mimic bark,
and the artist made the likeness of an affectionate wagging tail to quiver.

While Cadmus, turning the eyes of his well-turning face,
measured out the garden of the lords with his wandering gaze,
and the carvings and all the beauty of the painted hall,
seeing the bright glitterings of the stony metals,
meanwhile, leaving the assembly and the quarrels of the people,
bright, seated upon the back of his high-crested horse,
Emathion, holding Thracian Samos, the seat of Ares,
came to the royal house of his mother Electra,
who then alone ruled, guiding the reins of his brother's
sovereignty, since, leaving his fatherland's soil,
Dardanus had settled in the land's margin across the way,
scoring out the well-towered city named Dardania,
marking the Idaean dust with a ploughman's track;
and drinking the stream of Heptaporus and the floods of Rhesus
he left the heritage to his brother to hold, and the sceptre of the Cabeiri.
Dardanus, brother of Emathion, whom the bed of Zeus
begot, whom Justice the nurse cherished, when, taking
