the sceptre of Zeus and the robes of Time and the wand of Olympus,
the Hours ran to the house of royal Electra,
prophets of the unbreakable sovereignty of the Ausonians;
and they reared the infant, and by the unswerving voice of Zeus
the boy, springing up like the flower of ever-renewing youth,
left the house of Electra, when the flood of the third rain
towered with waves overwhelmed the seats of the universe.

For Ogyges first made trial of the sounding flood,
cleaving the air through the towering water,
when all the earth was hidden, flooded over, and the tip of the Thessalian
rock was covered, and on high the Pythian peak,
the cloud-near rock, surged with the snowy flood.
The second rain was when over the rim of the circling earth
the snow-laden water hid it with a raging stream,
when Deucalion alone, fellow-voyager with his agemate Pyrrha,
amid the perishing mortals, in a hollow ark cutting
the back-whirling flood of the unmeasured downpour
of the watery air, was ferried, a whirling sailor.
And the third rain of Zeus was when it washed the seat of the earth
and hid the cliffs, and even the unwetted back
of the Sithonian hill of Athos itself was covered,
when, cleaving the flood of the high-faring downpour,
Dardanus set foot on the ancient neighbouring Ida.

His brother then, lord of the snowy Sithonian land,
Emathion, leaving the heavy-sounding assembly,
marvelled at the man's form, since his inborn youth
mingled manliness and beauty in a matched shape,
he marvelled at so great a form; for of distinguished lords
the looks are themselves voiceless heralds, speaking unbidden.
And taking him in he gave him hospitality, and with weary Electra
he adorned the varied dinners of the rich table,
welcoming the stranger with friendly and blameless words,
setting much before him. But he, bowing his bent neck to the floor,
apart from the attendants, drew his eyes uncharmed,
and scarcely feasted; and as the hospitable bride
sat facing him, with a stealing glance from his face
he stretched in shame his chaste hand to the table.

And as they feasted, in close succession one after another
the breathing reed of Corybantian Ida crashed out;
and from the much-pierced passage, with the leaping of hands,
the dancing fingers, pressing the song,
beat out the concordant tune of the bellowing pipe;
and the booming cymbals, clashing with rolling shakes,
sounded a concordant echo with their double bronze
joined to the reeds; and beneath the plectrum the very
upright string of the seven-toned lyre quivered.

But when after the feast he had had his fill of the Bistonian pipe,
drawing near to the inquiring queen, who loves to ask,
Cadmus, setting aside the frenzy of his sea-wandering care,
told of his bright lineage, and a stream of ever-flowing words
he poured from his opening throat like a fountain:

"Dear lady, why do you ask me so much of the blood of my race?
I liken the race of swift-fated mortals to leaves;
the leaves that the frenzied breezes pour down on the earth
when the autumn season comes, and others in the springtime
season the wooded trees foster, in fresh bloom;
so the short-lived race of men: one is subdued
by destruction, having run its course of life, while another still flourishes,
that it may yield to another in turn; for, creeping back again,
the age of man flows from grey to new, taking shape afresh.
But I will tell of my far-famed, fair-childed race.
There is a city, glorious Argos, the equestrian seat of Hera,
the navel of the island of Tantalus; there a man
sowed a fair maiden with female-bearing seed,
Inachus, the famed citizen of the Inachian land,
a temple-keeper, who plotted the dreadful rites
of the city-guarding goddess with prophetic, mystic art,
an elder; and Zeus, the chief of the gods, the leader of the stars,
he refused to have as a son-in-law, keeping reverence for Hera, . . .
when, bull-formed, the heifer Io, her face changed,
was driven into the field-herd, a fellow-grazer,
and Hera set over the heifer a sleepless herdsman,
many-eyed Argus, adorned with unwandering eyes,
the watcher of Zeus' cow-horned wedding,
of unseen Zeus, and the girl went into the pasture
trembling at the eyes of the many-pupilled herdsman;
and Io, her body scored by the limb-devouring gadfly,
scored the swell of the Ionian sea with roving hoof;
she came even to Egypt, of my stream—which the citizens
called the Nile by a fitting name, because to the land
year after year, borne along, the watery bedfellow
with muddy flood throws around it new silt—
she came to Egypt, where after her cow shape,
changing the image of her divine horn,
she became the fruit-bearing goddess; and as the fruit is kindled
of Egyptian Demeter, of my horn-drawn Io,
the vapour rises, fellow-traveller with the fragrant breezes.
There she bore Epaphus to Zeus, since of her unsullied bosom,
of the Inachian heifer, the divine bedfellow had touch
with love-maddened hands; and from a god-begotten father,
from Epaphus, came Libya; and journeying to Libya's bridal chamber
even to Memphis came Poseidon as a wanderer,
tracking the maiden daughter of Epaphus, and then the girl,
receiving the dweller of the deep as a landward traveller,
bore Libyan Zeus, Belus, the ploughman of my race.
And the new oracle of Asbystian Zeus, an answering voice,
the thirsty prophetic sands proclaim to the Chaonian dove;
and as a father, equal in number to five,
Belus sowed a succession of children,
Phineus and Phoenix who left his city, with whom flourishing together
the citizen of cities exchanged in turn, the roaming Agenor
of unsettled life, my father, held his course
to Thebes after Memphis, to Assyria after Thebes;
and wise Aegyptus, the dweller of the Egyptian land,
of grievous birth, many-childed, who with male-born offspring
sowed the short-lived flocks of so many children,
and Danaus who left his fatherland, who armed against the male race
the female kind, stretching the wedding sword, when the bridal chambers
were reddened with the blood of slaughtered weddings,
and with hidden swords upon the iron-bearing beds
female Enyo lulled to sleep naked male Ares;
yet to Hypermnestra the evil-bridal slaughter was not pleasing,
but thrusting aside the grim-kindred ordinances of her father
she entrusted her father's word to the airy gust,
and kept her hand pure and bloodless of the iron;
and the marriage of both was holy. And my newly-blooming
sister the bold roving bull carried off,
if truly it was a bull; for I do not know how to believe
that bulls long for women's weddings.
And Agenor sent me, fellow-traveller with my brothers,
to track our sister and the wild ravisher of the bride,
the bull, the false sailor of the waveless sea,
for whose sake I come here, an unsteady wanderer."

Such things within the well-piped hall
Cadmus told, pouring forth speech from his eloquent throat,
telling of the child-saving frenzy of his father's threat
and the false-sailing bull-traveller of the Tyrian surge,
the unattainable, unknown ravisher of the Sidonian bride.
And Electra, hearing, cried out a comforting voice:

"Stranger, your sister and your fatherland and your father
give over to the whirl of Lethe and to forgetful silence;
for thus the life of mortals is borne, holding toil
on toil, since all, as many as a mortal womb has borne,
are enslaved to the compulsion of the Fates' spinning thread;
I am a witness, queen though I am, if ever of those
Pleiades I too was born one, whose mother once
brought to birth the female pangs within her bosom,
calling seven times upon Eileithyia at her childbed
to lighten the sting of repeated birth—
I am a witness; for far from my parents I dwell,
having neither Sterope nor Maia my fellow,
nor my sister Celaeno near as a hearth-mate; nor in my bosom
of my sister Taygeta have I held Lacedaemon with a double leap,
embracing the joyful boy with child-nursing arm;
nor near do I see the house of Alcyone, nor of Merope herself,
do I hear her speaking the mind-delighting word.
And besides, this I lament still more: for newly-blooming
my son who left his fatherland, when he had the down of first beard,
Dardanus, migrated to the bosom of the Idaean land,
and to Phrygian Simoeis gave the first-fruits of his hair,
drinking the alien water of the Thymbraean river;
and at the boundary of Libya my father still labours
with pressed shoulders, old Atlas bent over,
heaving up the seven-zoned hollow of the air.
Yet, having suffered so much, I feed a comforting hope
on the promises of Zeus, that with my other sisters
from the earth I shall come to the Atlantean pole of stars,
having heaven as my house, and shall be the seventh star.
And you too, soften your cares; for unforeseen,
rolling upon you the whirl of life-wandering fortune,
the dreadful thread of unmoving Fate has sealed it;
endure to bear, as one who left his fatherland, the unbending bond of compulsion,
feeding a higher hope as the herald of things to come,
if first-sown Io rooted your race,
if you have got from Libya the Poseidonian blood of your line;
remain among strangers, like Dardanus, dwelling in a house,
inhabiting a foreign city, as your father Agenor,
as Danaus your father's brother; for he too,
another man bearing his house, having the god-inspired race of Io,
a heavenly Zeus-fallen shoot, by name Byzas,
drinking the seven-mouthed water of the self-born Nile,
allotted a neighbouring land, where beside the Bosporus shore
the water crossed by the Inachian heifer is drawn,
giving light to all the dwellers around, when of that
unbending, maddened bull he bent the neck aslant."
She spoke, lulling to rest the cares of the son of Agenor.

And father Zeus sent the long-winged son of Maia
to the house of Electra, a swift messenger, that to Cadmus
he might give Harmonia for the harmony of wedlock,
a maiden migrant from heaven, whom for Aphrodite
in secret love the marriage-thieving Ares begot;
and the mother, ashamed of the babe, the self-announcer of her hidden bed,
did not rear her, but from her heavenly bosom
the nursling girl, reclining on her arm at the breast,
she brought to the house of Electra, fit for nursing, whose own child
the childbed Hours had brought to wet birth, whose dense breasts
still welled with swelling white moisture;
and receiving the bastard daughter by an equal law
the contemporary of Emathion she joined to one breast,
the newly-born girl, and with kindred-loving purpose
she lightened the double offspring with a nursing arm.

As some wild, twin-bearing lioness within the thicket,
shaggy, with milky dews
fitted her twin breasts to both cubs
and gave the divided teat to the twin young,
and licking their flesh and their still-hairless neck
reared the agemate brood with equal care:
so then with child-nursing loving teat she gave suck,
tending the yoked pair of newly-born children;
often she embraced the infant son, fellow with the agemate girl,
turning him here and there to the moisture of her rich breast,
with the loving hollow of her outstretched hand;
and on her knees she set the male child beside the female girl,
spreading her gaping thigh beside the neighbouring thigh,
widening the bosom of her deepening tunic;
and crying a sleep-charming melody to her children
she lulled both to sleep with nursing art,
spreading her arm to support the neck of the children,
and made her knee their bed, and over the two
she turned the edge of her robe, fanning their faces,
cooling the children, and quenched the rush of the heat
by pouring an answering blast, a made breeze.

While Cadmus sat near the prudent queen,
meanwhile, escaping the gatekeeper with his thieving foot,
unforeseen and unattainable, Hermes went into the house,
like a youth; and about his rosy face
the trailing track of his uncovered hair hung loose,
spreading wide, and crowning the edges of his new-haired cheek
the slender circle of his growing first-beard reddened,
freshly grown, running round on either side; and like a herald
he lifted his accustomed wand; and with face unseen,
adorned with clouds from head to the tips of his feet,
he came upon the finished dinners of the rich table;
nor did Emathion see him near, nor did
Harmonia herself, nor Cadmus the hearth-mate, nor the chorus of servant
men; but to god-fearing Electra alone appeared
Hermes of varied speech; and taking her into the recess of the house,
unforeseen he conversed and spoke with human voice:

"Mother's sister, bedfellow of Zeus, hail, of women
all the most blessed hereafter, since the son of Cronos
keeps the sovereignty of the universe for your children,
and all the cities of the earth your offspring will govern,
the bride-gifts of your love, and with my mother Maia
you may flash among the seven-pathed stars upon Olympus,
fellow-runner with the Sun, rising together with the Moon.
I am of your race, child-loving one, kindred Hermes,
the long-winged messenger of the immortals, and from heaven
your hospitable, high-ruling consort sent me
concerning your god-fearing guest; but you yourself
obey your son of Cronos, and your daughter Harmonia
send to go dowerless, fellow-voyager with her agemate Cadmus,
and do a favour to Zeus and the blessed; for the worn-out
immortals this stranger saved them all by singing;
this man came to the aid of your labouring consort,
this man spread a free day over Olympus.
Let not your daughter charm you with mother-loving lament;
but give her in marriage to the evil-averting Cadmus,
obeying the son of Cronos and Ares and Cytherea."

7. The seventh sings the white-haired suppliant prayer of Aion,
and Semele, and the love of Zeus, and the stolen marriage-bed.
Now, with the renewing fruit of everlasting life,
mingling the male, the seed of begetting, in the female furrow,
Eros plowed the unsown world, the husbandman of love;
and Nature took root, the nurse of all that is born,
and, blending fire with earth and water entwined with air,
she shaped the human race in a four-yoked bond.
But a sorrow of changing kinds held the life of mortals,
beginning in toil and never ceasing from care.
And to Zeus who rules over all, Aion his companion
showed the race of suffering men, with no portion of gladness;
for not yet, loosing the swaddling threads of childbirth,
had the father shot forth Bacchus from his pregnant thigh,
the rest from human care; not yet did the libation,
steeped in wine, make drunk the airy pathways with fragrant smoke;
and the daughters of the year, the joyless Seasons,
wove for the gods their garlands out of meadow-grass.
For there was need of wine; and the grace of a dance without Bacchus
was half-complete and useless; it charmed only
the eyes of the gathered crowd, when in his whirling sweeps
the dancer, turning many a circle, spun in a storm of feet,
his gestures speech, his hand a mouth, his fingers a voice.
But Aion of changing shapes, spreading on the knees of Zeus
his white hair, holding the key of all that is born,
stretched out the slackened tress of his beard in supplication,
and made his prayer; with his head bowed down to the floor
the curving neck pressed his back, drawn out at length;
and stretching out an endless hand from his bending knee,
the old shepherd of everlasting life spoke out:
Lord Zeus, look you also upon the griefs of a downcast world.
Do you not see how War has goaded all the earth,
reaping in season the corn of swiftly-perishing youth?
Not yet have those relics passed away, since you washed
all the nations of men with the flood, and the stream of the rain from the sky,
surging through the air, splashed up against neighbouring Selene.
Farewell to the life of short-lived mortals, over whose doom
I refuse the heavenly tiller; no longer will I steer
the cable of the world; let some other, better, of the blessed
receive the rudder of life that comes round again;
let another keep the running course of my years; for in pity
of their bitter affliction I have toiled over the much-enduring race of men.
Old age is no remedy, which withers youth
and makes a man slow with his head bowed down,
when, bent, with trembling, over-many-footed steps,
heavy-kneed he leans upon the familiar staff that tends old age;
death is no remedy, that often has hidden in Oblivion
the bridegroom newly come from the dance, the partner of his bride of equal age,
loosing the life-giving cables of a union that cannot be loosed.
I know indeed that marriage is full of charm, where there sounds
the flute of Athena, blending its voice with the pipe of Pan;
yet what profit is it, when beside the wedded chamber
the upright echo of the seven-stringed lyre rings out?
The harps do not loose our cares; nay, Eros himself,
dance-less at the wedding, has shaken off the bridal torch,
looking on the marriage-songs of those who lack delight.
But the life-saving remedy that brings forgetfulness of grief
took no root among much-toiling mortals; for that heavenly
lid of the jar Pandora should never have opened
for men, that sweet evil. Nay, even Prometheus himself
is to blame for the wickedness of mankind,
who cares for wretched mortals; for in place of fire,
the beginning of woe, the sweet nectar that gladdens the mind of the blessed,
he ought rather to have stolen, and granted as a gift to men,
so as to scatter with your draught the cares of the world.
But leaving the cares of clamorous life,
look upon your own downcast rites; does the wandering,
empty vapour of unceasing sacrifices charm you?
So spoke the old man; and for a while, in thoughtful silence,
Zeus the counsellor stirred his own boundless wisdom;
and he loosed the reins of his mind; with crowding counsels
the purposes of his teeming brain were set whirling.
And the son of Cronos raised to Aion a god-proclaiming voice,
declaring the higher oracles of the prophetic axle:
O father, self-sown shepherd of the everlasting years,
be not wroth; for mortal nature, untimely, never ceases
waxing and waning, the imitation of the moon.
Leave nectar to the blessed; and to men, a defence against grief,
I will give sweet wine, self-poured, the likeness of nectar;
another drink, fitted for mortals; but the primal world
still grieves, until I bring one child to birth.
I myself, the father, give birth, and in my male thigh I will endure
a woman's pangs, that I may save the offspring from its pangs.
Yesterday, at the nod of my Deo of the wide threshing-floors,
the earth, scored by the iron that woos the corn-ears,
bore the dry fruit of the sheaf-bearing ploughland.
Now my glorious-gifted child shall fix in the ground
the moist, fragrant fruit of pain-soothing autumn,
Dionysus the griefless, rearing the grief-dispelling cluster,
rival of Demeter; and you will praise me when you behold
the vine reddening with its wine-bearing dews,
the herald of gladness, and the country-folk beside the wine-press
treading the harvest with their heavy-laden feet,
and the phalanx of the Bassarids, lovers of the cry of Euoi,
shaking their loosened, frenzied hair into the air above their shoulders;
and, made frantic in mind by cup after cup,
all will raise the shout of Euoi at the loud-resounding table,
hailing Dionysus, the defender of the human race.
Him, when he has fought his contest, after the earth—companion of the stars,
after the war with the Giants, after the battle with the Indians—
the shifting heaven will receive, flashing his lightning beside Zeus.
And the god of the garden-vines, twining about his locks
the creeping serpent set upon the wine-dark ivy as a crown . . .
shall wear the serpent-headband, the sign of his new godhead;
and equal in honour with the blessed, named among men
shall be Dionysus of the vine, like Hermes of the golden wand,
like brazen Ares, like far-shooting Apollo.
So spoke the father; and the Fates consented; and around his word
the swift-footed Seasons, the heralds of things to come, sneezed an omen.
And so, when they had spoken, the two parted, the one coming
to the house of Harmonia, the other to the embroidered hall of Hera.
And Eros, self-taught and wise, who shepherds eternity,
striking on the dark gates of first-born Chaos,
brought out a god-driven quiver, in which alone
were kept, for Zeus, the fire-nourished arrows
that should turn him, fickle, to the desire of earthly marriages—
twelve of them; and a golden verse, measured out for each,
he had written on the middle back of the love-shooting quiver:
The first leads the son of Cronos to the bed of cow-eyed Io;
the second woos Europa with the ravishing bull;
the third leads the lord of Olympus to wed Plouto;
the fourth calls him to Danae as a golden bridegroom;
the fifth makes ready the fiery marriage for Semele;
the sixth grants the eagle to Aegina, the chief of the air;
the seventh joins Antiope to the crafty Satyr;
the eighth brings the wise swan to naked-bodied Leda;
the ninth bears the horse-bed to Dia of Perrhaebia;
the tenth charms Alcmene's three-moon husband;
the eleventh brings about the wedding of Laodameia;
the twelfth draws the thrice-coiling consort of Olympias.
But when Eros had looked over them all, handling them in order,
he let the other fire-pointed arrows lie,
and with his hand raised up the fifth and fitted it to the blazing string,
casting ivy upon the tip of the winged arrow,
that it might be a fitting crown for the vine-god,
dipping the whole shaft in the moisture of the nectar-bowl,
that Bacchus might make the nectared vintage grow.
While Eros was lifted to the house of Zeus on beating wings,
meanwhile Semele also, keeping pace with the rosy dawn,
was driving her mules, stretching the sound of her silver whip
through the city, and the slender, upright track of the well-wheeled car
scored the surface of the dust;
for, plucking from her eyes the Lethean feather of Sleep,
a wandering dream escorted her bewildered heart,
embroidering oracles, and with fresh-grown clusters
she thought she saw within the garden a tree of fair leaves,
green, weighed down with the swelling fruit of the unripe grape,
drenched with the growth-giving dews of the son of Cronos;
and suddenly a heavenly flame, falling through the air,
laid the whole tree low, yet did not touch its fruit;
but a wandering, long-winged bird snatched it up,
half-formed and lacking the birth that brings it to fulfilment,
and held it out to the son of Cronos; and the father in his sweet bosom
received and took it, and stitched it into his thigh; and in place of the fruit,
a bull-natured man, shaped with a horned form,
sprang up self-perfected above the loins of his sire.
And Semele was the tree; and the maiden, shuddering,
leapt up from her bed and startled her father,
telling of the gleaming vapour rising from the fair leaves.
And Cadmus the king was shaken, hearing that the tree of Semele
was burnt by fire; and calling his son, the god-voiced offspring of Chariclo,
early in the morning he told the smouldering dreams of his child.
And then, having received the inspired voice of Teiresias,
the father sent his daughter to the wonted temple of Athena
to make sacrifice to Zeus, the hurler of the thunderbolt—
a bull, the very image of the horned form of Lyaeus,
and a goat, the cutter of vines, the foe of the vintage to come.
From there she went out before the city, to kindle an altar to Zeus,
lord of the lightning; and standing beside the sacrifice
she steeped her bosom in blood, and the maiden was sprinkled with the slaughter;
and unsparing streams of blood wetted her tresses,
and her garments were dyed purple with the runlets from the ox;
and guiding her course beside the deep-rushy grass
she went to the ancestral water of neighbouring Asopus,
the maiden of the gleaming robe, to wash in the streams
her spotted garments, soaked with the many-spattering gore.
And looking on Semele bathing beside the streams of Asopus,
the Fury that roams in the air laughed,
remembering the son of Cronos, since with a common doom
he was to strike them both with the flaming thunderbolt.
There she cleansed her body, and naked, with her handmaids,
oaring her hands through the water, the maiden ran;
and with skilful art she held her head undrenched,
raised high above the swell, soaked to her hair,
and, laying her breast upon the stream,
with alternate feet she pushed the water behind her.
And she took up another offering, and high upon the neighbouring bank,
beside the eastern edge, to Dionysus the averter of ill,
into the stream, into the winds she shook off the fear of her dreams.
Not without the gods did she go to the streams; rather the Seasons,
prophetic, led her to the outpourings of that river;
nor did she escape the all-seeing eye of Zeus; and around the maiden
he turned, high-shining, the endless circle of his gaze.
And drawing in the air his bow, the helper of life,
Eros stood facing the father who was watching,
the unerring archer; and on the flower-tressed arrow
the bowstring flashed, and as the back-bent bow
was drawn, the echo of Euoi whistled forth the cunning shaft.
And Zeus the father, mighty as he was, was the target; to a worthless
Eros he bowed his neck; and like the track of a star
the bolt of the Loves, stirred with the wedding-whistle,
came to the heart of Zeus, swerving with thoughtful throb,
scoring with its topmost notches the fold of his thigh,
the herald of the birth to come. Then the son of Cronos,
bearing a restless eye, by the channelling constraint of earth,
was scourged toward the love of the maiden by the girdle of desire;
and gazing on Semele he leapt up, lest near the bank
he should see Europa again; and in his heart
he laboured once more, bearing a Phoenician longing; for of that same
beauty she bore the imprint, and ever about her face
shone the kindred radiance of his father's sister.
And Zeus the father changed his crafty form,
and for love of Semele, untimely, he flew as an eagle
high above Asopus, the daughter-begetting river,
bearing, like the prophet of Aegina's well-winged marriage,
the keen-eyed semblance of a bird's gaze;
and he left the upper air, and close beside the nearby bank
he measured the naked body of the fair-tressed maiden;
for he did not wish to see her from afar, but to gaze
close at hand on the all-white whole body of the bride,
because, sending everywhere his boundless eye,
so great and of such kind, the surveyor of the whole world,
it seemed to him not enough to see one unwedded maiden.
And the dark water was reddened by her rosy limbs,
and the river's stream became a lovely meadow,
flashing with the Graces; and gazing through the maiden
the naiad, unveiled, gave up a voice of wonder:
Surely it was not after the elder Cypris that Cronos, snatching away
their wedlock, cut the loins of his father, until again the wise foam,
bringing to a self-accomplished birth the shaping water,
brought to labour the younger sea-born Aphrodite?
Surely it is not that the river, after the sea, with like jealous births,
whirling the birth-bearing wave of the self-born swell,
bore another Cypris, and did not yield to the sea?
Surely it is not that one of the Muses entered my ancestral water
from neighbouring Helicon, and left for some spring
the horse-spring of Pegasus, the honey-dropping water,
or the stream of Olmeius? Stretched out in the streams
I behold a silver-footed maiden within the river;
I am persuaded that, wishing to come to the bed of Latmos,
to the couch of Endymion, the sleepless herdsman,
Selene is bathing in the Aonian outpourings;
but if she has cleansed her body for the grace of her sweet herdsman,
what need has she of Asopus, after the stream of Ocean?
And if she keeps her snowy, heavenly form,
what sign of the moon has she? For the yoke-straps of the unbridled
mules and the silver-wheeled car
are beside the shore, and Selene, the driver of oxen,
knows not how to yoke mules to the harness.
But if some heavenly goddess has come—for of the maiden
I see the grey, calm flashing of her eyes—
then perhaps, after the old quarrel of Teiresias,
grey-eyed Athena has bathed again, casting off her garment.
The rosy-armed maiden has a godlike form;
but if an earthly womb, glory-laden, bore her,
she is worthy of the heavenly bed of the son of Cronos.
Such words the voice from beneath the water spoke among the waves;
but Zeus, stirred by the fire-pointed goad of desire,
gazed on the rosy fingers of the swimming maiden;
and he turned the wandering circle of his unsteady eye,
now gazing on the spark of her rosy face,
now on the gleam of her ox-eyed lids, now on her hair
wandering in the winds, and, as her tresses were drawn aside,
he beheld the free, uncovered neck of the maiden;
and yet more he gazed upon her breasts, and, naked before the son of Cronos,
her bosom was armed, the archers of the Loves;
and he gazed on all her body; only the unseen, sacred
mystery of her lap his reverent eyes passed by.
And the mind of heavenly Zeus, creeping as a wanderer,
swam together with swimming Semele; and, charmed,
receiving the sweet-maddening spark in his accustomed heart,
the father yielded to the child; and with his feeblest dart
little Eros set the hurler of the thunderbolt aflame;
neither the showering of snow, nor against the fiery bearer
did the lightning avail; and even she herself was vanquished,
that so great a heavenly flame, by the little fire
of unwarlike Paphia; and little Eros with his shaggy quiver
vied with the aegis, the girdle with the shield, and to the love-breeding quiver
the heavy-thundering crash of the thunder was made a slave.
And Semele was stirred by the heart-charming sting of desire,
holding amazement; for love is the neighbour of friendly wonder.
And hardly did wily, high-ruling Zeus come back to the pole of heaven,
wearing again the inspired, recovered shape of his form.
And wishing to mount the nightly bed of Semele
he stretched his eye toward the west, for when sweet Hesperus should come;
and he blamed the long evening hour of Phaethon,
and with friendly lips he uttered a love-sick voice:
Tell me, lingering Night, when does grudging Dawn go down?
But you, lift up the torch, the forerunner of the Loves of Zeus,
prophesying the night-wandering lamp of Lyaeus.
Jealous Phaethon constrains me; can it be that he too
desires Semele, and grudges me in my longing?
O Sun, you trouble me, even if you have learned the goad of the Loves;
with sparing lash why do you whip your slow horse?
I know also another, swifter setting; if I wish,
I will hide both you and the dawn-goddess in my clouds,
and, with you hidden, day-time Night shall appear
as the bride-bringer of eager Zeus, so that there may shine
the stars at midday, and so that I may make the wonted escort of the Loves,
Hesperus, rise and never set.
But, drawing your forerunner the Dawn-star to the west,
grant a favour to you and to me in my longing, and all night long
have the joy of your Clymene, and let me come swiftly to Semele.
Yoke your chariot for me, light-bearing Selene, you also,
sending forth your plant-fostering radiance, since this marriage
ordains the birth of plant-rearing Dionysus;
and, rising over the lovely halls of Semele,
shine for me in my longing, together with the star of the Cyprian,
and lengthen the sweet darkness that ministers to the bed of Zeus.
Such words the father spoke, the things that desire knows how to bid.
But when, as he hastened, the earth-born leap stretching upward,
the topmost wide cone of mist ran up,
bringing the moist gloom of setting, the shadow opposite to Dawn,
then airy Zeus passed by the starry house
to the marriage of Semele, and with untraceable sandal,
leaping his first bound, measured with his sole the whole
airy path; and with the second he reached Thebes
like a wing or a thought; and as he rushed within,
the bars of the gateway opened of themselves.
And he embraced Semele with the loving clasp of his hand,
now over the bed lowing with the bellow of an ox,
bearing a horned aspect on his human limbs,
the very likeness, equal in growth, of bull-horned Dionysus,
now he put on the thick-haired form of a lion,
at another time he was a leopard, as begetting a bold son,
the driver of leopards and the charioteer of lions;
at another time the bridegroom, his hair coiled
under the spires of serpents, was bound with a vine-wreath,
whirling the wine-dark, twisting ivy of his locks,
the woven ornament of Bacchus; and a curving serpent, creeping,
licked the rosy neck of the trembling bride
with gentle lips, and, going down over her bosom,
it wreathed the rounded circle of her steadfast breasts,
hissing the marriage-song, and pouring out the sweet honey
of the well-hived bee, not the deadly venom of the viper.
And Zeus tarried at the marriage, and as beside a neighbouring wine-press
he thundered the cry of Euoi, begetting the son who loves the cry of Euoi;
and he set mouth upon mouth in love-madness, and, gushing forth
the lovely nectar, the consort made Semele drunk,
that she might bear a child, the sceptred lord of the vintage,
raising the care-banishing cluster, the messenger of things to come,
leaning his weighted arm upon the fire-bearing fennel-rod;
at another time he raised the thyrsus, much-entwined with wine-dark ivy,
bearing the skin of a deer; and on the woman-maddened bearer's
left arm shook the dappled fawnskin.
And all the earth laughed, and with self-grown leaves
a vine-bearing orchard ran round the bed of Semele,
and the walls budded with flowers from the dewy meadow
about the birth of Bromios; and on the cloudless bed,
with thundering crashes, Zeus within the chamber clashed
the drums, prophesying nocturnal Dionysus.
And after the bed he embraced Semele with loving speech,
consoling his bride with hopes of things to come:
I am, woman, the son of Cronos, your bridegroom; lift up
your proud neck on high, joined to a heavenly consort,
and do not seek a measure greater than mortal birth.
The marriage of Danae does not rival yours; nay, the wedlock
of the cattle-Loves even of his own father's sister
you have hidden; for Europa, glorying in the bed of Zeus,
went to Crete, but Semele comes to Olympus.
What more did you wish, beyond the heaven and the pole of stars?
And one day someone will say that the son of Cronos gave honour
to Minos below and to Dionysus in heaven.
But after the mortal son of Autonoe and the offspring of Ino—
the one fallen by his own hounds, the other doomed
to die at the winged arrow of his child-slaying sire,
and after the short-lived son of raving Agave—
you shall bring to birth an undying son, and I will call you immortal;
blessed are you, that for gods and men you shall bring forth a joy,
bearing a son who makes mortals forget their grief.

8. The eighth holds the shifting-worded, savage jealousy of Hera,
and the fiery marriage of Semele, and Zeus the slayer.
So speaking, the god went to Olympus; but in the high-roofed
hall his mind wandered near his bride,
holding a sting for Thebes greater than for heaven; for to the son of Cronos
heaven was lovely, the house of Semele, and about the wedding-chamber
the handmaids of Cadmus were the swift-footed Seasons of Zeus.
And with the marriage-droplets of the Zeus-sent wedding,
pressed by its swelling, the womb of Semele heaved;
and, as witness of the birth of garland-loving Dionysus,
she delighted her heart with a wreath, and on her flower-tressed head
she plaited the self-twining ivy of a maenad in her hair,
like a prophetess of the Bassarids, and to brides to come,
near their childbearing, she gave the late name of ivy.
And bearing the heavy weight of the god-begotten birth,
if ever some old shepherd made music on his pipe,
hearing the song of neighbouring Echo, the lover of the fields,
in her single tunic she went out of the chamber with maenad rush;
if the sound of the double flute was heard, the wanderer of the hills,
leaping unsandalled from the high-roofed halls,
self-bidden she went out to the ridge of the lonely woodland;
if a cymbal clashed, she was stirred with a throb of her feet,
bounding her curving step beneath her slanting sandal;
and if she heard the long-horned bull lowing,
with a like imitation she bellowed the cry of an ox from her throat;
often, beneath the shepherd's ridge, with maenad voice
she sang a song with Pan, and Echo joined her cry,
and, answering the country sound of the horned flute,
she bent her step into the dance; and the unborn, wise child
with hidden leaps bounded along with the mother who bore him,
a flute-maddened imitation, and a self-taught song,
half-formed, he sounded forth, pouring an echo from within her womb.
So he was swelling with the weight of the womb that bore a son,
the herald of gladness, a thoughtful babe; and about the boy
the Seasons, handmaids of the son of Cronos, crowned heaven.
And Envy, gazing on the marriage-bed of high-ruling Zeus
and the birth-pangs of Semele, the god-begotten labour,
took on a jealousy of Bacchus while he was yet within the womb,
self-suffering, loveless, smitten by his own venom.
And in his crafty mind he devised a twisted plan,
bearing the lying form of an Ares opposed to him
in counterfeit armour, and, as if with a stream of blood,
with a poisonous flower he scored the back of an ox-hide
with a feigned droplet, and, as though from slaughtered men,
dipping his treacherous fingers in like-coloured red,
he reddened his hands with a bastard, ruddy gore;
and from his throat he belched a nine-thousand-fold din,
pouring from his fearful mouth a man-rending voice;
and with thieving whispers he startled Athena,
and goaded jealous Hera yet more to wrath;
he provoked them both, and with such words he reproached them:
Seek for yourself another, new bridegroom in heaven, Hera,
another, since Semele has snatched away yours, who for the grace of her bed
treads the wedded ground of seven-gated Thebes
and rejects the seven-zoned heaven; and in your stead
he delights to hold in his arms an earthly, pregnant bride.
Where has my mother's jealousy gone? Can it be that even
the wrath of Hera herself has been softened toward the marriage of Semele?
Where are your stings, your unsparing gadfly? No longer in the sea
is the heifer driven, sea-frightened? No longer does the herdsman
Argus, with his sleepless, far-scattered eyes,
keep watch over the newer bed of the marriage-thieving son of Cronos?
But what is this Olympian crowd to me? Going down to earth
I will leave my father's heaven, and dwelling in our own
Thrace I shall not see the sorrows of my grieving mother,
nor Zeus the marriage-thief; and if ever he comes
to our land, desiring a Bistonian maiden,
he shall learn what Ares is when he is angered; for, bearing our own
death-bringing spear, the slayer of the Titans,
I will drive the woman-mad son of Cronos out of Thrace;
and taking as my pretext that he drags a maiden to his bed,
self-bidden I shall be the avenger of my own marriage,
because, consorting with earth-born weddings,
he has filled the dappled heaven with his loves.
May heaven be gracious, the house of mortals; do I tread the pole of stars?
Callisto wheels along Olympus, where the circle shines
of the high-crested Bear, named for the Arcadian.
I hate the course of the seven-pathed Pleiad; for in Olympus
Electra troubles me, flashing together with Selene.
Why are you now at ease? You afflicted Apollo, the son of Leto,
yet within the womb, and you do not stir against Dionysus?
When the Trito-born was born, Hephaestus, the labour-easer,
self-bearing Zeus shall bring to birth the son of a bastard wife,
bringing to labour another, higher birth in his male thigh,
and there is no more need of your axe. Yield, Athena,
cease crying out over the birth-arch of the head of Zeus,
because Dionysus disgraces the wise birth-pang of your
birth-perfecting head, in that, sprung from an earthly stock,
he will be self-born, an Olympian, like Athena,
hiding the boast of motherless Pallas. Nay, I myself
am ashamed far more, whenever some mortal says:
Zeus gave battle to Ares and gladness to Dionysus.
But leaving the pole of the son of Cronos to his bastard children,
I will come down from heaven, a wanderer; and let the water-frozen
Ister receive its sceptred lord roaming about,
before I see Ganymede here, the cup-bearer of Zeus,
the fair-haired herdsman, the citizen of Olympus after Pergamon,
handing the untouched cup of heavenly Hebe,
before I see Semele and Bacchus dwellers on Olympus,
and the star-wandering crown of earthly Ariadne
running with the Sun, the fellow-traveller of the dawn.
There I will stay, that I may not see the Sea-Monster, nor the sickle of Perseus,
nor the figure of Andromeda, nor the eye of the Gorgon Medusa,
which the son of Cronos may hereafter set in Olympus.
He spoke, and confounded the mind of self-born Athena,
and raised yet higher the wrath of heavy-jealous Hera.
And Envy darted swiftly off, and shaking his crooked knees
went by slanting paths through the air; and in his
eyes and his mind he rushed away, like smoke,
arming his telchin-mind for guile, for wickedness.
Nor did Hera, heavy in wrath, the consort of Zeus, grow slack;
but, darting along on her storm-swift sandal,
she ran through the dappled heaven adorned with bright stars,
through the countless cities, on a roaming sole,
seeking crafty Deceit, in case she might find her somewhere.
But when, high above the Dictaean rock of the Corybants,
she saw the birth-water of neighbouring Amnisus,
there the fickle mountain-roaming goddess met her;
for she always lingered by the false tomb of Zeus,
taking delight in the Cretans, since they were deceivers.
And about her loins flowed the Cydonian girdle,
in which lie all the cunning charms of mortals:
in it is crafty thievery, in it dalliance,
cajolery, in it manifold deceits, and in it also
the false oath that runs together with the airy winds.
And to crafty Deceit, with crafty speech, Hera
of cunning counsel made soft entreaty, warding off her consort:
Hail, goddess crafty-counselled, guile-wandering; not even
wheedling Hermes passes you by with his thieving whispers;
give me also the all-shifting girdle, which once Rheia
bound about her loins, until she deceived her consort.
I do not bear a rocky form against the son of Cronos,
nor do I beguile a consort with a deceitful stone,
but an earthly woman constrains me, for the grace of whose bed
raging Ares, heavy in wrath, refuses to dwell in heaven.
What profit is it that I am an immortal goddess? For a worthless
mortal holds my husband, whom no goddess, no Leto, snatched away;
it was not by Danae that rainy Zeus lay a second time,
but after the seal of the iron-bound chamber
the bride, blaming her golden marriage, sailed the sea,
and got for her love-gift the water of the salt sea; and in the deep
the chest, voyaging with her, swam upon the unsteady winds.
Nor after Crete did the bull of Olympus sail again,
he did not see Europa after her bed; but, soaked,
stung by the gadfly, horned Io swam.
Nor did a goddess have an unhindered marriage, but Leto herself,
bearing a burden in her womb, ran much-wandering,
restlessly gazing on the moving ankles of the wandering islands
and the unresting stream of the inhospitable sea,
and hardly did she see the free shoot of the birth-olive.
So much did Leto toil, and her consort did not help her;
and for the bed of one short-lived mortal bride
he refused the bed of his heavenly sister Hera.
I fear that the son of Cronos, my husband and my brother, hearing of it,
may drive me from heaven for the grace of a woman's bed,
and may make Semele the queen of his own Olympus.
But if you favour Zeus the son of Cronos rather than Hera,
and do not grant me your all-charming girdle,
so that my wandering son may come back to Olympus,
I will go to the farthest edge of Ocean,
leaving heaven for the grace of mortal weddings,
a hearth-fellow of first-born Tethys; thence I will come
to the house of Harmonia, and dwell near Ophion.
But you, honouring the all-mothering bride of Zeus,
grant me to have your helping girdle, that I may charm
raging Ares to flee and dwell in heaven once again.
To her speaking thus the goddess answered with persuasive words:
Mother of Enyalios, first-throned bride of Zeus,
I will give my girdle, and if you bid anything more
I obey, since you rule among the gods next to the son of Cronos.
Take this band; and clasping it about your bosom
you shall bring Ares to heaven; and if you wish,
charm the mind of the son of Cronos and, if need be, of Ocean
when he is angry; and leaving the wedding of earthly Loves
high-ruling Zeus shall come self-bidden to heaven,
bending his mind round with our deceitful girdle;
this puts to shame the heart-charming girdle of my Paphian.
So speaking, the crafty goddess fled, wind-borne,
passing through the air on her flying sandal.
And leaving the shield-brandishing cave of the Dictaean cliff
and the birth-grotto of the birth-perfecting goddess,
deceitful Hera came to the chamber of Semele,
snorting with jealousy; and, like a honey-tongued old woman,
she shaped her body to the form of a child-loving nurse,
a child-tender, whom Agenor himself had reared,
and gave her a portion, and bestowed the woman on a husband
as a father would; and she, repaying the grace of her keeping,
nursed Cadmus while he was yet an infant at her breast,
and cradled the babe Europa in her loving arms.
Taking a body equal to hers, Hera went into the house,
angry at Semele and Cypris and Dionysus
not yet having seen the light, and beside the newly-wedded chamber
she leaned her gaze toward the opposite wall,
turning aside her eye, lest she should behold the bed of Zeus.
Peisianassa, the handmaid of Semele, the offspring
of a Tyrian stock, seated her high upon a chair,
and Thelxinoe fitted carpets to the shining seat.
There the wily goddess sat nearby; and she found the maiden
heavy with the pang of her ripening childbirth;
and the birth, not touching the birth-perfecting Moon,
was proclaimed by the pale cheek of her unmarked womb
and the pallor before her wine-dark limbs; and as
lying Hera sat, her crafty body trembled with a feigned
throb, and below she bent down, nodding toward the ground,
her old neck bowed with hunched and pressing shoulders.
And hardly did she find a pretext; she groaned aloud in speech,
wiping a well-made tear from her face,
and she spoke a crafty word with a heart-charming voice:
Tell me, queen, why are your cheeks turned pale?
Where is that beauty of yours? Who, grudging your form,
has marred the purple sparks of your face?
And who has changed your roses into short-lived anemones?
And why do you, cast down, waste away? Can it be that you too
have heard those shameful things which the citizens cry out?
Perish the deadly mouth of women, the beginners of woe.
Tell me, do not hide from me the despoiler of your girdle;
which of the gods has defiled you? Who has snatched your maidenhood?
If secret Ares has wedded my maiden
and lay with Semele, scorning Aphrodite,
let him come to your bed, brandishing the marriage-spear;
your mother knows her steadfast sire.
But if swift-sandalled Hermes came reveling as your bridegroom
and for the beauty of Semele renounced his own Peitho,
let him grant his wand, the self-herald of your bed,
or let him adorn you with his golden sandals,
bringing a gift worthy of your bed, that you too
may be golden-sandalled, like Hera the consort of Zeus.
But if from heaven came a husband, fair Apollo,
and for the love of Semele forgot his Daphne,
without secret guile let him dance to you through the air,
delicate, riding the chariot of his singing swans,
bringing his lyre as the bride-gifts of your love,
a faithful sign of your chamber; for, beholding it,
Cadmus will recognize the heavenly cithara of Phoebus,
which he saw, shifting-voiced, beside the feast at his table,
singing the earthly weddings of Harmonia.
But if, mad for a woman, the dark-haired one constrained you,
and preferred you to the wise, far-sung Melanippe,
let him come reveling openly, and at the gates of Cadmus
let him fix the point of his bridal trident,
joining a like honour beside snake-haired Dirce,
as among the Argives, beside lion-feeding Lerna,
he set up a token of the marriage of Amymone, where still
a place is named after the trident of the Lernaean nymph.
But why do I call you the bedfellow of the Earth-shaker?
What signs have you of the bed of Poseidon?
With watery hands he embraced Tyro, poured out,
splashing in a deceitful stream, the counterfeit Enipeus.
But if also, as you say, your bridegroom is the son of Cronos,
let him come to your bed with the lovely thunderbolt,
armed with the wedding-lightning, that someone may say:
Thunderbolts are the bride-attendants of Hera and Semele.
Jealous though she is, the wife of Zeus will not be vexed at you;
for your mother's Ares would not allow it.
Blessed is Europa more than Semele, whom over his shoulders
horned Zeus lifted up; and on the love-stricken bull's
topmost hoof she ran dry over the water,
and so great a one was the boat of Eros. Ah, great marvel,
a maiden drove the charioteer of heaven.
I count Danae more blessed than Semele, through whose lap
golden, from the roof, rainy Zeus streamed down
in a rich droplet of woman-maddened snow;
yet the most blessed bride did not ask for golden gifts,
for she had her husband as the whole love-gift of Eros. But let there be
some silence between us, lest your sire Cadmus hear.
So speaking she left the house, and the bride still grieving,
holding the jealousy of Hera, of unmatched weddings,
blaming the son of Cronos; and by the back-returning path
she came within the heaven, and beside the heavenly seat,
beholding the weapons of Zeus lying apart from their bearer,
as though they could hear, with friendly speech she addressed them:
Thunder, has my cloud-gathering Zeus left you too?
Who has snatched you again, and stripped you of your bearer?
Thunder, you have been despoiled—Typhoeus is not the cause—
sharing the sufferings of Hera, my comforter; for rainy Zeus,
the bride-tender, rejects us both.
No longer is the earth dusted with snows, and, the moist-poured
rain failing, the drought feeds upon the furrow of the ploughland,
bearing a useless crop; and by the farmers
Zeus is called cloudless instead of dark-clouding.
Lightnings, break a fiery voice against the son of Cronos,
against woman-mad Zeus; friends, thunderbolts, cry out.
But you, the avengers of the heavy-jealous griefs of Hera,
go to Semele as bride-attendants, and as the gifts of her girdle
let her, entreating, receive her own flaming slayers.
Such things did Hera cry to the voiceless weapons of Zeus,
grieving, and the goddess heaved with jealous wrath.
And Semele, heavily bound by her newly-grieving heart,
longing for the lightning, the fire-bright escort of the Loves,
with blaming lips besought her consort,
wishing for the form of Hera's fire-crowned bed:
By Danae I beseech you, of the wealth-streaming weddings,
grant a favour, horned husband of Europa; for I am ashamed
to call you the consort of Semele, whom I saw as in a dream.
Acrisius is more blessed than Cadmus; but I myself too
would have wished, if I had seen the golden marriage, rainy Zeus,
had not the mother of Perseus snatched away this honour of yours;
I would have wished that you had carried me over the waters as a wandering bull
upon your shoulders, that my brother Polydorus too might wander
seeking the ravisher of the roaming bride,
like Cadmus, seeking my own son of Cronos as the bearer.
But what to me is the form of the cattle-marriage or of the snow?
I do not wish for an honour equal to that an earthly bride received.
Leave the bull to Europa, leave to Danae the shower of rain;
the jealousy of Hera's marriage alone holds me. If you honour me,
adorn my chamber with your heavenly fire,
darting the lovely gleam of the clouds, and as the lightning
show the bride-gift of my love to unbelieving Agave;
let Autonoe shudder beside my neighbouring chamber,
hearing the thunderous song of the bride-tending Loves,
the self-proclaiming token of your unannounced bed.
Grant me to embrace the dear flame and delight my heart,
touching the lightning and handling the thunderbolts.
Give me the wedded flame of your chamber; for every bride
has the torch as escort of marriage-perfecting weddings.
Am I not worthy of the thunderbolts of your marriage,
bearing the blood of Ares and of your Aphrodite?
Wretched am I; the marriage of Semele has short-lived fire
and earthly lamps, while, touching the thunderbolt
and handling the lightning, your Hera is wedded.
Bridegroom delighting in the thunderbolt, you in your many-gleaming chamber,
bearing your inspired form, go to the bed of Hera,
lighting up your bride with the lightnings of marriage,
fiery Zeus; but to Semele you come as a serpent or a bull;
she hears the heavy-thundering Olympian sound of the Loves,
but Semele, by a shadowy figure of form,
hears the bastard bellowing of a counterfeit bull;
soundless to my bed comes cloudless Zeus,
and the cloud-gatherer mingles with high-necked Hera.
And shunning the shame of his ill-married daughter, my sire,
shut indoors, your Cadmus, avoids the path of men,
ashamed to appear before the townsfolk, because the citizens
all mock at your secret weddings,
blaming Semele, that she had a stolen consort.
A fine love-gift you gave me, the reproaches of women;
and the band of handmaids blames me, and beyond others
I dread the headlong mouth of my unsilenced nurse.
Remember who, weaving a treacherous doom for Typhon,
gave you back the spark of the snatched thunderbolt;
show my sire what he gave; for old Cadmus
demands of me a token of your bed.
I have not yet seen the true face of the son of Cronos,
nor the light-bringing ray of his eyelids, nor on his face
have I marked the gleamings and his flashing beard;
I have not yet seen your Olympian form, but I behold
a leopard or a lion, and I have not seen my consort a god.
I look on you as a mortal, though I am to bear a god.
I have learned of another fiery marriage; for the Sun,
setting with the wedding-fire, embraced Clymene his bride.
So she spoke, asking for her own doom; for, equal to Hera,
the short-lived bride hoped to look upon for her marriage
the gentle spark of a calm thunderbolt.
And Zeus the father, hearing, reproached the jealous Fates,
and pitied Semele, untimely; and about Bacchus
he knew the crafty wrath of pitiless Hera.
And he bade Hermes snatch from the flaming thunderbolt
the new son of fire-stricken Thyone.
And the father spoke a word to the high-necked maiden:
O woman, surely the jealous mind of Hera has deceived you with guile;
do you indeed, woman, think that thunderbolts are gentle?
Endure to wait another while, since you still bear the burden,
endure to wait another while, since you carry my son;
do not, before the birth, demand of me the fiery slayers;
I did not despoil the maidenhood of Danae wielding the lightning,
nor the crash of thunder, and the thunderbolts did not wed
the marriage of Europa, your Tyrian bride,
the Inachian heifer did not see the flash; but you alone,
a mortal, demand of me what no goddess, no Leto, asked.
Such a word he spoke, and was unwilling to strive
against the threads of the Fates; and through the airy gulf,
flashing, he was borne, and the entreaty of his bride,
unwilling, he fulfilled, the husband Zeus who rouses the lightning,
and he danced toward Semele, stretching out with downcast hand
the bridal sparks of the marriage-destroying thunderbolt;
and the chamber gleamed with lightnings, and with the breath of fire
Ismenus blazed, and all Thebes flashed.
And Semele, beholding her flaming slayers,
raised her proud neck and spoke with high-minded voice:
I have no need of the clear-sounding harp, no need of the flute;
thunders are born to me, the pipes of the Loves of Zeus,
this Olympian sound is my flute, and the firebrand
of the heavenly lightning is the torch of my chamber; and of worthless
torches I take no heed; thunderbolts are my torches.
I am the wife of the son of Cronos; Agave belongs to Echion;
let them call Autonoe the wife of Aristaeus;
Ino has Nephele, but Semele got Hera as her fellow-bride.
I did not become the wife of Athamas, and I did not bear
the short-lived Actaeon, torn by his hounds, the comrade of the woodland.
I have no need of a lesser lyre; for the heavenly
Star-Cithara sings the wedding of Semele.
So she spoke, glorying, and wished to handle with her hands
the destroying lightning, and, scorning Fate,
with a daring palm she touched the deadly thunderbolts;
and the marriage of Semele was death-bringing, for whom by a single ordinance
the Fury made the wedding-chamber a pyre and a tomb;
and with birth-bringing rays the bridal breath of the thunderbolt,
since Zeus did not spare, burned the whole bride to ashes;
and the lightning was her midwife, and the thunderbolts her Eileithyia;
and as Bacchus leapt forth from the blazing lap of the mother who bore him,
the heavenly flame, sparing, served as his midwife,
while the weddings withered in the mother-slaying spark;
and the half-grown babe of the unharmed birth
the thunderbolts bathed with sparing breaths;
and Semele, beholding her fiery end,
perished rejoicing in her birth-doom; and one might behold
Desire, Eileithyia, and the Furies in a single chamber.
And Hermes brought the half-finished babe, born to its sire,
its limbs washed in the heavenly fire.
And Zeus, turning the mind of heavy-jealous Hera,
soothed her savage, ever-renewing weight of menace,
and Semele, the fiery one, removing her to the pole of stars,
to have heaven as her house, he led up, the mother of Bacchus,
a hearth-fellow of the heavenly dwellers, as the kin of Hera,
as the offspring of Harmonia from Ares, from Aphrodite;
and washing her new body clean in the blazing fire . . .
and she held the imperishable Olympian life; and in place of Cadmus
and the earthly ground and Autonoe and Agave,
she found Artemis sharing her throne, and consorted with Athena,
and received heaven as her gift, sharing one table
with Zeus and Hermes and Ares and the Cytherean.

11. The eleventh, watch, and you will mark lovely
Ampelos borne off by the man-slaying, snatching bull.
The contest was dissolved; and the lovely youth, glorying
in the sport-loving victory, leapt up, companion of his coeval Bacchus,
shifting his wandering sole around the rolling-footed circle,
leaning his all-white right hand on Dionysus;
and seeing him exulting, prancing on his feet with the double victory,
Iobacchus soothed him with a friendly word:
"Hasten again, dear boy, after the victory of swift feet
and after the contest on foot, to have yet a third other contest,
and swim, unreachable, with your coeval Bacchus as he swims.
Ampelos, having beaten me wrestling on the sands,
be lighter than Dionysus also in the streams,
and leaving the Satyrs still at play with their leapings,
hasten again, alone, to a third other contest;
may you win on land and in the waters, and after victory
I will crown your lovely locks with double clusters,
Lyaeus twice defeated, yet unvanquished.
This lovely stream suited you, it suited your beauty
alone, the beauty of your limbs, that Ampelos might be double,
cleaving the gold-gleaming waters with golden palm;
and as you stretch with naked limbs for victory,
the whole Pactolian water will adorn your beauty.
Grant the river an Olympian honour equal to your own, since Phaethon too
casts his rosy rays upon Ocean;
give Pactolus too your radiance, that Ampelos
may appear rising like the Morning Star; for this stream
flashes in both ways, with the reddening metal,
as you do with your limbs; and let the deep-rich stream
receive a youth of like colour and like form,
mingling beauty with beauty, that I may cry to the Satyrs:
how did rose come to rose? whence is one radiance mingled
both in the reddening skin and the flashing stream?
Would that here too, boy, there were the stream of Eridanus,
where the tears of the Heliades flow rich, that I might wash
your limbs in both, in gold and in amber.
But since I dwell very far from the Hesperian river,
I will come to Alybe, the neighbouring city, where nearby
the Geudis whitens with the draught of its wealth-bearing waters,
that you, washed from the river Pactolus,
Ampelos, I may brighten in the silvery streams too.
Let fair-flowing Hermus be a care to other Satyrs;
for it does not bear a stream of gold; but you alone
were a golden boy, may you have golden water too."
So speaking, he was borne through the water; and from the ground
Ampelos was lifted up and went along with Lyaeus;
and sweet was the course to them both, end from end,
as they swam in circles in the rich river.
And the god, holding a watery contest of swiftness,
ran unsteady in the water, casting his bare
breast on the streams, and shaking his feet and rowing his hands
he scored the unshaken back of the wealthy calm,
now keeping his course in company with the coeval boy,
now darting past, but guarded, only so far as he would leave
Ampelos running near the path, his companion, beside neighbouring Bacchus;
at other times wheeling his palms, as though tiring in the wave,
the swift-kneed god willingly gave the victory to the water-traveller.
And after the river's flood Ampelos went to the midst of the thicket,
holding his neck proud with the river victory.
And he girt his locks with a serpent cluster,
bearing a fearful mimicry of serpent-haired Lyaeus;
and often, seeing the spangled tunic of Bromius,
he fastened on his limbs a counterfeit, embroidered raiment,
and bound his light foot with a purple buskin,
wearing a dappled robe on his skin; and in a mountain-stalled car
watching Iobacchus driving leopards
he proudly displayed the sports of the crag-loving beasts;
now mounting the mane of a mountain bear
he reined back the grim mane of the hurrying beast,
now he lashed the shaggy neck of a lion,
at other times, mounted high upon spangled backs,
unshaken, he delighted to drive an unbridled tiger.
And seeing him, Dionysus, with a gentle threat,
spoke, consoling him with a friendly, prophetic word,
pouring a pitying voice from reproachful lips:
"Where are you borne, dear boy? Why does the wood please you so much?
Stay with me, hunting with hunting Dionysus;
when I touch the feast, feast together with Lyaeus,
reveling, when I rouse the revel for the Satyrs.
The leopard does not trouble me, nor the jaw of the wild bear;
do not tremble at the greedy mouth of the mountain-ranging lioness;
only fear the horns of the implacable bull."
He spoke, pitying bold Ampelos; and the youth
heard the word with his ears, but his mind played within him.
There appeared a great sign to loving Dionysus
announcing Ampelos short-lived; for from a crag
bearing a freshly grown fawn upon its back
a horned serpent rose, broad with scales,
and bearing it above the altar, on top of the foundations,
it dashed it down, thrashed by its fearful horn,
headlong, self-tumbling; and as the mountain-ranging fawn
bleated its shrill cry, its wandering life-breath flew away;
and as a libation was to be, self-heralding, with a draught of blood
the stone altar reddened with bloody dews,
bearing the likeness of wine poured out. And beholding
Euios the serpent, the horned snatcher of the fawn,
learning the horned destroyer of the witless youth,
he mingled laughter with grief, and held an unsteady purpose,
double, and was divided in his heart, lamenting the youth
near to his doom, laughing for the grace of sweet wine.
Yet he went, companion of the lovely boy,
to the mountain, to the flat rock, and to the course of the accustomed hunt.
And seeing him, Bacchus still rejoiced; for the eyes
never bring satiety of loves to those who gaze.
Often too, when Bromius sat beside the table,
the youth piped, rendering an unwonted Muse,
and poured forth the whole song of the reeds; and at the boy's
fair singing, even if he broke the strain of the song,
Bacchus, springing above the floor with a wind-like leap,
clapped with his hands, loud-sounding, and while the youth
was still singing, setting his lip about his mouth
he embraced, on the pretext of harmony, with a loving clasp;
and he swore by Cronides, that so great a rhythm singing Pan
never sang, nor clear-voiced Apollo.
And death-bearing Ate, seeing the bold youth
led astray from Lyaeus hunting in the mountains,
like to the graceful youth, his coeval boy,
soothed Ampelos the deluder with such a word,
doing a favour to the stepmother of Phrygian Dionysus:
"Your friend, fearless boy, is called Dionysus in vain;
what reward of companionship have you won? You do not drive Lyaeus's
wondrous chariot, you do not rein a leopard.
Maron has won the car of your Bromius, stretching his hand
with the beast-driving whip and the well-stoned bridle;
what gift is this you have from straight-thyrsus Lyaeus?
The Pans have the lyre and the din of sweet-sounding pipes,
and to the Satyrs your steward Dionysus gave the loud-roaring
circle of ox-hide, and the mountain-ranging
Bassarids themselves sit upon the backs of lions.
What gifts worthy of your friendship do you bring,
loved in vain by Bacchus, the driver of leopards?
Often, seated high upon the Phoebean car,
Atymnius, conspicuous on high, drove, cleaving the air;
you have heard of Abaris himself, whom into the air-walking course
Phoebus escorted on a flying, wandering arrow;
Ganymede too steered the eagle in the air,
the false winged Zeus, the father of your Lyaeus;
but Bacchus never lifted up Ampelos, the bird of the Loves,
raising your body with unscratching talons.
The Trojan wine-pourer was better, who has the court of Zeus,
the house. But you, boy, still bearing a longing for the car,
refuse to drive a colt into the unsteady course,
because, shaken by the swift-whirling draught of its feet,
the stormy horse shakes off its driver;
the raging horses dashed Glaucus down to the earth,
and Pegasus, swift-flying, sharing the Poseidonian blood
of the common stock, the airy offspring of the Earth-shaker,
shook off Bellerophon headlong.
Come with me to the herd, where clear-voiced herdsmen are,
and lovely oxen; and seated upon a bull
I will make you a conspicuous, ox-driving charioteer;
for your king, watching, will praise you far more,
bull-formed Dionysus, seated on the waist of a bull.
This is a course without fear, since even Europa, being a woman,
a maiden, mounted on bovine backs,
gripping the horn with her hands and not needing a bridle."
So speaking she persuaded him, and the goddess sank into the air.
And from a crag a wandering bull ran down,
unforeseen, and his tongue, the witness of his thirst,
he held forth from his throat with opening lips,
and drank; and about the boy, as though a herdsman present,
he stood, wholly like one who knew him; nor did he hold his horn
slantwise from his brow; and as the resistless bull
drank thickly, belching up the draught from his capacious gullet,
the dripping moisture of the dew wetted the youth,
as though a prophet of things to come, that with an earthly draught the oxen,
toiling about one endless circling turning-post,
water the vine-clad fruit with their waters.
And the bold boy stood above the bovine brow,
handling the curved horn with a fearless hand;
and goaded by the sweet sting of the woodland-grazing ox,
he wished to drive the unyoked, mountain-running bull.
And plucking leaves beside the deep-rushed grass
he wove a counterfeit scourge of green withies
with sharper shoots, and with a much-twisted cluster
bending the crooked rings he made the shape of a bridle;
and with dewy leaves he adorned the body of the bull,
and bound reddening roses round about its back,
and hung lilies and narcissus on its brow,
draping a purpling anemone on its neck;
and on either side he gilded both horns,
drawing up with his deep-digging hands yellow clay
from the neighbouring river. And spreading on high upon its back
a spangled hide, he mounted the spine of the bull;
and stretching a counterfeit whip along the bovine sides,
as though a fine-maned colt, he lashed his own bearer.
And the bold one cried out a word to bull-faced Mene:
"Yield to me, horned Selene, driver of oxen;
for I too am become horned in both ways, and I drive a bull."
Such a boastful word he cried to the rolling Moon.
And jealous Selene watched through the air with her eye
Ampelos borne by the man-slaying, snatching bull,
and sent him an ox-driving gadfly; and he, scored
in his body by the bitter, restless, roaming sting,
ran about the rough ridge, like a horse.
And the boy, seeing the unyoked bull with maddening sting
striking his track upon the high-crested hills,
terrified, before his doom, prayed with a wailing voice:
"Stand still today, bull, and tomorrow you will go swiftly;
do not kill me on a desolate height of rock,
that Bacchus may not hear of my doom unannounced.
Do not be angry, bull, because I gilded your horn;
do not be jealous, because Bacchus guards my friendship.
But if you kill me and care nothing for Dionysus,
and no pity holds you for a wailing charioteer,
because I am young, because I am also a friend of Lyaeus,
carry me to the Satyrs, and there, bull, you will overpower me,
that I may obtain, after death, my dust much-bewailed;
yes, I beseech you, dear bull; and I will think it a consolation,
that Dionysus, tearless, laments my doom.
If you deceive your horned charioteer
who has a likeness in form to your bull-faced shape,
become voiced and tell my death to Lyaeus:
bull, hostile to your Demeter and to Dionysus,
while Bromius grieves, bountiful Deo grieves with him."
Such a word the rosy youth spoke, neighbour of Hades,
ill-fated; and darting with the twin hoof of his feet
over the mountain's high peaks, hard to climb, the raging ox
shook off the youth headlong from his back;
and he fell self-tumbling; and as he fell upon his neck-joint
his slanting neck was split, faintly creaking;
and rolling him back over the ground in a whirl
with the sharp point of its horn it cast him down.
And the corpse was headless; and of the unburied corpse
the white body reddened with the reddening gore.
And one of the Satyrs, seeing lovely Ampelos
lying in the dust upon the ground, came as ill messenger to Bacchus.
And the god, hearing, ran swiftly like the breezes;
not so great a course did Heracles accomplish, when the Nymphs
hid soft Hylas in their jealous streams,
a bridegroom kept by the wet, snatching girl,
as then Bacchus rushed, mountain-running; and in the dust
he wept over the boy lying there, watching him as though alive.
And he wrapped a cloak about him, the breathless one, fastening from his shoulder
the fawnskin upon the cold breast,
and, though he was a corpse, bound buskins on his feet;
and roses and lilies he scattered on his skin, and about his hair,
as for a short-lived one fallen by a sharp sting,
he hung up the flower of the swift-perishing anemone;
and he gave a thyrsus to his hand, and covered him with his own robe
of purple; and as a gift from his uncut head
he cut one lock and laid it on the witnessing corpse
as a last offering; and taking ambrosia from his mother Rhea
he poured it on the wounds, whence the youth, changing his form,
transferred the fragrant ambrosia into his own fruit.
And as the graceful corpse was stretched upon the ground,
no pallor was poured about the rosy body; and of the swift-fated one
the graceful locks of the love-bearing head
quivered upon his face in the sparing breezes;
and there was a lovely one, dust-covered. And about the corpse
the Sileni groaned, and the Bacchae wailed.
Nor did beauty leave him, even though he died; and he lay
a corpse like a Satyr, wholly like one laughing, as though ever
pouring from voiceless lips a honey-sweet voice.
And gazing on the corpse, grief-soothing Dionysus
raised a wailing voice, holding a mirthless look:
"Let the jealous thread of the Fates fall; do bulls themselves too
prove jealous over youths, like the winds?
What Zephyrus, after Phoebus, assailed Dionysus too?
Blessed was Phoebus's Atymnius; for from a youth
he won this name; and of a Therapnaean youth himself
Apollo lifts a flower named for the medicine of the youth,
inscribing the dirge upon the petals of the hyacinth;
what garland have I too for my locks, or what flowers
do I wield that are voiced, consolations of my boy's grief?
But avenging your death, dragging him to slaughter,
I will lead the wandering bull to your tomb, untimely one.
I would not kill your slayer with an ox-axe,
that he might win a doom equal, his brow battered,
to bulls being slaughtered; but I would tear open the whole
bitter belly of the bull with the point of my own horn,
because it cast you down with its long-horned spike.
Blessed is the Earth-shaker, since he loved a neighbour of the homeland
of my boy, a Phrygian youth, and bearing him
led him up to the golden house of Zeus, a citizen of Olympus,
and to him, when he hastened to the horsemanship of Aphrodite,
he gave the dry car, the bridal chariot of Hippodameia.
I alone have a young one untimely; for lovely
Ampelos saw no life-giving marriage, nor did this youth
yoke my bridal car upon the marriage-bed,
but dying he left grief to the once-griefless Dionysus.
Not yet, dear boy, has Persuasion left your mouth,
but even though you are dead it dwells on your breathless lips;
and though you are a corpse your cheeks still glisten,
your eyes still laugh, and the snowy palms
of your two hands are still there,
and the shrill breezes still stir your lovely locks;
the death-bearing season has not quenched the roses of your limbs,
but all these things are still kept for you. Alas for the Loves,
what need was there that you should drive an implacable bull?
If the longing for storm-footed horses dismayed you,
why did you not tell me, that from neighbouring Ida
I might bring a chariot here, and from the ancient stock
might bring to you the Trojan race of heavenly horses,
plundering the homeland of Ganymede, whom Ida reared
with a body equal to yours, whom from the man-slaying bulls
high-flying Zeus lifted with sparing talons;
if you truly longed to slay beasts in the mountains,
why did you not tell me that there was need of a car?
And then you would have driven the harmless circle of my chariot,
and, receiving the untouched reins of my Rhea,
unshaken, would have lashed the car of gentle serpents.
No longer do you sing the wine-song with the Satyrs,
no longer do you command the castanet-loving Bassarids,
no longer do you hunt together with Dionysus hunting.
Alas, that Hades is not gentle, nor over a corpse
does he receive the splendid gifts of the deep-rich metal,
that I might make Ampelos, who died, alive again;
alas, that Hades is never persuaded; but if he should wish it,
I would freely give him all the gleaming wealth of Eridanus,
plundering the river trees, and I would bring
the flashing, gleaming Erythraean stone of the Indians
and all the silver of wealthy Alybe, and in exchange for the corpse
of my boy I would give the whole golden Pactolus."
So speaking he lamented the sweet corpse; and seeing him
lying in the dust he cried again with a mournful voice:
"Father Zeus, if you love me, and if you know the toil of loves,
set Ampelos speaking again for one hour,
a last hour and only, that he may utter one word:
'Why do you grieve, Dionysus, the one you do not raise with groanings?
I have ears, and I do not hear you crying out,
I have eyes, and I do not see you grieving;
grief-soothing Dionysus, do not shed tears for me,
but leave off your grief, since beside the murderous spring
the Naiads groan and Narcissus does not hear,
Phaethon does not know the mournful grief of the Heliades.'
Alas, that my father did not beget me a mortal, that I might be
a companion of the youth even in Hades, nor in Lethe
leave lovely Ampelos, fallen, alone.
In longing for a youth, Apollo is more blessed,
holding the beloved name of his boy; would that I too
were Ampeloeis, as Apollo is Hyacinthius.
How long do you sleep, and no longer, boy, do you dance?
Why today do you no longer go to the streams of the river
holding a fine-watered pitcher? In the mountain-stalled thicket
your season has come again for the accustomed dance.
If you are angry, dear boy, with love-stricken Dionysus,
speak to the Sileni, that I may hear your word.
If a lion overpowered you, I will destroy them all,
all that the crag of Tmolus bears, nor will I ever spare
the lions of our own Rhea, but I will overpower them,
if your slayers were born with grim jaws;
if a leopard cast down your body, flower of the Loves,
no longer will I drive the spangled body of leopards;
there are other beasts, and Artemis, mistress of the whole hunt,
drives a horn-drawn car of deer;
wearing a fawnskin robe I will ride on a car of fawns;
if shameless boars slew you, seizing them in one
I will kill them all, and I will not leave one boar alone
still living, left to the Archer-goddess;
but if a wanton bull slew you, with a sharp thyrsus
I would utterly destroy the bovine race, root and branch."
So he lamented. But Love stood near him
bearing the form of a shaggy, horn-drawn Silenus,
holding a thyrsus, and fastening a dappled skin on his body
he propped his frame on an old man's fennel-staff;
and to wailing Bromius he cried a consoling voice:
"With another love loose the sparks of your loves,
changing your goad to a new youth, a fresh one,
forgetting the dead; for of an older love
the medicine is always a new love; for time
does not know how to destroy love, even if it learns to hide all things.
But if you wish the pain-killing remedy of your grief,
embrace a better boy; desire knows how to wither desire.
The Laconian youth troubled Zephyrus; but when he died,
lovely Aetes, seeing Cyparissus the youth,
found a consolation for Amyclaean Hyacinthus.
If you wish, ask the gardener; for when he sees
a dust-covered flower lying on the ground, the ploughman
plants another, newer, as a medicine for the perished one.
Listen, that I may tell you a tale of men of old:
there was once a soft boy, surpassing his coeval youth,
beside the flood of Maeander, the many-branched river,
tall in his delicate form, swift of foot, with hair
straight, downless; and on both his cheeks
a natural Grace was leaping upon his face
with modest eyes, and from his eyelids ever
a far-shooting radiance flowed as his beauty cast its darts;
and he had a body wholly like milk, and about the white
a rose flushed, half-seen, with a two-coloured glow.
Him his dear father called Calamus, who through the earth
billowing below, drawing his crooked stream into the light,
creeping unseen, a slanting traveller beneath the ground,
leaping up sharply lifts his neck above the earth,
inner-recessed Maeander, leading his bosom-hidden water.
Such was lovely Calamus the swift. And the youth,
rosy-armed, delighted in his lovely coeval Carpus,
who won so great a beauty as no mortal man has won;
for if this youth had been among the men of former times,
he would have become the bridegroom of fair-haired Dawn,
holding a fairer form, with rosy skin alone surpassing
the splendour of Cephalus and the look of Orion;
nor would Deo have embraced with fruitful palm
Iasion as bridegroom, nor Selene Endymion;
but that youth, perhaps, on account of his nobler form,
as one husband of both, would have wedded the beds of both goddesses,
sharing the much-furrowed bed of fair-haired Deo,
and holding jealous Mene as a common bedfellow.
Such was the lovely one, dear to Calamus, flower of the Loves,
holding beauty; and both coevals upon the bank
of the neighbouring much-winding river sported together.
For them there was a winding course of the double track, and for both
there was strife; Calamus ran on like the breezes,
and bearing the elm as starting-line and the olive as turning-post
he ran along the river's banks from end to end . . .
and swift-kneed Calamus willingly fell to the ground,
and left a willing victory to graceful Carpus.
And as the boy bathed, the playful youth bathed with him,
and again they held another like contest in the waters,
and slow he swam in the streams, leaving Carpus
to go ahead, that swimming behind, cleaving the swell with his hands,
he might come second beside the ankles of swimming Carpus,
