watching the free back of the youth running before.
And there was a course from the watery starting-line; both contended,
which would beat which, that he might come back returning
to the bank, crossing both ends of the twin turning-post,
to the land on the other side, with their palms rowing;
and the flood was his path; but ever coming near him
the boy, sparing the rush of his hurrying hand,
watched the rosy-skinned fingers of their swimming hands;
and Calamus, leading the way, reined back his rush,
and yielded to the youth; and he ran on rowing his hands,
the storm-like boy, stretching his neck above the swell;
and now Carpus would have mounted from the surge onto the land,
and after the victory on land would have gained the river victory,
but Aetes, blowing against him, dashed him down,
and the implacable one slew the sweet boy; for as the youth's
throat opened, numberless water rushed in.
And Calamus, fleeing the storms of the jealous wind,
sank, away from the youth, onto the neighbouring shores;
and perceiving his friend not present and not hearing,
groaning lovingly he bellowed with a mournful voice:
"Naiads, speak, what Aetes snatched away Carpus?
Yes, I beseech you, grant me a last favour, come to another
spring, and flee the death-bearing water of my father,
nor drink the stream that slew Carpus.
Surely my begetter did not slay the youth; but in envy
Aetes, after Phoebus, destroyed Carpus for Calamus too,
and perhaps, longing for him, struck him with a jealous storm,
bringing a contrary breeze upon the youth after the discus.
Not yet has my star risen, bathed in the streams,
not yet has my Morning Star shone; but with Carpus
sinking in the streams, why should I still look on the light?
Naiads, speak, who quenched the light of the Loves?
Do you still linger, boy? Why does the water please you so much?
Surely you have not found a better friend in the waters, with whom staying
you have cast the longings of wretched Calamus to the winds?
If one love-stricken Naiad-Nymph snatched you,
tell me, and I will arm against them all; but if the wedding hymn
of marriage with our sister of the Loves delights you,
tell me, and even in the streams I will light your bridal chamber.
Carpus, do you float past me, forgetting the accustomed bank?
I grew weary calling you, and you do not hear me crying out.
If Notus or bold Eurus blew, let him wander himself,
pitiless, danceless, wanton, an enemy of the Loves;
if Boreas overpowered you, I will go to Oreithyia.
But if a wave covered you and did not reverence your form,
and my father took you with the unsparing draught of the wave,
let him receive his own son too in the man-slaying waters,
and let him hide Calamus near perished Carpus.
But falling headlong, where wandering Carpus died,
I will quench my hot love, drinking the Acherousian water."
He spoke, gushing forth the stream of his eyes; and about the corpse
he cut his dark lock with mournful iron,
which he had grown, which he had tended, and held out the mourning hair
to his father Maeander, and spoke his last word:
"Receive, after my locks, my body too; for I cannot
look upon the light for one dawn apart from Carpus;
Carpus and Calamus have one life, and both have won
a like goad of Love upon the earth; and let one watery
death be for us both, even in the streams.
Make, Naiads, on the high river-bank
a common cenotaph for us both, and about the tomb
let a word be inscribed in mournful letters:
'I am the grave of Carpus and Calamus, whom of old, both
longing for each other, the implacable water slew.'
And for love-stricken Calamus, though he is a brother,
dying, tear off one small cluster of his hair,
but for perished Carpus shear all his locks."
He spoke, and self-tumbling slipped into the stream,
drinking the child-slaying water of his refusing father.
And Calamus gave to reeds the shape named for him,
of like growth, and Carpus grew the fruit of the field.
Such things consoling, with a friendly word
did impetuous Eros soothe, lightening the sweet sting for Dionysus.
And his heart was lashed all the more with mournful grief
through the untimely doom of the youth.—And the unsteady
daughters of Lycabas, the storm-footed father,
the rosy-faced Hours, went to the house of the Sun;
of whom one, sending around her snow-shaded face
a thin gleam of dark-clouded radiance,
joined her cold feet to a hailstorm sandal,
and binding her locks upon her wet head
fastened a rain-bearing veil upon her brow,
and held a green wreath on her head, and with a snowy
white girdle covered her frosted breast;
and another spat out the mortal-delighting breeze
of the swallow-winds, breathing, and of her Zephyr-loving head
she girt the springtime hair with a dewy bond,
laughing flowery, and quivering through her robe
the long-shadowed fragrance of the morning, opening rose,
she wove a double revel for Adonis and Cytherea;
another Hour, together with her sisters, came as the harvest-Hour,
and the ear of grain, bristling round about with topmost clusters,
she lifted in her right hand, and the blade of the sharp-cutting sickle,
the messenger of the harvest, and the girl's body was girt
with white linen, and as she whirled in the dance
through her thin raiment the mysteries of her thighs appeared,
and as her face was loosed, the moist sweats
were dampened on her cheeks by the hotter Phaethon;
and another, the leader of the well-ploughed dance,
bound an olive shoot on her hairless temple
drenched with the waters of the seven-channeled river Nile,
and tending the thin, withering hair of her temple
she had a parched body, since, being autumnal,
she had shorn her tree-like hair to the leaf-shedding winds;
for not yet, with the plaited clusters of golden tendrils,
did vine-clusters flow upon the neck of the nymph,
nor, made drunk beside the wine-loving wine-press,
did the moisture of the dew of purple Maronian wine intoxicate her,
nor did the wandering ivy run up in a whirl;
but then the appointed time came, for the sake of which the Hours themselves
ran together in company to the house of the Sun.

12. In the twelfth delight your heart, where as a new flower of the Loves
Ampelos sent up his form into the vine-clad fruit.
So they, beside the brows of western Ocean,
were sailing to the halls of the generative Sun.
And as they journeyed the star Hesperus met them,
leaping from the hall; and hastening forth herself,
newly appeared, rose Selene, driver of oxen.
And before the eyes of the life-bearing Charioteer
they bent their fruitful track. He, having just finished his course,
returned from the air; and the radiant Morning Star
set down, near the four-horse car of the fiery-eyed driver,
the hot harness and the starry whip,
cleansing beside the streams of neighbouring Ocean
the bodies of the fire-fed horses, dripping with sweat;
and the colts, shaking the wet manes of their necks,
stamped with gleaming hooves in the glowing manger.
And the daughters of Chronos, around the fiery throne,
flying in a circle about the unwearied Charioteer,
the twelve circling Hours greeted the four,
handmaids of the Sun, companions of the glowing car,
ministers of Lycabas in turn; for to the primeval
ruler of the whole universe they bent a slavish neck.
And the grape-tending Hour cried out a word to him,
holding the autumnal sickle as witness of her supplication:
"Sun, grain-giver, planter, lord of fruits,
when will the vineyards grow the wine-bearing cluster?
And to which of the blessed does Aion betroth this honour?
Yes, I beseech you, do not hide it, for I alone
of all my sisters am without honour; for I grow no fruit,
no ear of grain, no meadow, and not the rain of Zeus."
She spoke; and the Sun encouraged the nurse
of the fruit to be, and beside the opposite wall
raising his finger he showed the circling girl
the unequal tablets of Harmony, on which there lie
in one all the oracles, all that were ordained for the world
that the prophetic hand of first-born Phanes inscribed,
and embroidered with his pen the fitting house for each.
And Hyperion, the steward of fire, spoke a word:
"On the third tablet, whence the wine-fruit shall come,
you will learn, where the Lion and the Virgin are; and on the fourth,
who is the sceptred lord of the cluster, where, drawing sweet nectar,
with painted hand Ganymede lifts the cup."
As the god spoke thus, the vine-loving girl ran,
turning her eyes about, and beside the wall of the oracle
she beheld the first tablet, coeval with the endless world,
bearing in one all things, all that the sceptred Ophion
accomplished, all that aged Cronos achieved, when, cutting
his father's male plough-share, he ploughed the bridal water,
sowing the unsown back of the daughter-bearing sea,
who once received his stone son in his gaping throat,
feasting on the counterfeit body of the lying Zeus;
and the stone delivered the brood of the children hidden within,
casting forth the burden of the pregnant throat.
But when the storm-footed Hour, the handmaid of Phaethon,
beheld the fire-bright victory of Zeus as he fought
and the hailing war-strife of the Cronian snow,
she looked in turn at the neighbouring tablet; and that one held
how the pine bore mortal offspring in travail, or whence suddenly,
unfolding its tree-like, generative childbearing,
the pine cast up an unsown, self-made son,
and whence rain-bringing Zeus flooded all the cities,
bringing the heaped-up water in towering seas,
how Notus from Boreas, and Eurus from Libs scourging,
lifted the wandering ark of Deucalion, neighbour of the Moon,
into an air-walking voyage, without a harbour.
And when the minister of Lycabas ran over the third tablet
with well-footed sole, the coiling girl halted,
gazing at the fated, many-turning oracles of the world,
reddening letters, inscribed with wise vermilion,
all that the various-storied, primeval mind had written,
such things prophesying, and she read on the tablets:
Argus, herdsman of Hera, will change into the shape of a bird,
keeping the bright form of his grim eyelids; but also
Harpalyce herself, after the bed of sinful unions,
having butchered her son for her daughter-wedding father,
will row her airy, winged journey
as a storm-like bird; and the web-toiling Philomela
will be a swallow with a spangled neck, twittering,
crying out the testimony of her tongueless silence,
having written speaking devices on a wise tunic;
and Niobe, beside the foot of Sipylus, a stone with sense,
lamenting with stony tears the rank of her children,
will stand as a piteous statue. And there will be a neighbour,
Pyrrhus, a Phrygian stone, love-maddened, still holding for Rhea
a lawless goad of unwedded unions,
and Thisbe a moist water, and Pyramus, both coevals,
longing for each other; and of the fair-crowned girl
Smilax, Crocus, longing, will be a flower of the Loves;
and after the bridal turning-post of the storm-footed weddings
and after the apples of the Paphian, into the shape of a lion
Artemis will goad transformed Atalanta.
And the restless Hour passed over all these things in one,
until she came to the place where fiery Hyperion
declared the symbols of prophecy to the storm-like girl,
where the Lion was wrought, radiant, where also
the starry Virgin herself was embroidered in a counterfeit shape
holding the wine-dark cluster, the summer-born flower of the fruit;
there the daughter of Chronos rested her feet, and read this:
Cissos, the high-flying, lovely youth, creeping into a plant,
will be the coiling ivy even among shoots; and of the youth
Calamus the upright reed, bent by the breezes,
will appear a thin shoot of the growth-giving field,
a prop of the vines; and changing his form into a plant,
Ampelos gives his name to the vine-clad fruit.
But when the harvest-girl beheld these oracles,
she sought that place, where beside the neighbouring wall
the image of Ganymede was inscribed with a fashioned form,
dripping the nectar-moisture from a golden cup,
where was the four-fold voice of the inscribed words;
there the grape-loving goddess reveled, and the nymph found
these oracles kept for ivy-bearing Lyaeus:
Zeus granted to Phoebus to have the prophetic laurel,
and reddening roses to rosy-skinned Cyprogeneia,
the grey-green olive-shoot to grey-eyed Athena,
and ears of grain to Demeter, and the vines to Dionysus.
Such things did the Bacchus-loving girl behold in the writings;
and rejoicing she darted off, and taking her sisters
she passed into the stream of eastern Ocean,
running together with the horsemanship of Phaethon.—But for Lyaeus
there was no remedy, with his comrade fallen, nor was there
memory of the dance; but with his mind shaken by the goad of love
he sang bitter dirges, and in careless silence
he left the bronze back of the unsounding ox-hide;
nor did the lyre delight him. And as, with mirthless face,
loving Dionysus piteously wailed,
the stream of the Lydian, reedy Hermus was stayed,
though it rolled swiftly with the windy beat of its current,
and longed not to flow; and with its deep-rich stream
saffron Pactolus reined back its mournful water,
bearing the likeness of a downcast man; and about the corpse
Sangarius checked the back-rushing draught of its spring channels,
pouring its Phrygian stream; and the breathless image
of the Tantalid, ill-bearing mother, drenched by the groanings,
shed double tears, as Dionysus lamented;
and the pine, wailing, companion of its coeval fir,
whispered faintly; and the laurel herself,
being the tree of unshorn Phoebus, shook off her hair
in the mournful winds; and the sleek, unpruned olive
poured its leaves to the ground, even though it was Athena's plant.
So, as tearless Dionysus groaned with longing,
the dread, unbound threads of the Fate were turned again;
and consoling the wail of grieving Dionysus
steadfast-worded Atropos cast up an inspired voice:
"Your youth lives, Dionysus, and he will not cross
the bitter water of Acheron; for your wail has found a way to undo
the unbending, recoverable threads of unswerving Fate;
Ampelos has not died, even though he died; for into a lovely
drink, into sweet nectar, I will change your boy;
him, with the dancing beat of the well-rolling hand,
the double-noted pipe, beating out the harmony of the feast,
will hymn, holding a Phrygian rhythm or a Dorian song;
or in the theatres a rhythmic man will sing of him,
pouring the Ismenian echo of the Aonian reed,
or to the dwellers of Marathon; and the Mysians will cry "Euoi"
for lovely Ampelos along with vine-clad Lyaeus.
And leaving the crooked, serpent girdle of your locks
you will wreathe clusters of grapes about your hair,
bringing envy to Phoebus, because he wields with his hand the mournful
tree-borne dirges of the weeping hyacinths,
while you have a drink, the rest of the mortal race,
the earthly likeness of heavenly nectar, and your flowery youth
will put to shame the boast of the Amyclaean boy;
and if that one's city raises warlike bronze,
your youth's land too will grow, light-bringing,
the moist rain of the reddening river-dew,
luxuriant wholly with gold, and rejoicing not in iron;
if it glories about the stream of a sounding river,
the Pactolian water is better than the Eurotas.
Ampelos, you gave grief to griefless Dionysus,
that, when your honey-dropping wine is grown,
you might give delight to the whole four-fold world
and a libation to the blessed and gladness to Dionysus;
lord Bacchus wept, that he might loose the tears of mortals."
So speaking the goddess went, companion of her sisters.
And a great wonder appeared to mournful Bacchus, the witness;
for the lovely corpse, springing up like a creeping serpent,
Ampelos, self-made, changed his own shape,
and became a sweet flower; and as the corpse was transformed
his belly was a tall bush, and the tips of his hands
put forth branches, and his feet were rooted,
his curls were grape-clusters, and the very fawnskin
was shaped into a many-figured flower of the growing fruit,
and the vine-cluster was his long-shadowed neck,
and like to his elbow the crooked tendril stretched,
swelling with grapes, and as his head was transformed
the bent, curved clusters mimicked the shape of his horn.
There were endless rows of plants; and self-made
the vine-clad row, coiling its green tendrils,
girt the neighbouring trees with the new wine-dark fruit.
And there was a new wonder, since the boy at play then,
coiling his slanting foot about a high-leaved plant,
high-flying Cissos made his form into a tree,
and became a curved shoot named for him, and girt
the newly grown row of vines with a crooked bond.
And with friendly leaves he shaded the overshadowed temple,
and intoxicated his locks from the wine-loving leaves,
Dionysus exulting; and of the growing boy
he plucked the fruit of the harvest just now ripening.
And the god, self-taught, without foot, outside the wine-press,
pressing the cluster with the heavy fruit of his palm,
squeezing the travail of drunkenness with entwining hands,
revealed the new-flowing mass of the purple fruit,
and found the sweet drink; the white fingers of wine-pouring
Dionysus reddened as they were drenched.
And he held a curved cup, the horn of an ox; and of the sweet-drinking
dew Bacchus tasted with the tips of his lips,
tasted also of the fruit, and delighting his heart with both
he cast up a word from his proud throat:
"Ambrosia and the nectar of my Zeus, Ampelos, you bring forth;
bearing two beloved shoots, the fruit, Apollo
ate not of the laurel, and drank not from the hyacinth;
no ear of grain travails a sweet drink; be gracious, Deo;
I will give to mortals food, and not only drink.
Ampelos, your doom too is lovely; truly the threads
of Fate herself were softened for you and for your beauty,
for you even Hades was pitying, for you even Persephone
herself changed her harsh purpose,
and brought you, a corpse, to life for your brother Dionysus.
You did not die as Atymnius died; not the water of Styx,
not the flame of Tisiphone, you did not see the eye of Megaera;
you still live, boy, even though you died; nor did the water
of Lethe hide you, no common tomb holds you; but the earth
herself was ashamed to cover your form;
but my father made you a plant, honouring you as a son,
lord Cronion changed your body into sweet nectar.
Nature did not, as on the inscribed Therapnaean clusters,
carve a dirge upon your unweeping leaves;
you keep your own colour, boy, even among shoots;
your end has proclaimed the radiance of your limbs;
your reddening form has not yet abandoned you.
But avenging your death I will never cease
pouring your wine as a libation upon your slayer
as he is sacrificed, the man-slaying one. And you bring reproach to the Hamadryads
with your lovely leaves; and from your fragrant clusters
the moistures of your Loves breathe about me.
When shall I mingle the fruit of the apple in the bowl?
When shall I drop the fig into the nectar-cup?
The fig and the apple alike have grace as far as the teeth.
No other plant can contend with your grape-clusters;
not the rose, not the fair-coloured narcissus, not the anemone,
not the lily, not the hyacinth equals the shoot of Bacchus,
because with the new drops of much-pressed fruit
your drink will receive all the flowers; one drink will be
mingled with all, and will come to one fragrance,
blended with flowers of every kind; for your flower
will adorn the whole springtime meadow-grass.
Yield to me, famed-archer, because you girt your griefless locks
with a mournful bond of many-wailing leaves;
dirges are inscribed upon your petals; but if in a garden
the famed-archer bears a garland, I draw sweet wine,
and put about myself a lovely garland, and the sweet-drinking
Ampelos himself I lift wholly within my heart.
Yield to the grape-rich one, glittering-helmed; for bloody Ares
pours gore as a libation, while the vine-clad one pours to Dionysus
the reddening dew of the wine-drenched cluster.
Deo, you are plundered after Pallas; for the olives
bring forth no gladness, and no ear of grain charms a man,
the pear has honey-sweet fruit, the myrtle grows
fragrant flowers, but they do not, with a mind-charming fruit,
cast human cares to the winds;
I have become far better than you both; for when our
wine is not present, joyless are the meals of the table,
when wine is not present, uncharmed are the dances.
If you can, grey-eyed one, drink the fruit of your olive;
my splendid-gifted harvest has conquered your plant,
because with your sleek oil athlete-men, joyless,
anoint their bodies; but the sorely-suffering man,
having cast wife or daughter into a common doom,
or having grief for perished children or mother or father,
when he tastes sweet wine,
will shake off the gloomy, swelling mass of his grief.
Ampelos, even after death you gladden the heart of Bacchus;
with all my limbs I will mingle your drink."
And all about, the trees with downward-nodding head,
like a suppliant, bend the curving neck,
and the aged palm bowed down its high-stretched leaves;
about the apple-tree you stretch your feet, about the fig-tree
spreading your hands you lean upon them, and your
harvest the handmaids lighten, as a mistress,
when, with the coiling beat of your stretching leaves,
you rise above the shoulder of the attendants; and of the neighbouring plants
the soft, many-coloured leaves of the wide-scattered clusters,
as though you slept, quiver upon your face,
cooling breezes with sparing breaths,
as an attendant shakes a thin, accustomed fan,
bearing an artificial breeze, cool, for her king.
But if you bring the noonday threat of Phaethon,
the Etesian breeze, leading the way for your cluster, comes,
lulling to rest the thirsty star of fiery Maira,
when the course of the summer-born Hour heats you,
warming with Sirian vapour the dew as it ripens.
He spoke, exulting, and cast away his former cares,
holding the fragrant harvest, the medicine for the youth.
And these things are sung about the vine-clad cluster,
how it became named for the youth. But of the singers
there is another, older story, how once upon the earth
from heaven the fruit-bearing Olympian ichor flowed
and brought forth the drink of the Bacchic cluster, and on the crags
self-grown, untended, the fruit of the harvest grew;
and not yet was the vine named for the gardener, but in the thickets
the wild vine, flourishing among the much-curved parsley-plants,
put forth a vine-rich wood of wine-bearing plants,
gushing up the moist, crammed mass of its dew;
and there was a great row, where, creeping up in order,
cluster upon cluster, reddening, shook as it wandered;
of which one, half-finished, swelling its travail,
flushing in changing hues, appeared with two-coloured fruit;
another, whitening, ripened, of a colour like foam,
and a great one, golden-formed, pushed its yoked
neighbour, neighbour against neighbour, and another in form was like pitch,
darkening its whole flower, and from its wine-bearing leaves
it intoxicated the whole splendid-fruited olive growing near it;
and over another, just-carved, with unripe fruit,
the self-rushing black air ran upon the silvery cluster,
bearing, in its cluster-laden mass, the swelling harvest;
and the coiling tendril of the harvest crowned the opposite pine,
shading the enveloping shoot with combined thickets,
and delighted the heart of Pan; and bringing its branches,
shaken by Boreas, near the vine-clad cluster,
the blood-dipped pine waved its fragrant hair.
And about it a serpent, coiled with crooked spines,
milked the dainty nectar of the well-dropping fruit,
and milking the Bacchic drink with grim jaws,
dropping into its throat the draught of the wine-drenched cluster,
the serpent reddened its chin with a purple drop.
And the mountain-roaming god marvelled, watching the snake
with its throat stained with the wine-coloured drop;
and coiling its dappled, turning track of scales,
it entered the neighbouring deep-bosomed crevice in the rock,
the spangled snake, having beheld the Bacchic juice. And gazing,
Bacchus marked the cluster pregnant with the reddening dew,
and recalled the older oracles of oracular Rhea.
And he dug into the crags, and with the sharp point
of his earth-digging iron he hollowed a recess in the rock;
and smoothing the brows of the deepening hollows
he made the trench into the shape of a fine-grape wine-press,
reaping the fresh-budding clusters with a sharp thyrsus,
making the likeness of the later-born curved-clawed sickle.
And there was a band of Satyrs, his companions; of whom one
leaned, gathering the vintage, another received the clusters
cut, in a hollow vessel, another, cutting the tangled leaves,
shook off the green refuse of the wine-loving fruit;
another, without thyrsus and without well-sharpened iron,
stretching his ironless right hand to the branches,
broke off the tips of the coiling cluster,
crouching, bent over, stretching his eye toward the vine;
and in a deep hollow he spread the heaped harvest,
heaping the centre-naveled back of the ravine with grapes . . .
he laid the coiling clusters one upon another in the hollow,
stretched out this way and that, and as he heaped up vintage-piles
filling the whole hollow he gathered them in the cavernous rock,
and trod the cluster with the dancing beat of his feet.
And the Satyrs, shaking their wild hair into the air,
learning the like mimicry of Dionysus,
binding dappled fawnskins about their shoulders,
shouted the song of the Bacchic, fellow-tongued echo,
with much-leaping feet pressing the harvest,
singing "Euoi"; and from the grape-rich hollow
as the wine gushed up the ravines grew purple;
and the harvest, pressed by alternating feet,
cast up the white foam of the reddening dew.
And they drew with bovine horns instead of cups,
not yet appearing, whence afterward, ever from that time,
this wondrous name belonged to the wine being mingled.
And one, gushing up the moisture of mind-charming Bacchus,
bent his crooked track of feet with a coiling beat,
shifting his right sole, changing from the left,
and wetted his shaggy beard with the moisture of Bacchus;
another leapt up, shaken by the goad of drunkenness,
hearing the fearful bellow of the struck ox-hide;
and one, drinking the irresistible stream of pain-healing wine,
reddened his dark chin with the rosy draught;
another, stretching his unsteady gaze up toward a tree,
watched the half-revealed, unfilleted neighbour Nymph,
and now into the high-leaved plant of the mountain wood
he would have crept with the curved-clawed sole of his slipping foot,
had Dionysus not restrained him; and about the springs
another, with a wandering beat of mind-rousing drunkenness,
pursued the watery, unrobed Naiad girl,
and now he would have embraced her as she swam with his shaggy arm,
had she not, anticipating him, hidden in the deep stream.
But to the wine-drinker Dionysus alone Rhea gave
the amethyst, the warder-off of raving compulsion.
And many of the fair-horned Satyrs, with sport-loving sole,
goaded into the dance, reveled; of whom one,
holding a hot, new goad beneath his heart, the escort of the Loves,
clasped a Bacchante about the middle with his hairy arm;
another, shaken by the goad of mind-wandering drunkenness,
touched the girdle of an unmarried, chaste maiden,
dragging back to Cypris the garments of the unyielding nymph,
and with a back-cast hand touched her rosy thighs;
and one reined back an unwilling initiate girl
lighting the night-dancing torch kindled for Dionysus;
another, casting his sparing fingers about her breast,
squeezed the swelling circle of her unbending bosom.
And after the revel of his sweet harvest, Dionysus,
exulting, entered the caves of the Cybelean goddess,
stretching the cluster-laden branches with flower-loving hand,
and taught his own Maeonia his sleepless festival.

15. In the fifteenth I sing of mighty Nicaea,
the rosy-armed beast-slayer who threatened the Loves.
So he spoke, and cloud-like the swarthy Indians flowed in
about the honey-breathing stream of the river; of whom one,
stepping close, planting his double step firm on the mud,
stood half-seen, wetting his navel in the water,
bent, stretching his stooped back into the river,
with hands hollowed deep he drew up the honey-dropping water;
and another by the outflow, gripped by burning thirst,
dipping his jutting beard in the purple wave,
spreading his breast from above on the river bank,
with open mouth drew up the moisture of Bacchus;
and another lay face down, bringing his mouth to the neighbouring spring,
and resting his wet hands on the sandy floor
with thirsty lips received the thirst-quenching water;
others drew the drunkenness with an earthen cup,
lifting the base of a broken jar;
and a great swarm drank from the reddening stream,
pouring with a wooden bowl the mass of the river's dew,
holding the rustic cup of sheep-tending men. And as the foes
belched up the wine from their capacious throats,
to their seeing eyes the crags were doubled,
and to their eyelids the water seemed twin-yoked.
And the outflow of the unmixed-wine-loving river gurgled,
spouting up the yellow stream of drunkenness; and of the sweet-drinking
wine the fragrant banks belched the streams.
And the strong-wine flood made the foes drunk. There a man,
an Indian, shaken by the frenzy of mind-stealing drink,
darted into the herd, and by the well-leaved thicket
led off a threatening bull, dragging it bound,
gripping the scored tip of its twin horns
with daring hands, as though by the twin horn
dragging bull-shaped Dionysus under a slavish yoke;
another, holding the dread jaw of an iron sickle,
cut through the throat of a mountain-grazing goat,
mangled by the whetted reaping-hook, as though cutting
the neck of well-horned Pan with hook-clawed bronze;
another destroyed the horn-drawn race of oxen,
as though mowing down the bull-faced shape of the Satyrs,
and one chased the race of long-horned deer,
gazing at the dappled, much-embroidered look of their hide,
as though destroying the line of the Bassarids; for by the cunning
fawnskins of like pattern his eyes were led astray;
and staining his whole corslet with murderous drops
the black Indian spearman reddened with gore.
And one, shouting, armed himself against a neighbouring tree,
lashing it on either side, and seeing in the spring
the coiling foliage of plants shaken by the winds
he destroyed the soft-haired shoots of the clusters,
splitting the leaves of the shaggy oak, as though with a sword
cutting through the lock of unshorn Dionysus,
fighting with leaves and not striving with Satyrs,
holding a useless delight in a shadowy victory.
And another band of the foes raved; and instead of a spear
one, taking up the deep-sounding timbrel by its shoulder-strap,
lifted it high, and with the double-beaten oxhide
struck up a bronze-clashing, twin-yoked echo of song;
and one, shaken by the cry of the many-holed flute,
danced unsteady with the coiling beat of his feet;
and one, setting the lotus-pipe to untried lips,
made the two-voiced harmony of the Mygdonian flute;
and one, leaping by the neighbouring root of an aged plant,
drew up the grey shoot of the well-dropping olive,
soaked with dewy rain, as though squeezing
with a wine-coloured drop the tip of his Maronian beard.
Others with swords, with spears, with helmets,
irresistibly raving, their minds undone by mind-stealing wine,
mimicked the rites of the shield-bearing Corybantes,
whirling their steps in an armed dance;
and with answering sweeps of their hands, coiling,
the shields were beaten with tumbling iron;
another, watching the rites of the revel-loving Muse,
leapt with the Satyrs in a mimic dance;
and one, hearing the din of the beaten oxhide,
took on a gentle temper, and with din-loving purpose
threw to the winds his dread quiver,
holding frenzy; and another, a woman-mad Indian chief,
seizing a high-necked Bacchant by her unbound lock,
dragging the untamed maiden recklessly to wedlock,
bound her over the ground, and stretching her in the dust
with love-mad hands unsealed her girdle,
borne on by a vain hope; for suddenly
an upright serpent crept hidden in her bosom, near her loins,
and darted at the foe's neck, and about his throat
with its tail-coils wove a round girdle;
and the dark-skinned man, fleeing with frightened feet,
shook off the hot goad of unwedded Loves,
wearing about his neck the snaky chain of the thorn.
While the wine-flushed Indians ran upon the mountains,
so long sweet Sleep, coiling his close wing,
fell upon the unbending, faltering eyes of the Indians,
and lulled them, their minds stung by measureless wine,
doing a favour to Dionysus, father of Pasithea;
of whom one slept face up with head bent back,
drawing wine-tottering breath through his sleepy nostril,
and one laid his heavy head on a stone,
sluggish, lying on the pebbled river bank,
and conversed with mind-wandering daytime dreams,
setting his stiff fingers upright about his temples;
and another lay stretched face down, and had both
hands let down, drawn equal along his twin thighs;
and one rested his head on the wrist of his own hand,
belching up wine; and another, bending his curved limbs
like a coiling snake, lay sleeping aslant.
And the band of foes, carried to the ridge of the wood,
one slept under an oak, another under an elm bush,
another, falling on his side, leaned against a holm-oak,
throwing his left hand on his frowning brow;
and a great swarm slept, a babbling corpse, sending to the air
the unbridled, meaningless din of a different echo,
wine-heavy; and another, with nodding head,
leaned his broad back on the trunk of an aged laurel;
and as he slumbered heavy on a deep-spread bed
of high-crested palm or well-flowering olive
a coiling shoot, fanned by the winds, whistled over him;
and one was stretched over the ground in the loose dust,
drenching his feet's ends in the river's outflow;
another raved with the beat of untried drunkenness,
and rested his heavy head on a neighbouring pine;
and the brow-sinews of another, snorting, were shaken.
And seeing the foes asleep, with laughing face
lord Bacchus spoke, pouring out a commanding voice:
"Indian-slaying servants of unconquered Dionysus,
binding the assembled sons of the Indians without battle
take them all alive in bloodless warfare;
and bending a slavish knee to mighty Dionysus
let the Indian serve my revel-loving Rhea,
shaking the wine-dark thyrsus, and casting to the storms
the silver greave let him bind his feet in buskins,
and crown his head with my ivy bond,
stripping the locks of his crest-lifting helmet,
and leaving the war-cry and the spear's echo
let him sing the euion to cluster-bearing Dionysus."
So he spoke, and the servants busied themselves; of whom one
coiling a snaky bond about the foes' necks
dragged a man fettered with a serpent-rope,
another, taking the slackened pull of a shaggy beard,
dragged a man up by his deep-flowing throat;
and one, stretching out his hands to the crook-haired temple,
dragged a spear-won man unbound by the hair;
another, fastening his folded hands behind the back,
wreathed the foe with a coiling bond of withies
about the neck; and with trembling beat Maron tottered,
lifting an Indian weighed down on his aged shoulder;
another, taking a spearman overcome by sleep,
dragging his neck wound about with a cluster-bond,
set him over the rim of the dappled leopard cars;
and over another lying down the euion-loving wandering swarm
bound his back-strained hands with an unbreakable bond,
and mounted the necks of the stiff-footed elephants;
and one, taking the strap of a well-rounded oxhide,
held an Indian fettered with a shoulder-thong.
And one, a Bassarid, lifting up a shepherd's crook,
foaming with the mind-soothing wave of frenzy,
an Indian explorer of the deep-rich sea
with daring hand dragged by his much-bending hair
to a slavish yoke. And as Lyaeus pressed on,
iron Erechtheus held a well-armoured foe
on his unbending shoulders; and the wine-tottering bearer's
black-skinned beast a mountain Bacchant drove,
lashing the haunches of the spear-won elephants;
and Hymenaeus lifted up a golden oxhide,
despoiling a man of his golden shield, and gladly
Bacchus looked on the youth with love-mad eyes,
shining bright in the armour of the sleeping bearer;
and the young man hurled a rich radiance in the gear,
as taking the arms of Lycian Glaucus Diomedes
flashed before the warriors, glittering with the rich shield.
And the army of the Bacchae plundered the other foes,
holding sweet sleep, companion of pleasant wine.
There a maiden, curved-bow archer, companion of the lonely wood,
reared with the Astacid Nymphs, bloomed in beauty,
fair-grown Nicaea, another hare-shooting Artemis,
a stranger to love, untried in Cytherea,
shooting beasts and tracking them over the hills;
nor was she hidden in the fragrant recess of a maiden's chamber.
And on the crags, beside the desert-roaming foot of the hills,
her bow was her distaff, and ever within the thicket
her long spinning-threads were winged arrows,
and the upright wood of her hunting-stakes the loom of mountain Athena;
and she kept company with the pure Arrow-pourer as fellow-toiler,
and on the crags she wove the net of her accustomed hunting,
dearer than the wrought thread; never with her bow
did she touch a feeble fawn of dappled form,
nor did she chase gazelles, nor lay hand on a hare,
but harnessing with a bloody bridle
she lashed the grey backs of shaggy-breasted lions,
and often she raised a spear against a raging she-bear;
and she blamed the far-shooting Arrow-pourer, that, leaving
the race of dappled leopards and the tribes of lions,
she yoked her car to worthless deer.
Nor did she care for perfume, but before honey-mixed cups
she preferred the watery drink of a ravine-spring,
pouring out cold water; and in the self-roofed hollow
was the maiden's hard-to-enter home, the desert crags;
and often, after the course of the easy, accustomed hunt,
she sat near the leopards, and under a single hollow rock
she stayed at noon, beside a lioness newly delivered;
and the gentle beast, under its calm brows,
licked the maiden's body with unrending jaws,
and like a whimpering dog with timid throat
it whined gently from the eager mouth of the raw-bearing lioness,
with sparing lip, and deeming her to be Artemis
the lion, lowering its suppliant head to the ground,
leaned against the maiden with its shaggy neck.
And in the woods a mountain-reared herdsman bloomed,
upright, of great stature, taller than youths of his own age;
his name was Hymnus, who in the midst of the wild wood
pastured his lovely cattle beside the neighbouring girl;
and shaking the herdsman's crook in his lovely hands
he came into deep love and no longer delighted in his flock,
like rosy Anchises, whom once Cypris
pastured his white line of mountain-grazing bulls,
lightening the cattle-driving girdle; and about the thicket
the herdsman, seeing the snowy girl hunting,
cared nothing for his herd of cattle; and wandering
of her own accord the lonely heifer grazed into the marsh,
strayed far from her old love-sick herdsman,
and the calf was carried about, leaping over the hills,
seeking the shepherd; and the young herdsman wandered
gazing at the rosy circle of the maiden's face.
And cunning Eros stirred the longing herdsman,
shaken by a more violent goad; for on the crags
as the maiden sped on the unapproachable course of the hunt
a light breeze swelled her whole robe into the air;
and the beauty of her flesh bloomed; her thighs gleamed white
and her ankles reddened, and like a lily, like an anemone
the rosy meadow of her snowy limbs shone forth;
and the young man, walking in longing with insatiate gaze,
watched the free rim of her uncovered thighs
The cluster of her back-streaming hair the breeze tossed,
lightening it on either side, and as her locks lifted
her bare middle neck flashed white-shining.
And the young mountain-roamer often went beside the girl,
now touching the hunting-stakes or handling the bow,
now, as the love-stricken arrow was drawn,
he watched the lovely girl's rosy-skinned fingers;
if ever, as she shot, she rounded the horn against the string,
and her hand was bared, the young man, unnoticed, with sidelong eye
watched the white archer-arm of the girl,
turning back his eye, the conduit of the Loves,
whether so great, like Nicaea, was white-armed Hera;
and to the western verge he stretched his gaze,
whether more silvery was the maiden, or Selene.
And the young man, tending the wound of the Loves beneath his heart,
near her and far from her thought of the girl,
how she drew her shaft to the mark against a mountain bear,
how she fastened her hand to a lion's neck,
curving her twin arm in a witnessing bond,
how again, sweating, she bathed in a spring's stream,
half-seen, and ever more he remembered her robe,
when, shaking it and lifting it as far as her navel,
baring the bloom of her flesh, the breeze hurled it up;
keeping that in mind he prayed to the sweet gusts
to lift again her deep-folded tunic.
And the unsteady young man, beside the well-horned flock,
seeing the neighbouring high-necked girl hunting
let fly such a word with envious voice:
"Would that I were an arrow, or a net, or a quiver,
would that I were a beast-slaying shaft, that with bare
hands she might lift me; and of her back-strained bow
I would far rather be the ox-sinew, that to her snowy
breast she might bring me, outside her chaste girdle—
yes, heifer, yes, calf, outside her chaste girdle.
Maiden, you lift a blessed shaft; and your
arrows are happier than shepherd Hymnus,
because they touch your love-bearing hands.
I envy your sweet, voiceless hunting-stakes;
nor does the longing for the stakes alone carry me; but I have
envy of the very bow and the breathless quiver.
Would that, resting at noon by a love-stricken spring,
she might cool her limbs, that I might see the high-necked girl—
yes, heifer, yes, calf, free of the envious tunic.
Have you not yet, Cytherea, pitied so great a constraint?
I know not Thrinacia nor the horn-drawn flock,
I pasture no cattle of Helios on these mountains,
my father told of no secret bed of Ares.
Maiden, do not chase me, even if I lead cattle to pasture;
herdsmen too have mounted heavenly beds:
rosy Tithonus was a bridegroom, whom for his beauty
light-bringing Dawn, halting her car, snatched away;
and the cup-bearer of Zeus was a herdsman, whom for his beauty
high-flying Zeus lifted up in sparing talons.
Come, pasture cattle, and I will call you a younger Selene,
with another cowherd, with Endymion;
throw your shaft and touch your crook, that one may say:
'Cytherea pastures the cattle of shepherd Hymnus.'"
So he spoke and entreated, and grasped her dear knees
with woman-mad hands, and followed her, and to tell her
he trembled at the goad of Eros, and blamed himself in his silence.
And once, taking courage, the underworker of bridal Loves,
he lifted up the hunting-gear of Nicaea lying there,
and raised the fierce spear, and under a greater goad of desire,
while the girl was angry, lifted her sweet quiver,
and kissed the silent nets and the breathless arrows,
setting the murderous shaft to his delighting lips,
and pressed it to his breast, squeezing with unsparing hand;
and he spoke a word in some soundless voice:
"By Paphia, speak again, oaks, as in Pyrrha's day,
as in Deucalion's, rebuke the raging girl.
Laurel, dear one, you too break a tree-voice;
would that fair Nicaea had lived before, and then Apollo
would have chased a more delicate maiden, and Daphne would not have become a tree."
So he spoke; and on his pipe, near the chaste girl,
witness of his pain, he made a bridal song.
And the maiden spoke, laughing at the herdsman:
"Sweet is your Pan, piping Paphia's song;
often he sang of love and was no bridegroom of Echo.
Ah, how much Daphnis the cowherd sang; and at his song
the maiden hid herself the more in untrodden crags,
fleeing the song of the shepherd's cry. Ah, how much of Phoebus
Daphne heard singing, and her heart was not charmed."
So speaking she showed the fierce spear to the foolish herdsman.
But he, struck by the raging sweet goad,
not knowing that the Amazon was so loveless,
let fly an ill-loving voice, herald of his own death:
"Yes, I beg you, send the dear spear, and with your snowy
hand kill me, and I rejoice; not your lance,
I do not fear, bed-shunner, your sword, because it would grant
a sharpest end, that I may at last escape the bitter,
fixed wound of Eros, the fire feeding under my heart.
Let me die, since the doom is lovely; but if with a shaft,
bow-bearer next after Cypris, you too will shoot me,
by Paphia, do not send it at my neck, but fix
your shaft in my heart, where the shaft of the Loves is.
Rather throw your spear at my neck, do not strike my heart;
I want no other wound. But if it pleases you,
I will endure another shaft, that earth may cover me
both holding the wound of fire and pierced by iron.
Kill me, the love-sick one, do not spare your string.
You unman the iron whenever you touch your arrows;
of my own accord I stand a mark, with delighted eye
watching the fingers glittering about the notches,
drawing out again your honey-sweet string,
brought near your rosy right breast.
I die, a willing corpse of Eros, by a sweet doom;
I care nothing for death and do not fear the cloud of shafts,
watching your bare snowy hand
touching the bow and the lovely arrow.
Against me let fly all the shafts of your quiver,
against me send the murderous shafts; for more bitter
are the other fire-pointed arrows that harry me.
But if you kill me with your heart-charming bow,
maiden, do not burn my body with the accustomed pyre;
I want no other burning; but you, girl,
only pour sweet dust over me when I am dead
with your own hand, a last small grace, that one may say:
'The maiden pitied as she killed the man she slew.' And of the dead
let no flute of mine, no harp lie about my tomb,
do not throw down the shepherd's crook, witness of my craft;
but fix your shaft of the slain one high over my tomb,
still bathed in the gore of my love-sickness.
And grant me one last other grace high over my tomb:
let the flowers of love-stricken Narcissus arise,
or lovely crocus or the bindweed flower of the Loves,
and plant the springtime short-lived anemone
proclaiming to all my short-lived youth.
And if no pitiless sea or hills bore you,
shed a little tear for me, only so much as with dews
to wet the rosy tips of your lovely cheek,
and with your hand carve this word in mournful red:
'Here lies the cowherd Hymnus, whom, denied his bed,
the maiden Nicaea killed and gave burial to when dead.'"
So he spoke, and Nicaea was angered; and raging
she bared the deadly lid of the venom-shooting quiver
and drew out a straight-coursing shaft, and stretching it out
she rounded the curved horn of the back-strained bow,
and the windy shaft against the herdsman's throat
as he spoke she let fly, and the irresistible wandering shaft
while he still poured out his speech sealed it with a bond in his throat.
But the corpse was not tearless then; for blaming
man-slaying Nicaea the mountain Nymph grieved,
mourning the dead Hymnus; and in her well-watered hall
the Rhyndacid girl, water-borne, unsandalled, lamented;
and the Naiads wept; and above Sipylus the neighbouring
rock of Niobe lamented more with self-poured tears.
And a younger girl, still untried in bridal Loves,
not yet companion of Bucolion's couch,
Naiad Abarbaree, often was indignant at the nymph;
and about the peak of Dindymon, near the thicket together,
the Astacid Nymphs reproached the ways of the Cybelean nymph,
and they uttered the dirge; and not so much over the burning doom
did the Heliades weep for dead Phaethon.
And gazing at the untamed heart of the murderous girl
Eros threw down his bow, and swore an oath to the herdsman
to yoke the unwilling maiden to Dionysus.
And with tearless eyes, upon her lion-car,
Dindymian Rhea lamented the fallen youth,
mother of Zeus, queen; and at the death of slain Hymnus
the maiden Echo, hating marriage, wailed.
And the oaks spoke: "Why did the herdsman sin so against you?
May Cytherea never, may Artemis never be gracious to you."
And Adresteia saw, she saw the murderous girl,
Adresteia saw the corpse twitching by the iron,
and showed the freshly-slain corpse to the Cyprus-born,
and blamed Eros himself. And by the well-leaved thicket
the bull's tears flowed in pity for Hymnus,
and the calf wept, and the grieving cow lamented
for the gasping shepherd, and seemed to cry out this:
"The fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him.
The maiden killed the one who longed for her, and instead of love-charms
gave doom as his wage, and in the love-stricken herdsman's
blood she dipped the bronze and quenched the fire of the Loves—
the fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him—
and grieved the Nymphs; she did not hear the mountain rock,
she did not heed the elm, nor reverence the pine
as it begged: 'Do not send the shaft, do not kill the herdsman.'"
And the wolf lamented Hymnus, the shameless bears lamented,
and with grim eyelids the lion wailed for the herdsman:
"The fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him.
Seek another rock, oxen, search out, bulls,
a strange mountain; for my sweet herdsman is dead with longing,
cut down by a woman's hand. To what thicket
do I lead my step? Farewell, pastures, farewell, beds of earth.
The fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him.
Farewell to me, peaks and mountains, farewell, springs,
farewell, Naiads, and my oaks. And both
Pan of the pastures and Phoebus cried aloud; let the flute wander.
Where is Nemesis? Where Cypris? Eros, do not touch the quiver;
pipe, sing no more; the clear-voiced herdsman is dead."
And the blameless gore of the wretched herdsman, slain by the Loves,
Phoebus showed to his sister, and Artemis herself lamented
the dead love of Hymnus, even if she was untried in the Loves.

16. In the sixteenth book I sing of bridal Nicaea,
the sleeping consort of unsleeping Dionysus.

Nor was the murder of the plaintive herdsman unavenged,
but taking up his bow and drawing his lovely arrow
impetuous Eros, unseen, armed himself against Dionysus,
who sat beside the bank of the smooth-pebbled river.
And swift Nicaea, after the course of her usual hunting,
streaming with unstoppable sweat from her labours among the loved crags,
washed her naked body in baths poured down from the mountains.
Nor did the far-shooting Eros delay: against the string
he set the tip-showing notch of the winged arrow,
he bent his bow round, and into the heart of love-maddened Lyaeus
he drove the whole shaft. And in the streams,
seeing the bare-skinned girl swimming, Dionysus
was shaken in mind by the fiery, sweet-maddening dart.
He went here and there, wherever the hare-club-bearing girl was,
now gazing at the curling locks of her hair
stirred by the circling breezes as she sped into her course,
now watching, where her tresses were drawn aside, the gleaming
nakedness of her neck, that sent out a light like the Moon's;
and he neglected the Satyrs and no longer delighted in the Bacchants;
and looking toward Olympus he spoke with a love-begetting voice:
'I will go where the dewy running-ground is, where the quiver,
where the arrow and the lovely bow, where too the very
couches of the unwed maiden breathe with perfume;
I will touch the nets' stakes and spread the toils with my hands;
I too will hunt, and bring down the familiar fawn.
And if, like some heavy-tempered Amazon, she should reproach me,
belching a womanish weight of honey-sweet threat,
to the knees of the angry girl I will bring my hand,
touching her lovely flesh as a suppliant — not lifting
an olive branch, since that is the tree of Athena,
the unwed and unbeguiled maiden, but instead of a bitter,
glistening bough, to my honey-sweet bride
I will lift up, in supplication, a cluster bearing the wine-dark fruit
of the honey-dripping vintage. And if she should be angered,
the maiden of the curved bow, let her not fix her spear in my flesh,
nor again draw the murderous arrow, but in shame
let her strike my body with the very tip of her sweet bow:
I care nothing for a stroke that charms the heart. And if she wishes,
let her seize my hair with her lovely hands,
tugging the willing locks of my bound tresses.
I will never restrain the maiden, but as though in anger
I will press her clenching right hand with a relentless grip,
taking her reddening fingers in a hooked clasp,
a comfort for the toil of Cypris — for the maiden
has plundered all the beauty of Olympus. Be gracious, Cerne!
Astacis has sprung up as a new rose-fingered Dawn,
another light-bearer has grown up — for the younger
holds her form unchanging: Nicaea is a Moon.
I longed, in my desire, to change my many-fashioned form;
were it not that reverence for my father's modesty holds me back,
I too, through the Tyrian water, a bull crossing the wet,
would carry my Nicaea unwetted over the seas
and swim — like the bridegroom of Europa — and unwilling
I would shake my back, so that, as the girl was tossed,
her all-white right hand might seize my horn.
I longed, were I a winged husband, that I might dance
lifting unshaken the woman upon my back,
as Cronides bore Aegina, so that after the bed I might make
the eagle, that other bird, a star to adorn the loves' wedding.
Yet I will not, by striking my wife's father with a thunderbolt,
grant my bride the wicked dowry of her father's ruin,
lest I grieve sweet Nicaea by his destruction.
Would I were a bastard bird with goodly wings, since she too,
our own maiden, loves winged arrows.
Rather, longing for Danae's watery shape of love,
I longed, were I become the golden shower as her husband,
myself the gift of wedlock, myself the spouse, that I might dance
pouring down on her the rich, loving shower of dew;
for it would befit my Nicaea, my fair-faced girl,
who has a golden form, to have a golden husband.'
Such words, raving with love, he cried in a frenzied voice.
And once, walking within a fragrant meadow,
he gazed at all the blossoming flowers, kin in hue to the girl,
and spoke a word to the misty breezes:
'Only now, scarcely, Nicaea, have I seen your shape here.
Did you not change your beauty into flowers? For gazing
on the fair-formed rose-bed I recognized your cheeks;
and your rose blooms unfading — for you wear
the inborn, never-ceasing, blushing anemone.
Turning my eye to the lily, I saw your snowy palms,
and beholding the hyacinth I saw your dark-blue hair.
Receive me as your fellow-traveller in the hunt; and if you wish,
I myself will bear the sweet burden of the stakes, I will carry
the high boots and the bow and the lovely arrows,
I myself — I have no need of the Satyrs. Did not Apollo himself,
beside the thicket, lift the nets of Cyrene?
What grudge is it, if I too handle the net? I do not toil
when I carry my Nicaea upon my own shoulders.
Nor am I greater than my father — for in the surging waters
the sea-crossing bull bore Europa undrenched.
Rosy maiden, why has the woodland so pleased you?
Spare your lovely limbs, and let no rocky,
unspread couch wear away your back upon the stones.
I will be your chamber-servant, if you wish; and in the hall
I myself will spread your bedding, and over it lay
the richly-dappled skins of leopards, and with them throw
the bristling, thick-haired hides of a lion's covering,
baring my own limbs; and you shall sleep sweet sleep
covered by the dappled fawnskins of Dionysus;
and a fitting screen of Mygdonian deer I throw on high,
stripping the Satyrs. And if you have need of hounds,
I will give you at once all my Pan's dogs together,
and bring other hounds from Sparta, those that my Carneian Apollo
rears for the loves of young men,
and I will summon the hunting hounds of Aristaeus;
and I will bring nets with their stakes and fitting gifts,
the high boots of Nomius and Agreus, who long ago knew
both the rich-meadowed pasture and the course of the toilsome chase.
And if you fear the flame of the summer-born thirsty season,
I will plant vine-shoots over your bed,
and the fragrant breezes of wine will breathe around you
as you lie within the midst of a covering of many grape-clusters.
Wandering maiden, of the love-stricken face,
pity your cheeks, smitten by Phaethon's heat,
lest the Sun's brilliance wither the beam of your limbs,
lest the winds spoil your perfumed locks:
sleep amid the roses and on the petals of the hyacinth,
resting your head on Dionysus your neighbour,
that you may kindle one revel for the four immortals,
for Phoebus and Zephyr and Cypris and Dionysus.
I would grant you, as plunder, a dark-skinned brood of Indians,
chamber-servants of your bridal bower — but why have I named
the dark race as escorts of your bed?
When does white Dawn ever mingle with black-cloaked Night?
Astacis, you are a younger Artemis — but I myself
will bring you sixty handmaids, dancers,
that I may make a countless choir to attend you,
equal in number to the handmaids of the mountain Archeress,
like the daughters of Ocean, so that Artemis
may not vie with you in hunting, even if she is mistress of the chase.
To you I grant the Graces of holy Orchomenus
as handmaids, taking over my children of Aphrodite.
But charm your unbeguiled heart with desire, and let my bed
receive you after the toil of the hunt, that you may appear
Artemis among the crags and Aphrodite in the bridal chambers.
What grudge is it, that you should hunt with hunting Lyaeus?
And if you have got a frenzy for battle, then, like a famed-bow Amazon,
you shall come to the Indian war, that you may be
Persuasion apart from strife and, when there is combat, Athena.
Take too, if you wish, the deer-slaying thyrsi of Lyaeus,
and become a fawn-slayer; and by your own hands
and by your own labours adorn my chariot,
yoking a leopard or lions to the bridle.'
So speaking he pursued the mountain girl, his neighbour,
crying out this word: 'Wait, maiden, for Bacchus your husband.'
But she, growing angry, raised up a mighty voice,
the maiden, hurling a furious mouth against Lyaeus:
'Go and say these things to some loving bride.
If you can drag the grey-eyed one or Artemis into wedlock,
then you have mighty Nicaea too as an obedient bride;
for I am companion-in-arms to both. But if there flees you
the unforeseen wedding of unlabouring Athena,
then neither will you charm the mind of the disobedient Archeress.
Do not seek the bed of Nicaea; nor let me see you
laying hand to bow and fingering the quiver.
Lest, after the herdsman Hymnus who perished, I bring you down too.
I will wound the unwounded Dionysus — unless against iron
you bear a flesh unscarred and unyielding to the dart.
I will imitate the high-crested sons of Iphimedeia,
and bind you with iron, inextricable chains,
just like your brother, and within a hiding-place
of bronze jars I will keep you too, after Ares,
until, fulfilling twelve circuits of the Moon,
you cast off your frenzy to the airy winds.
With woman-mad hands do not touch my quiver:
I have a bow, you a thyrsus; on the Astacian cliff
I send my arrow here against boars or lions,
Artemis' fellow-contestant, but over the rock of Lebanon
do you too hunt fawns, hunting alongside Aphrodite.
I do not accept your bed, even if you carry the blood of Zeus;
for if I wished to have a god as husband, I would not have
a soft-haired, ironless, feeble spouse of womanish form,
I would not have Dionysus, but there would be guarded for my bridal
a bridegroom either the famed-bow lord or bronze Ares —
one holding a bow, the other a sword as the loves' dowry;
but since I will accept none of the blessed ones, the frenzy
does not hold me even to call your father Cronion my father-in-law.
Seek another, Bacchus, a young and obedient bride.
Why do you hurry? You run an unattainable course, as once
Leto's son pursued Daphne, and as Hephaestus pursued Athena;
why do you hurry? This course is vain; for among the crags
the hunting-boots are far better than buskins.'
So speaking she left Bacchus. And ever beneath the grazing thicket
he sought the mountain-wandering maiden; and as he sped,
a hound ran with him, a faithful companion with a prudent heart,
which once, to mountain-loving Dionysus as he hunted,
high-horned Pan, the rearer of whelps, had given to keep as a gift.
And watching it as though it had understanding and a voice,
his fellow-ranger, his road-companion, his partner in toils,
Bacchus, raving with love, embraced it with a friendly speech:
'Why, wandering hound, are you the running-mate of Lyaeus,
you who deserve forever the longing Pan? Why do you alone
track with Dionysus as he tracks the maiden?
Has your keeper made you pitying toward loves?
Seek still our maiden, and do not, among the rocks,
leave Bacchus to wander alone over the mountains.
You alone pity me, and like a mortal, into the ridge of the woodland
you go after the leafy haunts of the wandering girl.
Toil for your king; and in return for your toils I will give you
a recompense: after the star Sirius of Maera,
I will lead you within the heaven and make you a star
near the earlier Dog, so that you too may ripen
the grape-cluster, shooting your gleam upon the Eileithyia of the cluster.
What grudge is it that a third Dog should rise? You too will shine
running beside the starry, hastening Hare.
If it is right, while pitying me, find fault with the chaste girl.
Turning a sidelong eye toward the ridge of Cybele's woodland,
because the woman still flees me, a god, as I seek her;
find fault with both, with Adonis and with Cythereia,
and pursue restless Echo, the wanderer through the mountain,
lest she make my bride still more a fugitive from the bed;
and do not leave your love-sick Pan near the girl,
lest he seize her and yoke her in compelled wedlock.
If you see the maiden, come swiftly, announcing it to Dionysus
by a witnessing silence or by intelligent barkings;
be the messenger of my desire; let some other hound wander
chasing either boars or lions from the crag.
Dear Pan, I call you most blessed, since even
your own hounds are born searchers-out of the loves.'
'You who play, many-shaped Fortune, with the mortal race,
be gracious, all-subduer; for after the mortal breed
you rule the whelps too, since this ill-fated wanderer
serves, after Pan, the longing Lyaeus as well;
find fault with the maiden, dear oaks; say it, you rocks:
even the hounds pity, and yet the Amazon did not show mercy.
There are prudent ones even among the whelps, to whom Cronion
gave a human mind, though he granted no mortal voice.'
He spoke near a plant; and through the leafy cluster,
hearing the voice of woman-mad Dionysus,
the ancient Melia raised a mocking cry:
'Others, Dionysus, are hunting here, urging on their hounds
for the Archeress, but you hunt for Aphrodite;
sweet is he who dreads the soft-skinned, unwedded girl;
bold Bacchus has become a suppliant, a servant of the loves;
with his Indian-slaying hands he begs a feeble girl.
Your father did not know how, with mind-charming speech of desire,
to lead an obedient girl into wedlock, into marriage;
he did not entreat Semele, until he won his love.
He did not persuade Danae, until he plundered her maidenhood;
you know Ixion's wife, joined to Zeus,
and the bridal neighing and the horse-wedding;
you learned the playful ordinance of the loves with Antiope,
and the laughing Satyr, the false, mimic husband.'
So she spoke, mocking the timid mind of Bacchus.
And she went within the oak, her coeval. And upon the hills,
grieving, Dionysus followed the frenzied girl
with love-maddened feet; and the swift-sandalled Amazon,
restless, went over the topmost heads of the trackless rock,
stealing away the footprint from the searching Lyaeus.
And as her skin was lashed by Phaethon's fiery brand,
the parched lips of the thirsty girl grew dry, unmoistened;
and not knowing the trick of woman-mad Dionysus,
she saw the yellow water of the wine-loving river,
and drank the sweet stream, whence the fiery Indians had drunk;
and her mind whirled, and the girl raved in drunkenness,
and she shook her head, shifting with a double throbbing,
and she thought she saw a twin, capacious lake
as she rolled her eyes; and as her head grew heavy
she beheld the doubled ridges of the beast-feeding hill;
and slipping on the dust with trembling feet
she was dragged, self-rolling, onto the wing of neighbouring Sleep;
and the heavy-kneed bride was charmed by the bridal swoon.
Seeing her asleep, Eros pointed her out to Bacchus,
pitying Hymnus; but Nemesis laughed to see it.
And crafty Dionysus, with noiseless boots,
crept soundless to the wedding with a cunning beat of his feet.
He came near the girl; and gently, drawing the topmost
fastening, the guardian of her inviolate girdle, he loosed it
with a sparing hand, that sleep might not let the maiden go.
And the earth, opening her fragrant childbed,
gave birth in travail to a plantation, in favour of Dionysus,
and lifting up a great vine-bearing canopy
the plaited stake was weighed down with clustering fruit;
and the bed was shaded with leaves — for of its own accord
the vine's tendril girdled the well-vined couch;
and many a wandering grape-cluster, high in the air with wine-dark fruit,
was shaken here and there by the breezes of Cypris,
and shrouded them both; and with celery-bearing cluster
the lovely shoot of the vine, its yoke-mate, made drunk
the woven ivy, climber upon the swelling vintage.
And the crafty wedding was like a dream-bed,
having sleep for its partner; and she was robbed of maidenhood,
the slumbering girl, and beheld, as escort of the loves,
sleep the under-servant of the wine-tottering wedding.
And the breeze, in the high-coursing leaping of the frenzied wood,
restless, self-shouting, wove a hymn of the loves,
and the wind-roaming song of the mountain-dwelling wedding
the maiden Echo answered with shamefaced lips,
the daughter of Pan, late-voiced; and dancing above the ground
the flute resounded, singing 'Hymen, O Hymenaeus';
this lovely wedding the mountain pine proclaimed.
And the wind-roaming soul of the herdsman, darting up,
stirred the sleeping maiden with nightly dreams:
'There are Furies even for one who loves, well-wed girl;
if you fled Hymnus your bridegroom, you have been wedded to Dionysus;
crookedly you give judgement, chamber-keeping maiden bride;
for you kill the one who loves, and pursue the one who does not woo.
Maiden, you gave brazen sleep to Hymnus who loved you;
maiden, sweet sleep has destroyed your maidenhood.
Pitifully, laughing, you saw the blood of the herdsman struck down;
more pitifully, lamenting, you have seen the blood of your maidenhood.'
So speaking, like to shadowy smoke,
the tearful soul of the love-stricken herdsman sped away,
and unreachable plunged into the all-receiving hall of Tartarus,
bearing envy of Bacchus and his wine-tottering wedding.
And striking out a bridal sound on his clear reeds,
hiding the envy beneath his heart, the hymn-singing Pan
spoke a reproachful song against another's wedding.
And one of the love-maddened Satyrs, beside the neighbouring thicket,
an insatiable gazer at the unseen wedding,
told the Bacchic tale, having seen the fair-maiden bed:
'Horned Pan, do you still alone run after Aphrodite?
And you too — when will you be the bridegroom of the pursued Echo?
And you too — when will you contrive such a helping trick,
an aid for your own unwedded wedlock?
Dear Pan, become you too a planter instead of a herdsman,
and renounce the shepherd's crook, and beside the rock
leave the cattle and the sheep — what will the herdsmen do for you?
Wake, and plant you too the wedding-arranging wine of the loves.'
The tale was not yet ended when the goat-feeding Pan cried out:
'Would my father had taught me the trick of marriage-fulfilling wine!
Would that, like Bacchus, I ruled the mind-deranging grape!
Then I too would have fulfilled the much-wandering frenzy of my loves,
seeing sleeping and drunk the ill-maiden Echo.
Be gracious, this pasture of mine, since beside the neighbouring spring
I water these sheep, but with the wine-loving stream
Dionysus drags unbeguiled maidens into wedlock.
He has found a drug for love, his own plant: away with the milk
of goats, away with the milk of our sheep — for it cannot
bring sleep upon desire or drag a maiden into wedlock.
I alone, Cythereia, am forced — alas for the loves!'
The pipe of Pan fled the unwedded wedlock
and hailed with joy the just-accomplished wedding of Dionysus
with self-sounding strains; and the more — to his accustomed song
the answering Echo replied as Syrinx sounded:
'Dionysus, mortal-charming shepherd of the bridal wine,
you alone have become blessed, since, when the bride refused,
you found wine, the wedding-arranging helper of the loves.'
Such a word the love-sick, grieving Pan recited,
holding envy and longing for marriage-fulfilling Lyaeus.
And having accomplished his love and his desire of the wayside bed,
Dionysus rose up on his unspeakable sandal.
And the bride, waking, blamed the river spring,
angry at sleep and Cypris and Dionysus,
drenched with a tearful rain; and grieving
she heard still the remnants of the Naiads' bridal song,
and the herald of the bed of love-stricken Lyaeus —
shaded by the leaves of the vine she saw the couch
covered with the bridal fawnskins of Dionysus,
self-announcing the secret bed; she saw too
her own maiden girdle filled with the bridal dew.
And she gashed her rosy cheeks, and beating
both her thighs she roared with a plaintive voice:
'Alas for my maidenhood, which the Euian water snatched away;
alas for my maidenhood, which the sleep of the loves snatched away;
alas for my maidenhood, which wandering Bacchus snatched away.
Away with the deceiving drink of the Water-nymphs, away with the bed!
Hamadryad nymphs, whom shall I blame? For my maidenhood
sleep, Eros, trickery, wine have plundered.
Even Artemis has renounced maidens — but she herself,
why did Echo, all her body, not tell me, "flee the bed"?
Why into my ear, only that I might not hear Bacchus,
did Pitys not whisper, and Daphne not speak,
"Maiden, beware of drinking the deceiving water"?'
She spoke, and gushed up a much-weeping rain of the eye.
And now she longed to press a sword against her neck,
now, self-rolling, she wished to fall from the mountain
headlong at the last, slipping in the dust;
and she longed to wipe out the drink of the bridal spring,
had not the earlier flood, changed from the moisture of Bacchus,
murmured white water and no longer the stream of Lyaeus.
And she entreated Cronides and Artemis, that he might dry up
the courts of the Naiads, made dusty in thirsty ground.
Often she strained her eye through the mountain, in case she might find
the unsteady footprint of the unseen Dionysus,
that a woman might strike the god with her bow, that she might subdue
the cluster-bearing deity; and she wished still more to destroy
with fiery fire that whole bridal vine.
Often, beholding through the mountain the tracks of Bacchus,
she shot, aiming her arrows at the airy gusts;
often she lifted her spear and stood facing her mark,
that she might strike the body of the unwounded Dionysus;
but in vain she let fly, and did not hit Lyaeus.
And she was angry at the river and swore that never from its spring
would she drink the deceiving water with thirsty lips;
she swore too to keep a sleepless eye through the nights,
she swore to sleep no other sweet sleep in the mountains.
And she was angry at the guardian hounds, because they too
had not then armed themselves against woman-mad Lyaeus.
And she sought a high remedy against death by hanging,
crushing her neck, entwined in a strangling bond,
shunning the mocking blame of her companion youth.
And unwilling she left the ancient beast-nurturing wood,
ashamed to appear before the Archeress after the bed.
And filled with the drop of holy Lyaeus' seed
she bore a burden in her womb; and when the labour was fulfilled
the life-warming Hours delivered a female birth,
and confirmed the nine-circuit course of the Moon;
and from the wedlock of Bromius the god-sped girl flowered,
whom he named Telete, ever rejoicing in festivals,
the night-dancing girl, follower of Dionysus,
delighting in castanets and in the double-beaten oxhide.
And beside the wine-loving lake the god built
a fair-stoned city, Nicaea, which he called
by the name of the nymph Astacis, after his Indian-slaying victory.

19. In the nineteenth, beside the tomb of Staphylus,
Bacchus rouses a delightful contest over a fragrant mixing-bowl.

So he spoke, and the youth, with a heavy goad in his fresh-grieving heart,
sealed his lips in a speechless silence,
overcome by tears that poured of themselves; and at last the mother,
Methe, who rejoiced in Lyaeus, recited her piteous words:
"The sleepless watcher of your dancing-round,
your own Staphylus, Dionysus, a sleep of bronze has lulled to rest;
your own Staphylus, Dionysus, the breezes of Charon have snatched away.
A double heavy grief has rushed upon me: the vine-clad
Bacchus has forsaken me, and my husband has fallen sick;
and I bore a common sorrow over them both,
over Staphylus dying and Lyaeus not at hand.
But of your richly-streaming fruit, dear Bacchus,
give me your cup brimful, that drinking
I may lull my heavy grief asleep with your sorrow-banishing wine.
You are my hope, Dionysus lover of the cry: only the fruit,
only let me see the mixing-bowl, and I shed no tears again."
So she spoke, and he pitied her, and mixing in a cup
the care-loosing liquor of evil-warding wine he offered it
to the young boy and the downcast mother; and both drank
the honey-flowing weight of the fruit in a heart-cheering draught;
and Methe's groaning was soothed, and Botrys' grief;
and the woman spoke some word to heart-charming Bacchus:
"You have come to me, dear Bacchus, dear light; no longer sorrow,
no longer grief holds me now that Dionysus has appeared;
you have come to me, dear Bacchus, dear light; for with your
drink of healing wine I have soothed my tears.
Not for my husband, not for my father's death do I mourn; nay, even from the cluster
itself, if you wish, I will part; for in both alike
I have Bacchus—as begetter and as son and as bedfellow.
I will follow, if you wish me, and come to your house;
let me be a fellow-traveller of the Bassarids; and if you wish,
I will carry your wands and your lovely fruit,
and to my lips I will press the wine-press flute.
Do not leave me a widow, lest I swell a double pain
for Staphylus dead and Dionysus gone away.
You have the cluster for your servant; let him be taught the dances
and the rites and the offerings and, if you wish, the war with the Indians;
and let me see him laughing beside the wine-loving press,
treading out underfoot the birth-pangs of your fruit.
And remember the aged Wine-jar; do not leave him
untaught of your rite or without his share of the sweet wine."
So she spoke, and with a smiling face the lord Bacchus
heartened Methe, and to the wine-loving nymph said this:
"Lady, giver of splendid gifts, second only to golden Aphrodite,
bestower of mirth . . . joy-giving mother of the Loves,
feast together with Lyaeus, who touches the banquet;
be a garland-bearer for Dionysus, like Aphrodite,
crowned with flowers and well-grown clusters;
the wreaths of your tresses shall make Victory jealous.
I will make you cup-bearer, second after gold-throned Hebe;
you shall rise together with the vine-clad Lyaeus,
a fellow-traveller and attendant of the Bacchic cups,
and they shall call you Methe, the mortal-delighting surfeit of wine;
the cluster I will call the care-banishing fruit of my harvest,
and the grape that bears the cluster I will name from Staphylus,
the birth-pang of the vines and the dew of the vineyard.
Nor apart from Methe shall I be able to feast,
nor apart from Methe do I ever raise the revel."
So speaking, beside the tomb of Staphylus the wine-fallen
Dionysus, banisher of grief, set up a willing contest;
and dragging forth a fine-bearded goat and a male bull
he set them as a double prize, and called the players of the lyre
to compete, the contestants of the Pierian song;
he set them as a double prize, and urging the competitors,
the men skilled in the sweet-sounding lyre, he coaxed them with a word:
"Here we raise an Attic revel; for to the prize-winning
man who conquers I will grant the pale-hided bull,
and to the man defeated I will hand over the shaggy goat."
So spoke Bromios, and a man who strikes the lyre leaped up,
Oeagrus, a citizen of the chill Bistonian soil,
holding the plectrum that hangs beside the lyre; and after him
rose Erechtheus, dweller in hymn-singing Attica.
Both came into the midst as competitors of the contest,
players of the lyre; and they wreathed their hair
with leaves of bay; and they girded up their robes.
Beginning, they made their fingers quiver with the accustomed beat,
pressing the answering string of the outstretched gut in turn,
clasping the ends, that it might be neither too high-pitched,
nor ever, slackened, soften the manly song.
And first, having won the lot, with skilful rhythm
Erechtheus, dweller of Cecrops' land, struck the lyre,
singing the ancestral hymn: how in holy Athens
Celeus also gave hospitality to Deo, all-mother of Life,
with her boy Triptolemus and old Metaneira,
and she gave them grain, when, sowing snow on the furrow of earth,
Triptolemus found seed upon his ear-bearing car;
and beside the new-built tomb of Celeus dead,
with tearless eyes Deo lamented the harvest-feast,
yet, consoling them again with a heart-charming word,
she quenched the heavy grief of Triptolemus and Metaneira;
so too the king of the Assyrians gave Dionysus
hospitality in his own hall; and the lord, in return for his table,
granted him the Euian gifts and the vine-clad fruit,
and when Staphylus the wine-loving king had died,
he stayed his son Botrys from lamenting care,
and lulled the sorrow of his mournful wife Methe.
Such things the skilful lyre-striker played; and at the rhythm
all alike were charmed; and together with thyrsus-bearing Lyaeus
they marvelled at the fitting, lovely-voiced Attic song.
Second, lord Oeagrus, weaving a shifting hymn,
as the father of Orpheus, sharing the hearth of his familiar Muse,
struck up a two-line harmony with a Phoebean strain,
brief of word, clear of speech, in some Amyclaean fashion:
"Fair-haired Hyacinthus Apollo brought back to life,
and Staphylus Dionysus will make to live forever."
Not yet had the revel ceased, but the people cried out
with auspicious words from throats of one tongue,
and the Satyrs roared all together; and from his seat
Bacchus leaped up restless, shaking up and down
his right hand, and Botrys ran forward, with the cry of "euoi"
honouring the well-rhythmed harmony of the singer;
and the lord crowned the head of Oeagrus with ivy,
and the father of Orpheus, striking the earth with his foot,
gladly received the unyoked bull as the wage of his song;
and around him in rows his comrades leaped for joy.
And the wide-bearded goat, swelling his grief and his envy,
with shamed hands the citizen of Athens led away.
Then fair-haired Iobacchus, bringing them with unsparing hand,
set worthy prizes for the dance-weaving victory:
an aged mixing-bowl pregnant with fragrant wine,
golden, that held measures past telling, gushing for the thirsty earth
the four-year-old liquor of Lyaeus,
the skilled Olympian work of Hephaestus, which once Cypris
gave to her vine-clad brother Dionysus;
and a smaller bowl he set in the midst of the contest,
of silver, gleaming, round, which once to Bacchus
the king of Alybe gave as a guest-gift, dwelling in his halls
beside the wealthy soil, where in the recess of the earthly mine
the black hollow whitened with elbows of silver;
about its rim, upon the bossed crown of its edge,
ran twining ivy, and round about it was wrought with golden ornament;
this he brought and set, with its deep-hollowed belly,
a wine-vat still breathing the younger weight of the fruit,
must, the drink of unwedded intoxication; for there is no blame
that the man defeated should drink the unsobering dew.
But when Bacchus had set the prizes in the midst of the contest,
