he called those skilled in the dance with a summoning voice:
"Whoever shall compete, wheeling with skilful foot,
and conquer in the judgement of the running foot, let him take
both the golden mixing-bowl and the pour of sweet-drinking wine;
but he who falls, shaken by the slip of an unsteady foot,
and dances the worse, let him receive the lesser gifts as well;
for I am not the same to all; but to the prize-winning
man who has conquered in the graceful dance-treading contest
no gleaming tripod, no swift horse will I grant,
no spear and breastplate stained with the blood of Indians,
rousing the javelin-throwers to the straight-coursing discus;
no course of fleetness is stretched out here, no point of a spear
that carries far; but to Staphylus, the king who has perished,
a man who loved the leap, I honour the play-loving feet;
nor do I hold out gifts for the fly-strong wrestling,
nor is there a horse-race, nor are these the games of Elis,
nor the bridegroom-slaying course of Oenomaus; for our
turning-post is the dance, our starting-lines the leaping of feet,
the nimble hand and the twisting bound, and the nod of a face
ever-moving restlessly, and the speaking silence
that wheels the fingers and the dancer's glance."
At such a word from him horned Silenus rose up,
and thrice-old Maron, with heavy-sounding foot, leaped forward,
eyeing the great golden flashing mixing-bowl,
not because it was golden and the better, but because alone
it held the richly-streaming, most ancient weight of dew
up to the very edge of its rim; and love of the sweet wine
made him young, and the Bacchic scent overpowered his grey hairs;
and he twirled his feet, testing his own strength,
lest heavy old age had stopped his limbs that had forgotten the dance.
And the old man with his voice appeased the soul of Staphylus,
pouring a sober word from his shaggy chin:
"I am Maron, the fellow-contestant of grief-free Lyaeus;
I know not how to weep; what have tears to do with Dionysus?
The circles of my feet are my burial-gifts beside your tomb;
receive me smiling; Maron knows no cares,
Maron knows no wailing, no weight of mourning sorrow;
I am the lovely servant of grief-free Dionysus.
Be gracious to your Maron, even if you have drunk the waters of Lethe,
grant the grace that I may drink the pour of ancient wine,
and let Silenus drink the new weight of the new fruit.
And for Staphylus after death, as for one alive, I will dance,
since I prefer the dance to the savoury-loving table;
for you, Staphylus, living and not breathing, I dance,
striking up a revel over your tomb; I am Bacchus' man,
not the servant of Phoebus, and I have not learned to sing dirges,
such as among the Cretans lord Apollo trilled,
weeping for lovely Atymnius; and of the Heliades
I was a stranger, alien to Eridanus
I am, no kinsman of Phaethon the perished charioteer;
I am no dweller of Sparta, I lift no mournful flower,
shaking the delicate petals of the much-wept hyacinths.
Today, whether you sit beside Minos and judge alike,
or whether you hold the flowery court of Rhadamanthys,
walking softly in the groves of the Elysian meadow,
hear your Maron; and I, in place of cups,
with truceless lips belch out a thoughtful libation;
be gracious to your Maron, and grant me a wine-dark victory,
a victory that all admire; and I, above your tomb,
will pour the fair first-fruits of my golden cups,
beginning from my bowl, after the prize of my victory."
So speaking, Maron danced with twisting foot,
shifting his right foot to take the place of the left,
tracing an intricate silence with a voiceless hand;
and he rolled his wandering eyes, the image of words,
weaving an intelligent rhythm with a cunning gesture;
and he shook his head and wished to toss his locks,
had not the bare brow of his hairless head lacked them.
Nor, as an old man bearing Titan blood,
did he picture with eloquent gesture the Titan race,
not Cronus or Phanes the elder, nor the offspring
of the Sun-Titan, coeval with the equal-aged universe;
but leaving all this and the flood of ancient matter,
in skilful silence he figured the cup-bearer of Cronides,
stretching the goblet to Zeus and cheering the choir of the other
immortals ever with cups close-following one upon another,
or pouring the holy dew down into the mixing-bowl;
and his harmony was a sweet drink; nay, even
the maiden Hebe he danced, drawing the nectar;
and looking toward the Satyrs he pictured the form of Ganymede
with speechless hands, and whenever he looked toward the Bacchants,
in thoughtful silence he showed the gold-sandalled Hebe.
Such things Maron traced, plying his versatile fingers,
and he reined in the skilful onset of his well-rhythmed foot,
completing the many-bending measures of the restless dance.
And he stood trembling, watching with a sidelong eye
who would conquer whom, who would reach his own house
bearing the larger mixing-bowl, brimming with drink.
And Silenus danced; and of his much-turning art
his silent hand traced the cunning tokens.
And then such was the figure of his hands: as once a great
contention fell upon the son of Cyrene and Dionysus
over the drink, and the blessed ones came together; not then was there boxing,
not running, not then the discus for prizes: for the son of Phoebus
the cups lay as the instruments of care, and for Dionysus,
and two mixing-bowls, the one a pour of aged wine,
the other bearing the new gifts of the branch-loving bee;
and Cronides sat as judge, and for the prize-winners
a delicate contest was stretched out over the honey-dripping victory;
the cups lay as instruments; and, like gold-winged Hermes,
Love himself, the lovely, stood as steward in the midst,
holding in one hand both ivy and a shoot of olive,
to Bacchus the ivy-flower, to Aristaeus holding out
the shoot of olive like the wreaths of Pisa,
the holy emblem of Pallas. And in a honey-mixed cup
first Aristaeus, mixing the birth-pang of the bee,
offered the immortals a skilful draught, cheering
one after another, and dealt the goblet to each in turn;
to them at the beginning of the richly-dropping dew
the surfeit came most sharp, but as the cups were drawn
they refused the third, and touched not the fourth,
and blamed the swift surfeit of the honey; but of the sweet-drinking
Dionysus, in his soft tunic, drawing from the mixing-bowl,
lifted two cups and held them out with a twin motion,
the first to Cronides, the second he gave to Hera,
the third goblet to his father's brother, the Earth-shaker;
and in order he mixed for all the gods together and for Zeus his father,
who delighted; and to the one downcast alone,
smiling, he stretched the goblet to jealous Phoebus;
and they were charmed in mind by the many-scattered cups,
and grew ever the thirstier the more they drank,
and asked again for another, and there was no surfeit of cups.
And the immortals raised the cry, and entrusted to Bacchus
the right to bear the prize of victory for the sweet-drinking vine;
and drunken, unconquerable Love, the steward of the contest,
crowned the hair of Lyaeus with clustering ivy.
This with skilful hand horned Silenus wove,
and he stayed his right hand, and on a much-leaping sandal
he was lifted from the ground and sent his glances into the air,
now joining his feet yoked together one upon the other,
now, parting them, he sprang with a counter-shifting art;
at another time, much-twisting, dancing above the floor,
upright upon his heels he shook with a winding leap;
and on his right foot, unbending, he propped himself,
holding the fingertip of the other foot, or bending his knee
with joined hands, or the outstretched fold of his thighs—
Silenus heavy-kneed, holding the upright onset of his foot;
and he raised his left foot upon his flank and shoulder,
lifting it in a spiral, and by a backstrained art
he raised the curved foot aloft, winding it about his neck;
and in the swift whirl of the homeward-circling dance,
on his back, self-twisting, he bent with a circular art,
showing his outspread arched belly to the air,
crossing the same unending turning-post like a garland;
and his head was carried sidelong, as though ever
touching the floor and yet not grazing the dust;
and with shaggy foot Silenus tore the ground,
unstable here and there, in a Bacchic frenzy of leaping feet.
And then his knees grew weary, and as his head shook
he slipped, on his back, self-rolling, upon the field;
and he was shaped into a river: his body gushed water
in self-flowing streams; and as his forehead changed
his horns surged into an arching channel,
and the surge crested, churned high upon his head,
and his belly, full of fish, was hollowed into sand;
and as Silenus was poured forth his hair changed
into self-grown rushes; and over the river, close beside,
the sharp-pointed reed whistled, shaken by the breezes,
self-grown. And Maron bound up the sweet victory,
holding in his arms a mixing-bowl crammed with sweet wine;
and as Silenus was poured forth, as a prize, like a libation,
he took the silver mixing-bowl and flung it into the streams,
and made drunk the pourings of the dance-weaving river,
whence the place is named from the mixing-bowl, and of the sweet-drinking
Silenus murmuring the Euian water is heard.
And Maron spoke some word to the river-spring:
"Maron does no violence to you, Silenus; but into you I will cast
the reddening wine, and call you the wine-receiver.
Receive, you insatiable of drink, your own wine; receive Bacchus'
silver mixing-bowl, and you shall be silver-eddying.
Rolling-footed Silenus, even in your pourings you dance,
the whirl of your feet even in the surges you keep,
still you revel in your watery form; but be gracious
to the Bacchants and the Satyrs and the wine-giving fruits,
and guard the Silenoi, the offshoot of your stock;
and to deep-drinking Maron be kind, and let me not see you
stealing away the eagerness for victory even in the rivers.
With your waters rather swell the wine of the Maronian fruit;
be of one mind with Dionysus even among the rivers.
Foolish one, who taught you to contend with your betters?"
Another Silenus again, exchanging an overweening pipe,
lifted his proud neck and came into strife with Phoebus;
but he, stripping the hairy skin, binding him to a shoot,
made of him a breathing wineskin, and high upon a tree
hidden within he bellied out the mimic shape of the wind,
as though once more the unsilent herdsman were singing;
and pitying him, Delphic Apollo gave him form,
and made a river of the same name; still of that
shaggy Silenus the winding water is told,
and it belches a wind-roaming din, as though ever
the Phrygian pipe were piped on answering reeds.
And you too changed your body, having kindled strife with a better,
wholly like the former Silenus. But may you no more
seek the unsandalled, familiar Bacchant nymph,
the loose-haired mountain Bacchant; for the boundless brood
of the loose-locked Naiads delights you.
No more seek the serpent-bonds of Lyaeus,
plying eels, the crooked birth-pang of the streams,
and, fitted with spotted scales instead of serpents,
fishes creep upon your streams.
And if you have been parted from clustering Dionysus,
the more I count you blessed; for you too swell the cluster;
what more would you wish, bearing as the nourisher of your floods
Zeus after Bacchus, the begetter of the whole brood?
In place of your Satyrs, ranks of rivers; in place of the wine-press,
you dance upon the back of roaring Ocean.
A like form you have even among the waters; and there is no blame
that Silenus, his brow plumed with ox-horns,
should hold a bull-shaped, horned river-form."
So spoke Maron; and all marvelled to see the winding water
of Silenus the wide-poured tumbler,
the equal-natured likeness of the much-bending river.

21. The twenty-first holds first the wrath of the Earth-shaker
and the man-breaking battle of Ambrosia and the ambush of the Indians.

Nor did the son of Dryas forget his former fight;
but taking up the ox-cleaver a second time within the thicket . . .
seeking the tribes of the Bassarids. And on Ambrosia
heavenly Zeus bestowed might and war-mad courage,
and she then, frenzied, possessed by the swell of madness,
lifted a stone, hurling it at Lycurgus,
and dashed the heavy helmet from his hair.
But he, full of courage, fought back with a larger stone,
rough, and struck the breast of the ox-eyed Nymph;
yet he did not lay her low, and in wrath he raised his voice:
"Ares, lord of war, father of mighty Lycurgus,
look in shame upon your offspring, who in place of Lyaeus
shoots at a worthless, ironless woman.
The sea does violence to my ox-cleaver; for in the surges
Dionysus was hidden, and I, journeying baffled,
shall come to my own city, and give up the unfinished toil."
He spoke; and Ambrosia, seizing her about the middle with a limb-strong grip
in his hand, he pressed; and he wished to fasten bonds upon her,
as though dragging a spear-won captive to an alien house,
bearing the thiasos-loving Nymph, the nurse of Bromios,
pricking her servile back with the two-edged ox-cleaver.
But he did not check her as she stood, nor did he redden her
with fresh-poured gore as he struck at her head;
but she fled the bold man, and prayed to her mother Earth,
saffron-robed Ambrosia, that she might escape Lycurgus.
And Earth, fruit-bearing, opening her hollow,
received the handmaid of Bromios into her loving bosom,
Ambrosia living; and the vanished Nymph
changed her form into a plant and became a vine-shoot;
and twining a self-coiling cord about Lycurgus
she throttled his yoked neck with a strangling bond,
fighting after the thyrsus with a threatening cluster.
And vehement Rhea made the plant gifted with voice,
granting it as a grace to Dionysus, king of the vines;
and Ambrosia cried aloud and uttered a living voice:
"Not even as a plant shall I ever escape strife with you,
I will wound your body even among my shoots, and in place of a chain
of bronze I will gird you tight with unbreakable leaves;
against you, vine-clad, I arm myself, that one may say:
'The Bassarids slay murderers even with their leaves.'
Beware the warlike vineyards; for the vines
strike their foes, and the fruits hurl their spears.
Living I fought you, and dying I will subdue you;
so do the nurses of Dionysus prove their valour.
You have heard of the sea-ship-stopper, how in the deep
a small, feeble fish has often beset sailors,
checking them back, and with the little gulf of its throat
has stopped the long ship, held fast by a bond?
Receive me, the land ship-stopper, receive of my leaves
the self-fetter, ironless, of the cluster-strong war.
Wait for me, here wait, awaiting the son of Thyone,
until he returns from the bays of the sea."
Such things the long-leaved vine-clad Ambrosia spoke
with cluster-bearing voice, as Lycurgus was struck;
and held fast by the green bonds, the wild man,
unshaken by the unbreakable inescapable fetters of leaves,
fastened all around, shouted, threatening Dionysus;
nor had he strength to flee, but in vain by compulsion he shook
his throat entangled with worthless coils;
nor through his windpipe was a voice carried in the midst
as he was squeezed in a garland; and the Bacchants encircled
his neck, girdled in the midst by a throttling cluster.
And spear-wielding Ares snatched away the dread axe
of his own son; for he feared the raging Bacchant of Bromios,
lest with the murderous ox-cleaver she should strike the body of Lycurgus;
nor did he free the son of Dryas from the green bonds,
much though he longed to, but he yielded to his father's lightning,
hearing the threatening thunderous crash of Zeus.
And falling forward upon the head, full upon it,
Polyxo tore the hair of the irresistible man;
and casting her maddened hand upon the belly of her foe,
gripping his breastplate, she wrenched with a snatching jerk,
and in wrath she rent it—warlike Muses, tell,
what a marvel it was then, of the tunic torn apart
by female nails, iron though it was—;
and weaving a coiling cord of long withies
loose-haired Cleite and vine-clad Gigarto
with a leafy lash reddened the body of Lycurgus,
with bloody welts upon his furrowed back;
and Phleio scored his foot with broader thorns,
raging madly; and Erphe, fellow-traveller of the Vine-god,
gripping the middle of his shaggy chin,
strove to throw the man to the ground; and fighting,
Phasyleia, steerer of the Bacchic dance,
scored her foe's belly with a sharp goad;
and Theope armed herself, the nurse of Lyaeus,
with a skin-piercing fennel-stalk; and she struck the body of Lycurgus,
and Bromie, named after Bromios; and with them the Nymph
Cisseis, lover of clusters, lashed the man with ivy.
And as Lycurgus was overpowered in the woody war,
another and worse calamity appeared again; for against Arabia
mountain Rhea armed the sea Earth-shaker,
the spear-hurler of foundations split with a crash;
and the deep-bosomed bar of the ground
the sea-ruling Earth-shaker dislodged, wielding his trident,
its hollows lashed by winds within,
earth-toiling winds, since with a guiding heave
the lurking blasts hollow out the gaping chasms;
and the unshaken bosom of Arabia's soil was shaken,
and the cloud-near halls were loosed by the quaking heave;
and oaks fell to the ground, and struck by the trident
the Nysaean Arabian floor danced, writhing about;
and the elm lay on the ground, and the laurel dusted its foliage,
and the pine, self-uprooted, leaned upon the neighbouring fir.
While the Earth-shaker, a furious wind beneath the earth,
uprooted the recess of the nether haunts,
meanwhile there came another, newer evil; for the wood-dwelling
Nysaean women, smitten by the lash of serpent-haired Megaera,
bellowed like bulls,
destroyers of their own children; and rushing,
one hurled into the air a wandering boy
who from the air slipped headlong into the dust,
another dragged her own babe, and remembered not the breast;
another reddened her hand with child-slaying iron,
having carved up her son, and became a maenad like Agave.
And they ran upon their own children, and the newborn
sons, whom they had borne, they cut up with the knife . . .
another, cowering beneath the maddening lash of Pan,
an Arabian shepherd raved into the field-dwelling battle-cry.
Such things the herdsman, surging with frenzied guile,
carved up his own children, and feasted on his sons
with child-devouring jaws; and of the mind-shaken herdsmen
the belly entombed the unnursed male offspring . . .
by the hands of the Nymphs. And by the much-bending leaves
fastened all around he was fettered, and bent no knee to Lyaeus,
stretched no hand to Zeus, the warder-off of necessity,
held no fear of thunder; but threatening with his face
he raged against the Bassarids; and as it rushed upon his head
he marked the lightning, and yielded not to Lyaeus.
He was struck here and there, and against the scattered volleys
he stood, awaiting their counter-onset so great,
having Ares alone for helper, alone contending
with Zeus, Poseidon, Rhea, Earth, Nereus, Bacchus.
And toiling he hurled out an unbridled cry:
"Kindle fire, let us burn the whole plant; into the fire let these
Bacchic leaves be cast, and through the sea, ablaze,
let us hurl the vines upon Dionysus beneath the waves,
the token of Arabian manhood; but even
Thetis herself, receiving on her wave the fire-burnt fruit,
let her quench the vine-ash in the sea.
Loose these phantoms and the shifting witchcraft of bonds;
these I deem the Nereids' Poseidonian witchcraft;
loose them, and bring me near the surges; for against
the prophetic, sorcerous Proteus I arm myself; kindle the pine,
that going beside the sea, with my avenging heart,
I may burn down Melicertes, the host of Bromios."
He spoke, threatening both Nereus and Dionysus . . .
He came near to Arabia; and her son weary of
the woody fray, the son of the War-god, she revived,
holding the iron sword of Ares, and against the Bacchants
she bared the gleaming back of the demonic knife,
flashing it to terror against the female Cybelid war;
and cutting through the leaves of Ambrosia with the iron
she unbound the clustering bonds of Lycurgus.
And she soothed the dark-haired shaker of the earth,
her own brother, and Zeus her husband, and her mother Rhea,
rescuing Lycurgus, that he might be numbered
among the immortals; and the Arabs upon their savoury altars,
as to a god, propitiated the son of Dryas with sacrifices,
instead of Dionysus's honey-dropping fruit
pouring gore in libation to unbacchic Lycurgus.
And so old Time was destined to accomplish these things late;
but Zeus the father, lest any proud mortal man,
another bearing the likeness of spear-bold Lycurgus,
should raise reproach against blameless Dionysus,
made maddened Lycurgus a blind wanderer,
a wayfarer turning back and forth through an unknown city,
seeking a guide for his needful path,
often stumbling against his own self with his sandals.
And these things were among the crags. But in the Erythraean sea
the daughters of Nereus within the deep-billowed court
propitiated Dionysus at a sea-table;
and casting off her envy of Semele's heaven-sent bed,
striking up a bold hymn to wine-nurturing Lyaeus,
the nurse of Dionysus sang, sea-dwelling Ino;
and for Bromios, drawing sweet nectar from the bowl,
his foster-brother, equal in years, Melicertes poured the wine.
So he abode there within the deep-billowed court,
holding the wide sea for his house, a wanderer beneath the waves;
and poured out he reclined in the weed-grown bosom of Thetis;
and unsated he embraced his Cadmean nurse, fair in children,
the very sister of his mother Ino,
and often clasped Palaemon with a friendly embrace,
his foster-brother, equal in years. But with noiseless sandal,
no longer striking up the much-coiling dance,
since Bacchus was not present, the Mimallon was distraught,
seeking the tracks of sea-faring Lyaeus;
and the toil-loving Satyr, with an unlaughing face,
wearied with a strange grief, and on mountain-roaming hooves
the frenzied wandering Pans ran through the woods,
the Pans, searchers for the unheralded Dionysus;
and Silenus, undancing, casting away the heedless cymbals,
lay downcast; and the Cronian Nymph
Macris was distraught, the nurse of grief-free Dionysus,
the chariot-mate of the well-greaved Bacchic wagon.
So they were shaken, downcast; and to the grieving ones
Scelmis, leaving the recess of the waveless sea,
drove his father's wagon, untouched by water,
heralding the return of the coming Dionysus.
While Bacchus was busied with the sea-nourished feasts of the table,
meanwhile through the Caucasian mountain to the city of the Indians
the wind-footed herald of wine-nurturing Bromios came,
bull-shaped, holding a counterfeit form in his horn-drawn shape,
the answering likeness of the lunar horns,
having fastened about his body the skin of a mountain-roaming goat,
let down from the collarbone over one shoulder,
hanging from the right side to the fold of his thigh,
shaking the ears on either side of both cheeks,
like a long-eared ass, shaggy of body; and from the middle
of his loins a kindred tail trailed self-coiling.
And around him laughing the swarthy Indians flocked,
until he came near, where on a twin-yoked car
sat towering Deriades, leader of men,
checking the standing tread of his lofty elephants.
And laughing at the Satyr he cried out a mocking voice:
"What two-coloured men bull-shaped Dionysus
sends to Deriades, the playthings of war,
of strange nature, not men of wholly mortal form,
but holding the shape of beasts, since with twin form
they are mongrels, both bulls and men; for both
the shape of an ox they hold and a man's face."
He spoke, and displaying the forewarning signs of war
he struck his dappled-backed shield with his unsparing knife
upon the midmost circling boss; and from the oxhide
the bronze, as it was struck, boomed a deadly echo.
And loosing his lips, amazed before the grim king,
the swift-running herald spoke the message of Bromios:
"Deriades, sceptred lord, the god Dionysus commands
that the Indians, receiving the wine of the care-banishing fruit,
pour libation to the immortals, without wars, without toils;
but if they will not receive it, he arms himself, until with his thyrsoi
he bends the servile knee of Hydaspes to the Bassarids.
You have heard the true message; speak also yourself
to me who ask some word, that I may report it to Dionysus."
So he spoke, and the sceptred king belched out a raging voice:
"Alas, what a word the bold man-beast has spoken.
I am ashamed to subdue a herald with warlike hand,
who holds no rushing spear and touches no oxhide.
I have heard all that your champion has suffered; Ganges has heard
of the weakness of Bromios and the manhood of Lycurgus;
I know your king, a bastard god, when fleeing
he slipped into the deep of the evil-warding sea.
And your Bacchus is reported fiery, since from his mother's
flanks he rose, of thunder-stricken Thyone;
and water is far stronger than fire; if he wishes,
with his seething flood my father, the Indian Hydaspes,
could quench the fire-breathing blast of Zeus's thunderbolt.
And if you wish, bend your foot to the neighbouring land of the Medes;
going there, proclaim the dancing-rounds of Dionysus.
Plunge into the Bactrian soil, where the god Mithras arose,
the Assyrian Phaethon in Persia; for Deriades
has not learned the dance of the heavenly blessed ones, nor honours
the sun and Zeus and the choir of bright-shining stars.
Not Cronus, not Cronion the destroyer of his father did I learn of,
not crooked-counselled Cronus, the devourer of his own children,
who reaped the plant-sowing swarm of the Loves of heaven.
I know not your gifts and what you have named the fruit;
I receive no other drink after golden Hydaspes;
my wine is the spear, and my drink in turn is the oxhide.
Semele did not bear me in a fire-stricken wedding,
receiving the murderous flame in her chamber, but bronze-clad
Enyo, insatiable of battles, reared me.
I care not for the blessed children of Zeus; for both
alone are gods to me, both Earth and Water.
Go and proclaim these things to war-shunning Dionysus;
begone, fleeing unattainable, while I still hold back my bow,
begone, fleeing my spear; and arming for battle
your half-formed beasts and your unarmoured women
make war against Deriades, and after the Indian victory
I will in turn drag you as a runner-mate to spear-won Dionysus.
Yet I will not make you my messenger; for you cannot
hold a servile, house-keeping task; but with your long
ears flapping at the feasts I will let you be."
So speaking he sent him off with a threatening face;
and scoring the middle hollow of a folded tablet
the swift-tongued one wrote such a word on the two-leaved board:
"If you can, Dionysus, arm yourself against Deriades."
Hearing such things the loud herald ran back again.
And he found the Silenoi rejoicing; for coming up
from the surges Dionysus mingled with the mountain Nymphs;
and the Satyrs leaped, and the Bacchants danced,
and with aged feet Maron led the song,
leaning his arm upon the neck of a double Bacchant,
in the midst, gushing forth the fragrant pour of wine;
and unveiled the Mimallon shouted out a song,
singing of the track of homeward-returned Dionysus.
And the vine-god cast off his former cares,
and entered upon delight, since within the sea he had learned
all things, hearing from Toronaean Proteus,
the earth-shaking heave of the unhospitable Arabs' soil,
and tottering Lycurgus, a blind wanderer on his own foot;
he heard too of the death-bringing frenzy of the herdsman's compulsion,
how the choir of the field-dwellers was driven raving, how in the glens
the women carved up their own offspring;
and he heard of the choir of the heavenly Hyades, he heard of
Ambrosia herself, rising after earth to Olympus,
Ambrosia arming herself against unwearying Lycurgus,
and the leafy fray and the vine-clad war.
And as they delighted the herald came running back,
unharmed, much-prayed-for, to exulting Dionysus,
telling of the high-necked folly of Deriades,
holding the twofold tablet pregnant with war.
Nor did the lord neglect it; and to battle the warriors
he boldly summoned, knowing the forewarning
signs of Deriades scored upon the witnessing tablet.
And calling the wandering Rhadamanes, whom once from the soil
of Crete Minos drove unwilling from the land
to the shore of Arabia, he bade them at Rhea's nod
fasten ship-timbers for a sea-war against the Indians.
And swiftly he drove his Eastern car to the region of the land,
flashing in his arms like the Morning Star; and around the rock
Caucasian, passing through its crested hollow,
he skirted the light-bearing shore of the Eastern soil,
journeying to the noonday starting-post of the sun.
While the voice of thyrsus-bearing battle was heard,
and the near-marching army of mountain-dwelling Dionysus,
meanwhile Deriades set a thick ambush of Indians,
sending his army unyoked to the opposite land,
entrusting all his guile-contrived hope of war
to bronze-clad Ares; and he sailed high upon his ships,
having oared his host across the Indian Hydaspes.
And in two armies the war of the Indians was divided
on either shore of the spear-bearing river:
Thureus by the ankle of Zephyrus, and Deriades
came near the opposite bank by the wing of swarthy Eurus.
And there was a shady place there, where with thick
shoots of every kind the wide-stretching ridge of the wood
was girt, and there was a hollow cave; and flying
never did the wandering arrow score those trees,
if one should shoot, and never in the midst of the thickets
was the sun carried, rushing down with a swift heave,
scoring the close-woven leaves with its inmost rays,
nor did the air-roaming flood sink through the shady wood
from rainy Zeus, but scarcely, with a trailing of water,
did Zeus's high-shining shower wet the tips of the leaves.
There in the long-trunked groves thievish Ares
was hidden among the green clusters of the lofty plants,
unforeseen, unshaken, and in the woody bosom
he held the guarded gait of his noiseless sandals,
not raking through the leafy thicket with secret foot,
holding no fear of a crouching foot, no chattering echo
with stammering lip, and no pallor about his face;
but he held a bold and steadfast mind, and on the ground-couch
sleeping a measured armoured sleep upon his eyelids . . .
awaiting the well-ordered battle-cry of the coming army.

22. The second-and-twentieth book sings the strife of Bromius and the deeds
that Aeacus accomplished on the plain and at the Hydaspes.

But when the company of Bacchus came on foot to the ford
of the pebble-strewn river, there where, in its deep-eddying gulf,
the Indian Hydaspes pours out its sailable water like the Nile,
then the women's song of the Bassarids made melody,
striking up the Phrygian revel-rout for Lyaeus the Lord of Night,
and the chorus of shaggy Satyrs roared with the mystic voice;
all the earth laughed, and the rocks lowed in answer,
the Naiads raised the ritual cry, and over the river the Nymphs
girdled themselves in spiral coils with the silent streams
and sang in tune the partnered measure of the Sicilian song,
such as the hymn-singing Sirens used to strike up
from their honey-tongued throats; and the whole thicket quivered,
and the wise oaks uttered a melody like the pipe,
and the Hamadryads shrilled, and on a leafy spray
a Nymph, half-seen, peered over a cluster and sang.
With snow-white milk the welling spring turned pale,
though it was all of water, and in the ravine's hollow
the Naiads bathed in milky streams,
and drank the white milk; and from its reddening breast
the hard rock blushed, belching out wine,
spurting new must from the unplanted hill
in pleasant-to-drink trickles; and from self-flowing bosoms
poured the sweet gifts of the honey-dripping bee
with no need of hives; and from bushes new-born
the apple of the sharp-haired thorn ran up downy;
and as oil flowed of itself over the topmost boughs,
the tree of Athena was bathed in unpressed moisture.
And hares embraced the dancing hounds;
the long serpents reveled in the dance,
licking the footprints of viper-haired Dionysus,
bending their necks aside, and one over another belched out
a gentle hiss from its rejoicing throat;
the delighted serpent kept then a measured rhythm,
and the coiling trail of its long spine wound about
as it leapt around the fearless feet of Dionysus.
Spiraling and bounding over the Indian crag
the tigers sported; and within the thicket a great swarm
of mountain-roaming elephants sprang up.
And then over the rugged glens the wandering Pans
ran across the unwalkable mountains on slender hooves,
the shuddering heights, where no bold light bird flew as wayfarer . . .
he measured the high-pathed wings with twin beating
and, tossing the loose tress beside his throat,
the lion as comrade danced opposite the leaping boar;
and the birds cried aloud the likeness of human song,
filching its imitating, half-finished strain,
prophesying the victory of the India-slaying struggle,
and over their green limbs they shook out at length
the upright trailing tail; and in the same eager dance
the leopard, high-leaping, ran beside the bear as its running-mate.
And Artemis reined back the rush of her dappled whelps
when she saw the gentle lioness make its dance-treading leap;
ashamed, she unstrung her well-curved bowstring,
that she might not shoot with shafts the beasts at their delight.
And one who beheld the strange marvels of Bacchus,
casting his eye through the topmost dense cluster,
folding the leaves about the watching circle of his sight,
let himself see only so much as a man peers around
with painted eyes peering through a helmet's slot,
or as when a man skilled in the tragic chorus,
holding a fearful bellow from his long-sounding throat,
strains his inmost eye through a fashioned eye,
wearing the false semblance of a mortal face.
So he, hiding from all the marvels beneath the shady wood,
watched unseen with a face that stole its glances;
and he reported to the foe; and Thoureus quivered with fear,
finding fault with Morrheus and with senseless Deriades.
The Indian host trembled, and heedless of battle
shook from their fearful hands the bronze armor,
gazing at the trees shaken by the frenzied rush.
And now the Indian host would have taken from the neighboring bank
the gray olive-bough, witness of supplication,
and bent a slavish neck to unconquered Dionysus;
but Hera of many devices, changing her shape,
emboldened the enemy and deceived the chief of the Indians,
fastening upon Dionysus a Thessalian magic hymn,
and the brew of Circe with god-summoning incantations,
such as the enchantment of a river beyond all enchanting.
And she persuaded the foe, quick to obey; and she told each
that no one, held fast by burning thirst, should ever stumble
by drinking the beguiled water of the mind-stealing river.
And now, leaping out from the unseen river-bed,
the fiery Indians would have fallen on the feasting armies;
but a Hamadryad Nymph, peering over a wind-stirred cluster,
sprang up from the leafy hollow;
holding a thyrsus in her hand, in form she seemed a Bacchant,
her hair wreathed in mimic ivy of the oak;
and telling of the foes' guile, with a silence that signals treachery,
she whispered into the ears of clustering Lyaeus:
"Vine-clad Dionysus, plant-tending lord of fruits,
your plant will grant grace and beauty to the Hamadryads;
I was not born a Bassarid, I am no comrade of Lyaeus,
only in my hand I lift a counterfeit thyrsus;
I am not from Phrygia, your fatherland, nor do I dwell
in the land of the Lydians by the stream of the wealth-flowing river;
I am a fair-leaved Hamadryad, here where the warriors,
your foes, lie in ambush; and, careless of my own country,
I will save your army from death; for to your
Satyrs I bring loyalty, Indian though I am,
and instead of Deriades I am of one mind with Dionysus;
for I will grant you the grace I owe, because the moist pangs
of his streams, and the oaks he ever nourishes
with rainy drops, great father Zeus the Rain-giver supplies.
Give me your leaves, and here I will plant them;
give me your clusters, which loosen cares.
But, dear one, do not hasten to cross the river's flood,
lest the neighboring Indians press upon you in the water;
turn your eye to the trees, and beside the leafy thicket
spy out unforeseen the ambush of men in hiding.
Yet what will the cowards within the thicket do to you?
The foes live only while you still hold back your thyrsus.
Be silent on our account, lest the enemy hear nearby,
lest Hydaspes report it to the hidden Indians."
So saying, the Hamadryad Nymph turned back and departed,
like a wing or a thought, and changing her form,
like a bird she ran through the wood of her lair,
darting up to her own oak; while in silence
he mingled with the Bassarids, and of the Hamadryad goddess
spoke the word into the ears of each of his champions,
nodding with his glances, and in thoughtful silence bade them,
armed in their gear, to feast among the oaks,
and told of the guile of the hidden, plot-weaving Indians,
lest the warriors press upon them unarmored,
while they still feasted through the host; and they obeyed
Lyaeus when he called, and were ready for battle
beside the silent dinner of the spear-bearing table.
And after the swift meal the shield-bearers flowed in
from the neighboring river to drink the after-dinner water,
at the divine nods of all-clever Dionysus,
lest drink and slumber and darkness lull the host to sleep.
And here and there the army fell on a war-loving bed,
snatching a little sleep upon the shield of battle.
But father Zeus, turning aside the guileful mind of the Indians,
checked the evening battle with a bellowing roar,
pouring out the boundless din of an all-night rain.
But when snow-footed Dawn, scoring the darkness away,
gathering the morning, blushed upon the dewy rock,
the foes, peering over the topmost screen of the battle-rousing wood,
rushed forward in a mass; and Thoureus led them,
the monstrous champion of the Indian war, like in his charge
to towering Typhon darting down at the thunderbolt.
And the armies, at the cunning nod of wise Bacchus,
held a feigned fear, undismayed, and from the battle
withdrew of their own will, willingly, until the Indians
poured out into the plain, having left the cover of the thicket.
In rich armor the Lydian man was arrayed,
bearing the gold-gleaming likeness of Lycian Glaucus,
proclaiming his own land, where on the bank of the Pactolus
the bright wealth of the reddening dew glitters,
and he flashed with rosy gleams facing the Dawn,
shaking the golden front of his wealth-flowing helmet,
that Lydian man, far-conspicuous, and from the breast of the bearer
a radiance shone from his reddening tunic;
and shaking the gleaming helm upon his temple,
another champion from Alybe, excelling for Dionysus,
displayed his fatherland's wealth, and from his bright head
the marble gleam of the silver helmet shone,
casting a light equal to the snowy Moon.
And the god, never standing still, terrified all the warriors
of the foe, holding no bared sword, brandishing no spear,
but borne through the midst of the champions, like the breezes,
he wheeled the right wing of the battle from the left,
hurling the long-shadowing thyrsus, with the flower of the earth,
cleaving the cloud of Indians with his ivy-spear.
Neither did high-headed, so-mighty Thoureus drive him back,
nor the host, nor any other champion; poured upon one another
they gave way here and there before onrushing Dionysus.
And Oeagrus shook up the dark War-goddess,
insatiate, mowing the ranks of close-pressed men,
cutting the helmet-glancing harvest with his Bistonian spear.
As when a river, pouring forth its stormy strength,
restless, comes down from the crag in a ravine-cut stream,
borne onto the plain, and not even the vineyards themselves
with unbroken fences hold it back
as it scrapes the midst of a stone bridge's back;
many a pine was rolled along, and many a fallen
high-seen fir, torn up by the roots, was dragged in the flood;
so he ranged the army of the foes, one after another,
slaying the footmen as he turned about with his Sithonian lance,
and they ringed him round, and built up about him
what the warriors call the mimic tortoise of shields;
foot was set firm to foot, and shield leaned
against shield, in turn each neighbor's shield crowding the next,
and crest nodded to crest, and near at hand
man touched man; and as the dust rose
the warriors whitened with the hooves of horses.
There whom first, whom last, sending to Hades,
did Oeagrus, citizen of the Bistonian soil, reap,
slaying one here and another there, having fulfilled for his wife
the deeds, said to fall short of the famed Calliope?
This one above the breast with his swift spear, that one cleaving
with the hilted sword across the neck, and another
maddened foe he pierced beside the navel, and from the deadly
wound he drew out his spear, and as it was dragged
he tore out the warm bowels with the bloody iron;
and at another's fighting he ran down dragging his sword,
and with the keen blade he cut off the hand, and it, falling,
blood-soaked, quivered upon the ground, the leaping hand;
and the hand was severed, yet did not let go the shield,
gripping at the edge the dusty shield-strap;
and the wind-roving soul, leaping up from the dead man,
longed for the wonted vigor of the body it had clasped.
Another he crushed, striking with his unsparing spear,
piercing the tips of the arm with the whetted point,
and with the sword he struck the shield, and as it was beaten by the iron
the unbroken, central-bossed back of the oxhide rang.
But he, shaken by the raging frenzy of battle,
brandished his spear, shifting it with circling craft
either on both sides of the flank, or of the neck, or near the shoulder;
and shaking here and there the back-whirling point,
he cut through the midst of the crowded battle-press,
swift, seated high upon his crest-lifting horse.
As when, after the dark season of chill winter,
the air appears, stripped bare of unsheltered clouds,
receiving the clear gleam of the springtime light;
so he, reveling, the fearless man, stripped bare
the middle battle of the splitting Indians' close ranks.
And then one, driving his bronze against a champion's mouth,
struck the right jaw-beard with his ghastly knife;
and one, hurling a din against the foes through the air,
sent a wandering stone toward a high-pathed mark,
and the air-roving rock crashed upon a head,
and dashed away the crest of a well-helmed plume,
when the neck-fastening bond was loosed beside the throat;
and as it rolled the head of the bearer was laid bare.
Not the men alone roared then, but the very
horses, bronze-clad, crashed in War,
trumpeting Ares with their warlike neighing.
And the maiden of the later voice, from the mountain-dwelling throats,
answering their din with her rocky mouths,
imitating Echo neighed the war-song.
And many a newly-slaughtered corpse rolled on the fields,
spitting out the warm stream of blood; and as men perished,
some hung dead upon their sides,
one, struck, writhed with his gashed flank,
another rolled over the ground in the poured dust,
another was propped beside the navel, and one upon the earth
leapt over the head of a quivering man,
and one, falling, cried out, struck in the throat,
and twisted his feet about in the dance of death;
and another lay face-down, and as though wroth with his slayer,
wide-mouthed he clenched the earth with maddened tooth.
As another was struck by the long-barbed iron,
the white tunic reddened with gore from the spearman;
as another fought, from the stretched bows
his blood-soaked thigh was grazed by the winged arrow.
And one, pressing his trumpet vainly to his lips,
that hostile man, sounded the strain of battle-rousing echo,
drawing his shrinking, fleeing host into the fray.
And the Indians, hearing the cry, streamed to the tumult.
Emboldened, they laid hold of the returning struggle,
ashamed to appear before their king outside the victory.
And many a well-armored warrior, crown-like in one place,
ringed round Aeacus where he sped.
But he, hemmed in their midst, was overborne—not by helmet,
not trusting in shields nor in the breastplate of battle;
but, sheathed instead of iron in his father's gift,
Athena walled him round wholly with unbreakable clouds,
with which once she quenched the drought of the rainless field,
bringing life-giving water to the thirsty earth
when Zeus rained, and of the sheaf-bearing earth
the well-laboring furrows were wedded to the plow;
and in the midst of his foes, ringed round, the inspired man
crushed some with his swift spear, some with the sword,
some with hard stones; and the ground reddened with gore
as the Indians were slain, and by the unbending man's spear
lay a heap of widely-scattered corpses, of whom one
half-dead still quivered, another, beating the ground with his feet,
on his back, self-rolling, kept company with a neighbor's doom;
and they crowded the ground, and corpse leaned on corpse
laid down by measure, and from the freshly-cut throat
the cold body was warmed by the reddening gore;
and the slaughter was unspeakable, and as men fell one upon another
the earth grew dark, drenched with the channel of blood,
and pitying her sons, in a ravine-voice she spoke:
"Son of Zeus, life-giving, blood-stained—for you rule too
over the fruit-bearing rain and over the bloody snowfall—
with rain you watered all the teeming vineyard
of Hellas, but the Indian furrow you flooded with gore;
once sheaf-bearing, now death-bearing; for the husbandmen
your snowfall found the ear of grain, but you reaped the Indian host,
mowing men like a harvest; and you bring both:
from Zeus you lead the rain, from Ares you snow with blood."
So spoke life-bearing Earth. But the son of Cronus
roared from heaven, and to the slaughter of the Indians
the trumpet of Zeus summoned Aeacus with thunderous crashes.
And one among the foes, stretching his eye toward Aeacus,
sent a shaft, and Athena turned aside the arrow,
which but grazed the thigh, only so much as to scratch the skin's surface.
But still more, painless, Aeacus fought into the midst of the Indians,
never standing still, since the shaft touched his thigh
like a man's slender fingernail, when it scratches the skin's edge.
And one man, unovertaken, withdrew, a footman wayfarer,
on swifter feet, and wished to plunge into the neighboring
thicket where before he had hidden; and pursuing him
Erechtheus drove his wind-footed horse in the chase;
but when he had reached him by as much as the upright rush
of a flying spear stretches when a champion has cast it,
then, throwing himself behind his back, the footman stood
facing him, awaiting the horseman; but he, bending,
fixed his left foot to the earth on bent knee,
aslant upon his flanks, and of his back-strained ankle
he raised the sole high in the air, stretching upright
the toes of his right foot fixed firm to the ground,
holding an Indian shield of seven oxhides, the likeness of a tower,
holding a bared sharp sword; and thrusting before his face
his bronze-backed shield, the proud Indian rushed on,
either to die, or to strike the man, or to drive off the horse
with daring blade; and with the bossed iron,
aslant, checking the horse's jaw across its path,
on foot he shook the horseman above him;
and now he would have flung to the ground the citizen of motherless Athena,
but Erechtheus pierced him with his spear beside the navel's edge,
and the man, transfixed through the middle by the deadly sharp bronze,
he hurled to the ground; and he, in whirling rushes,
slid headlong from the air into the dust,
turning his head like a tumbler in a dancer's leap.
Leaving him gasping, turning his horse's course,
the citizen of Athena charged upon other foes.
. . . bending his bow, and laying upon the string
upright the arrow stretched to the very iron tip,
he drew the shaft toward the mark; and to the noble-bearing bride
Calliope he entrusted all the hope of victory.
Nine long-barbed arrows he sent forth,
and slew nine men; and there was an equal number
of arrows sent and of warriors slain;
of these the wandering shaft split the brow's edge of one,
of another it scored the rim of the shaggy-breasted nipple,
another above the loins, and another, falling on the belly,
was borne into the very midst of the gashed flank,
and one ran through the side, and one, fixed upright
in the storm-swift sole of a fleeing man's feet,
pinned his foot to the ground with a binding fetter.
And he drew out the wind-roving shaft; and from his quiver
another being sent after another, one upon another,
a downpour of arrows rushed in an airy whirl.
As when a man driving bronze on a bronze anvil
with tireless hammer sends out a fire-roaring sound,
striking the neighboring lump of metal, and many leap forth,
bounding sparks from the beaten iron,
warming the air, and with alternate blows
one was foremost, one near, another, leaping up,
overtakes another still leaping with fiery bound;
so he, shooting at the host of Indians facing him
as they fought, scattered them from his unwearying bow,
slaying one here, another there, with arrow upon arrow.
And as the middle phalanx shrank from the cloud of shafts
the space was laid bare, the likeness of the horned Moon
shining on both sides, when, gleaming a little from her horn,
she has filled the two tips with new-born radiance
and with leaning rays scores the middle of her circle,
divided by twofold soft fire; and the middle
of the still-gashed Moon's disk was seen laid bare.
Nor did Aeacus cease from battle, fighting beside Dionysus,
undismayed, and he reveled in the tumult,
slaying here and there; and pursuing them from the plain
he led the wandering folk into the river's mouths.
United, the warriors ringed round a single man
struck with swords, yet heeding neither blade
nor winged shaft; and with blow upon blow
the swift man mowed the iron harvest of the dark battle
and fought against all, some on the banks,
others below in the river, slaughtering with warlike hand;
and he filled all the stream with corpses; and as men perished,
murmuring with blood, the white Hydaspes reddened.
And one man, fleeing the windy rush of the champion,
headlong, self-rolling, slid into the stream,
and many a freshly-slaughtered corpse, by the spearman's iron,
was dragged, borne in the wavy flood,
its limbs swollen; and in the gore beneath the water
the Naiads bathed in the blood-red stream,
and the black water was reddened with bloody trickles.
And many in the river-mouths, casting away their points,
showed forth supplication, unarmed, one on the banks,
one stretched out beside the sands, and one on the ground
upright on bent knee, bending his curving neck;
but Aeacus refused their prayers with face uplifted,
raising unbending wrath against his foes;
and the spearman without iron, still touching prayer,
not one Lycaon alone he slew, but his foes,
rolling on the ground with unarmored hands,
he slaughtered without number, defiling the river's stream;
and the Hydaspes received many an Asteropaeus as a corpse.
Nor was it without a god that Aeacus too made war; for his foes,
as the father of Peleus, slaughtering within the river,
he held a watery battle and a watery War,
as though prophesying about the flood of the river Scamander
the half-finished struggle to come for Achilles;
and the battle of the grandsire foretold the battle of the grandson.
And one Nymph in the river-mouths cried out, sandalless,
a Naiad without veil, peering over the streams:
"Kinsman of the Naiads, bearing Zeus-descended blood,
pity the holy water of the Zeus-fallen river.
Your spear has slain Indians enough; cease for the Nymphs
to rouse tears in the tearless Naiads;
a watery Naiad was your mother too;
for I hear that your Aegina is the daughter of a river.
Remember who bore you, and no longer defile the stream.
I will go to another stream undefiled, I go into the sea.
And sea-Thetis receives me; but let this bloody stream
be the care of the Fury and of Dionysus."

24. The four-and-twentieth holds the boundless lament of the Indians,
and the shuttle of the loom-laboring Aphrodite, and her distaff.

But father Zeus turned aside the threat of his angry son,
lashing the din of the close-woven clouds with thunder;
and he soothed the wrath of boundless Ocean,
restraining the fiery battle of Dionysus.
And Hera crashed a boundless echo through the air,
checking the wrath of fire-mighty Dionysus.
And stretching out a watery hand to merciful Bacchus,
to the fiery son of Zeus old Hydaspes shouted,
welling up a suppliant word from his throat:
"Spare me, Dionysus, the Zeus-fallen river,
showing favor to my fruit-bearing waters; for from your
waters there sprang up the fair-clustered vintage.
I erred, fire-nurtured Dionysus; for the heavenly
gleam of your torches proclaimed your lineage.
But longing for my children compelled me; for to Deriades,
my son, bringing loyalty, I roused the threat of my surges,
rolling a helping swell for the slaughtered Indians.
I am ashamed to appear before my father, because to the sea
I drag streams mingled with murmuring blood
and defile Poseidon with bloody drops;
this, this it was that armed me to strive with Dionysus.
But by your father of hosts and of suppliants,
have shame for the Hydaspes, hot and seething with your fire.
The Naiads flee my stream; and around my springs
one dwells in a watery home, another in the thickets,
companion of the Hamadryads, exchanging her plant for the sea,
another holds the Indus as an exile, and one, fleeing
on dusty feet, plunged into the thirsty Caucasian rock,
and another, darting away to the Choaspes,
dwells in foreign streams and no longer her father's water.
Do not destroy the reeds, the offspring of my streams,
on which, as they grow, leans the shoot of the vine,
the grape-bearing shoot; for the reeds, bound to one another,
buoy up your well-watered vintage;
do not burn the reeds, from which come your Mygdonian pipes,
lest your music-loving Athena ever reproach you,
she who once, finding the grim likeness of the Gorgons' heads
as they cried out, devised the Libyan form of the paired pipes;
and have shame for the song that steers your mystic strain,
the harmonious melody of the Pan-pipe;
cease to wither the river's stream with your fennel-stalk,
since the river's stream nourishes your fennel-stalks.
You have not crossed a foreign stream that bears your name; for another,
a different Dionysus I made bright in my baths,
the namesake of the younger Bromius, when the son of Cronus
entrusted Zagreus to my child-nurturing Nymphs;
and you too bear the whole body of Zagreus; but to him
grant a late-fulfilled favor, from whom you sprang; for from the heart
of that first-born, the much-sung Dionysus, you arose.
And honor the youth-nurturing water of your Lamus;
remember Maeonia your fatherland; for of your
gracious Pactolus the Hydaspes is the brother.
And you, now stretching one favor to so many rivers,
my kinsmen, rein back your radiance;
do not burn with fire the flood of waters; for from waters
sprang the lightning, the rainy fire of your Zeus.
But soften your wrath, since I fall at your knees,
spreading out a gentle, suppliant stream; for in his wars,
if Typhoeus had bent his bold neck and been gentle,
and, casting away the swelling, recoverable mass of his threat,
your father, high-ruling Zeus, would have checked the lightning."
So he spoke, and Dionysus reined back his pine-torch.
And the Northern wind fanned the river-mouths
with its wintry lash, bringing a stormy breeze,
cooling the stream of the fire-struck river,
honoring the sun and Bacchus and Zeus together,
and quenched the unquenched divine fire of the surges.
While Bacchus still sailed across the watery Hydaspes,
meanwhile, with the daring of Ares, an overmighty rush,
Deriades armed the Indians for the eponymous strife,
setting his ranks about the stream, that the warriors
might hold back the host of the Bacchae as they were still coming up.
Nor did it escape the all-seeing eye of Zeus; and swiftly
he was borne from heaven to shield Dionysus.
And going as helpers to their own, one after another,
with Zeus all the gods, dwellers of Olympus, came
with winged leap; and for the sake of Aegina's bed
the eagle hovered, a second time the high-flying Zeus,
after the stream of Asopus, and air-roving Aeacus,
gripping him with sparing talons, with snatching foot
he lifted and brought him into the war of Deriades,
to the Indian land; and from the broad-pathed gulf
his father Apollo saved his son Aristaeus,
bright, borne on his chariot of evil-warding swans,
keeping the memory of his bridal chamber with lion-slaying Cyrene;
and prevailing, long-winged Hermes snatched up his son,
the son of Penelope, horn-spreading, long-haired Pan;
and Urania rescued Hymenaeus from death,
namesake of her fruitful son, and the airy
paths she scored, like the track of a star,
showing favor to her clustering brother Dionysus;
and Calliope lifted Oeagrus on her shoulders;
and Hephaestus took thought for his children, the Cabeiri,
and snatched up both, like a swift flame;
and Pallas Athena of the headland saved Erechtheus,
the India-slayer, dweller of god-founded Athens;
and the Hamadryad Nymphs all the dwellers of Olympus
rescued, all who cared for the dear oaks; but beyond the rest
the laurel Apollo, appearing, saved the laurel-nymphs,
and together with him his mother helped them, his fellow-traveler,
Leto, still honoring the childbed-trees.
And the phalanx of the Bassarids and the cluster-bearing women
from the deep, loud-roaring tumult were rescued
by the daughters of Cydnus, the Zephyr-loving river,
who knew the watery floating course, whom for victory
in the Indian war their father gave to Bacchus,
Naiads skilled in battle, whom once the art of war
Cilician Typhoeus taught, when he warred with the son of Cronus.
And the host accompanied them, traveling together; but the eager ones
Euius outran, all of them, on his mountain-dwelling chariot
scoring the stream with the track of his unwetted axle;
and he held a course companioned with the Satyrs, with whom went the Bacchae,
water-faring, and the Pans as fellow-travelers; but beyond the rest
swifter the Telchines upon their sea-bred horses,
drivers of their father's sea-founded car,
joined the course of hastening Dionysus.
Others were behind, and they pressed on by the crossing,
coming up from another unseen path,
where the god led the way; since, gently quivering his wing,
the eagle led, Zeus in counterfeit form, across the mountain,
with sparing talons bearing his son aloft,
Aeacus borne high upon the airy path.
And they danced, leaping over the Indian crag,
and chased over the rocks, and dwelt in the thickets,
and pitched their tents in the gently shadowy wood . . .
and others held the fawn-chasing hunt of long-horned deer
along with their hounds; and with the Hamadryad Nymphs
the Water-nymphs of plant-loving Dionysus mingled.
And the phalanxes of the Bassarids, beside the Erythraean thicket,
nursed the cub of a mountain-dwelling lioness,
and their breasts welled up with the moisture of self-flowing milk;
another, pursuing her longing for the snaky cluster,
searched the caves of venom-shooting serpents through the mountain,
and displayed her hunting-craft; and with the casting thyrsus
one struck the storm-footed fawn; another, unseen,
with a maddened leap ran down a raging bear;
and one gripped the spine of black-hided beasts
and climbed the mane of the mountain-roaming elephants.
And one of the archers fitted a shaft to the curved string
and shot an elm; but another took an olive for his mark;
and another struck a pine; and a great whistle of arrows
sent forth hissed in the air toward a neighboring fir.
For them the mountain-sounding revel roared. But grieving,
Thoureus came to king Deriades, a bringer of ill news,
announcing with speechless tears the slaughter of the Indians,
and scarcely from his mouth lifted up his mournful voice:
"Sceptered Deriades, god-born scion of Enyo,
we went, as you bade, to the crag over against us,
we found in the glens a lonely neighboring thicket;
there we set our ambush and waited, until there should come
the thyrsus-mad Dionysus; and as Bacchus came on
the pipe crashed out, and as the rough oxhide
was beaten on both sides there was a bronze-clanging echo
and the noise of the syrinx; and the whole thicket quivered
and the oaks spoke and the hills danced;
the Naiads raised the ritual cry. And I armed the warriors,
shrinking, trembling, dragging the unwilling into battle.
And the god, whom they call by name, shaking his pointed thyrsi,
shooting the Indian race with his worthless leaves,
slew on the plain a boundless host struck by the sharp thyrsus,
and in the surges destroyed the remnant of the Indians.
But let us ask the wise Brahmans, that you may learn
whether this is a god come against us, or a mortal man.
Do not raise a useless nightly battle,
do not destroy your army in lightless war;
already the misty gloom is stretched out; and near at hand
the Evening Star gleams, checking the strife.
But if longing holds you for the hard-faced tumult,
hold back the Indian today, and tomorrow you draw them into battle."
So speaking, he persuaded the unyielding Deriades,
won over not for weakness' sake, but as one
finding fault with the setting Sun and not yielding to Lyaeus.
And withdrawing the Indian phalanx from the river,
overmighty Deriades retreated in mournful frenzy,
seated on the manes of his returning elephants.
And the Indians here and there with their towering king
sped into the city in flight, within their walls
hearing of the victory of war-mad Dionysus.
And already a mournful rumor flew through the town,
announcing the kindred slaughter of the newly-slain Indians.
And the lament was boundless; and of the dirge-loving women
the circles of their faces were scored with mourning nails,
and the tunics were rent at the middle of the breast,
baring their bosoms, and with alternate blows
beaten by their hands the rim of their breasts was reddened,
blood-soaked. And a gray old man on the threshold of old age
cut his snowy lock with downcast iron,
hearing that his four youthful sons had perished,
whom Aeacus had subdued with a single ghastly sword,
slaughtered piteously; and of the heavy-suffering women
one mourned her brother, another her father;
another, a bride with varied tears, lamented
her bridegroom newly-wed, like Protesilaus,
another a Laodameia; and of the newly-yoked bride
the unbraided, veilless cluster of her hair was torn.
And one, the helpless wife of a fallen Indian,
having fulfilled the near-birth pangs of childbed
and beholding the tenth childbearing circle of the Moon,
much-weeping, mourned her husband's watery death,
and wrathful at the river broke into a wailing cry:
"I will never drink my bitter fatherly Hydaspes;
no longer do I pass by those streams, no longer, wretched,
shall I touch the river that has hidden your corpse,
no, by you and by your burden that I bear within my womb,
no, by the love that time does not know how to wither.
Who will take and carry me to where my dead husband fell,
that I may embrace the watery corpse, that the wave
may hide me too with my water-faring husband?
Would that I had borne a son and reared him; but now, wretched,
the swell of my belly holds me, my childbirth ripening.
And if I ever bear a child and he asks for his father,
to my son, calling for his papa, how shall I show his father?"
She spoke to the husband who did not hear, lamenting.
And another mourned the unwedded wedding-songs
of her dying suitor, whom the marriageable season did not see
crowned with a bridal wreath, nor in the bridal chamber
did the sweet-sounding, life-saving pipe of the Loves sing.
For them in their grief was the lament. But around the thickets
Bacchus, with his Satyrs and his India-slaying warriors,
held a feast; and bulls were carved,
and heifers in rows were cut up with the knife,
struck with axes, and from the Erythraean flock
thick herds of spear-won sheep were sacrificed.
And sitting in throngs at the well-rounded table
the Sileni and the Satyrs with fair-thyrsused Dionysus
with their many hands touched a single feast;
and boundless wine was drunk in turn; and the cup-bearers
emptied the fragrant, countless wine-jars,
drawing the blameless grape of the nectarous vintage.
And as they took their delight, singing beside the mixing-bowl,
the Lesbian, self-taught Leucus wove a song,
how the former Titans armed themselves against Olympus;
and he sang the true victory of high-ruling Zeus,
how broad-bearded Cronus, sinking beneath the thunderbolt,
he sealed in the dark Tartarean gulf,
armed in vain with the watery weapons of winter.
And Lapethus, citizen of the unarmed Cyprian soil,
sat beside the thoughtful harper, and offered him
a rich portion of the feast, and asked him to sing
that delightful tale, dear to never-silent Athens,
of loom-laboring Cythereia striving with Athena.
And he, playing the lyre, struck up to sing of Cypris,
how once, holding the goad of distaff-loving care,
with unpracticed hands she went after the loom of Athena,
lifting the shuttle and no longer the girdle of the Loves.
And the thick thread of the Paphian was stretched, like a long
twisted withy-cord, well-plaited, such as by some craft
in long stretches an old shipwright stitches,
fencing the newly-finished, gaping timbers of ships;
and she all day and all night beside the loom
made and unmade Pallas' work, and with a strange,
unwonted toil she wore out her untoughened hands;
and with the many-toothed comb scraping the cloth
and hanging the dancing weight at the middle
of the shuttle, she wove a robe, and Cypris became Athena;
and the toil was without laughter; and as the robe was woven
the broad thread swelled monstrous; and of themselves
the warp-threads broke as the cloth thickened;
and she had as witnesses of her twofold labor's craft
the sun and the lamp and the necessary Moon.
Not for her did the dancing handmaids of the Paphian
dance the dance of Orchomenos; but with a whirling rush
Pasithea twirled the spindle, and Peitho became a wool-worker,
and Aglaia gave the thread and the spun yarn to her mistress.
And the life of mortal marriages wandered astray; and the harmony
of unwedded wedding-songs, useless,
old Aion, charioteer of life, lamented in dismay;
and unhonored Love unstrung his fiery bowstring,
gazing at the unbegotten, unplowed furrow of the world.
Then was no lovely sound of lyres, then no syrinx,
no clear pipe sang, shrilling "Hymen, O Hymenaeus";
but as life dwindled and the race was lashed,
the bars of the indissoluble yoke were heaved aside.
And toil-enduring Athena saw the labor-loving Paphian,
and held wrath mingled with laughter, when she saw the long,
rough cord of the labor-untried Cythereia;
and she announced it to the immortals; and with heavy-jealous purpose
she spoke, finding fault both with Cypris and with her father:
"Your gift, heavenly Zeus, comes shifting and inconstant;
no longer do I hold the gift of the Fates; for the loom-laborer,
your daughter Aphrodite, has plundered my lot.
Lady Hera did not seize Athena's lot,
the sister and consort of my Zeus, but she vexes
Agelaia, armed with shields from birth,
that steward of bridal chambers, the tender goddess. But of your kind
when did unwarlike Cythereia fight in the front of Olympus,
or what Titans did she destroy with her womanish girdle,
that after wars she now does me violence? But you yourself,
tell me, Archeress, when from the midst of your forest
did you ever see Athena shooting or hunting?
Who calls on the gray-eyed one when women are in labor?"
As she spoke, the gods, dwellers of Olympus, gathered,
wishing to see Aphrodite plying the loom.
And beholding the labors of the battle-untried Cythereia,
in wonder they ringed round the goddess's counterfeit work;
and laughing, mockery-loving Hermes spoke again:
"You hold a loom, Cythereia; leave your girdle to Athena.
If you handle the thread, if you stretch the shuttle with your hands,
take up also the rushing spear and the aegis of Tritogeneia.
I know, Cythereia, from where you weave the much-clattering loom;
your guile does not escape me; perhaps your bridegroom Ares
demands of you lovely tunics for the wedding.
Weave a robe for Ares; but on the newly-spun robe
do not embroider a shield; for what has Aphrodite to do with shields?
Make Phaethon the light-bearing witness of your bed,
announcing the thief who plundered your couch in secret;
if you wish, embroider also your ancient bonds,
and let a modest hand fashion the god, the bastard husband;
and you too, Love, after your bow, twirling your spindle,
make threads for your mother, distaff-loving Cythereia,
that after the winged one I may call you a loom-laborer too,
and after the ox-string sinews behold the fiery god
drawing out the spool past the thread instead of arrows.
In gold fashion Ares beside golden Aphrodite,
carrying a shuttle in his hand and not brandishing an oxhide shield,
embroidering a double cloak with the work-laboring Cythereia.
But, goddess Cythereia, from your distaff-loving hands
cast the threads to the winds and busy yourself with your girdle-strap,
and take thought for wedlock a second time; for the first-born
world still wanders astray, while you still weave a robe."
So he spoke, and they smiled, all the dwellers of Olympus.
And casting away the half-finished thread of the cloth,
ashamed before the gray-eyed one, Cythereia went up
to her own Cyprus, the nurse of the human race;
and Love once more fitted the shifting-formed life to his girdle,
sowing the childbed-circle of the well-plowed world.
Such a lovely-voiced song Leucus wove,
hymning Aphrodite, untaught in the distaff,
who had raised a great quarrel with the work-laboring Athena.

But when there was satiety of the wine-loving table,
welling up wine, they fell on the lonely bed;
some on the broidered fawnskin, some on leaves
spread out, others, above the poured dust,
strewed a pallet for themselves with goatskins;
and others kept company with battle-rousing dreams,
spreading their bronze bodies in warlike sleep,
of whom one struck an Indian seated high upon a horse,
another pierced an Indian on the neck, and one, slaughtering,
struck a footman with his sword, and one wounded Deriades;
and another, sending his air-roving shaft high,
struck the towering elephants with a dreaming arrow.
And the breeds of leopards and the wild tribes of lions
and the hunting hounds of desert-roaming Dionysus
kept the sleepless watch of alternate guard,
waking all night within the mountain wood,
lest the battle of the dark Indians rush upon them;
and torches in rows flashed toward Olympus,
the lamps of the sleepless Bacchic dance.

25. In the twenty-fifth you have the contest of Perseus
and the judgment of Heracles against the valor of Dionysus.

Muse, make war once more on the cunning fray with the wise thyrsus;
for not yet has the Eastern War-god bent a slave's knee under Dionysus
and lulled to sleep the seven-year struggle;
but, awe-struck still at the dragon-bearded crest
of the Indian plane-tree, its nestlings cry out again,
foretellers of the Bacchic war. I will not sing
the first six years, when the Indian host was inside its walls;
but, completing my work in mimicry of Homer's pattern,
I will hymn the last year of the wars, and I will inscribe
a battle matched in number to the seventh year of my sparrow.
To seven-gated Thebes I will mingle my song, since she too,
maddened, runs in Bacchic frenzy about me, and like a bride
has bared her breast above her downcast robe,
remembering Pentheus. And to urge me to my singing
old Cithaeron held out to me his grieving hand,
ashamed, lest I cry aloud the lawless bed
or the father-slaying husband, the son who lay beside her who bore him.
I hear the Aonian lyre's voice. Tell me, Muses,
what Amphion again draws the breathless stone into the dance?
I know the source of this sound: to Thebes that is being sung
the Dorian echo of the Pindaric lyre rang out.
But let us again slay the race of the Red-skinned Indians;
for never has time looked upon another fray to match it
before the Eastern war, nor after the Indian struggle
has it seen another late-accomplished Enyo to balance it,
nor did so great an army come to Ilion, nor a fleet of men
so vast; but, contending with the young and the firstborn alike,
I will raise up the well-toiled sweat of Dionysus,
judging the valor of the sons of Zeus, that I may understand
who labored at such a contest, who proved equal to Bacchus.
Perseus, indeed, swift of knee, plying his well-feathered track,
held a course near the clouds, a wayfarer on foot in the air,
if truly he flew. But what was the greater feat, if, plying his ankles,
he swam a strange rowing with his windy sole,
in that, with the plundering grip of his deep-sunk hand,
seizing the wandering eye of sleepless Phorcys's daughters,
guarded by the noiseless leap of his point-piercing sandals,
he mowed the snaky harvest of Medusa alone—
whose womb, still swelling with offspring, was pressed,
in labor with Pegasus, and the bride's pregnant neck,
the Gorgon's, the travail-bringing sickle reaped,
the harvest of that horse-bearing throat? And, of a war he never fought,
swift-sandaled Perseus lifted up the tokens of victory,
breathless, the snake-coiled crop of the Gorgon's hair,
the relics of a head streaming with bloody drops,
the half-completed hiss from the newly-severed throats
thinly murmuring beneath. And he stood not in manly combat,
nor was there then the din of land-battle, nor on the sea
did the seaman War-god billow out for warring Perseus
the warlike sails of ships with battle-rousing winds;
nor with murderous spray did Libyan Nereus turn crimson,
nor did the deadly water receive a corpse rolled in by its own course;
but, trembling at the hiss of the dragon-tressed hair
of raging Stheno, winged Perseus spun about,
and bearing the helmet of Hades and the sickle of Pallas,
and holding the wing of Hermes and Zeus for his father,
the fugitive was lifted aloft on swifter sandal,
hearing the bellow of Euryale and not the trumpet,
having plundered a small cave of Libya. He slew no army of men,
he laid no city in ashes with the flaming brand.
But not such was the fray of Bromius: not creeping on foot
was Bacchus armed, a guileful champion, nor by ambush
of the wakeful circle of the eye that passes back and forth,
the ever-shifting watch of Phorcys's daughters borrowed from Sleep,
did he accomplish the womanish feat against unarmored Medusa;
but, cleaving through the ranks of his foes with twofold victory
of war on land and battle through the waters,
he drenched the earth with gore, and mingling the wave with blood
he made the Nereids crimson with the reddening stream,
slaying barbarian tribes. And many upon their mother Earth,
the high-crested harvest of the Indians, were entombed headless,
and many, perished in the deeps beneath the sharp thyrsus,
were ferried of themselves as voyagers over the sea,
the dead throng of the Indians. And for unconquered Lyaeus,
when the battle-rousing river fought with its waters,
I pass by the billowing War-god, when the Bacchic pine,
smoldering, set the barbarian water aflame
with its sodden spark, and watery Hydaspes seethed
with hot wave, gushing up his river smoke.
But you will say that Perseus slew the sea-bred monster:
with the Gorgon's eye he turned the beast of the sea to stone.
What was the greater feat, if, watching for the eye of murderous Medusa,
Polydectes, changing the alien form of human limbs,
was molded of himself into stone?
But the mighty toil of Indian-slaying Bacchus was no single Gorgon,
no air-roaming, sea-beaten stone, nor any Polydectes;
but he mowed the stalk of dragon-haired Giants,
Bacchus excelling with his little, man-breaking thyrsus,
when, hurling the warlike ivy at Porphyrion,
he struck Enceladus and drove back Alcyoneus,
fighting with leaves. And the thyrsi were shot as arrows,
slayers of the earthborn, defenders of Olympus,
when the coiling people of the Field with two hundred hands,
pressing the starry rim against their many-ridged temple,
bent the knee to the slender spear-flinging cluster,
to the ivy-spear—and not by the fiery thunderbolt
did so great a swarm fall as by the man-breaking thyrsus.
But, friends, let us judge. In the eastern field, indeed,
the Sun, beholding the Indian-slaying sweat of Dionysus,
was amazed; and over the western gulf
the Evening Moon saw long-winged Perseus,
who had toiled at a small labor with his curved-claw bronze;
and by as much as Phaethon won glory above the Moon,
by so much will I declare Bacchus mightier than Perseus.
Inachus was witness of them both, when with ivy
and murderous fennel the Mycenaean spears contended,
heavy with bronze, and, fleeing the ivy-loving war of the Satyrs,
sickle-bearing Perseus yielded to thyrsus-bearing Bromius,
and instead of warring Lyaeus he hurled his rushing spear,
casting at worthless, ironless Ariadne;
I do not admire Perseus for slaying one woman,
still breathing the Loves in her bridal raiment.
And if he boasts because of the golden bed of Zeus,
rainy Zeus did not carry Danae up to heaven,
honoring the maiden-loving shower of fertile dew,
that little stealthy union; but Semele set foot on Olympus
with Zeus, with the blessed ones touching one table,
seated beside her clustering son Dionysus.
Danae won no Olympian home, but, being inside
a sea-faring chest, the bride of Zeus went sailing,
blaming the deceitful shower of wedded Loves,
that held an unstable fortune of a short-lived snow.
I know of Andromeda, that she shines within Olympus,
but again she suffers even in the heavens; and perhaps, poor wretch,
often she has spoken such a word in an indignant voice:
'What is the more, if you carried me to the heavens, bridegroom Perseus?
A fair Olympian bride-gift you gave me; for the starry
Monster troubles me still even here, and a new one, another
counterpart of the former, after the earth and the terror of the brine,
I still wear chains even among the stars. Your sickle
did not save me in heaven; in vain for me within Olympus
the gentle eye of starry Medusa gleams;
the Monster troubles me still, and you spread no nimble wings.
My grieving mother constrains me, since she too,
poor Cassiopeia, sinks through the heaven into the sea,
dreading the Nereids, and blesses the course of the Bear,
unwetted by Ocean and not touching the sea;
and, seeing the terror of Andromeda and the Monster of Olympus,
aged Cepheus laments here too after the earth.'
Such a word the chain-bound bride often cried aloud,
calling on Perseus, and her husband did not help her.
And if Perseus glories in the stars of Andromeda,
turn a sidelong eye through the heaven, where there shines
the gleaming Serpent-bearer lifting the coiled Serpent,
and you will see the round Crown of Ariadne
running with the Sun, rising together with the Moon,
announcing the desire of crown-loving Dionysus.
I know of the war of Minos, which the womanish Enyo gave him,
lifting up the love-girdle and not the strap of the oxhide shield,
when Cypris was the helmet-shaker, when Persuasion
brandished the bronze spear and became Pallas Athena,
fellow-traveler to warring Minos; and in the battles
the marriage-marshalling swarm of Loves, untrained in war, shot their arrows,
and Desire the lovely, the city-sacker, when to the people
of Nisaean Megara the Cydonian trumpet roared,
when, seeing Fear and Panic as fellow-laborers of the Loves,
bronze Ares retreated with shamefaced steps,
beholding Aphrodite lifting the shield
and Desire wielding the spear; and for the well-armored fighter
delicate-robed Eros wrought a fair-haired victory:
for Scylla, while her unshorn father slept,
sheared the coeval cluster of his purple hair,
and sacked the whole city with a single cleaving iron,
mowing the lock of her city-guarding head.
Minos the city-sacker once, by his own naked beauty,
found the end of the battle, and conquered—not by iron,
