but by desire and love. But when Lyaeus was arming,
no Desire soothed the fray of the spear-bearing Indians,
no Paphian armed herself to fight beside Lyaeus,
conquering by beauty; no single maiden
frenzied with passion brought aid, in love with Dionysus,
no lovely guile, no locks of Deriades;
but, of the far-scattered wars, the strange-tempered Indian
held the boast of an ever-renewed victory. And if you honor
the Inachian Heracles, I myself will refute his whole toil.
I know, indeed, that, twisting his slanting arm about the lion,
he encircled its neck with a well-handed clinging bond,
bringing a death without iron, where through the life-sustaining throat
the breath of the windpipe passes midway through the air;
I do not admire even this: by a leafy thicket once,
excelling with lion-slaying hands, Cyrene
the maiden wrought a like deed, in that she too
mastered the male beast with an unyielding female bond.
But Bacchus, a child still in his first bloom, sporting in the mountains,
gripping with one hand the shaggy chin,
dragged the bloody lion, and held out to his mother Rhea
the gaping beast, pressing the lock of its neck;
he dragged it still living, and, binding it tight with a collar,
he yoked the beast with a guiding bridle,
fastening the slavish jaws, and, seated on high in his car,
he lashed with his whip the wild backs of trembling lions.
And the breeds of leopards and the race of flesh-eating bears
were enslaved by the infant hands of Dionysus.
I know also the Arcadian mountain-ranging boar; but to Lyaeus
boars and tribes of lions were playthings while a child.
What greater thing did bold Heracles accomplish, if, with much labor,
he loosed some small snaky spring of Lerna,
cutting the self-renewing harvest of the lurking hydra,
the many-necked field sprouting up with serpents?
Would that he had slain it alone, and not, toiling, called upon
Iolaus, the smiter of the newly-grown heads,
lifting the light-bearing torch, until the two of them
laid low the female serpent. But I do not know how to honor
two men contending against a single worthless viper;
one toil was divided between them both. But the thyrsus-bearer,
alone cutting off the snaky sons of the Field,
Euios assailed them all, the champion of Zeus, from over whose shoulders
broad and on either side hydras flowed by turns,
far greater than the Inachian hydra, and instead of Lerna
they hissed unsteady in the air, neighbors of the stars.
Be gracious, Iolaus; for you burned the body of the hydra,
yet Heracles alone, alone, snatched the name of victory.
No little Nemea did my champion, no Lerna
did Bacchus revive from many-throated jaws,
cutting the snaky thicket of the self-renewing hydra;
but, bearing the South Wind and the Northern feet and the wing of Eurus
and the West Wind as herald, with fourfold victory
he filled Ocean, earth, and sea with his contests.
If a serpent brings glory to a man, if lurking hydras,
these are the natal garlands of Bacchus, these of Lyaeus
the dread snake-coiled bonds of dragon-locks,
ever since he left the offspring-completing fold of his father's thigh.
I will be silent about the golden horn of the deer; I will not blame
so great a Heracles as the slayer of a single doe.
Make no mention of the trembling deer; for to the fawn-slaying
Bacchant the deer-coursing hunt is a small plaything.
Leave aside the Cnossian toil of Heracles; for that frenzied
bull which he drove I do not admire, in that, brandishing
so great a club, he cut off a little horn;
often one woman has done this, often a Bacchant
has carved up the boundless herd of well-horned bulls,
a worthless handmaid of bull-horned Dionysus;
and, dragging up the sharpened, curved horn,
often, if the maddened ox fought with its horns,
she bent the bull to its knee, the assailer of lions.
Leave aside too the heads of three-crested Geryon;
for my own Dionysus, with his flesh-cutting ivy,
crushed Alpos, the god-fighting son of the Field,
Alpos haired with a hundred snaky heads,
touching the sun and again dragging down the Moon,
crowding the starry dance with his tresses.
The labors of Heracles, whom immortal Zeus begot,
holding the three-mooned, child-sowing bed of Alcmene,
were a worthless mountain-bred toil; but the deeds of Bacchus
were either a many-cubited Giant or the high-crested champion of the Indians—
no deer, no ranks of an ox-herd, no shaggy boar,
nor a hound, nor a bull, nor self-rooted fruit
gold-gleaming, nor dung, nor a wandering, restless bird
holding a worthless, ironless, feathered point,
nor a horse's stranger-slaying jaw, nor one little girdle
of Hippolyta—but the victory of Dionysus
was boundless Deriades or twenty-cubit Orontes.
All-radiant son of Meles, undying herald of Achaea,
gracious be your book, coeval with the dawn;
I will not make mention of the Trojan struggle; for I do not liken
Dionysus to the son of Aeacus, nor Deriades to Hector.
Your Muse ought to have hymned so great and such a contest
and Bacchus, the spear-flinger against the Giants,
and to have left the toils of Achilles to other singers,
had not Thetis seized that prize. But to sing clear
breathe upon me your god-sped breath; for I have need
of your eloquence, since, singing of so great a War,
I dim the Indian-slaying sweat of Dionysus.
But, goddess, carry me a second time into the midst of the Indians,
holding a breathing spear and the shield of father Homer,
to fight with Morrheus and witless Deriades,
armed together with Zeus and Bromius; and in the battles
let me hear the army-rousing sound of the Bacchic pipe
and the unceasing din of Homer's wise trumpet,
that with intelligent spear I may slay the remnant of the Indians.

So upon the well-pastured ridge of the Indian wood
sat Bacchus and his throng, a citizen of the desolate crag,
in the truce of the war. And Ganges quivered in fear,
pitying his children; and over the fate of the newly slain
the whole city was shaken; and with the mournful clamor
of dirge-loving women the streets rang loud.
And Deriades was shaken by fear and wonder and shame;
for now he had heard all; but the more, with sidelong eye,
he grieved as he gazed, in that, changing its marvelous form,
black Hydaspes murmured with billowing wine.
There too the broad-bearded one, plying his sluggish foot,
the wretch, holding a misty, blinding fog upon his eyes,
sprinkled the golden dew of toil-loosing drunkenness
upon his gummed eyes; and as his face drew up
the wine-dark drops, his eyes were opened.
And with delighted feet the old man danced, singing aloud,
of the crimsoning moisture of the evil-averting river;
and with his aged hands drawing up the stream cloud-like,
he filled the fragrant skins with purple drunkenness,
and kindled an altar to Zeus and to wine-pouring Dionysus,
beholding the late radiance of the unwonted Sun.
And the boy, leaving the wine-drunk hounds on the shore
lapping the sweet water of the reddening river,
the hunter, fellow-rover of the mountain Archer-goddess,
turned his step toward the city, to disbelieving Deriades
announcing the sweet flood of the drunkenness-staggering river.
And now the vine-scented odor ran through the town
and with warm breezes made drunk all the streets,
foretelling the victory of Indian-slaying Lyaeus;
and on the lofty towers the citizens lodged
in fear, and the guards girdled the wall with oxhides,
of the high-crested city. And on the hilltops,
grieving, Dionysus often reproached Hera,
that, grudging again, she had reined back the battle of the Indians,
when the returning Moon had filled ten circles,
measuring the thirtieth dawn's course of the war;
and the winds fanned up every hope of victory.
And gazing at his lions by their idle manger,
like a lion he roared and groaned within the thicket
with tearless eyes; and to downcast Bacchus
trailing-robed Attis came through the Scythian mountain,
unsown, lashing on the wandering car of lions,
swift messenger of divine Rhea, who once with bronze
made bloody the fruitful stalk of marriage-completing youth,
and cast away the loving furrow of unmarried plows,
the harvest of male reaping; and with bloody,
child-begetting drops besprinkling the fold of his thigh,
he made his warm body female with the smiting iron;
he then, driving the car of the Cybelean goddess,
came as a comforting messenger to grieving Lyaeus.
And Dionysus, seeing him, sprang up, lest he come near
bringing all-subduing Rhea to the battle of the Indians.
And, halting the wild car, drawing the reins through the rail,
and showing the unscarred tips of his rosy beard,
Attis spoke a word to Bacchus, pouring forth a shrill cry:
'Vine-clad Dionysus, child of Zeus, descendant of Rhea,
tell me at my asking, when will you return to the land of the Lydians,
having destroyed the wool-haired race of the Indians?
Not yet has Rhea looked upon the dark-skinned captives,
not yet, after the strife, beside the mountain-stalled manger,
has she wiped the Mygdonian sweat of your lions
beside the wealth-flowing stream of Pactolus; but the whirl
of the noiseless, ever-flowing years of battle you keep rolling;
not yet to the beast-rearing Mother of the gods have you brought
the tokens of victory, the eastern tribes of Indian lions.
But from Hephaestus and from your immortal Rhea
receive these arms, which the Lemnian anvil wrought,
holding the sea with the earth and the air and the dance of stars.'
Not yet had the speech ended, and proud Bacchus cried out:
'Hard are the gods, and jealous. In the wars, indeed,
in a single dawn I shall be able to destroy the city of the Indians
with my ivy-spear; but the victory
my stepmother's grudge, the envy of Hera, turns me away from against my will.
Openly against Deriades stands wild Ares as champion,
fighting against the Satyrs; and I have often longed to wound him
with the thyrsus; but, threatening, the son of Cronos
with thundering crashes reined back my onset.
But may heavenly Zeus this very day lull
the din of the heavy-crashing clouds, and tomorrow I will bind Ares,
until I cleave the well-helmeted stalk of the Indians.'
So spoke Dionysus, and the Lydian Attis answered him,
brandishing the starry, unwounded shield of the air:
'O friend, would you not fear the wrath of Ares, the envy of Hera?
Nor the whole rank of the blessed ones, while you have all-mother Rhea,
nor the curved-bow army—so that, hurling spears,
you might not strike the Sun or wound the Moon?
Who would dim the sword of Orion with his blade,
or shoot at Bootes with earthly arrows?
But you will say it is the horn-trailing father of Deriades:
to Hydaspes, who bears Ocean, what could he do to you?
Take courage and fight a second time, since of the battle
my Rhea has prophesied the late-accomplished victory;
for there will be no end of the war before in the combat
the four-yoked Seasons fulfill the sixth year;
for so the eye of Zeus and the threads of unbending Fate
yielded to the nods of Hera; and in the coming
seventh year you shall shatter the city of the Indians.'
So saying, he gave the shield to Bromius; and, delighting his heart
with the goblets, lovers of unmixed wine,
of toil-loosing wine, he touched the feast; and, pleasing his spirit
at the table, he turned back again and lashed the backs of his lions,
guiding his mountain-coursing car homeward to Phrygia.
And he drove past the crags of the Caucasian glens,
and the heights of the Assyrians and the hard-trodden mountains of Bactra,
and passed the watchtowers of Lebanon and the spurs of Taurus,
until he set foot on the land of Maeonia; and the self-built,
marvelous hall of mighty-childed Rhea he entered;
and he loosed the flesh-eating lions from their collars,
and tied them near the manger and gave them ambrosial fodder.
But he, instructed in his mother's inspired oracle,
thyrsus-maddened Dionysus, mingled with the mountain Bacchants,
leaving to the winds the burden of downcast grief,
shaking in his hand the much-wrought shield, the weapon of Olympus,
the wise work of Hephaestus. And the peoples gathered,
gazing at the varied Olympian marvels of art,
the gleaming wonders that the heavenly hand had wrought,
fashioning the many-colored shield, in whose midst
he had made the encircling earth, and around the earth
he had rounded the heaven, engraved with the dance of stars,
and he made the sea yoked to the earth; and in the upper sky
he wrought with gold the Sun mounted on the fiery rim of his car,
and from silver metal,
whitening, he made round the whole wheeling Moon;
and there all the constellations that, in the many-shining order,
the coiling sky has girdled like a crown and made varied,
about its seven zones, and by the axle's circle
the unwetted twin pole of the heavenly Wain;
for both run beside the turning-post, higher than Ocean,
in line with each other at the flank, and ever by so much
the head of the setting Bear is bent below
as the neck of the other rising Bear is stretched up;
and he wrought the Dragon midway between the two Wains,
which, joining the divided limbs of both that lie near,
is bent in the coiling track of its heavenly belly,
drawing back again its glancing body, like the coiling stream
of slanting, roaring Maeander, which, through the land,
turning its curved water aslant, travels in spirals,
stretching its facing eye toward the head of Helice,
girdling its body with starry scales, ringed about
with the constellations of the Bears; and on the tip of its tongue
a forward-stretched star gleams, spitting out light,
sending its many-toothed flame near to its lips.
Such things upon the central surface the wise smith fashioned
of the well-made shield; and, doing grace to Lyaeus,
he wrought the ox-built walls of lyre-built Thebes,
of the seven-passaged, alternating gateways
being raised; and Zethus was there, toiling for his fatherland,
lifting a rocky burden on his straining shoulder;
and Amphion sang, the lyre-striker; and to his song
into a self-rolling course the coiling hill danced,
as though enchanted even on the shield; and perhaps you would say . . .
though it was painted, that, sporting with a leap,
the light quiver of the unmoving crag was set astir;
and, watching the man absorbed in his silent lyre,
striking a rapid melody on the deceitful string,
you would have hastened to draw near, that, leaning your ear
to the tower-building lyre, you might delight your mind as well,
hearing the stone-moving sound of the seven-toned music.
And the well-whirling shield, where the glancing dance of stars,
held its fitted ornament, since within the hall of Zeus
the Trojan cupbearer was wrought with sacred art,
holding the well-made eagle, the winged bearer,
as in paintings too, gripped by the seizing wing;
and Zeus, in terror, seemed to fly through the air,
lifting with untearing talons the awe-struck boy,
sparing him in the onset of his gently moving wings,
lest, plunging headlong from the air, Ganymede
be hidden in the murderous surge of the sea;
and he trembled the more for the Fates, lest, having first given
the lovely youth, who had bestowed his name on the neighboring sea,
he should snatch a late prize reserved for Helle;
and beside the heavenly table of the gods' feast
the boy was fashioned just like one drawing wine; and of the self-poured
nectarous dew he held a brimming bowl,
and offered the cup to feasting Zeus; and Hera sat
as though in anger even on the shield, with form for witness
holding the jealousy of her soul, and to the goddess seated beside her,
to Pallas, she pointed out the boy, that the sweet nectar of Olympus
a star-roaming herdsman, Ganymede, was pouring,
plying in his hand the cups that maiden Hebe had as her lot.
And Maeonia he fashioned, since she was the nurse of Bacchus,
and Moria and the dappled serpent and the divine plant,
and the boundless dragon-slaying son of earth, Damasen,
and Tylos, scarred by a sharp, venom-shedding doom,
the short-lived dweller of Maeonia, who once walking
by the brows of the Mygdonian river, neighboring Hermus,
touched a dragon with his hand; and it, stretching out its broad neck,
and raising its head with the boundless gaping of its jaw,
rushed against the man, and, scourging the man's flanks,
shook its tail in a stormy assault,
and, fastening its back upon the mortal flesh like a garland,
leaping about the circles of the youth's neck,
scoring the tips of his cheeks with its many-toothed furrow,
with its venom-shedding jaws it spat out the moisture of Fate,
and, as it leaped upon him, over his weighed-down shoulders
the man's neck was girdled midway with its tail-coils,
holding the snaky necklace of Hades, neighbor of Fate.
And the corpse fell to the earth like a plant of the field.
And, pitying the youth newly fallen by a witnessed doom,
a veil-less Naiad mourned over the neighboring corpse,
and then held back the monstrous beast, that it might be slain;
for it slew not one wayfarer alone nor herdsman,
nor killed only untimely Tylos, but in its lair
dwelling it fed even upon beasts, and often, dragging
the unstable, self-rooted tree beneath the grinding of its teeth,
it hid the trunk in its musty throat,
again drawing back the grim blast of its jaws;
and often, dragging back the spun-around traveler,
with its inward-drawn pantings, terrified, dragging him into its mouth,
the far-seen beast received the whole man into its gaping throat.
And Moria watched the slayer of her brother,
gazing from afar, and the nymph quivered with fear,
seeing the long-ranked furrow of its venom-shedding teeth,
and she saw the garland of death coiled about a throat;
and, wailing often beside the dragon-pastured thicket,
she met with towering Damasen, the son of Earth,
whom once his mother bore in birth-pangs of her own begetting,
attending from his birth his hairy circle of beard;
and at his birth Strife was his nurse; and spears
were his breast, and his washings were slaughters, and his swaddling-cloth a breastplate,
and, weighed down with the broad burden of his long limbs,
an infant wielding the spear, a valiant babe, neighbor of the air,
from birth he brandished the kindred spear, and the newly-appeared
Eileithyia armed the cradle-shield-bearer.
Beholding him beside the slope of the well-pastured wood,
she bent in supplication, and, weeping, the nymph pointed out
the boundless serpent, the slayer of her brother,
and Tylos newly-scarred, still gasping in the dust;
nor did the Giant, the monstrous champion, neglect her; but, pressing
the tree by its very root, he tore it from his mother the field,
and stood slantwise against the flesh-eating dragon;
and the coiling champion fought for snaky honor,
sending the hiss of battle from its neck-trumpet,
a serpent of fifty acres, wreathed in its coil;
and with a double clasp it fettered his feet with a bond,
and, scourging the body of Damasen with crooked coils,
with a raging chasm it opened the gates of its teeth,
shooting from its lips the wet shaft, shaking its eyes,
raw, breathing slaughter, and at the Giant's face
it spat from its rainy jaws the springs of venom,
shooting the pale, long-shadowed foam of its teeth;
and it leaped upon the high-crested Giant's head,
darting upright with an earth-shaking quiver of its limbs.
But the dread Giant shook off the burden of the dragon's spine,
shaking limbs like crags;
and in his hand he brandished his long-leaved point,
hurling upright the oaken shaft; and about the temple
he fixed the tree by the roots, where about the round neck
the bond of its spine was joined by the throat-point;
and the tree was rooted a second time; and upon the earth
lay the dragon, unshaken, a coiling corpse. But suddenly
the female serpent, scraping the ground with a homeward coil,
the mate, wreathing herself about, sought her slanting consort,
like a woman longing for her dead husband; and to the crags
she stretched out more swiftly the coil of her long spine,
hastening to the herb-bearing mountain; and about the thicket
plucking the flower of Zeus with her snaky jaw,
with her uttermost lips she brought the pain-killing plant,
and to the grim corpse, as a warder against destruction,
she fitted it to the dry nostril, and to the dead,
venom-stricken serpent she gave back a flowering life.
And the corpse, self-coiling, leaped; and part of it
was breathless, but another part moved on, and another, shaking,
was a half-completed corpse, holding a self-stirring tail;
and with cold jaws, drawing a breath restored,
in its opening throat by little it hummed in wonted fashion,
pouring forth a recovered hiss; and late, going
homeward, it slipped back into its ancient lurking-hole.
And Moria lifted the flower of Zeus, and over the corpse
to its life-bearing nostril she fitted the life-giving plant.
And the life-bringing herb with its pain-healing clusters
breathed soul into the cold body of the renewed corpse.
And the soul came into the body a second time; and in its inmost recess
the cold body was warmed by a helping fire;
and the corpse, tending the recovered beginning of life,
quivered the sole of its right foot, and about its left,
straightening its standing step, it propped itself on the whole sole,
holding the same likeness of a man who, sleeping in his bed,
shakes off morning slumber as his eyes open.
And again the blood seethed; and of the newly-breathing corpse
the hands grew light; and harmony came to its form,
walking to its feet, light to its eyes, voice to its lips.
And Cybele was carved newly-delivered, as though in her lap
lifting a mimic, child-less childbirth
with fashioned arms, and to her loveless consort
guileful Rhea offered the stone birth-pang,
a chill, heavy meal; and he, hiding the mortal-shaped
form, the marble son, the father, in his devouring throat,
feasting on the false body of a sham Zeus;
and lifting within his loins the birth-bringing stone,
he cast up his oppressed, many-childed offspring,
spitting out the burden of his pregnant throat.
Such manifold works of laboring art
the warlike, many-fountained shield of Olympus held,
the Bacchic shield, which, beholding, they marveled one upon another,
and they ringed the bearer of the wheeling shield,
praising the fiery Olympian hearth.
And as they delighted, Dawn measured out the setting,
withdrawing the light of her fiery-eyed face;
and silent Night blackened the whole shadowy earth.
And the peoples, here and there on couches strewn upon the ground,
after the evening meal, sank down on their mountain bed.

26. The twenty-sixth has the deceitful shape of Athena
and the great battle-rousing host of the gathering Indians.

To Deriades, sleeping high upon his downcast bed,
came rushing Athena, bringing faithful tidings to Bacchus,
and devised for her kinsman another victory yet to be;
and, changing her form into the very likeness of Orontes,
she mimicked the son-in-law of high-crested Deriades;
and as he had cast off the murderous sting of Enyo,
the mimic vision of a deceitful dream beguiled him,
crying aloud such a word, and over the fate of the slain
she emboldened the fearful man to the battle of Dionysus:
'You sleep, Deriades; and I blame you; for it is alien
to city-guarding kings to take an all-night sleep;
the counsellor keeps the measure of sleep. About the towers
the foes press hard, and you do not lift your rushing spear,
you do not hear the rushing din of the drums, nor the song of pipes,
nor do you hear the army-rousing sound of the murderous trumpet.
But pity your young daughter, the mourning widow,
Protonoe, lamenting her husband,
and do not leave your Orontes unavenged, sceptered king.
Slay my destroyers, the unarmored; for though your son-in-law,
swift-fated, is dead, his slayers still live.
Look at my breast, struck by the sharp thyrsus;
alas, that warlike Lycurgus does not dwell here,
alas, that you rule not over the overbearing Arabs;
Dionysus was no god, who, pursuing into the swell of the sea
a mortal man, made him a wanderer beneath the waters.
I saw Deriades putting to flight the womanish Enyo.
Be a fearless lion, since, fleeing the bronze-clad man,
fawn-clad Dionysus became like a fawn.
He did not slay the war-mad race of the Indians,
but your own father slew them; for in the wars,
seeing your champions in flight, Hydaspes destroyed them.
You are not like other men; for the heavenly
blood of your grandfather, blazing Phaethon's daughter,
you bear; you have no mortal body; no sword
nor weapon will master you, bearing down upon Lyaeus.'
So saying, much-counseling Athena went to Olympus,
changing the shape of her dream-borne face.
And Deriades at dawn, from cities, from islands,
bade his heralds gather the far-scattered nation;
and many a herald, here and there with stormy sandal,
went from city to city, mustering the host
along the eastern shore; and the war-mad fighters
gathered from every side at the king's summons.
First the helmsmen of Enyo armed themselves,
Agraeus and Phlogios, leaders who came together,
after the newly-completed tomb of their lately-perished father,
the two sons of Eulaeus; and there campaigned with them the peoples,
all who dwelt in Cyra and, beside the broad barbarian water
of the Indian river, Baedion of Ombelos,
and well-towered Rhodoe, the plain of the war-mad Indians,
and rugged Propanison, and all who held the round of the island
of the Graiai, where the children, instead of their usual mother,
have the male breast of a milk-bearing sire,
stealing the dew with their uttermost lips;
and those who held steep Sesindion, and those who, with a flax-fenced circle,
towered Gazos with thread-woven dwellings,
unbreakable, well-made with well-spun foundations,
an unbending bulwark of war, and never has a hostile man
with bronze broken the rank of the linen-cloaked towers.
And against these marched bold warriors,
the Dardae and the armies of the Prasioi, and the tribes of the Salangoi
who bear gold, whose wealth is shared in their homes, whose custom it is always
to eat the pulse-fruit as their daily living; and instead of grain
they grind it with the wheeling circle of the mill;
and the ranks of the crooked-haired Zabioi, whose prudent
champion was Palthanor, who loathed Deriades,
agreeing in his pious ways with Dionysus;
him lord Dionysus, leading after the battle of the Indians,
gave as a foreign dweller to lyre-built Thebes;
and he abode with Justice, leaving his native Hydaspes,
having drunk the Ismenian water of the Aonian river.
And against these, exulting, Morrheus armed a boundless army,
the son of Didnasos, fellow-traveler of his father, who then,
holding a grief mingled with woeful old age, took up the battle,
brandishing the much-wrought shield with his aged hand
and shaking his chin shadowed by a hoary meadow,
the unbidden herald of long time,
still groaning for his short-lived son, Indian Orontes—
Didnasos of the shifting tears; and lord Morrheus followed him,
holding the upright avenging spear, that he might master
the whole host of Bromius, and he wished alone to contend
with brother-slaying Bacchus, and the unwounded son of Thyone
he longed to wound, the slayer of his kinsman.
And there followed them the race of the many-tongued Indians,
those who held the city of the Sun, fair-built Aethra,
the foundation of a cloudless soil, and those who held both
the thicket of Anthene and the reed-bed of Orycie,
and fiery Nesaea and storm-free Melaenae,
and the well-whirling plain of sea-girdled Patalene;
and against these the close ranks of the Dyssaeoi, with whom too
the dread tribes of the shaggy-breasted Sabeiroi armed themselves,
who have shaggy hairs upon their hearts, for whose sake always
they hold courage of soul and do not cower before Enyo.
With these campaigned also the Ear-sleeper men,
whose custom is to slumber upon their long ears;
to them came Phringos and Aspetos, drawing them to battle,
and proud Danyclos their comrade, with whom, marching together,
far-shooting Morrheus went as fellow-laborer of Hippouros;
and, holding a single purpose, the whole Ear-sleeper host
five bloodthirsty leaders marshaled.
Tektaphos came far-shooting to the battle, who once, from his daughter's
hungry lips drew, as defenses against doom,
the streams of her father-nursing, guileful breast—
Tektaphos, withered, dry of skin, a prudent corpse—
when the sceptered king, holding a loveless threat,
Deriades, pressing him with many-woven cords,
shut him bound in a musty pit,
unfed, squalid, his body worn out with hunger,
deprived of the sun and the well-rounded moon.
And the man was hidden, fettered, in an earthy depth,
bringing no drink, no food, beholding no man,
but beneath the hollow rock of his ground-dug flanks
he lay suffering; and with long hunger he wasted away,
stretching out the feeble breath of his hungry lips,
breathing yet, like the breathless; and as from a corpse
foul breezes blew from his withered skin.
And there was a guard of watchmen keeping the imprisoned man,
whom then his cunning daughter, with deceiving speech,
beguiled; and she cried a heavy-groaning, suppliant voice,
shaking her treacherous robes, the newly-delivered bride:
'Do not kill me, guardians; I carry nothing,
I came bringing no drink and no food to my father;
tears, tears only I bring to my father;
my hands declare them free; if your minds,
if your minds are distrustful, loose my blameless girdle,
cast aside my veils for me, shake my tunic with your hands;
I came bringing no life-sustaining drink. But hide even me
myself with my father in the underground pit;
I am no terror, no terror, even if the sceptered king should hear;
who is angered at one who pities a corpse? At a wretchedly-fated
dying man, who is wrathful? Who does not pity the breathless?
And I will close the drooping eyes of the prisoner;
hide me; what envy is there in death? Let one tomb
receive us both as we perish, father and child.'
So saying, she persuaded them. And the girl ran into the recess,
a light-bearer to the dark prisoner; and in the pit
she poured into her father's mouth the milk of her evil-averting breasts,
fearless; and hearing the deed of the god-fearing Heavenly one,
Deriades marveled; and, like the image
of the over-thoughtful girl, he loosed her father from his bonds;
and a far-shouted rumor was heard, and the host of the Indians
praised the guileful breast of the evil-averting bride.
He then was conspicuous among the Bolingoi, as, amid the stars,
the Evening Star gleams, brightening the air,
the Evening Star, herald of the lightless gloom that follows.
And high-headed Gingles and high-stepping Thyraeus
and high-clouded Hippalmos, from beyond the last edge of earth,
armed the glancing tribes of the spear-bold Arachotoi
and the comrade phalanxes of the Dersaioi, who with iron
hide in heaped dust those slain in war by iron
(they entombed in dust those slain in the strife).
And, having mustered the curved-bow army of allies,
slow Habrathoos came; and ashamed of his newly-cut
locks he armed himself, nursing wrath and grief
at the ox-horned king, since in foolish madness
overbearing Deriades had shorn off his whole hair,
a bitter reproach to the Indians. And the constrained warrior
came scarcely to the battle, and with high-crested helmet
he hid the mangled, hairless circle of his head,
keeping hidden wrath in his heart; and in the battles
by day he fought, but ever in the all-night hour
he sent to Bacchus a faithful attendant,
a messenger announcing the designs of Deriades;
and secretly he was armed for Deriades and openly for Dionysus.
And the wild tribes of the Xouthoi and the battle-rousing Arienoi
and the offspring of the Zoaroi he armed, and the tribe of the Earoi
and the breed of the Kaspeiroi and Arbis, and those who held
Hyspor itself, gleaming with its radiant stream,
haired with electrum from its deep-rich veins,
and those who held sunny Arsanie, where the women
in a single dawn, at the wonted loom of Pallas,
with swift hands complete a whole tunic.
And against these were arrayed in the tumbling battle
the Kyraioi, skilled in the sea-beaten round of the islands,
knowers of sea-warfare; but water-faring
merchant-ships they do not know, but on untanned oxhide
they sail in a skillful copy of wooden ships;
with skins they steer a bastard voyage, in which the sailor
sits, faring over the waveless swells,
scoring the sea's back with mimic merchant-ships.
These Thyamis marshaled, and Holkasos, the leader of men,
the two sons of Tarbelos, the spear-bearing father.
And a great swarm came, leaving Areizanteia,
nurse of strange wooden honey, where the trees,
having drunk the airy, life-giving Eastern watering of dew,
their leafy boughs, honey-flowing, as from hives,
bring forth the cunning travail of the wise bee,
the green drink of the self-born petals; for into the plain
the newly-appeared Sun, when he bathes in Ocean,
shakes off the nourishing moisture of his Eastern hair,
sprinkling the plant-nursing furrow of the life-bearing earth.
Such honey Areizanteia bears, in which delighting,
swimming on its wings, dancing above the petal,
the boundless bird flies; and a certain crooked serpent, creeping,
girdling itself in coils, entwined with the sweet tree,
draws the lily moisture with its seizing throat,
licking with its lips the sweet travail of the clusters;
and the dragons, gushing up the tree-dew,
pour out sweet honey, and they spit out a wandering venom
not so bitter as the bee's sweet stream is sweet;
where, upon the honey-dripping branches, sings
the orion-bird, the sweet bird, like a sensible swan;
it strikes up no note in chorus with the Zephyr's breeze,
sending a windy whistle of hymn-bearing wings,
but with wise mouth it sings, like some man
striking a bridal hymn on the bride-tending lyre.
And the katreus foretells the coming pour of rain,
golden-formed, clear-voiced; and from its eyelids the radiance
is sent in morning beams, matched against Dawn;
and often, singing clear above the windy tree,
in chorus with the orion-bird it wove a neighboring song,
adorned with crimson wings; and perhaps you would say,
hearing the singing katreus chant its eastern hymn,
that a morning, glancing-throated nightingale wove a revel.
There too was the host of the battle-rousing mortals, whom for combat
fearless Pyloites, son of Hippalmos, armed,
holding his brother Billaeos, a fellow leader.
And against these were armed the Sibai and the people of Hydarkes,
and another army came, leaving the city Karmina;
of these together Kyllaros was lord, and Astraeis, champion of the Indians,
the twin sons of Brongos, honored by Deriades.
And another fleet came from three hundred islands,
which lie ranked one beyond another, each in turn
neighbors to one another, where, in a far-stretching channel,
the two-mouthed Indus, bearing its wandering, curving water,
creeping little by little from the Indian reed-bed,
slanting over the soil beside the mouth of the Eastern sea,
goes self-rolling above the Aethiopian ridge;
where, raised in the coil of its summer-born waters,
with self-born streams it grows cubit upon cubit,
and the watery consort embraces the rich earth,
delighting the thirsty bride with moist kisses,
holding the many-cubited frenzy of his sheaf-bearing wedlock,
in alternate measure begetting ever-renewed streams—
the Nile in Egypt and the eastern Indus, Hydaspes.
There, scoring the black-pebbled stream with its hoof,
swims the watery river-horse, the wanderer,
such as, scoring the summer-born swell of my Nile,
dwells, a watery wayfarer through the deep water,
with its long jaws; and onto the beach it walks,
splitting the ridge of the wood with its jagged-toothed point,
and, holding its wet, unscarred jaw, a snatcher of crops,
with a mimic sickle it cuts the grain-bearing harvest,
an ironless reaper of the sheaf-bearing birth;
such things they say the Indian river bears,
a might like the seven-channeled Nile. And those who left
the curving rounds of the islands and the seats of the neighboring Indus,
the warlike men armed themselves, whose champion man,
Rhigbasos, led, holding the likeness of the Giants.
Nor did old Aretos fail Deriades
when he called to battle, a heavy man; but, fastening
the bronze-heavy tunic upon his shaggy breast,
he lifted the oxhide over his aged back,
hanging the strap about his bent neck.
And the constrained warrior armed his army
with his five sons, Lycos and his comrade Myrsos,
Glaucos and Periphas and the late-born Melaneus.
And, binding his hoary lock fast with the helmet,
he took the left wing of the well-wheeling battle,
leaving the right horn of the war to his sons,
whom nature had sealed with the bond of voiceless mouths,
binding their tongue, the channel-cutter of wise speech;
for when, dancing beside the doorposts of the bridal chamber,
Aretos pledged Laobie by the law of yoking marriage,
consorting in child-begetting wedlock,
a divine portent came to pass, since beside the marriage altar,
toiling at the bride-tending sacrifice to Aphrodite,
the newly-dancing bridegroom—in the well-hymned hall
a many-bearing sow, croaking aloud the birth-din of her throat,
a prophet of things to come, was burdened,
lifting a strange and unbelievable delivery,
and bore the bastard race of finned creatures, and from her flanks
she cast up a wet, fish-like offspring,
having borne, instead of an earthly birth, a birth of the brine.
And of the fish-bearing sow many-mouthed Rumor flew,
gathering the people; and the far-scattered citizens
gazed at the many-childed earthly offspring,
a likeness equal in nature to a sea-born delivery.
And he questioned the prophet, the spokesman of the god; and to his asking
he declared a coming rank of voiceless children,
the image of the tongueless sea-born offspring.
And then the prophet said to hide the fore-announcing oracles,
that he might appease the long-winged son of Maia,
the leader of the tongue, the guide of wise speech.
And Laobie was in labor, and with an alternate delivery
she bore, equal in number to the sow's young, a rank of children,
like the voiceless fishes, whom after the victory
lord Bacchus pitied, and from their voiceless throats
he loosed the bond of the tongue, and drove away their coeval silence,
and joined to each a late-accomplished voice.
With these campaigned shield-bearing warriors,
those who dwelt in Pylai and those who held, near Eurus,
inhabited Eukolla, the abode of warlike Dawn,
and sacred Goryandis, the well-sown furrow of the earth.
And against these were armed all who held the borders of Oite,
the tree-bearing mother of the measureless-lived elephants,
to whom nature granted to live the rounds of two hundred years
in the much-bending course of ever-flowing time,
or of three hundred; and one grazes upon another,
from the tip of its foot to its head, black-skinned;
holding in its long jaws projecting tusks,
twin, in the reaping fashion of the curved-claw sickle,
a sharpened cutter, it traverses the rank of trees
with its long-shanked feet; and holding the likeness of camels
and an arched crest, on its capacious back
it bears a countless swarm of crowded riders,
wheeling its standing step in the unbending track of its knee,
and the broad-browed shape of a snaky head,
holding a small, arched neck; and it has a slender
likeness of a swine's face, with eyes of the same form,
high-appearing, vast in measure; and as it moves on its way
its fleshless ears, dangling beside its neighboring temple,
are fanned by the small breeze of slender winds;
and, often scourging its body with a guiding quiver,
its slender, scanty tail shakes restlessly.
And often in wars, shaking its projecting jaw,
the towering bull-headed beast assailed a man,
bearing a strange, jagged-toothed, double-mouthed sickle,
wheeling on either side the innate point of its chin;
and often a well-armored, uplifted shield-bearer
it raised upright, pierced by its seizing throat,
and laid the man low with its jagged-toothed point,
and hurled the self-rolled corpse, the wanderer turned about,
from on high into the whirl of dust,
tossing in coils the rim of its crooked chin,
jagged here and there beside the projecting teeth,
answering in spirals the snaky spine,
stretching to its feet the scored sword of its teeth.
These lord Dionysus, leading after the battle of the Indians,
beside the Caucasian shore of the Amazonian river,
roused to terror the well-helmeted women,
seated upon the crests of the towering elephants.
But these things were after the strife. To the battle of Lyaeus,
when Deriades summoned, then came champion Pyloites,
driving the straight-footed elephant through the tumult,
the war-mad blood of the fair-childed race of Marathon;
and to the battle there followed him, his other-tongued neighbor,
the people, leaving fair-veiled Eristobareia.
And the offspring of the Derbikes followed Deriades,
the Aethiopians and the Sakai and the varied nations of the Bactrians,
and a great army of woolly-haired Blemyes. And a strange-seeming
fashion the Aethiopians use, a cunning device of battle:
for, bearing the rim of a dead horse's head,
deceiving, they hide the true circle of their face,
and bind a mortal head with another face,
having shaped the breathless into the breathing; and in the battles
they harry the foe who knows it not with the bastard head;
and the champion sends from his mouth a deceitful sound,
pouring a horse's neigh in a human voice.
These were mustered at the king's summons.
And over all the lord of the Indians led the way to battle,
whom in wet love his father Hydaspes begot,
having consorted in the well-travailing wedlock
of Astris, the daughter of the Sun. And there is a tale that his mother,
a Naiad, the offspring of Ocean, Keto bore,
whom once, creeping about the seething bridal chamber,
the bridegroom Hydaspes embraced in watery wedlock,
bearing the true Titanian blood; for from the primal
bed of Thaumas, rosy-armed Electra his consort
bore a twin race, and from her bed
both a river sprang and a messenger of the Heavenly ones,
stormy Iris and swift-flowing Hydaspes,
the one quickening the course of her feet, the other of his streams;
and both pursue an equal, opposite-going journey,
Iris among the immortals and Hydaspes among the rivers.
So great, then, was the army that came; and the city was straitened with the host;
and the well-helmeted ranks were girdled with comrades,
filling in the city the rounds of the four-fold roads;
some at the crossways, thronging, some in trenches,
others before the towering wall, others upon the towers
slept sweet sleep on spear-bearing beds.
And the phalanxes of the leaders Deriades entertained in his own hall,
and all, upon alternating seats,
touched one table with the host-receiving king.
For them there were evening meals and the wing of nightly Sleep
to care for, and the army slept armed, neighbor of war;
and as they slept they kept company with a battle-rousing dream,
raising a mimic Enyo against the Satyrs.

28. Survey the twenty-eighth, where you may behold
the Cyclopes' fiery War-rage rolling abundant.
There a strife arose past all soothing; for the two,
Faunus and Aristaeus, drove one common War,
and Aeacus marched beside them, doing deeds worthy
of Zeus his own father, stretching across his back
a bronze shield of cunning workmanship, in whose round
many marvels were studded, the labour of the Lemnian anvil.
And the host had armed itself, of many fashions, for the fray with the Indians
who pressed on in their droves; one, guiding his richly wrought car
swiftly into the conflict with flesh-cutting ivy,
mounted upon leopards; another, with bristling harness,
yoked the mountain-ranging chariot of Erythraean lions
and drove the grim pair; and another, dismayed by none,
hurling at the dark ranks of the Indians,
unshaken, took joy in lashing an unbridled bull,
and one, springing up onto the back of Cybele's bear,
charged at the foe, and whirling his wine-dark thyrsus
put to flight the drivers of the long-shanked elephants;
another, casting at the host with flesh-cutting ivy,
held neither sword nor round shield, nor the deadly
spear of battle, but, shaking the curling leaves of plants,
slew a bronze-clad man with a slender frond.
And a thunderous din crashed out, like a pipe's blast;
the Sileni shouted; the Bacchant women advanced to war,
flinging fawnskins like breastplates across their bosoms.
And one of the mountain-roaming Satyrs, as though driving a colt,
with legs astride sat upon the back of a lioness.
The Indians raised their answering war-cry, and, mustering its fighters,
the barbarian pipe of War, host-gathering, blared aloud;
garlands were on their helmets, breastplate clashed on aegis,
the thyrsus rioted against the spears, and against the buskins
stood matched the answering greaves; and of the yoke-fellow bearers
the lines of oxhide shields leaned one against another,
and footmen against footmen, and against the high-crested head
the Pelasgian helmet thrust the Mygdonian helmet.
And there was a turmoil of champions, each in his own kind: one, lifting himself,
whirled the airborne leap of the Bacchic dance,
one, fallen, groaned, another beat time with his sandal,
one, struck, gasped out his life, another bounded for Lyaeus;
another, hurling a martial sound from his lips,
sang the spear of Ares, while one sang the banquet of Dionysus;
and War crashed in concert with the rite of Bromius,
the euhan rattles rang out, and, leader of the tumult,
the trumpet, mustering the people, sounded with the lyre,
mixed gore with the libation, and stirred slaughter into the dance.
There by far the first, light on his own foot springing forth,
Phalineus hurled his javelin against Deriades,
and struck the unbreakable iron tunic;
yet the deadly point, for all its straining, did not touch the flesh,
but, glancing aside, fixed itself in the ground; and in his fury
valiant Corymbasus, marking the foe rushing close
upon Deriades, came upon him, and as he sped on
severed his throat full in the middle, striking with his blade,
and reaped off his head; and as the skull was cleft
Phalineus, blood-stained and headless, fell to the ground.
And about him a clamorous battle rose; the very tip
of Phlogius' brow Dexiochus shaved away with bronze,
striking the brow's edge as the helmet split in two;
but he, in terror, shifting his knee a little from his knee,
sheltered beneath the long oxhide of his brother,
as when Ajax received his brother, the archer Teucer
of Dardanian stock, into his sevenfold shield,
hiding the kinsman who shared his toil behind a father's buckler.
At once Corymbasus, drawing his sword from the sheath,
flung Dexiochus headlong with a stroke across the neck;
and swiftly, leaping upon the gasping corpse, ran about it
frenzied Clytius, leader of the footmen; and high-plumed,
quick and dismayed, he hurled at Deriades;
but Hera turned the champion's spear aside,
angered both at Clytius and at India-slaying Dionysus;
yet the swift leader did not wholly miss; for, piercing
the monstrous throat of the irresistible beast,
he slew the straight-standing elephant of Deriades;
and, labouring in its anguish, the towering beast, ambidextrous,
shook the whole car with its dark neck;
and tossing the crooked jaw that juts before its face,
blood-stained, it strained back the bonds of the yoking harness;
but the swift-handed driver, bending the well-fastened yoke
with his sword, cut the team-binding traces
of the neck-straps; and from the broad stall
Celaeneus took another, high to view, and yoked it new.
And Clytius was bold, in the hope of unreproached victory;
he called out to the slayer of Dexiochus in a raving voice,
pouring a deadly word upon the insolent throat:
"Stand, dog, do not flee, Corymbasus, and I will teach you
what manner of javelin-men attend on Lyaeus.
You I will carry off as spoil to Phrygia, and the cities of the Indians
this spear of mine shall ravage, and after India-slaying victory
I will make Deriades the servant of Dionysus;
let some unwooed girl loose her maidenhood,
receiving the shaggy-breasted wedlock of a Satyr,
an Indian woman defiled beside the Mygdonian Hermus."
So he spoke, and Corymbasus was wroth, and while Clytius
uttered his late-battle words, he sheared through his throat;
and the head flew up aloft at the leap of Fate,
sprinkling the dust with bloody drops.
And, leaving the dancing corpse to whirl back again,
Corymbasus put the Sileni to flight, foremost of the Indians,
foremost in manhood after Morrheus and the king.
And striking the spearman Sebes above the rim of the breast
he drove the bronze spear into his flesh, and as the bloody
shaft was dragged out he laid him in the heaped dust.
Then he rushed at Oenomaus; he, fleeing like the winds,
withdrew to the host of Bromius with terrified foot;
and marking him, Corymbasus pursued behind, and in his back
full in the middle drove the spear; rushing in its onset,
the point sprang out by the navel through the belly's far side;
and he, pierced about with the bloody iron,
fell forward, freshly slain, and slid into the dust;
and over his eyelids the death-bringing darkness covered him.
Nor did the monstrous champion cease from battle; but four
well-helmeted fighters were slain by one slayer,
Tyndarius and Thoon and Autesion and Onites.
And many a freshly slaughtered corpse there was, not falling
forward to the ground, nor stretched supine on the floor;
but, dead, unshaken, it propped itself upon the earth,
altogether like a champion still fighting, as though brandishing a spear,
as though stretching the swift bow and drawing the shaft at its mark.
And a valiant corpse, longing for War even after its doom,
forced the threads of the Fates, like a light spear
poised to strike, pierced from the scattered bows
by their shafts from head to the very feet,
an upright image of Ares; and the fighters gazed
with marvelling eyes upon the spearman who was dead,
still gripping his spear and not casting away his shield,
a dead javelin-man and a breathless shield-bearer.
And one, struck by the Athenian's grim iron,
reaped off his right hand, smiting the arm's end;
and the hand, tumbling in a dancing leap of slaughter,
fell freshly severed, entwined with its fellow shoulder,
streaking the streaming back with tawny dust.
And now, drawing the long spear of the leaping hand,
with far-flung shaft he would have had his War recovered,
and the left hand, spear-wielding, fought in turn its match;
but the hostile man, coming from the opposite path, forestalled him,
and with answering blade struck the left hand off at the root;
and the palm fell to the ground, and, casting at the slayer,
the far-flung stream of bloody dew sprinkled it
in crimson drops, and over the floor the wretched hand,
self-rolling in its leaps, bounded in its frenzy,
reddened with blood, and its curved fingers upon the ground
it locked with deft middle and hooked-nail grip,
as though clasping again the strap of the oxhide shield.
And it spoke a word, shedding the tears of Ares:
"Yet another hand I long for, that I may accomplish
with three palms deeds worthy of Tritogeneia;
even without hands I will pursue the hostile man;
this is the remnant of my manhood still left, that one may tell
the dexterous boast of the Athenians, that they too,
excelling even with their feet, fight on when their hands are cut away."
So speaking, he ran upon the champions like the winds,
making ready, weaponless, a battle for the destroyer.
And they, beholding him, marvelled each at the other,
and the fighters ringed the half-finished champion about
in throngs; but he alone received with unsparing blade
the alternating stroke of iron answering iron;
and hardly did he fall to the ground; he was a likeness of Ares,
guarding for a late-born dweller the memory of a father.
Not then alone was the company of foot-travellers cut down,
but among the horsemen too was slaughter; one marched on
bringing doom to another; driver overtook driver,
either cleaving with his spear the back of one who fled before,
or striking on the breast one who came against him near,
and thrust him from his horse, freshly slain, into the dust.
And a horse, struck above the flank by an arrow,
flung headlong to the ground its hurled-off driver,
just as the swift-flying Pegasus, companion of the wandering breeze,
borne aloft, shook off Bellerophon;
another, in his terror, from the slippery back,
upright, falling through the horse's belly to the ground,
stuck head-foremost, hanging, and about the earth,
casting his head, rolled, leaving his feet upon the horse's back.
And the mighty Cyclopes ringed the fighters about,
helpers of Zeus; and against the misty host
Argilipus blazed, lifting a light-bringing brand.
And he was armed with the earth-born, fire-pointed thunderbolt,
fighting with torches; and the swarthy Indians trembled,
astounded at the fire that answered the heavenly bolt;
and a fiery champion he was; upon the heads of his foes
the sparks of the earth-born thunderbolt were shot;
and the Cyclops conquered ash-spears and countless swords,
shaking hot bolts and the smoking point,
holding the brand for a bow; and one Indian after another,
countless, he burned up, the man, with his archer's flame,
no single Salmoneus, but with a bastard thunderbolt he confounded them;
not one god-fighter alone did he slay; not for one alone
did Evadne lament, as her Capaneus withered away.
And Steropes had armed himself, whirling a mimic flash,
bringing against the lightnings of heaven an answering gleam,
holding a quenchable glitter, which the Western flame begot,
seed of Sicilian fire and of the smouldering hearth;
and he had a covering like a cloud, and in its inmost depths
hid and again revealed his flash with a double quiver,
bearing the likeness of the heavenly light; for the lightning,
coming, holds its gleam fleeting yet recovered again.
And Brontes fought, striking out a ringing strain,
pouring an answering echo with thunderous crashes;
and with the strange drops of an earth-born snowfall,
shedding a made, short-lived, fair-weather water
in mimic streams, he became a bastard Zeus without clouds.
And, leaving the cunning crash of his counterfeit thunder,
he armed himself with Sicilian iron for the slaughter of the foe,
and, brandishing his hammer aloft above his shoulders,
he battered the heads of his enemies thick and fast with the iron;
he struck the dark ranks turn and turn about, as ever
he beats the forge-wrought anvil with Aetna's clangour.
And, breaking off the crag of a long-based watch-rock,
with a rocky spear he charged down upon Deriades;
and hurling a vast stone with unsparing hand
against the black-skinned king as he armed for battle,
he struck his shaggy breast with the ravine-point;
and he, drunk with so great a millstone of a rock,
was weighed down over all his breast; and Hydaspes warded off
the slaughter of his stricken son. But the bold one, faint from his wound,
shook from his tireless hands his rushing spear,
the bronze, twenty cubits long, and flung his shield to the ground
with shame-filled palms; and drawing a feeble breath,
struck on the rim of the breast by the marble point,
he fell head-foremost from his lofty car
like a vast, towering fir—and the fir, falling,
runs about the boundless bosom of the wide plough-land—.
And the Indians, pouring round him, lifted him into the chariot,
fearing the misshapen Cyclops, lest with some cast
he take up yet another high-stretched crag of the hill
and slay the king with the rugged bolt,
having a length equal to that of high-crested Polyphemus.
And in the middle of the grim champion's brow blazed
the round flash of his single-eyed face;
and, cowering before the grim Cyclops' glance,
the dark-skinned Indians were shaken with astonished fear,
thinking from heaven that the Olympian Moon,
rising against the face of the earth-born Cyclops,
flashed at the full, shielding Lyaeus.
And father Zeus, beholding the Cyclops' mimic battle-rage,
high in the clouds laughed, because, receiving from the earthly clouds
a strange rain through an untried bosom,
the earth was snowed upon then, yet the thirsty air,
bearing its naked back unwetted, held no streaming dew.
And Hypsachis armed himself; marching beside his brother,
shaking with a towering hand a shield as great as a cliff,
high in the clouds Elatreus held a vast fir-tree,
cutting the heads of foes with his tree of a spear.
Euryalus armed himself; and, cleaving in the tumult
the great host that fled the plain as far as the sea,
penning the ranks of the Indians into the fishy gulf,
he conquered the foe across the spear-bearing deep,
whirling his sword, twenty cubits long and upright, through the water;
and with his long ox-cleaver, cutting a sea-neighbouring rock,
he flung it at the foe; and many of the unburied
learned the nets of a twofold, sea-drenched Fate,
by the surging War and by the jagged bolt.
With them another kinsman, excelling, Halimedes,
a monstrous Cyclops, raged in Bacchic frenzy with his towering limbs,
and put the foe to flight; and guarding his face
he held before it the bossed back of his round oxhide shield.
And, marking him, Phlogius, avenger of the slain Indians,
bent his bow, and, drawing a winged shaft, was minded
to strike him full in the middle with the arrow;
but, learning of the onset aimed straight at him,
the high-headed Cyclops, swerving sidelong, avoided
the cast of the rushing arrow; and he, shaking a crag,
flung the rugged bolt at Phlogius; but he, fleeing,
stood beside the car of ox-horned Deriades,
and hardly avoided the air-roaming marble point,
staying there; and, wroth at Phlogius' escape,
Halimedes, splitting open his deadly throat,
slew twelve men with one bellow of his voice,
pouring forth the man-destroying roar of his raving cry.
And the Cyclopes' war-shout crashed upon Olympus
with terrible tongues. And the dancers of War,
the Dictaean Corybantes, advanced to the tumult.
Damneus made war, pursuing the hostile tribes . . .
and on the plain was the war-cry; and to the troubled Bacchants
Prymneus came, calm, like a stern-wind breeze
that saves a sailor riding the road with the storms;
and much-prayed-for he came to the host, as comes
to the storm-tossed ships the calm Polydeuces,
lulling the heavy wave of the storm-breeding sea.
And with lighter feet Ocythous startled the fighters;
many he slew with a swift doom,
one mastering with his spear in close fight, one with a bolt
from afar, another cutting down with his grim blade;
another still running before, fled like the winds,
the frenzied one overtook, plying his wind-swift knees,
in his running altogether like Iphiclus, who, hastening
the soles of his feet, grazed the surface of the untrodden calm,
and held his airborne course above the ears of corn,
treading the topmost unbending path of the asphodel with his feet.
Such a storm-foot was Ocythous. And in the tumult
Mimas set up the whirling-foot of rhythmic War,
and startled the host, whirling his dance-beating sword,
holding the mirthless armed leap with knowing foot,
as when, rousing a din in the ears of Cronus,
Pyrrhichus, beating his Idaean shield with the swords,
raised the battle-cheering strain of lying Echo,
stealing away the hidden, again-grown youth of Zeus;
with such a mimic armed leap of the dance
bronze-clad Mimas whirled his airy lance;
and, cutting the heads of foes, the iron harvests of battle,
with India-slaying axes and the double-striking blade,
he held up the first-fruits of the enemy, with Bacchus for witness,
and, in place of the ox-sacrifice and the wonted wine,
pouring a libation of blood upon Dionysus.
And, wheeling on his restless foot with knowing tread,
helmet-flashing Acmon went, the comrade of Ocythous;
he fought unshaken, like a forge-wrought anvil,
lifting his Corybantic shield, in the midst of which
often the infant Zeus slept his sleep upon the mountains;
and the house of Zeus was a little cave, where that
holy goat nursed him with her false, milky teat,
welling up the strange wise milk, while the oxhide,
with theft-hiding crashes, made the shield-wielding Echo roar,
struck in the midst of its back by the tumbling iron.
For which cause Rhea, fashioning a false stone,
set it as the antidote for the son of Cronus on Cronus' table.
And bright-eyed Idaeus entered the revel of War,
a dancer of battle, whirling his nimble step,
irresistible, driven by the goad of India-slaying strife.
And Melisseus startled the whole dark rank,
with unshaken courage; and, keeping faith with his name,
he mimicked the dread stings of an armed bee;
and aiming his marble at the javelin-man of the dappled Curete,
at his match Melisseus, Morrheus missed,
he missed; for it is not fitting to destroy the Corybantes with a millstone.
And, coming together into one, the dancers of joyless Ares
held a common yoke of War; and about the car
they wreathed Deriades round with oxhide shields, garland-wise,
clashing their armour, and in the rhythmic tumult
they ringed a tower about him with shield-bearing dances.
And the air-roaming echo ran up to the halls of Zeus,
and the fair-footed Hours feared the din of both.

38. The thirty-eighth book, where with the blazing brand
you have the doom of poor Phaethon the charioteer.

The contest was dissolved; and the peoples went to the haunts of the thicket,
and gathered each in his own quarters; and the country-ranging
Pans lodged in their cleft-rock chambers,
dwelling in the self-built caves of the lonely lioness,
at evening; and the Satyrs, sunk into the bear's den,
with sharpened claws and not with cutting iron
hollowed out a scant rocky bed upon the ground,
until the light-bearing dawn shone forth, and freshly risen
the light of calm Morning rose for both,
for Indians and for Satyrs; for then, at the circling turn,
the spiral of time stretched out a respite
from the Mygdonian war and the Indian battle-din; and for them
there was no slaughter, no strife then; and far from the fight
lay the cobwebbed six-year ox-hide shield of Bacchus.

But when the Seasons brought the seventh year of the wars,
then a heavenly sign, a herald, appeared to wine-dark Bacchus,
an incredible marvel; for darkness in mid-day,
unforeseen, was spread out, and in a blackening robe
the noonday mist held Phaethon hidden,
and as the ray was stolen the hills were shadowed over;
and many a wandering torch fell here and there,
streaming down from the heavenly chariot; and the tops of the earth
a numberless rain drenched, and the rocks billowed
with the showers from the air, until at last, scarcely, high upon his car,
the fiery Hyperion rose again in lofty splendor.
And to grieving Bacchus through the air there flew a favorable sign,
a high-coursing eagle, carrying a horned serpent
in its sharpened claws; and the serpent, bending its bold neck,
fell head-first, rolling of itself, and slipped into the Hydaspes.
And a trembling silence held the whole numberless host;
but Idmon of varied counsel, since he had learned the rites of the heavenly Muse,
who knows the well-rounded circle of the stars,
stood alone unafraid, since he had learned by skillful art
the shadowed orbs of the Moon interwoven with Phaethon,
and the gleaming flame beneath the dark-shaped cone
of stolen Phaethon's unseen passage,
and the thunderous crash of the colliding clouds,
the bellowing of the upper air, and the lightning comet,
and the beam of the meteors, and the fiery leap of the thunderbolt;
such works, learned from the goddess Urania,
he stood with a heart of courage; but the limbs of every man
were loosened; and the prophet, the old man, with a smiling face,
Idmon, holding steadfast persuasion upon his lips,
heartened the whole people, since after the long battle-din
he knew that victory was near, to come after a little while.
And Erechtheus questioned the much-knowing Phrygian seer,
watching for the tokens of Zeus on high, whether the fight was
of good omen for the enemy or for Dionysus the slayer of Indians,
not so much longing for the issue of the battle as to hear
the tale of Olympus dear to the mystic discourses,
and the ranks of the starry coils and the circling Moon,
and the daytime setting of the Phaethontian light bereft of its gleam
when stolen away. For always, concerning god-spoken tales,
the citizens of ancient Attica are eager to learn.
Nor did the old prophet neglect him, but shaking the Euian wand
of Lyaios and not the Panopean laurel,
he uttered such a prophetic word from his throat:
"Do you wish to hear a heart-charming tale, Erechtheus,
which the gods alone, the dwellers of Olympus, know?
I will tell it, as my laurelled Apollo taught me.
Do not tremble at the lightning, do not fear the wandering torch,
nor the dark course of the Sun, nor the bird of Olympus,
the first herald of the victory that shall be Lyaios's;
for as it was wounded by the points of sharpened claws,
pierced by the keen talon of the seizing bird,
the horned serpent slipped into the river's mouths,
and old Hydaspes hid the dead crawling thing,
so the ancestral flood will cover Deriades,
who has a form like his bull-horned father."
Such words the god-speaking old man uttered; and at the tale
of the prophet the whole host rejoiced; but beyond the rest
the citizen of motherless Athena mingled joy with wonder,
being so disposed in sweet hopes, as if in the midst
he were reveling at Marathon after the war of Deriades.

And then to lonely, crag-loving Dionysus, set apart,
his brother came from heaven, Hermes the messenger of Zeus,
and spoke a word, comforting him about his victory:
"Do not tremble at this sign, even though there was a daytime night;
this your father Cronion has revealed to you, fearless Bacchus,
as a herald of your Indian-slaying victory; for to the sun
flashing forth I liken light-bearing Bacchus second to it,
and the bold black-skinned Indian to the murky mist;
for in the sky this likeness is the same; and as the gloom
dimmed the light of the bright dawn when it was hidden,
and again, rising high upon his fire-gleaming car,
the sun shot away the gloomy mist,
so you too, having shaken far away from your eyelids
the gloomy, unseen darkness of the Tartarean Fury,
will flash in battle a second time, like Hyperion.
So great a marvel old Aion the nurse never brought,
since the time when, struck by the breath of the demonic fire,
half-burned Phaethon fell head-first from the light-bearing car of the Sun
and was hidden in the Celtic river;
and beside the brows of Eridanus the Heliades
still mourn the bold youth with their wailing leaves."
So he spoke, and Dionysus rejoiced in the hope of victory;
and he questioned Hermes, and wished the more to hear
the tale of Olympus dear to the Western Celts,
how Phaethon rolled through the upper air, or from what cause
the very Heliades beside the stream of mournful Eridanus
were changed into a plant, and from their fair-leaved trees
let gleaming tears drip down into the streams.
And to him as he questioned gentle Hermes opened his mouth
and uttered a wondrous word to inquiring Bacchus:
"Dionysus, shepherd of human life that delights mortals,
if the sweet sting of ancient stories drives you,
I will tell in order the whole tale of Phaethon.
Loud-sounding Ocean, girdled by the rim of the world,
leading the earth-encircling water round the watery turning-post,
having joined in the primal marriage of Tethys,
the watery bridegroom begot Clymene, whom once Tethys
nursed, greater than the Naiads, at her moist breast,
a younger maiden of fair arms, at whose beauty
the Sun, wheeling round the twelve-month year,
journeying garland-wise round the seven-zoned rim of the air,
the steward of fire grew faint with another fire; and the flame of his car
and the gleam of his rays the torch of the Loves overpowered,
when over the horn of reddening Ocean,
bathing his fiery body in the Eastern waters,
he saw the maiden near his path, when, naked,
she swam, sporting in her father's streams,
and as she bathed she flashed; and she was like, as when
filling the wheeling brightness of her double horn,
the bountiful evening Moon shines through the water.
Half-seen, unsandaled, in the waters stood the girl,
shooting at the Sun with her rosy cheeks;
and in the streams the shape of her body was traced; no girdle then
covered the maiden's breast, but, lighting up the pool,
the fair-rounded rim of her silvery breasts grew red.
And the father yoked the girl to the heavenly driver;
and the fair-footed Seasons sang aloud the marriage-song of Clymene
and the light-bearing wedding of the Sun; and round about the Naiad
Nymphs danced; and beside the watery bridal chamber,
in a flashing wedding, the girl, with happy travail, was wed,
and with her cold limbs received her hot bedfellow.
And the gleam of the starry host was the bride-chamber's attendant,
and the star of Cypris wove a song for the marriage-hymn,
the Morning Star, leader of the union; and instead of the pine-torch
the Moon held a bridal ray to deck the wedding;
and the Hesperides shouted; and along with his bride Tethys
Ocean sounded a song with his many-fountained throat.
And the womb of Clymene swelled with the fruitful wedding;
and travailing with the child as the birth ripened
she bore a wondrous, light-bearing son. And round the boy
as he was born the ancestral air sang a song;
and the daughters of Ocean, as the son leaped forth from the birth,
washed him clean in his grandsire's baths;
and they wrapped him in swaddling-clothes; and the stars with fiery leap
darting into the stream of accustomed Ocean
circled round the boy, and the Moon, as Eileithyia,
sent forth a light-bearing gleam; and the Sun
gave his son to bear his own name with a witnessing form
that fitted it; for on the flashing face of the youth
shone the kindred splendor of his sire the Sun.
Often in his child-nursing haunts, gently playing,
Ocean lifting Phaethon, whirling him round again,
held him up by the middle of his belly, and through the high-coursing path
he received the boy back from the air into his palm,
restless, self-whirling, running with the wandering breeze,
and again hurled him up; and the boy with wheeling spin
of his well-twisting hand, swerving from Ocean,
fell with a whirling eddy into the black water,
a prophet of his own death; and the old man groaned as he understood,
knowing the oracles, but hid them in wise silence,
lest he should wound the griefless heart of child-loving Clymene
by foretelling the bitter threads of Phaethon's Fate.
And the boy, lately reared, with the first down on his lip,
now tended the house of his Clymene, now also
he went to the meadow of Thrinacia itself, where often,
lingering, he stayed with Lampetie, herding the oxen and the flocks . . .
Carrying a longing for his godlike father the charioteer,
he fitted an axle with skillful binding of timbers,
rounding out a wheel's shape for a make-believe car;
and fashioning traces, and from flower-tressed gardens
plaiting with slender osiers a thrice-twined whip,
he set new bridles upon four rams;
and making a fine counterfeit Morning Star
of white flowers, like a wheeling circle,
he set it before his well-greaved wagon,
bearing the shape of the Eastern star; and about its mane,
fixing a fiery brand upright here and there,
with mimic rays he imitated his sire,
riding garland-wise round the sea-beaten rim of the island.
But when he grew up, bearing fair-flowering youth,
often he laid hold of his father's flame, and with a small hand
lifted the hot traces and the star-spangled whip,
and tended the wheel, and handling the horses' bodies
with snowy palms the boy delighted in his play;
and with his right hand he touched the fire-stricken bridle.
He was mad, holding a longing for horsemanship; and sitting
at his father's knees, shedding suppliant tears,
he asked for the fiery car and the course of the heavenly horses.
And the father refused; but the more, with sweet speech,
asking, he entreated; and consoling the young son
about the high-coursing car, with a loving voice he said:
"O child of the Sun, dear offspring of Ocean,
seek another gift; what have you ever to do with the car of Olympus?
Let alone the unattainable course of horsemanship; for you cannot
guide my car, which I myself scarcely drive.
Never has impetuous Ares been armed with the fiery thunderbolt,
but he strikes a tune on the trumpet and not the thunder;
Hephaestus does not gather the clouds of his father,
nor is he called the cloud-gatherer like Cronion,
but beside the hearth he strikes the iron anvil,
pouring out a man-made breeze with man-made bellows;
Apollo has the winged swan, and not the swift horse;
Hermes does not lift up the fiery lightning of his father,
holding his wand, nor raise his father's aegis.
But you will say: To Zagreus he gave a spark of the thunderbolt.
Zagreus lifted up the bolt, and met with destruction.
Have a care, child, lest you too suffer like sufferings."
He spoke, and did not persuade him; and the boy, stinging his father,
wet his tunics with hotter tears;
and with his hands he touched his father's fiery beard,
crouching on the ground, bending his bowed neck,
in supplication; and the father pitied his son as he watched.
And wailing Clymene asked the more; but he in his heart,
firmly knowing the unalterable threads of Fate,
grieving, gave his consent, and wiping with his tunic
the rain from the joyless eyes of weeping Phaethon
he kissed his son's lips, and spoke so great a word:
"Twelve in all are the houses of the fiery upper air,
fixed upon the rim of the rounded zodiac circle,
ranged in order, close-set, in which alone
lies the slanting, much-winding path of the wandering planets
that never stand still. And each house spiral Cronos changes,
crawling heavy-kneed, until at last, scarcely, late, he completes
thirty circuits of the returning Moon,
above the rim of the seventh zone; and high above the sixth
Zeus, set opposite, holds a swifter course than his father,
and runs his course in a year; and in the third . . .
in sixty days fiery Ares passes,
the neighbor of your father; and rising in the fourth
I myself garland-wise cut through the whole pole with my car,
driving the many-curved circles of the heavenly Coils,
bearing the measures of time, wheeled round by the four Seasons,
about the same turning-post, until I journey through the whole house,
filling out the accustomed month to its completion; nor, leaving
my course unfinished, do I journey on a backward path,
nor again on a forward one, since the other much-curving
stars run their opposite ever-wandering courses,
and again reining back, both forward and behind,
they keep the half-done, ever-loosened measures of the path,
receiving from both sides my otherward-darting gleam;
among whom the horned Moon, whitening the pole,
having filled out the whole circle, with wise fire brings the month to birth,
half-shown, then waxing, then full with her whole face;
and opposite to the Moon I, wheeling spherewise,
the brightness that feeds the sheaf-bearing birth,
journey the endless circle round the zodiac turning-post,
begetting the measures of time, and changing house to house,
and having completed one circle I bring round the whole year.
But beware the ends of the bond, lest, creeping close,
having wound the dark cone with your car,
it should steal the whole light, shadowing your chariot;
nor ride past the rim of the accustomed circle;
nor, with the much-curving bond of the far-stretched coils,
watching for the rim of the five parallel circles,
have a frenzy, and leave your father's wonted turning-post,
lest the roving horses lead you astray in the air;
nor, gazing at the twelve circles of the journey,
hasten from house to another house; and with your car
riding the Ram do not seek to drive the Bull;
do not seek out the neighboring herald of the chariot-pole,
the star-faring Scorpion, driving him beneath the Balance,
until you have filled out thirty degrees.
But listen to my word; and I will teach you everything.
The center of the whole world, the mid-navel star of Olympus,
the Ram, holding which, rising high, I make the spring grow,
and treading the tropic rim, the herald of the West wind,
balancing the night equal to the morning,
I guide the dewy course of the swallow-Season;
and changing to the lower house opposite the Ram,
in the twin Claws sending equal-day light,
turning back I make the day equal-yoked with mist,
and lead the leaf-shaking course of the autumn Season,
driving with lesser light to the low turning-post
in the leaf-shedding month; and to men I bring the rainy winter
over the back of the fishy Goat,
that for the countryfolk the earth may bring forth her life-giving gifts,
having the rain as bridegroom and the dew as midwife;
and I make ready the summer, the corn-tressed herald of harvest,
lashing the fiery earth with hotter rays,
high-stretched beside the turning-post when I drive in my course
to the Crab, opposite the unwarmed Goat,
making both the Nile and the grape-cluster grow together.
And beginning your course, go after the neighboring Cerne,
following the Light-bringer, guide of the unwandering path,
the forerunner of horsemanship; and in alternating journey
twelve circling Seasons guide your course."
So speaking he set upon Phaethon's head
the golden helmet, and crowned him with his own fire,
twining seven-corded rays upon his locks,
and wound garland-wise a white girdle about his waist;
and he clothed him in his own fiery tunic,
and bound his foot with a reddening sandal.
And he gave the car to his son; and from the eastern manger
the Seasons brought the fiery horses of the Sun;
and bold Lucifer came to the yoke, and round the bright
horse's neck he fastened the slave-collar with the trace.
And Phaethon mounted; and the Sun his father gave him
to wield the reins, the gleaming reins and the shining whip;
and the Sun trembled in fearful silence,
knowing his son short-lived; and near the bank,
half-seen, Clymene, the child-loving mother,
gazing at him mounting the fiery car, leaped for joy.
And now the dewy Light-bringer gleamed, the star,
and Phaethon rose, treading the Eastern rim,
washed in the ancestral waters of his grandsire Ocean.
And the bold high-running driver of the bright horses
gazed upon the sky scored with the dance of stars,
wheeled about with seven zones; he saw the wanderers
running opposite, and saw the earth like a center
fixed in the middle, raised up with long crags,
everywhere towered round with vaulting winds;
and he gazed at the rivers, and the brows of Ocean
reining his stream back again into his own water.
While he stretched his eye to the upper air and the pouring of the stars
and the dappled tribes of the earth and the restless backs of the sea,
gazing in circles at the seats of the boundless world,
meanwhile the fiery horses, wheeling beneath the yoke,
passed by the rim of the accustomed zodiac circle.
And Phaethon, untaught, holding the fiery whip,
seemed to lash the horses' crest; and they, gone mad,
shrinking from the goad of the unsparing driver,
unwilling, beyond the starting-line of the ancient path,
the wandering horses ran past the axle's turning-post,
expecting another stroke from their accustomed driver.
And by the Southern goal and the northern back of Boreas
there was tumult. And standing by the heavenly gate
the fair-footed Seasons marveled at the strange counterfeit day;
and the morning trembled; and Lucifer the star cried out:
"Where are you carried, dear boy? Why do you madly drive the horse?
Spare your haughty whip; and beware both
the wandering stars and the chorus of the fixed,
lest bold Orion slay you with his sword,
lest old Bootes strike you with his fiery club;
spare yet your wandering horsemanship, nor let
the Whale of Olympus entomb you in its long belly in the air;
nor let the Lion carve you, or the Bull of Olympus,
arching his neck, strike you with his fiery horn;
have a care for the Archer, lest from his stretched string
he slay you with a fire-barbed arrow.
Let there be no second chaos, and let the stars of the air appear
while the day still stands, and to your car at noon
let the restless morning meet the Moon."
So he spoke, but Phaethon drove on the more, dragging his car
to the South, to the North, near the West wind, close to the East.
