And there was tumult in the upper air, and it shook
the harmony of the unmoved world; and the very axle,
pierced through the middle, was set aslant in the whirling air.
And scarcely lightening the self-turning pole of the stars,
crouching, Libyan Atlas stood bent over,
holding a greater burden; and outside the Bear, the equinoctial
circle, grazing it with the winding drag of his belly,
the Serpent hissed, running with the starry Bull;
and to the Dog blazing as Sirius the Lion roared from his throat,
warming the air with raging fire, and bold he stood
driving the eight-footed Crab with shaggy-haired leap;
and beside the hinder foot of the heavenly Lion
the thirsty Tail lashed the Virgin near his path;
and the winged maiden, darting past Bootes,
came near the axle and consorted with the Wain;
and by the western goal, sending wandering light,
the Morning Star pushed the opposite Evening Star;
and the morning wandered; and instead of the accustomed Hare
fiery Sirius seized the thirsty Bear;
and parting two ways, the one to the South, the other to the North,
the starry Fishes leaped upon Olympus,
neighbors of the Water-pourer; and with a tumbler's spring
running with the Goat, the curling Dolphin danced;
and the Scorpion, wandering from the curving Southern path,
near his neighbor, touching his own sword,
Orion trembled even among the stars, lest, creeping slowly,
he should scrape the tips of his feet a second time with the sharp sting;
and spitting from her face the half-finished gleam,
darkening at her edge the noonday Moon leaped up;
for no longer, stealing her counterfeit gleam from the male fire
of opposite Phaethon, did she milk her brother's splendor;
and the spiral seven-starred echo of the Pleiad host
roared upon the seven-zoned sky with circling voice;
and shaking forth a din from their equal-numbered throats
the stars, running opposite, the wanderers, raved in bacchic frenzy;
Cypris thrust Zeus, Ares thrust Cronos, and near the springtime
Pleiad came my own migrant star,
and mingling kindred light with the seven-coursing stars,
half-shown, it rose beside my mother Maia,
swerving from the heavenly car, with which it is ever
either running together or the morning forerunner, and in the evening
sends its later light when the Sun is setting;
and when it journeys with an equal course, equal-portioned,
the wise in stars have named it the heart of the Sun;
and stretching his neck wet with dewy snowflakes
the Bull of Olympus, the bridegroom of Europa, bellowed,
straightening his curved foot to the course; and sharp-pointed,
slanting his horn at Phaethon from his crooked forehead,
he struck the heavenly rim with his fiery hooves;
and bold Orion drew his sword aslant from the sheath
upon his blazing thigh; and Bootes brandished his crook;
and tossing aloft the knees of his starry foot
Pegasus neighed, and shaking the pole with his hoof
the half-seen Libyan horse ran past his neighbor the Swan,
and in anger shook his wings, that again he might
hurl another charioteer from the air, even as he himself
shook Bellerophon from the heavenly rim,
and no longer near the high-coursing Northern turning-post
did the wheeling Bears dance upon each other's loins,
but they mingled with the South, and beside the Western pool
they washed their unwetted feet in the strange Ocean.
But Zeus the father struck Phaethon down with the thunderbolt
from on high, rolling of himself over the stream of Eridanus;
and binding the harmony recovered again with its ancient bond
he gave the horses back to the Sun, and the heavenly
car he gave to the dawn-rising, and beside the ancient turning-post
the fair-footed Seasons, attendants of Phaethon, ran their course.
And the whole earth laughed a second time; and from the air
the rain of life-begetting Zeus cleansed all the fields,
and with its moist drop quenched the wandering torch,
all that over the whole earth from their fiery throats
the blazing horses, neighing, spat from heaven.
And the Sun rose, guiding his car that ran its course again;
and the seed grew, and the threshing-floors laughed again,
receiving the former life-giving gleam of the air.
And Zeus the father set Phaethon among the stars of Olympus,
like the Charioteer, and named after him; and the heavenly
gleaming Car, stretched out with his shining forearm,
he holds in the likeness of the Charioteer darting to the race,
as though again, even among the stars, longing for his father's car.
And the fire-burned river rose up into the pole of stars
with Zeus's approval, and in the starry circle
the curved water of fiery Eridanus wheels round.
And the sisters of the swift-fated, fallen charioteer
changed their form into a plant, and from their mourning trees
they let a rich dew drip from their leaves.

39. In the thirty-ninth, after the waves, you behold
Deriades fleeing the fire-blazing fleet of the Indians.

So speaking, Hermes, beyond overtaking, went to heaven,
leaving joy and wonder to his brother Dionysus.
While Bacchus was still marveling at the disordered pouring of the stars
and at fallen Phaethon, how among the Celts
he slipped, fire-burned, into the Western stream,
meanwhile the foreign ships drew near, which on the sea,
guiding them in lines to the sea-fighting War of the Indians,
the Rhadamanes sailed over the unwashed brine,
striking the sea with alternating strokes,
drivers of the watery battle; and for eager Lyaios
the escorting wind hissed against the answering hulls.
And Lycus led the way, driving his car upon the waters,
grazing the unscored stream with his horse's hooves.
But measureless Deriades, towering high above the racing towers,
gazed cloud-wise upon the sails of the ships
with an angry eye, and, hearing in his arrogance
that an Arab craftsman had built the war-rousing ships,
he swore to bring War against the woodcutting Arabs,
and threatened to lay waste the city of Lycurgus,
mowing down the Rhadamanes with the destroying iron.
And the fearless Indians, gazing at the fleet, trembled,
watching the sea-beaten War, until even
the knees of bold Deriades himself were loosened;
but with a feigned laugh on his calm face
the Indian king commanded from three hundred islands
of his elephant-grazing land, along the hard-trodden ankles of its shore,
to lead a host; and the swift herald went upon the path,
walking on his many-winding feet from land to land;
and the keen fleet came from the scattered islands
at the king's call; and he, stretching his bold neck,
drawing the fair-helmeted ships to the war of the sea,
heartened the whole host, and spoke with a high-minded voice:
"Men, whom my steadfast Hydaspes reared,
now fight again with confidence; and bring
blazing fire to the war, and kindle boundless pine,
that I may burn the newcome ships with the blazing brand,
and hide the water-coursing host in the sea
with their spears, with their breastplates, with their hulls, with Dionysus.
If Bacchus is a god, with my fire I will destroy Bacchus;
is it not enough that, sprinkling his many-faceted drugs in the streams
with Thessalian flowers, he reddened my Hydaspes,
and seeing it I kept silence, and quietly still
endured to look upon the yellow streams of the polluted river?
For if this stream had been from a stranger river,
and my father had not been warlike Indian Hydaspes,
then I would have filled this flood with poured dust,
abolishing the grape-laden smell of Dionysus,
and journeying through the drunken stream of my father
with dusty feet I would have run across the unwetted water,
as is told among the Argives, how the Earth-shaker
made the water dry, and the horse's hoof scored
the Inachian dust of the parched river.
He is no god, no god, this man; he has lied about his lineage.
For what Olympian aegis of Cronion does he brandish?
What spark has he of the Zeus-hurled thunderbolt?
What heavenly lightning of his father does he lift?
The son of Cronos does not arm for war with wine-dark ivy;
I do not liken the clatter of tambourines to the thunder's tune,
nor will I call the wands like the bolts of Zeus,
nor will I name his earthly breastplate equal to the cloud of Zeus;
when do I liken his dappled fawnskin to a spangled star?
But you will say that he received the grape and the pouring of wine
as gifts from Cronion his plant-nurturing father;
to one who bears Trojan blood and is some country herdsman,
Zeus gave to wine-pouring Ganymede the nectar of Olympus,
and wine was not like nectar; give way, you wands.
Bacchus feasts with the Satyrs upon the earth;
Ganymede feasts with the heavenly immortals.
And if this man were mortal, sprung from a heavenly father,
with Zeus and the blessed ones he would have touched one table.
I have heard how once his own throne and the scepter of Olympus
Zeus gave as a gift to Zagreus, an elder Dionysus,
the lightning to Zagreus and the vine to wine-dark Bacchus."
He spoke, and rose to battle; and the peoples thronged together
with spear, with shields, and the late hope of victory
in the land-war they removed to the sea.
And to his champions Dionysus called with a frenzied voice:
"Brave children of Ares and of well-armored Athena,
whose life is the works of war and whose hopes are contests,
hasten to abolish the race of the Indians upon the sea too,
having achieved a sea-victory to follow your victory on land.
But, the carriers of the sea-fight's slaughter,
doubling your spears, twin-plaited in a paired bond,
the sea-fighting joined together, clad about the mouth with bronze,
mingle with the enemy a sea-startling Enyo,
forestalling them, lest, lifting the fire-gleaming brand in his hand,
Deriades burn the warlike timbers of the ships.
Fight without fear, Mimallones; for the watery-warring
hopes of the enemy are empty boasts; and if, after toil,
the lord of the Indians did not finish the fight on land,
seated on the crests of his towering elephants,
cloud-high, beyond reach, unwounded, neighbor to the air,
yet I never lack champions, nor will I call
another helper besides Cronion my father,
the driver of sea and air; but if I wish,
I arm Poseidon my father's brother
to abolish with his trident the whole Indian line;
and a broad-bearded champion, offspring of the Earth-shaker,
Glaucus I have as my fellow in arms, neighbor of my Thebes,
the sea-citizen of the Aonian field of Anthedon;
Glaucus I have, and Phorcys; and as it is lashed by the sea,
Melicertes will sink the hull of Deriades,
honoring kindred Dionysus, whose mother once
nursed the infant Bacchus, since sea-dwelling Ino gave
one milk to both, to Palaemon and to Dionysus;
and of the prophetic old man, who once foretold our victory
that should come upon the sea with his deep-sea voice,
I am the friend, of Proteus; and my Thetis
arms for the fight the daughters of Nereus, and in the battle-din
my Ino, fellow in arms of the Bassarids, puts on her armor;
and I will arm for war Aeolus too, that I may see
Eurus hurling his javelin and Boreas wielding his spear,
the son-in-law of my champion, the ravisher of the Marathonian bride,
and the Ethiopian South wind, the shield-bearer of Lyaios;
and Zephyrus much more, in the storm-driven din,
will harm the hulls of the enemy; for he has
as bedfellow my Iris, the messenger of Zeus. But in silence,
far from the good-wand war of the Indian battle-din,
let rough Aeolus stay quiet, having bound with the accustomed bond
the windy bag he tightened, nor upon the sea
let the winds prevail with Indian-slaying blasts;
but I will finish the fight, brandishing my ship-destroying wands."
So speaking he armed his confident leaders.
And already the herald trumpet of war stood ready,
and the pipes of Ares sounded forth a battle-rousing tune,
gathering the host, and the smitten ox-hide shield
rang out the bronze-clashing echo of the sea-fight,
and the army-rousing pipe shrieked a din that thudded with it;
and instead of the rock-voice, the war-remnants of sound,
the sea Echo answered the late-speaking Panian voices.
For them as they fought there was tumult, and a cry arose
of men calling out; and the host fought with accustomed skill,
ringing round the whole army garland-wise, and in the midst
the Indian fleet was hemmed by the even-rowing ships
into the likeness of fish caught in a net; and to the Aeacids
Aeacus, foretelling the watery War of Salamis,
as the battle began, uttered a god-fearing voice:
"If once before, hearing my suppliant cry,
you drove the seedless drought from the broad-acred field,
bringing life-giving water to the thirsty land,
grant again the same late-fulfilled favor, Zeus of the rain,
honoring me with water here too; and let someone say,
beholding our victory: as upon the earth
Zeus honored his own son, so on the seas he honors him.
Let another, an Achaean man, say: in one ordinance
Aeacus is Indian-slaying and life-giving; for he does both,
cutting off the heads of enemies and giving fruit to the furrow,
he brought joy to Demeter and gladness to Dionysus.
And rescue the voyage of our ship; and as into the parched
and earthly hollow I led the life-bringing water,
so I proclaim a death-bearing surge from the deep flanks
fighting against the armies and hulls of Deriades.
But, father, lord of life, lord of the battle-din,
send me the eagle bird, the herald of my race,
on the right for my champions and for your Dionysus;
and let another bird come on the left for the enemy;
and let these be the diverse tokens for both:
the one I shall behold, carried on a seizing talon,
scored with the sharp sting of its sharpened claws,
lifting up a huge dead horned serpent,
announcing the end of the horned enemy;
and to the host of the enemy let another, black-skinned, come
with dark wings, foretelling the slaughter of the Indians,
the black sign of self-wrought death; and if you are willing,
with thunderous crashings prophesy my victory,
and sending the lightning of Bromios as childbed-fires
honor your son again with fire, and let the thunderbolts
shoot at the fair-helmeted hulls of the enemy.
Yes, father, remember Aegina, lest you shame your bride's
bridegroom, the wing-shaped bird of the Loves."
So speaking he made war, and casting his eye
to the airy paths, full against the returning Bear,
Erechtheus entreated his son-in-law and cried out a word:
"Boreas my son-in-law, arm yourself, and for your bride's
fighting father straining your helping breath
grant a sea-victory as the bride-gift of your chamber;
to the hulls of Bromios bringing a ship-saving breeze
give a favor to both, to Erechtheus and to Dionysus;
but lashing the maddened sea against the ships of Deriades
arm your storms with a billowy blast—
for you are experienced in battle, since you yourself
dwell in Thrace, experienced, just like Ares—
and bringing a storm-breath against the enemy's phalanx
arm yourself against Deriades with a frosty spear;
and setting a storm-driven Enyo against the enemy
shoot the foe with a hail-shaft,
bearing faith to Zeus and to Pallas and to Dionysus.
Remember Cecropia of fair maidens, where the women
embroider with the shuttle the marriage-hymn of your Loves;
and honor Ilissus the wedding-decker, where the bride,
the Attic girl, your long-since consort, the seizing breezes carried off
as she sat unshaken on your unmoving shoulder.
I know that another wind will come as fellow in arms,
the Eastern, neighbor to the enemy; but in the battle
I do not fear bold Eurus, since the winged winds
all, as many as breathe, are attendants of Boreas;
and let the champion of the Ethiopians, upon the Southern edge of the field,
Corymbasus, return no more, but be subdued,
having as hot fellow-fighter his own Ethiopian South wind,
having drunk the cold death-bearing water over the sea;
I care nothing for Zephyrus, when Boreas arms.
Show your accord with your father-in-law; and from heaven
with you for my Bacchic armies will fight
with his trident Poseidon, and Athena,
she for her own dwellers, he for the offspring of his brother;
and fiery Hephaestus, honoring the blood of Erechtheus,
will come kindly to the watery War,
whirling his battling flame upon the hulls of Deriades.
And grant me to conquer in the waters too, and after the victory
let Erechtheus bring his host unharmed to Cecropia,
and let Athens sing of Boreas and Oreithyia."
Crying out such a word, the sea-whirling man laid hold of the fight
with his skillful spear, and like a dweller of Marathon
he had a longing for the sea-fight; and in the oar-loving battle-din
Ares was then a fair-armed sailor, and in his palm
Fear held the rudder, and the steersman of the battle-din,
Terror, loosed the cables of the javelin-bearing ships.
And the phalanxes of the Cyclopes sailed the sea,
shooting at the hulls with the crags near the shore;
and Euryalus cried his war-cry, and in the sea-roaring din
cloud-high Halimedes was stung to battle.
And against the twin armies sea-Ares thundered
after the land-fight, and with a sea-roaring shout
upon the Bacchic hulls the hulls of the Indians flowed on;
and there was slaughter on both sides, and the waves boiled with gore,
and a great host of both fell; and with new-shed
blood the back of the dark sea grew red.
And many here and there, falling in the pouring of death,
the swollen sailors floated upon the sea;
and with the eddies, having the ferrying winds for whirling,
the dead crowd was dragged along, running with the unsparing breeze;
and many beneath the self-rolling whirl of the battle-din
slipped into the stream, and drinking by necessity
the bitter water perceived the threads of underwater Fate,
weighed down by the breastplate; and the black water of the swollen sea
covered the like-colored bodies of the dark dead
in the seaweed depth, and with the water-coursing wearer
the bronze tunic was buried in the muddy clay;
and the sea became a tomb. And many were entombed
in the jaws of sea-monsters, and in its fishy throat
a seal, tossing the breathless corpse, entombed it,
belching forth the yellow stream of blood. And of the slain
the sea drank up the armor, and of the newly-slaughtered wearer
of itself the crested helmet floated through the water
as the bond was loosened, and on the storm-driven
flood of the wandering sea the rounds of many an ox-hide shield swam
with their wet baldric. And much beneath the wave-tips
the reddening foam bubbled up from the gray brine,
flecking the all-white pouring with a bloody trail.
And Melicertes was reddened with bloody drops;
and Leucothea raised her cry, the nurse of Lyaios,
holding her neck high, and for the Indian-slaying victory
the Nymph crowned her hair with the flower of the seaweed;
and Thetis without her veil, leaning up out of the sea,
propping her hands on Doris and Panopeia,
stretched a glad eye toward good-wand Dionysus.
And from the deep Galatea, through the sea's gulf
half-seen was borne, grazing the calm,
and at the sea-startling Enyo of the murderous Cyclops
gazing she was shaken, and changed her cheeks with fear;
for she hoped to see Polyphemus in the Indian battle
fighting in arms with Lyaios against Deriades;
and trembling she entreated sea Aphrodite
to save the son of Poseidon doing valiant deeds,
and besought the dark-haired, child-loving sire
to shield Polyphemus as he fought, for his son's sake.
And the daughters of Nereus circled round the bearer
of the deep trident; and propped upon his trident
the sea Earth-shaker gazed at the neighboring battle,
and watching the host of well-armored Dionysus,
jealous as he saw the Enyo of the other Cyclops,
to watery-warring Bromios he broke out with a much-reproachful voice:
"To the battle-cry, dear Bacchus, gathering so many Cyclopes,
and leaving one alone far from the fight,
for seven years' time you have a many-circled contest,
feeding the shifting hope of an endless war,
since the champions of your great contest
all need one unconquered Polyphemus;
but if my son the Cyclops had come to your fight,
and had brandished the prong of my father's trident,
then, fighting in arms with Dionysus over the plain,
he would have crushed the breast of bull-horned Deriades,
and cleaving the great dread throng with my trident
he would have killed the whole race of Indians in one dawn.
My other son of old, holding a hundred hands,
helped your father, the destroyer of the Titans,
many-armed Aegaeon, when, drawing Cronos to flight,
he stretched out the wide-scattered tribe of his towering palms,
having a high-necked mane that shadowed the sun,
and the grim Titans were banished from Olympus,
cowering before the Enyo of skillful Briareus."
Such a word he spoke in envy with an indignant voice.
And Thoosa in shame held her cheeks downcast,
since love-mad Polyphemus was not present at the war.
And as the toil of the loud-roaring battle-din came to its end,
Nereus beheld his accustomed sea streaming with blood;
and the Earth-shaker marveled at the yellow back of the sea,
seeing the man-eating fish and, with the multitude of corpses,
the unwetted back of the neighboring sea bridged over . . .
And the Bacchic phalanxes flowed on against the blazing host.
And the boundless army of the enemy lay dead, of those who in the fight
were struck with swords and sharp-piercing arrows.
On one a shaft fell above the flank, and another, struck
with the bronze spear above the rim of the middle temple,
had his wound dug deep as his head was scored.
And many here and there of the wide-scattered rowers,
cleaving the sea with alternating oars,
whitened the dark, close-following pouring with foam,
and there was useless toil for the eager rowers,
and the bound cables, with the helping iron,
the steersman cut, and split the rope with his sword.
And of both phalanxes, sending a whir through the air,
flowed the long-shadowed rain of unwandering arrows;
of which one struck the very middle of the mast, and another, passing through,
made the well-twisting sail boom, running with the breezes,
another was fixed in the forestays, and another in the mast-step
lay fallen, and another, a shaft wandering through the air,
hit the topmost of the high-crested yard-arm,
and another was stretched out on the benches; and close at hand
others, straying from the steersman's path,
unsteadily grazed the tips of the rudder's peak;
and Phlogios famed for the bow, drawing a wind-swift shaft,
struck the ship's deck and did not hit Lyaios.
And one might see upon the sea a fine-winged wandering shaft
twined about the curving folds of a crooked octopus;
and one missed another; and with the Erythraean iron
another, hurling at Dionysus, struck a pompilus fish;
and Corymbasus shot with his spear, that he might hit
a Satyr's oar-blade, and the lance, darting past,
scored the double tail of the water-coursing fish
with its sharpened point; and aiming his iron
at the useless mark of unwounded Dionysus
Deriades sent his spear, and straying from Bacchus
the deadly point busied itself with the back of a dolphin,
where the curving neck of the fish joins its crest,
and the dolphin, self-twisting at the accustomed circling goal,
half-dead leaped with the spring of dancing Fate;
and many here and there, tumblers of destruction,
the fish danced as their backs were scored.
And Steropes fought in front; and high-footed Halimedes,
taking in his hand a crag of the sea-born hill,
hurled it at the enemy; and the wandering ship sank,
struck by the rough stone in its wheeling round.
And one lance, thrown across one hull, neighbor to a hull,
yoked both, the sea-running point of the spear,
binding the two ships in a common bond
as they were crowded cloud-wise; and there was a discordant echo.
And the fleet of both held a four-yoked Enyo,
of which one was about the back of the opposite blazing Eurus,
another by the wing of dewy Libs, another by Boreas,
and by the Southern edge. And with alternating gusts
swift-kneed Morrheus, stepping from hull to hull,
frightened the sea-startling Enyo of the Bassarids,
doing valiant deeds in the waters too; but with his wand
Euios wounded him and drew him back from the watery fight,
and toiling in pain Morrheus went to the city.
While the divine wound that had fallen to his lot the demonic hand
of the pain-loosing Brahman healed with Phoebean art,
murmuring a chattering hymn beneath a divine song,
meanwhile against the enemy Lydian Ares pressed on.
For them there was a battle-rousing voyage, and Enyo held
the lead of the sailing, and of the sea-clashing battle-din
there was a tumult of both kinds; for of the enemy
all who were shot with hard arrows
or with murderous leaf-points or spears or swords,
oaring their unaccustomed hands into the black water
with unsteady strokes were entombed in the sea;
but if any warrior of Bromios fell into the brine struck,
tossing his palms he swam, cleaving the waves
with sea-fighting hands, and in the sea-roaring din
fighting in the surge he split the water along with the men.
And Cronion inclined the scales of the sea-battle,
making ready a watery victory for Dionysus;
and with the deep trident the dark-haired god armed himself,
fighting against the foe, and driving the unwetted
car of Poseidon, Melicertes raved in bacchic frenzy.
And riding on four storms across the sea,
towering up the waves, the winds armed themselves,
wishing to abolish the line of the enemy's ships,
some helpers of Deriades, some of Lyaios;
and Zephyrus was armed, and the South wind hissed against Eurus,
and Boreas, bringing the opposing Thracian blast,
lashed the wild back of the maddened sea.
And guiding the battling fleet of Deriades
Strife led the way of the fight; but of the ships of Dionysus
with Indian-slaying hand Victory swelled the sails.
And setting his battling conch to his wet lips
Nereus bellowed a tune with the sea-trumpet;
and Thetis rang out the tune of the war-Echo,
shielding Lyaios with her father's waves.
And Eurymedon the Cabeirus, lifting his accustomed brand,
found a stratagem to help the fight; for his own
long ship he set ablaze, kindling a willing fire;
and at the Bacchic nods, leaping about the sea,
and with slanting curves stepping from hull to hull,
the wandering torch swam into a self-twisting circle,
burning here and there the line of the wide-scattered ships.
And seeing the glare of the fire-stricken sea
a Nereid without her veil sank into the depths of the deep,
fleeing the watery fire through the blazing water.
And the Indian throng withdrew to the land, leaving the sea;
and Phaethon laughed, that after his former bonds
out of the fire of Hephaestus the sea-fighting Ares fled again.
And Deriades, beyond reach, seeing the flame running with the breezes,
flew to the plain, tossing his knees more swiftly,
fleeing the watery War of sea-battling Dionysus.

47. Come to the forty-seventh book, where Perseus is,
and the death of Icarius, and soft-robed Ariadne.

Now here and there through the city flew Rumor,
the self-crying herald that vine-rich Dionysus
had come to the land of Attica; and for sleepless Lyaeus
fair-laboring Athens were stirred into the Bacchic dance.
And the great revel roared; and the gathered citizens
draped the streets with broidered garments
by their many scattered hands; and for plant-increasing Bacchus
Athens were wreathed of their own accord
with the leaves of the vine; and the women, with mystic breasts,
girded their cups of wine over their iron-bearing bosoms,
and maidens danced, and crowned their heads,
twining the Attic hair with the flower of ivy.
And Ilissus rolled its living water about the city,
glorifying Dionysus; and in rival dance
the banks of Cephisus beat out the Euian song.
And the orchard sprang up, and from the bosom of the earth,
self-grown in the ripening of a sweet birth,
the cluster reddened upon olive-bearing Marathon,
and the oaks whispered, and as their leaves opened
the Seasons of the meadow belched forth the two-colored rose,
and the hills brought to birth the self-fulfilled lily.
And to the Phrygian pipes the pipe of Athens sounded in answer,
and the Acharnian reed sang out a twin music,
pressed by hands; and from throats of one tongue
the deep-roaring native Bacchant, singing in unison
with the Mygdonian unwed girl, raised a two-throated harmony,
leaning her arm upon a young Pactolian nymph,
and held up the night-dancing flame with a double torch
to first-born Zagreus and to late-born Dionysus;
and remembering Itylus and the loom-toiling Philomela,
the Attic nightingale of changeful throat cried out in answer,
and the talking bird of Zephyr poured her song beneath the eaves,
casting all memory of Tereus to the storm-winds.
Nor was anyone in the city without a dance. But Bacchus, rejoicing,
came to the house of Icarius, who was, beyond all other
husbandmen, more skilled at planting strange trees.
And the old vine-dresser danced with rustic feet
when he beheld Dionysus come as a guest, and welcomed
the lord of fair-planted vines with a humble table;
and Erigone mixed it, drawing the milk of goats;
but Bacchus stopped her, and to the kindly old man
he gave wineskins teeming with toil-loosing draught,
and holding in his right hand a fragrant cup of sweet wine
he offered it to Icarius, and greeted him with friendly words:

"Receive, old man, this gift, which Athens does not yet know.
Old man, I count you blessed; for the citizens will sing you,
crying such a word, that Icarius found fame to surpass
Celeus, and Erigone to surpass Metaneira.
I have envy for Demeter of old, because she too,
to another tiller of the soil, Deo gave the corn-blessed ear.
Triptolemus found the ear of corn, and you the wine-dark cluster of harvest;
gracious one, you alone vie with heavenly Ganymede,
more blessed than Triptolemus before you; for the cares
that gnaw the heart, ears of corn do not loose them, but the wine-bearing
clusters are the healers of human grief."

Such a word he spoke, and to the hospitable old man
he gave a delicate cup full of mind-rousing wine;
and the old planting vine-dresser drank cup after cup,
holding an insatiate frenzy for the well-dripping dew;
and the girl, drawing a stream of wine instead of milk,
held out the cup with her hand, until she made her father drunk.
But when he found his fill of the cup-receiving table,
weaving his slipping step, turned this way and that,
with alternating feet the vine-dresser leaped up,
striking up the Euian hymn of Zagreus for Dionysus.
And to the rustic old man the plant-tending god gave
clustering vine-branches, the Euius-loving gifts of the table;
and the lord taught him, by some plant-increasing art,
to break them, to dig the trenches, and to set the branches in the round pits.
And to other husbandmen the old planting vine-dresser,
bearing the gifts of Bromius and the vine-borne harvest,
taught the wine-growing husbandry of Dionysus;
and casting an unspeakable flood of wine into the shepherd's bowl,
he gladdened the feasters with cup after cup,
opening the fragrant flow of the wine-holding skins.
And one of them, drinking the stream of sweet mind-rousing wine,
soothed the father of Erigone with a friendly word:

"Tell me, old man, where on earth did you find the nectar of Olympus?
You do not bring it from the yellow water of Cephisus,
you do not carry the honey-sweet gifts of the Naiads;
for the springs do not gush forth honey-flowing streams,
nor is the stream of Ilissus reddened in its poured channel;
this was no drink of the shoot-loving bee,
bringing the sharpest fill to mortals; this is a strange thing,
and sweeter than sweet honey you bring a sweeter water;
this is no native drink the Attic olive brings to birth;
sweeter than milk you have a drink, lasting forever,
in the gathered drops of a honey-mixed potion.
And if the rose-armed Seasons knew how to bring to mortals
a drink from the calyxes of the plant-increasing gardens,
then I would have called this the spring drink of Adonis
or of Cytherea, the fragrant dew of roses.
You bring a toil-loosing and a strange drink; for it has scattered
my cares, that wandered upon the airy winds.
Did not immortal Hebe give you a gift from the upper air?
Did not your city-guarding Athena bring you this?
Who has seized the bowl from heaven, from which Ganymede draws,
mixing the cup for Zeus and the immortals?
More blessed than guest-receiving Celeus, did not you yourself
receive in your hall some gracious dweller come from heaven?
I am persuaded that some other god revelled in your house,
and gave this drink of your friendship, through the feast of your table,
as a gift to Attica, as Deo gave the corn."

So he spoke, marvelling at the sweet drink; and from his lips,
sweetly maddened, he raised the cry, pouring out a rustic song.
And the husbandmen, drawing cup after cup,
were all stirred into Bacchic frenzy by the mind-robbing wine;
and their eyes wandered, and with the strong-wine cups
their silvery cheeks grew purple, and the breasts of the tillers
grew warm, and their heads were weighed down with drink,
and the veins of their swelling heads surged;
and as they gazed, the bosom of the field seemed to shake,
and the oaks danced and the crags leaped;
and full of the unaccustomed wine, with slipping steps,
each man fell rolling of himself, on his back, to the ground.
And the band of husbandmen, shaken by a murderous frenzy,
ran upon wretched Icarius in raving madness,
as though he had mixed the drugged guile of wine,
one holding an iron ox-axe, another arming
his hands with a mattock, another lifting the ear-cutting
sickle, and another raising a vast stone,
another was driven on, brandishing a crook in his hand,
and they struck the old man; and one, seizing a goad close by,
pierced the body of Icarius with the flesh-cutting point.
And in his anguish the old planting vine-dresser fell to the ground,
struck with their clubs, and stumbling against the table
he struck the wine-bowl, and into the flood of dark wine
he rolled half-dead; and as his head was weighed down,
struck by the alternating blows of the husbandmen,
the bloody dew reddened the wine of like color.
And scarcely from his lips, neighbor now of Hades, he cried out a word:

"Wine of my Bromius, the rest of mortal cares,
the sweet that to me alone is pitiless; for joy
it gave to all men, but to Icarius it gave death;
the sweet that is the enemy of Erigone; for our mournful
girl, the sorrowless Dionysus has made full of sorrow."

Not yet did his speech cease; but death outran his voice.
And the corpse lay there, far from the prudent girl,
with eyes wide open. And on an unbedded couch upon the ground
the murderers slept a sweet sleep upon the floor,
heavy with wine, like corpses; and when they awoke,
they groaned for the man they had killed unknowing; and high upon their shoulders
lightly lifting the corpse they carried it up to the wooded ridge,
their minds now sober; and in a well-watered stream
they washed his wounds beside a mountain-poured spring;
and the freshly-slain corpse, whom they had killed in mindless madness,
the murderers buried with their man-slaying hands.

And the soul of Icarius, all like smoke, rushed
to the house of Erigone; and equal to a mortal form
was the light phantom of a shadowy dream-seen sight,
all like a man newly slain, and the wretched thing wore
the spotted tunic, the herald of an unrevealed murder,
reddened with blood and squalid with dust,
torn by the alternating blows of iron.
And it stretched out its hands; and it showed the wounds
of its freshly-slaughtered limbs for the neighboring girl to see.
And the maiden cried aloud in her lament-loving dreams,
when she saw so many wounds of the head, when the wretched one saw
the freshly-flowing gore of his reddened throat;
and the shadowy father spoke a word to the mourning girl:

"Awake, wretched one, and seek your father;
awake, and hunt out my drunken murderers;
I am your heavy-grieving father, whom for the sake of wine
the dreadful husbandmen slew with iron.
O child, I count you blessed; for of your slain father
you did not hear the crash of the battered head,
you did not see the gray hair reddened beneath the gore,
you did not see the freshly-slain corpse twitching in the dust,
you did not behold the father-killing clubs; but a god
kept you far from your father, and guarded your sight,
that you should not look on the death of your slaughtered father.
Look on my tunics, purpled with blood;
for yesterday the husbandmen, made drunk with alternating cups,
gushing with the moisture of unaccustomed Bacchus,
circled around me; and as I was slaughtered with iron
I called the shepherds, and they did not hear my cry;
only Echo of the after-voice heard my crash,
mourning your father with answering laments.
No longer lifting your crook in the midst of the wood
do you come to the flowering pasture and to the meadows,
feeding your herd with your rustic husband;
no longer, handling your tree-tending mattock,
do you bring channel-water to the fruitful garden;
but insatiate of my honey-dripping harvest,
weep for your father, me, fallen dead; and I shall see you
living an orphan, untried in marriage."

So speaking, the winged vision of the dream ran past.
And the girl, awaking, tore her rosy cheeks,
and with mournful nails she scratched her firm breasts,
and tore up by the roots the cluster of her long hair;
and seeing the oxen still standing by the rock,
the maiden, grieving, roared out with a wailing voice:

"Where is the corpse of Icarius? Speak, dear hills;
tell me, you familiar bulls, the death of my father;
of my slain father, who are the murderers?
Where has my sweet father gone? Is it that, teaching
a neighbor the young shoots of the fair-planted harvest,
he wanders, sitting among the husbandmen, or with some herdsman
of the trees he stayed, sharing the feast as a guest?
Tell me, who mourn, and I will endure, until he comes.
If my father still lives, the shoots of the garden
I will water, living again together with my father;
but if my father is dead and plants no more trees,
I will look on a death equal to my dead father's."

So speaking, swift-kneed she ran up to the wooded ridge,
seeking the tracks of her freshly-slaughtered father.
But to her question the bold goatherd did not tell,
nor by the thickets did the herd-tending oxherd, pitying
the maiden, tell of the unmarked track of her unheralded father,
nor did the old shepherd show the corpse of Icarius;
but in vain she wandered; and hardly did the vine-dresser find her,
and with mournful lips cried out an ill-tidings voice,
and showed the nearby tomb of her newly-buried father.
And the maiden, hearing it, raged with prudent madness;
and tearing her locks she laid them by the dear tomb,
a maiden unveiled, unsandalled, and with self-poured
ever-flowing tears she kept her tunic bathed.
And with speechless lips she sealed silence
for a time; and a faithful dog, Erigone's companion,
went with the mournful girl, lamenting with a whining cry,
and grieved together with her as she grieved. And in her madness
she ran up to a high-headed tree; and about the tree
binding her twined neck with a strangling bond,
the maiden died aloft in a self-slaying whirl,
swinging both her feet in a dancer's plunge;
and she died, and met a willing death; and about the girl
the dog often shook itself, and cried out a mournful echo,
shedding intelligent tears from its bestial eyes.
Nor did the dog leave the maiden unguarded and forlorn,
but stayed by the tree, chasing off any wild beast that came,
leopard or lion; and to the wayfarers who passed
with speechless gestures it pointed out the unwed girl
entangled in strangling bonds high upon the tree.
And they, pitying her, climbed up to the woodland tree
on the tips of their feet, and from the fair-leaved boughs
brought down the untamed maiden; and the nearby
ground they hollowed out with earth-digging mattocks.
And with them the dog labored too, with prudent heart,
and in its grief deepened the ground with skilful foot,
scoring the surface of the loose earth with its sharp claws.
And the wayfarers gave funeral rites to the freshly-slain corpse;
and bearing in his heart the weight of a shared grief,
each ran back to his own work with hurrying foot;
but the dog alone stayed by the neighboring tomb,
out of love for Erigone, and perished by a willing death.

And father Zeus took pity; and in the starry circle
he fixed Erigone beside the Lion's back;
and the rustic maiden holds an ear of corn; for she would not
lift the wine-dark cluster, the murderer of her father.
And the old man Icarius, fellow-traveler with the neighboring girl,
leading him to the star-wandering pole, he named Boötes,
shining bright, touching the Arcadian Bear of the Wain;
and he made the gleaming Dog, that rushes down upon the Hare,
a fiery star, where about the circle of Olympus
the sea-faring Argo sails in starry form.
And these things Achaean legend has fashioned, mixing
its familiar persuasion with falsehood; but the truth is this:
Zeus the lord on high assigned the soul of corn-bearing Erigone
to the heavenly star of the Maiden as her yoke-mate; and near
the ethereal Dog he set a dog of like form,
Sirius, whom they call the harvest-star; and the soul of Icarius,
air-wandering, he joined to Boötes.
And these things the son of Cronos gave to the wine-growing land of Attica,
preparing one honor both for Pallas and for Dionysus.

And leaving the honey-flowing streams of Ilissus, Bacchus,
delicate, revelled toward the vine-clad circle of Naxos;
and about him bold Eros shook his wings, and as Lyaeus came,
about to wed, Cytherea led the way before him.
For just now, leaving sleeping upon the shore
the maiden fled from her fatherland, pitiless Theseus sailed away,
and committed his vows to the winds. And seeing
Dionysus the sleeping, forsaken Ariadne,
he mixed love with wonder; and to the dance-weaving Bacchants
with marvelling tongue he spoke a guarded word:

"Bassarids, do not shake your rattles, let there be no noise
of foot or pipe; let Cypris sleep;
but she does not wear the girdle, the token of the Cyprus-born.
I am persuaded that Grace is wedded to wily Sleep;
but since dawn has shone and Eos appears nearby,
wake the sleeping Pasithea. Who beside Naxos,
who has wrapped Grace, the unclad? Surely it is not Hebe?
But to whom did she leave the cup of the blessed? Surely beside the sea
the gleaming Selene, driver of oxen, does not lie reclined?
And why does she sleep apart from her familiar Endymion?
Surely it is not silver-footed Thetis I behold upon the shore?
But she has no naked rosy body. If it is right to speak,
the Archer-goddess of Naxos rests from the toils of the hunt,
having wiped off in the sea the sweat of beast-slaying;
for toil always begets sweet sleep; but who in the thicket
has seen Artemis with trailing tunic? Wait, Bacchants.
Stand, Maron; do not dance here; cease your shrilling,
dear Pan, lest you scatter the morning sleep of Athena;
and to whom has Pallas left her spear? And who lifts
the bronze helmet or the aegis of the Trito-born?"

Such things Bacchus said; and from the sand the wretched
ill-fated girl, scattering her sleep, awoke,
and saw not the fleet and not her deceiver husband;
but with the halcyons the Cydonian bride lamented,
haunting the shores, the deep-roaring dowry of the Loves;
and she named her young man; and beside the sea she raged
seeking the ship; and she was wroth with envious Sleep,
and far more she blamed the mother of the Paphian, the sea;
and she made supplication to Boreas, and named the wind by oath,
named Oreithyia by oath, that back to the land of Naxos
he might bring the youth, and she might see the sweet ship a second time;
still more she asked of Aeolus the unsoftened; and to her prayer
he yielded and consented, and sent a contrary wind
to blow; but for the love-stricken girl
ill-fated Boreas cared nothing; nay, the very breezes
were soon jealous and angry with the maiden,
and they carried the ship back to Attica. And at the maiden
Eros himself marvelled, and on sorrowless Naxos
he thought he beheld Aphrodite lamenting;
for she was brighter even in her griefs, and grief
adorned her sorrowing; and to mourning Ariadne
laughter-loving Aphrodite gently yielded the judgment,
smiling with desire, and the eyes of Persuasion yielded,
and of the Graces, and the lovely tears of the girl outshone Eros.
And late, in tears, she uttered such a voice:

"Sleep came sweet to me, while sweet Theseus departed;
would that he had left me still in my delight; for in my sleep
I saw Cecropia, and within the court of Theseus
there was a delicate wedding-song, and Ariadne was sung,
and a dance, and my own delighted hand adorned
with spring leaves the flowering altar of the Loves;
and I held the bridal wreath; and Theseus was near me
in bridal garments, sacrificing to Aphrodite.
Alas, what sweet dream I saw; but fleeing me
he went away, leaving me still a maiden; be gracious, Persuasion;
these the misty bride-decking darkness gave me,
and envious light-bringing Eos snatched all these away;
and waking I found not my beloved. Truly even the very
images of answering dreams are jealous Loves,
because the deceiving sight of marriage-fulfilling dreams,
a lovely one, I saw, and lovely Theseus fled.
To me even dear Sleep is hostile; tell me, rocks,
tell me, the ill-loved one, who has stolen away the citizen of Athens?
If Boreas should blow, I come to Oreithyia;
but Oreithyia is angry with me, because she too
bears the blood of Marathon, whence dear Theseus came.
If Zephyr drives, show to the Zephyrian bride,
to Iris, mother of Desire, Ariadne forced;
if Notus, if bold Eurus, I come to the dawn-born,
blaming the surging winds before their ill-loving mother.
Give again, Sleep, your dear empty grace, sending,
equal to that one, another lovely dream, that I may see
the sweet deceiving bed of sleeping Cypris;
only linger upon my eyes, that I may behold
the breathless frenzy of Love's dreamed-of marriage.
If to the Attic land, deceiving bridegroom Theseus,
the snatching breezes have led your voyage from Naxos,
tell me, who ask, and to Aeolus at once I go,
blaming the envious and unholy winds;
but if he set me, the exile from my fatherland, on forsaken Naxos,
and unknown to you the pitiless sailor sailed away,
he sinned against Theseus and against Justice, against Ariadne;
may that sailor never again see a guiding wind,
nor may gentle Melicertes ever gracious behold him
riding with the unsteady storms;
but let Notus blow when there is need of Boreas;
let him see Eurus when he wants Zephyr; and when the spring
winds blow for all seafarers,
let him alone consort with a wintry sea.
That sailor sinned, the lawless one; but I myself
went astray, longing for the citizen of prudent Athens.
Would that I had not loved him, ill-fated as I am; for as he was
lovely to the Paphian, so wild was Theseus;
he did not tell me this while he still held my thread;
he did not tell me this beside our labyrinth.
Would that the pitiless bull had killed him; cease, my voice,
from folly, do not slay the sweet young man; alas for the Loves;
Theseus sailed alone to fair-laboring Athens.
I know whence he has left me; perhaps of one of the maidens
he conceived a fellow-voyaging love, and dances in Marathon
toward another's marriage, while I still travel to Naxos.
Naxos was my bridal chamber, deceiving bridegroom Theseus;
I have lost both father and bridegroom; alas for the Loves;
I see not Minos, and I behold not Theseus;
I have left behind my Cnossus, and I have not seen your Athens;
I am bereft of father and fatherland; ah, most wretched,
the dowry of my love is the water of the sea; to whom do I flee?
What god will snatch me and bear me to Marathon,
Ariadne contending in judgment for Cypris and Theseus?
Who, taking me, would carry me through the swell? Would that I too
might see another thread, the guide of our path;
such a thread I too would wish to have, that I might escape
the swell of the Aegean sea and cross to Marathon,
that I might embrace you, even if you hate Ariadne,
that I might embrace you, the oath-breaking husband.
Receive me as the chamber-maid of your bed, if you will;
and I will spread your couch . . . after Crete, Ariadne,
like one taken captive; and for your most blessed bride
I will endure, as a handmaid, to weave the loud-clattering loom,
and to lift on my envious shoulders the unaccustomed pitcher,
and to bring water for the meal to sweet Theseus;
only let me see Theseus; for our mother too
once served the husbandmen, and bowed her neck to a herdsman,
and dallied with a grazing speechless bull,
and bore a bull to a cow; while the herdsman played,
she had no desire for the lyre, only to hear the bellowing.
But I would not touch a crook, nor by the manger
will I stand; but I will be close beside our queen,
while Theseus speaks, and I will hear no bellowing;
and I will sing the lovely wedding-song of your marriage,
hiding my envy of your newly-yoked bride.
Stop, as you sail by the Naxian shores,
stop your ship for me; why, sailor, do you too grieve me?
So then you too are of Marathon; if you come
to your lovely land, where is the home of the Loves,
receive me, wretched as I am, that I may see the city of Cecrops;
but if you will leave me and, pitiless one, sail away,
tell your Theseus that Ariadne mourns,
blaming the unfulfilled deceiving oath of the Loves.
I know whence Eros, heavy in wrath, made the promise
of deceiving Theseus unfulfilled; for instead of Hera,
whom they call the Yoker, he swore the marriage-oath
of the virgin goddess, of unstained Athena;
he swore the oath of Pallas; what have Pallas and Cytherea to do with each other?"

Such things as she mourned Bacchus delighted to hear;
and he knew Cecropia and learned the name of Theseus
and the deceiving voyage from Crete; and near the girl,
with his inspired form, he gleamed; and the maiden
to a stronger love for another, raving Eros,
the wandering one, lashed with his goading girdle,
that the Minoan girl, persuaded, he might yoke
to his brother Dionysus.
And consoling the mournful, ill-loved Ariadne,
Bacchus spoke such a word with his heart-charming voice:

"Maiden, why do you grieve for the deceiving citizen of Athens?
Let go the memory of Theseus; you have Dionysus for a husband,
an immortal husband instead of a short-lived one; and if the mortal body
of a young man your own age delights you, never could Theseus
contend with Dionysus in valor and in beauty.
But you will say: the dweller of the earth-dug labyrinth,
the double-natured man yoked with a bull, he reddened with blood;
you know your helper, your thread; for the citizen of Athens,
the club-bearer, did not find a contest to fight,
had not the rose-skinned woman defended him; I will not teach you
the Paphian and Eros and the distaff of Ariadne.
You will not say that Athens is greater than the upper air;
Minos, your father, was not all like to all-ruling Zeus;
Cnossus is not the equal of Olympus.
Nor in vain did this voyage set out from my Naxos,
but Desire kept you for a better marriage;
blessed are you, because, leaving the inferior bed of Theseus,
you will behold the couch of lovely Dionysus.
What greater boast did you wish for? For you have both
heaven for your home, and Cronos' son is your father-in-law.
Cassiepeia will not be able to vie with you
because of her daughter's Olympian glory; for the ethereal
bonds of Andromeda among the stars Perseus gave;
but for you I will make a starry crown, so that you may be called
the gleaming consort of garland-loving Dionysus."

He spoke consoling; and the girl leaped with joy,
casting all memory of Theseus into the sea,
having received the heavenly wooer's promise
of marriage. And Eros adorned the bridal chamber for Bacchus;
and the wedding chorus rang out; and about the chamber
all flowers bloomed; and with spring leaves
the dancing women of Orchomenus circled Naxos;
and the Hamadryad sang of the bridal chambers, and about the springs
the unveiled, unsandalled Naiad Nymph approved
Ariadne joined to the vine-clad god;
and Ortygia cried aloud, and to the kinsman of city-guarding Phoebus,
Lyaeus, striking up a bridegroom's hymn,
she leaped into the dance, immovable though she was.
And weaving a circling flower of purple roses,
the fiery prophet Eros plaited a crown, of one hue with the stars,
the herald of the heavenly Crown; and about the bride
of Naxos leaped the bride-decking swarm of the Loves.
And consorting in the bridal chamber with yoking marriage-songs,
the Gold-fathered husband sowed a many-childed seed.

And rolling the long whirl of gray time,
he remembered his own fair-laboring mother Rhea;
and leaving Naxos, full of the Graces, blameless,
he went through all the cities of Hellas; and near horse-pasturing
Argos he came, even if Hera held Inachus.
But they did not receive him, and the dance-weaving women
and the Satyrs they drove off, and refused his thyrsi,
lest Hera should ever harm the Pelasgian seat,
the jealous one, heavy in wrath, bearing down upon Lyaeus;
and the old Silenoi they held back. And grieving,
Dionysus drove all the women of Inachus to frenzy;
and the Achaean women cried aloud with bellowing; and against those who met them
they rushed at the crossroads; and upon their own
newborn babes the wretched ones sharpened their knives,
of whom one drew her sword and the mother killed her son,
another shattered her three-year-old child,
and one hurled into the air a wandering boy
still seeking his dear milk; and at the destruction
of the newborn babes Inachus raged at the fate;
and the mother killed her son, and there was no desire for the breasts
that nurse the child, no memory of the necessary birth-pang;
and at Asterion, where many first-fruits of riper youth,
the flower of the young men's hairless heads were shorn,
it received the boys themselves and no longer the locks of their hair.
And one, seeing a servant of approaching Lyaeus,
spoke such a word, a citizen of the Pelasgian land:

Such a word he spoke, laughing in scorn at Dionysus.
And Pelasgian Hera armed the Argive phalanx;
and she likened herself to the prophet Melampus; and in anger
she broke out a warlike voice to Gorgon-slaying Perseus:

"Offspring of a heavenly line, helmet-flashing Perseus,
lift up your sickle, lest with some unwarlike thyrsus
feeble women lay waste your Argos;
do not fear one single snake, the girdle of his locks,
since your blood-red beast-slaying hook
mowed the harvest of so many serpents of Medusa;
arm against the phalanx of the Bassarids; and of the bronze-roofed
chamber be mindful, where through the bosom of Danae
rainy Zeus poured the golden bride-stealing shower,
lest Danae, after her bed, after the golden marriage,
should bend a slavish knee to worthless Lyaeus;
show that you bear the true blood of Cronos' son,
show that you have a golden race, and proclaim
the bed of the rich heavenly snow;
and war with the Satyrs; and against arming Lyaeus
stretch out the bloody eye of snake-haired Medusa,
and after the bitter lord of sea-washed Seriphos
I shall behold another new stony Polydectes.
With you all-subduing Argive Hera arms herself,
the stepmother of Bromius; and defending Mycenae,
lift up your city-saving sickle, that I may see
spear-won Ariadne following Perseus;
kill the rank of the ox-horned Satyrs; and of the Bassarids
with the Gorgon's eye change the mortal sight
into a self-made image of like form; and with answering
stony beauty adorn your streets,
making varied statues in the markets of Inachus.
Why do you fear Dionysus, whom the beds of Zeus did not beget?
Tell me, what could he do to you? When will a footman on the ground
ever overtake the winged one, riding aloft through the air?"

So she spoke, emboldening him; and Perseus flew into battle.
And calling the citizens, the Pelasgian trumpet roared,
of whom one lifted the spear of the warrior Lynceus,
another that of older Phoroneus, another of Pelasgus,
another raised the Abantian shield in his hand
and the ashen spear of Proetus, and the quiver of Acrisius
another man lifted, while another, bold, stood for battle
holding the sword of Danaus, with which once, lifting it bare,
he armed his daughters for man-slaying marriage,
another wielded a great axe, which beside the altar
Inachus, the inspired priest of city-holding Hera,
once stood lifting, the cleaver of oxen's foreheads.
And the battle-rousing army upon high-stepping horses
ran behind warring Perseus; and one stood by
hurling the war-cry from rough lips,
a footman, and fitted his bow to the curving string,
and lifted the hollow quiver upon his back;
and the champion of the Argives was sickle-bearing Perseus,
and he laced his feet in airy sandals,
and lifted the head of unseen Medusa.

And Iobacchus armed his free-tressed women
and the horned Satyrs; and he was stirred into Bacchic frenzy in the din,
seeing the airy course of the winged champion;
and in his hand he lifted the thyrsus, holding before his face
the adamant, the stone turned to rock by the rain of Zeus,
the defender against stony-eyed Medusa,
that he might escape the hateful gleam of the unseen face.
And seeing the phalanxes of the Bassarids and the sacred things of Lyaeus,
laughing dreadfully, helmet-flashing Perseus spoke:

So speaking he fought in the front; and he frightened the Bacchants,
arming for war and the reaper of Medusa,
Hera the all-subduing; and flashing down upon Bacchus
the likeness of lightning, a god-sped leaping fire,
she hurled against Bromius the light-bearing fiery spear.
And laughing Dionysus answered with a raving voice:

"You have no point so flashing, an unarmed point;
you cannot rout me, even if you got a fiery spear;
nor does the lightning of Zeus harm me; for half-finished,
an infant still, Bacchus the thunderbolts washed,
pouring an unburning breath upon unharmed Dionysus.
And you, proud one, sickle-bearing Perseus, cease;
this is no battle of a lesser Gorgon, no single bride,
heavy-bound Andromeda, the prize; but with Lyaeus
you wage strife, who has the race of Zeus, to whom alone
Rhea once offered the life-bringing breast, whom once with the fire
of the bridal lightning the gentle flame brought to birth,
whom the West, whom the Morning-star marvelled at, to whom the ranks of the Indians
yielded, whom even Deriades and Orontes feared,
who, holding the boundless likeness of the towering Giants,
fell, to whom bold Alpos sank down, the son of Earth,
holding a vast cloud-near body, to whom the Arab
people bend the knee, while the Sicilian sailor still sings
of the bastard sea-roving shape of the Tyrrhenians, whose form,
human, I changed to another, and instead of men
dancing fish leap in the sea.
You heard the lament of seven-gated Thebes; I will not teach you
dread-mad Pentheus and child-slaying Agave;
you have no need of report or witness, that of Lyaeus
your Argos made trial, while the Achaean women themselves
still groan over their own birth-pangs.
But, friend, make war, and soon, pierced by my clusters,
you will praise Bacchus, because you will see the wings of your sandals
yielding to my unbroken buskins;
never will you scatter the battle of the Bassarids, never will I cease
sending the wine-dark thyrsus, until I show your throat
in Argos pierced by the ivy-spear,
and your sickle conquered by leaves; nor will Zeus,
my father, save you, nor your gray-eyed kinswoman, nor your Hera,
much though she rages against war-steadfast Dionysus;
but I will kill you, and proud Mycenae
will see the reaper of Medusa reaped;
or binding you fast in a chest with a greater bond
I will hurl you afloat a second time on the familiar sea;
and if you will, go up again at last to your Seriphos.
But if you boast about your golden race,
have for fellow-laborer worthless golden Aphrodite."

So speaking he fought in the front; and the Bacchants advanced,
and the Satyrs warred. And above the head of Bromius,
fluttering his light wings, aloft flew Perseus;
but Iobacchus, raising his body, neighbor to the upper air,
wingless, high-pathed, was lifted on a greater stride
higher than flying Perseus, and to the seven-pathed
air he brought his hand, and consorted with Olympus,
and pressed the clouds; and Perseus quailed in fear,
beholding the unreachable right hand of Dionysus
touching the sun and reaching the moon.
But leaving Dionysus he fought against the raving Bacchants;
and shaking in his hand the death-bearing eye of Medusa
he made stone the arming Ariadne.
And Bacchus roared the more, seeing his bride turned to rock;
and now he would have sacked Argos and overthrown Mycenae
and mowed down the whole rank of the Danaans, and now
he would have wounded the very Hera, fighting unknown and unwounded,
in the false mortal form of the answering prophet,
and now swift-sandalled Perseus would have perished beyond his fate,
had not Hermes, appearing behind him with winged sandal,
seized his golden tress and reined him back,
and soothed him with a kindly, harm-averting word:

"True blood of Zeus, bastard child of jealous Hera,
you know how I saved you from the Zeus-sent fires,
and gave you, still a child, to the Nymphs, the daughters
of the river Lamus, and again, taking you in my arms,
brought you to the house of your child-rearing Ino;
and you, showing gratitude to your rescuer, the son of Maia,
kinsman, lull to rest this kindred battle; for both,
Perseus and Dionysus, are the offspring of one father;
do not blame the Argive army, do not blame the sickle of Perseus;
for not willingly does he arm for war; but Hera
armed him, and in the form of the prophet Melampus
he fights openly; but you, hold off and let the strife alone,
lest crafty Hera bear down on you again.
But you will speak of your wife's death; in a glorious fate
fighting she died, and dead Ariadne
you ought rather to count blessed, that she found so great a slayer,
born of a heavenly and not a mortal stock,
the reaper of the sea-beast and of horse-bearing Medusa;
the threads of the Fates obey none; for of heavenly stock
died Electra, the consort of Zeus, and she herself departed,
wedded to that Zeus, the sister of your Cadmus,
Europa, after the Olympian bed, and your own
mother died still bearing your seed in her womb;
Semele did not pass the gates of Olympus before her death,
but when she received her fate. And dying, your bride
will come to the star-wandering heaven, and near
our seven-pathed Pleiad, Maia, she will appear.
What more dear did she wish than to shine upon the earth,
dwelling in the upper air after Crete, Ariadne?
But lay down your thyrsus, and leave Enyo to the winds,
and the self-made image of earthly Ariadne
fix where the heavenly image of Hera stands.
Do not sack the city where the blood of your forebears is,
but honor the land of your ox-horned Io,
lulling your thyrsus to rest; and the Achaean women
you will praise hereafter, when an altar of ox-faced Hera
they will raise, and of your fair-chambered bride."

Such a word he spoke; and leaving horse-pasturing Argos,
back to the pole he came, having blended for both,
for Perseus and for Dionysus, a law of concord.
Nor did Argive Hera remain there for long;
but changing her false mortal form,
taking her divine shape, she returned again to Olympus.
And to the host of Inachus old Melampus spoke,
the god-fearing blood of Lynceus, first-born of Pelasgus:

"Obey the prophet, and shake the wine-dark Bacchus;
shake the bronze rattles and the Euian drums of Rhea,
lest he lay waste the whole race of Inachus,
lest after the infant children he destroy the young men,
lest after the death of the children he kill the women;
but make a god-pleasing sacrifice to Bacchus
and to Zeus, and dance for Perseus and for Dionysus."

So speaking he persuaded them; and the people gathered,
striking up for Bacchus a night-dancing song,
and set up the rites; and in god-summoning dance
the rattles rang out, and feet beat the ground,
and torches blazed; and the gathered citizens
smeared their cheeks with the mystic white gypsum;
and the drums rang out, and as the bronze was struck
a twin clattering din roared; and the altars reddened
with the slaughter of bulls in ranks, one upon another,
and countless sheep were killed; and the men at the blazing altar
appeased Bacchus, and the women made him gracious;
and the air-wandering melody, a female cry, sounded,
answering the revel that ransoms life; and the Inachian
maenads cast their mind-banishing madness to the winds.

48. Seek the blood of the Giants in the forty-eighth book,
and look for Pallene, and the child of sleeping Aura.

But riding upon the rim of his chariot of leopards,
Bacchus revelled, wandering through the Thracian land,
leaving the horse-pasturing soil of first-born Phoroneus.
Nor did Inachian Hera soften her relentless wrath
now that Argos was driven to frenzy, but keeping the memory
of the madness of the Achaean women, she armed herself again against Bacchus.
And she revealed her crafty prayers to all-mothering Earth,
crying out the deeds of Zeus and the manhood of Dionysus,
who had destroyed the boundless cloud of earth-born Indians;
and when the life-bearing mother heard that the child of Semele
had wiped out the swift-doomed Indian race,
remembering her sons she groaned the more; and against Bacchus
she armed the mountain-running tribes of the self-born Giants,
rousing her high-crested children to the din of war:

"My children, make war against cluster-bearing Dionysus
upon the steep crags, and the destroyer of my race,
the Indian-slaying son of Zeus, overtake; let me not see
the bastard scepter-bearer of Olympus ruling beside Zeus.
Bind, bind Bacchus, that he may be a chamber-servant,
when I grant Hebe in marriage to Porphyrion
and Cytherea to Chthonios, when I sing the gray-eyed goddess
the consort of Enceladus and Artemis of Alcyoneus;
bring me Dionysus, that I may vex the son of Cronos
beholding the slavery of spear-won Lyaeus;
or, wounding him with the destroying iron,
kill me him, all like to Zagreus, that someone may say,
either a god or one of mortals, that at the offspring of Cronos' son
Earth in her wrath armed twin slayers,
the elder Titans against the former Dionysus,
and the younger Giants against the later-born Dionysus."

So speaking she roused the whole rank of the Giants.
And the phalanxes of the earth-born advanced to the din of war.
One, holding a Nysaean crag, another, with iron
chiseling out the cloud-high ravined hollow,
armed himself with rocks to hurl at Dionysus;
another a stony crest of the sea-based land,
another, breaking off the ridge of the sea-girt isthmus,
hastened to the battle-cry. And with boundless hands
high-headed Pelorus hurled up Pelion,
laying bare the hollow house of Philyra; and as the unroofed
crag was snatched away, old Chiron quailed,
man-formed, unfinished, twined with the horse his age-mate.
And holding a cluster of the vine, the destroyer of Giants,
Bacchus ran down upon high-crested Alcyoneus,
not holding a rushing spear, not lifting a bloody sword,
but he tore the scattered hands of the Giants,
striking with his garlands; and with the strong-wine leaf
the dreadful tribes of earth-nurtured serpents were torn apart;
and as the snake-haired heads of a Giant were struck,
their reaped necks danced in the dust.
And countless tribes were killed; and as the Giants were torn,
rivers of ever-flowing blood ran, and with freshly-poured
purple streams the ravines reddened.
And the phalanxes of the earth-born serpents raged in Bacchic terror,
fearing the locks of snake-haired Dionysus.
And with fire Bacchus fought, hurling into the air a brand,
the destroyer of his foes; and along the high-pathed track
the self-whirling Bacchic flame ran leaping,
darting with limb-devouring spark upon the Giants;
and one, bearing the gleam upon his threatening chin,
half-burnt, the serpent hissed with fire-heated throat,
spitting out smoke, no longer sending deadly venom.
And the tumult was boundless; and above the heads of his foes
Bacchus was lifted up, raising his warlike brand,
and with the earthly firebolt he heated the bodies of the Giants,
an answering likeness of the Zeus-hurled thunderbolt;
and the torches blazed; and upon the head of Enceladus
the wandering fire whirled, heating the air;
but it did not overcome him, and by the breath of earthly fire
Enceladus did not bend his knee, since he was kept safe from the thunderbolt.
And boundless Alcyoneus leaped against Lyaeus,
armed with Thracian crags; and against Bacchus
he lifted the cloud-high ridge of wintry Haemus
to a useless aim, against unwounded Dionysus;
and he hurled the peak; but touching the unbroken
fawnskin of Lyaeus the hills were split apart;
and young Typhoeus laid bare the heads of Emathia,
high in view, all like to the former one, who once lifted
many a torn hollow of his mother the earth,
casting stony shafts at Dionysus.
And drawing a sword from one of the Giants writhing on the ground,
Bacchus the lord armed himself against the Giants' heads,
reaping the snaky harvest of their venom-shooting locks;
and slaying the self-made host with unarmed hand
he fought in frenzy, the rider upon green trees,
holding the long-leaved ivy, the spear-thrower against the Giants.
And now he would have slain them all with his man-breaking thyrsus,
but turning back he withdrew willingly from the fight,
keeping his foes alive for his father.
And now swiftly he would have run to Phrygia with quick foot,
but another labor held him back, that of so many dead
he might kill one man, a murderer,
the death-bringing father of Pallene, who once,
holding a lawless frenzy for his daughter's ill-mated marriage,
broke off her wedlock, and slaughtering countless
would-be suitors he reaped them down, beneath whose gore,
as they were killed, the wrestling-grounds reddened with clamor,
until Bacchus came, the champion of Justice; and standing
beside the ill-loving father of marriageable Pallene,
he asked for the wicked marriage of the chilling girl,
and offered varied gifts; and to Lyaeus, who asked,
the dreadful man proclaimed a wrestling-match for the marriage;
and leading him he set him in the ill-guesting wrestling-ground,
where the bold spear-shaking girl stood,
lightly bearing on her shoulders the bridal oxhide.
And then Cypris was the contest-judge; and in the midst
naked Eros stood, and held out the bridal wreath to Bacchus,
and the wrestling was the bride-decker; and in silvery
raiment Persuasion clothed her delicate body,
foretelling the victory of marriage-bound Lyaeus.
And the girl stripped the garments from her strong limbs,
and laid down her rushing spear for the wedding, and more delicate
the Sithonian girl stood, unveiled, unsandalled,
womanlike, unarmed, and with a reddening band
she girdled the rounded ring of her firm breasts;
and her body was uncovered, and the unbound locks
of her boundless hair flowed over the girl's neck,
and she bared her legs and the folds of her uncovered thighs,
the naked knee showing; and about her thighs
she fitted a white woven cloth, the covering of a woman's modesty;
and her skin she had smeared with oily ointment,
and her hands far more, so that from his unbreakable grip
the girl's slippery body might slide away when pressed.
And threatening Lyaeus with grim lips,
she stood by the bride-decking suitor, and a double
bond she cast about his neck with the pull of yoked arms;
but turning back Bacchus loosed his own neck,
casting off the girl's soft-skinned fingers,
shaking his twined neck free of the womanish bonds;
and circling his two hands in a ring upon her waist
he shook Pallene with a counter-pulling heave of his feet;
and he gripped her rosy hand, and held it,
the Cyprian consolation, pressing the snowy hand;
nor did he so much long to roll the girl upon the ground
as to touch her soft skin, delighting in the sweet
labor; and he toiled, drawing a deceiving breath
like a mortal, and by a willing delay he gave up the victory.
And lovely Pallene, with the skilful heave of wrestling,
lifted the body of Lyaeus with her womanish hands;
nor did she raise so great a weight, but wearying
she left the male limbs of unmoving Dionysus.
And the god, with an answering bond of clasping hands,
seizing the lovely maiden, as one lifting a thyrsus,
lightly raised her aslant and twined high above his shoulder;
but with sparing hand he shook off the heavy girl,
and stretched all of unshaken Pallene upon the ground;
and with crafty eyelids he turned his gaze,
beholding the dusty limbs of the soft-haired girl
and the soiled locks of her uncared-for head.
But turning back, leaping up from the dust,
upright the girl planted her feet a second time;
and Dionysus, with a rolling unsparing thrust of his knee,
gripping the belly of Pallene with a counter-pulling heave,
longed to roll the maiden upon the ground,
and shifted his hands, twining them about her sides,
arching her neck crosswise, and about her middle
back he circled his fingers bent behind,
watching to catch either ankle or shin or knee.
And the god, self-rolling, willingly fell to the ground,
conquered by a worthless hand; and a lovely
drug of love he had, and in the sweet dust,
lifting the lovely burden of the Loves upon his belly,
he himself stayed on his back, and did not shake off the girl,
but bound her with the heart-charming bond of desire.
And she, with a swift-whirling guiding heave of her feet,
lifted her step, and from love-maddened Lyaeus
loosed his male hand; and the god, with a lesser thrust,
turning his limbs, stretched out the rosy girl,
laying her on the ground; and the girl lay upon the earth,
spreading out her hands; and as she stretched along the ground
with skilful hand he yoked her neck in a binding bond.
With swifter feet the father, rushing into the midst,
reined back his daughter, who wished to keep contending,
and broke off the marriage-contest of the wedding,
entrusting the lovely victory to Dionysus,
lest she kill him, holding him in an unyielding bond.
And when Zeus had praised the prize-winning victory,
Eros crowned his kinsman with the bride-leading cluster,
who had completed the lovely wrestling of marriage.
And such a contest was like to it, as when the girl
Atalanta, hastening, was conquered by Hippomenes,
who rolled the golden-gleaming bridal gifts before her.
But when Bacchus had finished the contest of the bride-decking
wrestling, still dripping the marriage sweat of the toils,
he overthrew Sithon, struck by the sharp thyrsus,
the slayer of suitors; and as he rolled in the dust
he gave the girl the murderous thyrsus, the dowry of the Loves.
And the marriage was much-hymned; and in the unsilent chamber
the Silenoi sang, and the Bacchants danced,
and the drunken Satyrs wove a hymn of the Loves,
singing the union of the prize-won marriage.
And the phalanxes of the Nereids beneath the foot of the neighboring isthmus
girdled Dionysus with a bridal dance,
and sang a song, and by the Thracian sea
old Nereus, the host of Bromius, danced,
and Galatea, leaping about the bridal sea,
sang of Pallene joined to Dionysus,
and Thetis leaped, though she was unskilled in the Loves,
and Melicertes crowned the bridal ridge of the sea-girt isthmus,
crying the wedding-shout for the marriage of Pallene;
and one of the Hamadryads, by fiery neighboring Lemnos,
the Athonian, kindled the bridal Thracian pine.
And consoling his bride with friendly words
as she mourned her father, the Euius-loving husband said:

"Maiden, do not lament your ill-loving father;
maiden, do not lament the suitor of your virginity;
what father begot and led a daughter to marriage?
Let go your empty grief, that over your slain father,
your Sithon, Justice dances laughing,
and with maiden hands kindling the bridal fire,
she who knows no marriage still sings your marriage,
beholding another Oenomaus dead;
Oenomaus perished, and at her father's death
Hippodameia rejoices with her newly-wed husband.
And you too, casting the longing for your father to the storm-winds,
delight, joined to your cluster-bearing husband,
escaping your father's reproach; I will not teach you
the hateful love of Sithon and his delay of marriage,
who, lifting in murderous hand the son-in-law-slaying spear,
made you grow old, untried in Aphrodite,
and broke off the union of your unwedded bed.
Behold the rotted remains of the dead suitors,
whom the Paphian adorned and the raging Fury killed;
behold those heads, the first-fruits of your halls,
still dripping with the gore of the ill-guesting marriages.
You do not have the earthly race of Sithon; but heavenly,
I am persuaded, your Thracian Ares begot you,
I am persuaded that Cytherea bore your race;
and you stamped yourself with the laws of your twin parents,
having the temper of Ares and the splendor of Aphrodite;
I am persuaded that the contest-lord Hermes begot you,
coming to the delicate marriage-fulfilling bed of Persuasion,
and taught you wrestling, the escort of the Loves."

He spoke, consoling her grief with a healing word,
and lulled the lovely tears of the mourning girl.
And for a time he lingered near his bride,
delighting in the love of the newly-yoked marriage.
And leaving the halls of Pallene and Thracian Boreas,
he came to the house of Rhea, where by the Phrygian foot
were the Cybeleid courts of the fair-laboring goddess.

There, hunting by the foot of the Dindyma rock,
the Rhyndacian maiden Aura grew up, the mountain-roamer,
still unskilled in love, fellow-runner of the Archer-goddess,
fleeing the thoughts of unwarlike maidens,
a younger Artemis of Lelantos, whom once the Titan,
wedding Periboia, the offspring of Ocean,
the elder-born Lelantos begot, a storm-footed girl,
a girl who matched men, untried in Aphrodite.
She grew up taller than her age-mates,
lovely, rosy-armed, ever delighting in the hills;
and often hunting she ran down the raging bear,
and sent her rushing spear to cast at the lioness,
not killing deer and not shooting hares;
but lifting the blood-red quiver
she shot with beast-slaying arrows the mountain-running tribes
of flesh-devouring lions; and in name and in deed
she had the swiftest course, running with the mountain breezes.
And once, in the fire-bright hour of thirsty heat,
the maiden, sleeping, rested from the toils of the hunt;
and stretching her body high upon the Cybelean grass,
laying her head against the shoot of a chaste laurel,
she slept at midday; and of the marriage to come
she saw a lovely prophetic dream-vision,
that the fiery god, stretching his arrow on the burning string,
rushing Eros, the hare-shooter, shot within the thicket,
shooting the rank of beasts with worthless arrows;
and with the boy as he hunted, the son of Myrrha,
Cypris went laughing; and the maiden Aura stood,
behind the bow of Artemis, from her shoulder above
lifting the quiver of huntsman Eros;
but he slew the beasts, until he had his fill of the string,
shooting the grim mouth of leopards and the jaw of a bear,
and capturing a lioness alive with his all-charming girdle
he showed the pressed beast to his playful mother;
and the maiden thought in the dark that her, too,
leaning her arm upon Adonis and Cytherea,
greedy Eros provoked, bending to Aphrodite
as a captive, the slavish knee of an arrogant lioness,
crying out such a word: "Garland-bearing mother of the Loves,
I bring you maiden-loving Aura, bowing her neck to you;
but, dancing women of love-stricken Orchomenus,
crown the bride-decking girdle-strap, since so great a will
he has conquered, of the unconquerable lioness."
Such a prophetic word the mountain-girl Aura saw;
nor was the dream of the Loves in vain, since they too
bring a man into the net and hunt a woman.
And the girl, awaking, raged at the prudent laurel,
and fought with the Paphian and Eros, and more with Sleep
she was angry, the bold one, and threatened the Dream,
and blamed the leaves and spoke with a voiceless voice:

"Laurel, why do you rout me? What have Cypris and your tree to do together?
I went astray, sleeping beneath your neighboring branches,
thinking your plant maiden-loving, but of your report
I did not get truth, nor of hope; so then, Laurel,
changing your body, did you find a way to change your mind?
Surely you do not serve marriage-loving Aphrodite after your fate?
