This tree is not of a prudent maiden, but of a newly-wed bride;
it is no wonder to see these dreams beside the myrtle;
this is a dream worthy of a wanton; surely Persuasion,
surely your laurel-Apollo planted you with his hand?"

She spoke, angry at once with the plant and Eros and Sleep.
And once, hunting through the mountains, the mistress of the chase,
her skin lashed with the smoky heat of fire,
Artemis prepared her chariot, that with the Naiad Nymphs
she might cool her hot body in the mountain-poured baths,
when it was midsummer, blazing, when, brandishing
the fiery midday sound of his parching whip,
the sun shone upon the Lion's back.
And the deer in their yoking harness
Artemis the mountain-roamer fastened together; and mounting the chariot
the maiden Aura took the whip and the reins,
and drove the horned, storm-swift wagon.
And the bandless daughters of ever-flowing Ocean,
handmaids, rushed together with the Archer-goddess,
of whom one, swift-kneed, ran before her mistress,
another, equal in pace, drawing up her tunic,
was near, and another, touching the wicker-body
of the long-greaved wagon, kept a fellow-running course.
And the Archer-goddess, gleaming the light of her face,
flashed brighter than her handmaids, as when in her
ethereal chariot, sending the flame of sleepless torches,
shooting cloudless rays, Selene
rose full-shining among the fire-fed stars,
dimming the whole heavenly rank with her face;
with a light equal to hers Artemis ran through the wood,
until she came to the place where, with sounding stream,
the Zeus-fallen water of the river Sangarius is drawn.
And Aura reined in her twining whip,
and checking the deer with golden bridles
she halted the light-bringing chariot of her mistress beside the streams;
and the goddess ran down from the chariot; and from her shoulders
Oupis took her bow, and Hecaerge her quiver,
and the daughters of Ocean the fair-plaited hunting-nets;
and the hounds . . . and Loxo loosed the buskins from her feet.
And she, at midday, kept the maiden-loving reverence of modesty
in the river's flow, creeping through the streams
with sparing steps, and from foot to head
drawing up little by little her dipped tunic,
clasping her feet about with her twin thighs,
the girl bathed her whole hidden body in measured fashion.
And looking sidelong through the water, sharp-eyed Aura
with bold eyelids of a shameless face
measured the holy body of the unseen girl,
beholding the marvelous form of her prudent mistress;
and stretching out her feet, with arms outspread,
the maiden Aura swam together with the swimming goddess.
And half-seen, unfinished, within the river-bank,
wiping the wet drops from her hair . . .
Artemis the huntress; and close to her rustic Aura,
fingering her breasts, cried out a god-fighting voice:

"Artemis, you have only the maiden-loving name of a girl,
since across your bosom, with the loose ring of your nipple,
you have the female breast of the Paphian, not the male breast of Athena,
and your cheeks shoot rosy sparks;
but, taking on the body of a love-stricken goddess,
do you too be queen of marriages with soft-haired Cytherea,
receiving some bridegroom in your chamber; and if you will,
lie with Hermes and Ares, leave Athena;
and if you will, lift the arrow and bow of the Loves,
if you handle the bold frenzy of the arrow-bearing quiver.
Be gracious, your form; I am far better than you;
behold, how I bear my strong body; behold the male form,
and the step of Aura, swifter than Zephyr;
behold, how my arms swell; behold the breasts,
unripe, swelling, milkless; surely you would say
that yours gush a milky dew;
how do you have a soft-skinned hand? How do your breasts
have no rounded circle, like those of Aura,
the self-made heralds of unrobbed virginity?"

She spoke in mockery; and downcast in silence,
her companion, the goddess, surged with swelling wrath,
and her eyes shot murderous sparks;
and she leaped up from the flood, and put on her tunic again,
and on her pure flanks a second time fitted her girdle
in grief. And she pursued vengeance; and she found the girl
high in the clouds beside the Bull, where, by neighboring Cydnus,
she had stilled the high-necked boast of Typhaon's threat;
and a self-rolling wheel was beside the feet of the mistress,
signifying that she drags all the proud to the ground,
whirling them from on high with the avenging circle of justice,
the all-subduing goddess, turning the course of life;
and about her, by her throne, flew an avenging bird,
a winged griffin, and was lifted on the beat of four feet
as the goddess flew, the self-announcing sign that she too
passes through the four-divided seats of the world,
binding the high-crested men with an unbreakable bridle,
an answering likeness, and as with the whip of evil,
as with a self-rolling wheel, she rolls the proud man.
And she knew, when she saw with greening face the goddess,
Artemis grieving, full of murderous threat,
and asking her she soothed her with a friendly word:

"Your wrath, Archer-goddess, your eyes cry aloud;
Artemis, what god-fighting son of Earth routs you?
What Typhoeus has sprung up again upon the ground?
Surely Tityos, returned, stretching his love-mad eye,
has not touched the untouched garment of your mother?
Artemis, where are your arrows and the shafts of Apollo?
Who again does violence to you, another Orion? He still lies there,
the wretch who touched your tunic,
a breathless corpse within the bowels of his mother; but if some man
with love-stricken hands seized your robes,
breed another scorpion, the avenger of your girdle;
and if again bold Otus or arrogant Ephialtes
longed for the unattainable union of your Loves,
kill the suitor of your unwedded virginity;
and if some woman of many children grieves your Leto,
let another stony Niobe weep her offspring;
what envy is there if I make another stone above Sipylus?
Surely your father does not vex you over a bed for the gray-eyed one?
Surely Cronos' son did not nod your marriage to Hermes,
as the wedding of pure Athena to Hephaestus?
And if a woman routs you, as your mother Leto,
I will be the avenger of the grieving Archer-goddess."

Not yet did her speech cease; and to the harm-averting goddess
forestalling her, the dog-rearing girl cried out such a word:
So she spoke, and the goddess emboldened her and answered with a word:

"Daughter of Leto, bed-fleeing, dog-driver, sister of Phoebus,
I will not subdue the Titan child with my sickle,
nor will I make her a stony bride in Phrygia,
since I too am born of the most ancient blood of the Titans,
lest father Lelantos ever blame me when he hears;
but one thing I grant you, Archer-goddess: rustic Aura
has reproached your virginity, and she will be a maiden no more;
and you shall behold her through her mountain-poured bosom
still lamenting her girdle with welling tears."

She spoke, consoling her; and the girl left the hills,
Artemis, seated in the four-yoked chariot of deer,
and went to Phrygia. And with a like-zealous course
the maiden Adrasteia pursued hard-fighting Aura,
yoking contending griffins beneath the bridle;
and swiftly she was borne through the air on her swift chariot,
and stayed her course above the heads of Sipylus
before the stony-eyed face of the Tantalid,
clasping the crooked bridles of the winged four-foots.
And she came near proud Aura; and the high-minded
neck of the wretch she struck with her snaky whip,
and shook her with the wheel-like circle of justice,
and bent the mindless mind of the unbending one; and about the girdle
of the maiden she whirled her viperous whip,
Argive Adrasteia; and to please the goddess,
though her brother Dionysus was very angry,
she armed another love, though she was unskilled in the Loves,
after the bed of Pallene, after the death of Ariadne,
the one left in her fatherland, the other in an alien
land turned to stone, like the image of Achaean Hera,
and far more than Broe over an unfulfilled bed.
And Nemesis flew off beside the snow-struck Bull,
until she came a second time to Cydnus; and about the girl
Eros stirred Dionysus to frenzy with a sweet-shooting arrow,
and wheeling his wings the light one flew back to Olympus.
And the mountain-roaming god was lashed with a greater fire;
for it was no slight consolation; he had then no
Cyprian hope of the girl, no drug of the Loves;
but Eros burned him the more with his heart-charming fire
for the late-fulfilled marriage of raving, unyielding Aura.
And in pain he hid his desire, nor in the thickets
did he hold converse with Aura in Cyprian words,
lest she flee him. What is more wretched than when men alone
long, and the women feel no desire?
And he kept in his heart the fixed arrow of the Loves,
to see if the maiden held a dog-driving course within the thicket;
and as her tunic was lifted by the Cyprian winds,
gazing at her thigh, the wandering Bacchus grew womanish.
And late, shaken by the seething desire of Aura,
helpless Bacchus cried out a word with a raving voice:

"I have the likeness of ill-loving Pan, since she flees me,
the wind-roaming maiden, and with desert sandal
wanders unsteadily, more than unseen Echo.
Blessed Pan, far more than Bromius, because seeking
you found the cure of love in a heart-charming voice;
your sound the after-voiced, unstable Echo answers,
uttering a like talking sound; would that she too,
the maiden Aura, would belch one word from her lips.
This love is not like all others; for she herself
does not nurse a temper like that of other maidens.
What cure is there for my pain? Shall I charm her
with a Cyprian nod? When, ah when is Aura charmed
by moving eyelids? Stretching a love-mad eye,
who with marriage-words leads astray the mind of a bear
to the Paphian, to Eros? Who has held converse with a lioness?
Who has spoken a word to an oak? Who has deceived the breathless pine?
Who persuaded the cornel-tree, and led the rock to marriage?
What man could charm the unmoved mind of Aura?
What man could charm her? And to the ungirdled girl
who could speak of marriage or the girdle, love's helper?
Who of the sweet sting of Eros or the name of the Cyprus-born?
Athena would sooner be persuaded; nor does fearless Artemis
flee me so much as maiden-loving Aura.
Would that with friendly lips she would speak only this word:
'Bacchus, you long in vain, do not seek the maiden Aura.'"

He spoke, walking within the flowering meadow
with the spring breezes, and beside the fragrant myrtle,
sweetly at midday he lulled his feet to rest, and against a tree
he leaned, holding the hissing Zephyr-breeze,
held fast by both weariness and love; and as he sat,
of its own accord, peering over a neighboring cluster,
a maiden, an unveiled Hamadryad Nymph, spoke,
bearing faithful tidings to Cypris and to lovely Lyaeus:

"Bacchus can never lead Aura to his bed,
unless he fetter the heavy-bound one with chains,
twining her feet and hands with Cyprian bonds,
or, yoking her in marriage as she sleeps,
steal the dowerless virginity of the maiden."

So speaking she went back and hid in the cluster of her age,
entering again her oaken house; but Bacchus, in his toil,
sent his mind wandering in love-bearing dreams.
And the wind-roaming soul of dead Ariadne,
standing beside sweetly-sleeping Dionysus,
jealous after her death, spoke with a dream-voice:

"Forgetful Dionysus of your former marriage,
the jealousy of Aura holds you, and you care nothing for Ariadne;
alas for my Theseus, whom the bitter wind snatched away,
alas for my Theseus, whom Phaedra got for a husband.
It was not fated for me to escape my oath-breaking husband,
if the sweet young man left me sleeping, and instead of him
I was wedded to ill-loving and deceiving Lyaeus.
Alas, that I had no swift-doomed mortal husband,
for then, armed against love-mad Dionysus,
I too would have been one of the Lemnian women.
But the suitor of a much-scattered bridal bed,
the oath-breaking bridegroom, after Theseus I will call you too;
and if your bride asks of you a gift of Eros,
receive my distaff, the love-gift of the Loves,
that you may give, lawless one, to your crag-loving bride
the gifts of your wife the Minoan, that someone may say:
'She gave a thread to Theseus and a distaff to Dionysus.'
And you too, after Cronos' son, changing bed for bed,
have imitated the deeds of your woman-mad father,
holding an insatiate frenzy for changeful love;
of your Sithonian wife and the newly-yoked marriage,
of Pallene, I know, and of the wedding of Althaea;
I will be silent about the love of Coronis, from whose bed
three yoked Graces were born; but, Mycenae,
cry out my fate and the wild eye of Medusa,
and of jealous Ariadne forced into love;
shores of Naxos, cry out: bridegroom Theseus,
the Minoan calls you, angry at Dionysus.
But why do I remember Cecropia? For to the Paphian
I make my complaint against both, Theseus and Dionysus."

So speaking she rushed away, all like to shadowy smoke.
And bold Bacchus woke, scattering the wing of Sleep,
and pitied the mourning Ariadne of his dream.
And he sought a shifting trick, the escort of the Loves;
and he remembered his former bed with the Astacid nymph,
how he had wed the lovely girl with a guileful drink,
having Sleep for the escort of the drunken-staggering marriage.
While Bacchus wished to prepare the trick of the bed,
meanwhile the roving girl of Lelantos ran,
seeking a spring, gripped by burning thirst.
Nor did the mountain-running, unstable Aura escape Dionysus
in her thirst; and swiftly leaping to the base of a rock
he struck the earth with his thyrsus; and the hill, splitting,
brought forth of itself wine from its fragrant breast,
in a purple stream; and to please Lyaeus
the Seasons, handmaids of the Sun, marked with flowers
the topmost brow of the spring, and with fragrant breezes
the sweet air of the new-grown meadow was lashed;
and it had the leaves of the cluster named for Narcissus,
the graceful youth, whom by leafy Latmos
his bridegroom Endymion of horned Selene begot,
who once, fair of skin, in the deceiving mute form,
seeing the water shaped into a self-made image,
died, gazing at the shadowy phantoms of his form;
and it held the living plant of Amyclaean hyacinth;
and flying in flocks upon the flowering cluster
the nightingales of spring sang above the leaves.
And there, thirsting, the midday Aura ran,
to see if anywhere, thirsting, she might behold the stream of Zeus
or some spring or the flow of a mountain-poured river;
and about her eyelids Eros poured a mist.
But when she saw the deceiving Bacchic spring,
then Persuasion drove the shadowy cloud from her eyes,
crying out such a word, the first herald of marriage to Aura:

"Maiden, come here, and of the marriage-fulfilling spring
receive the streams into your mouth, and into your bosom a husband."

And gladly the girl saw it; and bending over the spring
with opened lips she drew up the moisture of Bacchus.
And the maiden, drinking, uttered such a voice:

"Naiads, what is this wonder? Whence came this sweet water?
Who poured out this drink? What heavenly womb bore it?
At any rate, having drunk this, I no longer go to my running;
but my feet grow heavy, and I am charmed by sweet sleep,
and I send a stumbling, soft-sounding noise from my lips."
"You hunt, Dionysus; and the maiden Aura awaits you."

So speaking he hastened to Olympus, and waving his wings
he withdrew among the spring leaves, having carved this:
"Bridegroom, finish the bed while the maiden still sleeps;
in silence to us, lest sleep let the maiden go."

And seeing her, Iobacchus, upon her unbedded couch
plucking the Lethean wing of bridal Sleep,
soundless on the tips of his unsandalled feet creeping,
went after the dumb couch of speechless Aura;
and with sparing hand he laid aside the hollow quiver
of the maiden, and hid her bow in a hollow rock,
lest she shoot him, shaking off the wing of Sleep;
and with unbreakable bonds he yoked the girl's feet,
and with twining hands sealed the cord upon her hands,
lest she escape him; and spreading her on the dust,
the maiden heavy with sleep, all ready for Aphrodite,
he stole the marriage-harvest of sleeping Aura.
And he was a dowerless husband; and upon the ground the wretched one,
heavy with wine, unshaken, was wedded to Dionysus;
and with shadowy wings clasping the body of Aura,
Sleep was the bride-decker of Bacchus, because he himself
made trial of the Paphian, and is the yoke-mate of Selene,
and is the fellow-escort of nightly love, of the Loves;
and the marriage was as a dream. And with much-leaping dance
the hill leaped up into a self-whirling dance,
and half-seen the Hamadryad shook her age-mate pine;
only the maiden Echo did not dance among the hills,
and ashamed, unattainable, hid at the base of a rock,
lest she behold the marriage of woman-mad Dionysus.
And having fulfilled the wedding upon the noiseless bed,
the vine-clad bridegroom, lifting his guarded step,
kissed his bride's lovely lip, and loosed
her unbending feet and hands, and from the rock the quiver
taking in his hand, and the bow, he laid them again beside his bride.
And he came near the Satyrs, still breathing of the marriage,
entrusting the bed of sleeping Aura to the winds.
And the bride rose from her love; and the limb-loosing
sleep, the witness of the unheralded Loves, she shook off;
and gazing in amazement, outside her prudent girdle,
at her bared breast and the folds of her uncovered thigh
and her tunic spotted with the marriage-drops,
proclaiming her ravished, dowerless virginity,
she raged as she gazed; and she fitted her circling girdle,
shadowing her breast again, and the ring of her familiar breast
with the maiden belt she bound in vain with a bond.
And in grief she cried aloud, held in a leap of madness;
and she chased the husbandmen, and near the leafy bank,
avenging her guileful husband with a punishing law,
she slaughtered the shepherds; and with pitiless iron
she killed the oxherd the more, since she had learned that the bridegroom of Eos,
graceful Tithonus, was an ill-loved oxherd man,
because Selene the ox-driver too had loved
Latmian Endymion, busy with herds of oxen;
she heard too of the Phrygian, whom another maiden killed,
the bitter love of song, of the love-stricken herdsman;
she killed the goatherd the more, killed the whole flock of goats,
suffering terribly, because the girl had seen ill-loved Pan
holding the like form of a shaggy goat's face;
for she expected just this, shaken by desire for Echo,
that the shepherd Pan had forced the sleeping girl;
she subdued the tillers far more, because they too
serve Cypris, since a tiller of the soil was the man,
Iasion, the consort of Demeter who bears the sheaves;
and she killed the huntsman, persuaded by an older tale;
for she heard that Cephalus, the citizen of motherless Athena,
the hunter, was the husband of rose-crowned Eos;
and she slaughtered the servants of the Bacchic harvest,
because, gushing the dew of strong-wine drunkenness,
heavy with wine, ill-loved, they are the attendants of Lyaeus;
for not yet had she learned the guile of Dionysus
and the deceiving drink of strong-wine Cytherea,
but she emptied the huts of the crag-loving shepherds,
sprinkling the hills with reddening blood.
And shaking her mind, held in a leap of madness,
she came to the house of Cypris; and loosing the threatening girdle,
the belt of her newly-spun tunic,
she lashed the delicate body of the unconquerable goddess;
and snatching the image of marriage-fulfilling Cytherea
she came near the Sangarius, and as it rolled in the streams
she gave naked Aphrodite to the naked Naiads.
And after the divine image and the self-whirling whip
she hurled the delicate likeness of Eros into the dust;
and she left empty the house of the Cybeleid foam-born goddess.
And roving, unattainable, she entered her familiar thicket,
and touched her hunting-stakes, and remembered the hunt again;
and with wet eyelids she lamented her virginity,
and crying out shrill she uttered such a voice:

"What god loosed the bonds of my virginity?
If, as I slept upon my desert bed,
counselor Zeus, stealing his form, forced me,
nor reverenced even our neighbor Rhea,
after the wild beasts I will shoot the pole of stars;
and if Phoebus Apollo lay with me sleeping,
I will sack the whole stony, famous Pytho;
and if my Cyllenian Hermes plundered my bed,
I will destroy Arcadia root and branch with my arrows,
and make golden-circleted Persuasion my handmaid;
and if with the marriage-tricks of dream-weddings
unseen Dionysus plundered my virginity,
I will go where the house of Cybele is, and from high-crested
Tmolus I will chase frenzied Dionysus;
and hanging the murderous quiver on my shoulders
I will arm against Paphos, against Phrygia; for against both
I will stretch my bow, against Cypris and Dionysus.
With you, Archer-goddess, I am more angry, because you, girl,
did not kill me still a sleeping maiden, nor against him,
your own bedfellow, did you arm with your pure arrows."

She spoke, and reined in her trembling voice,
overcome by tears. And full of the seed of marriage-fulfilling
child-begetting Lyaeus, ill-maiden Aura
lifted a double burden; and the woman raged at her load,
maddened past bearing by the seed, ill-maiden Aura . . .
whether a self-born seed or from a man's marriage
or from a guileful god; and she remembered the bride of Zeus,
Plouto of dread offspring, the Berecyntian, from whose bed
Tantalus sprang. And she wished to cut open her womb,
that from her torn belly, in mindless madness,
she might wipe out the unnurtured, half-finished offspring.
And she lifted a sword, and through her naked breast
with her right hand she longed to drive the unsparing blade.
And often she went to the cave of a newly-delivered lioness,
that she might slip into the net of a willing Fate;
but the mountain-roaming beast, frightened, fled from her,
lest she kill it, and hid in the recess of a rock,
entrusting its cub to its desert bed.
And often through her swollen woman's bosom
the self-slayer longed to drive the willing sword,
that, self-slaughtered, she might escape the reproaches of her belly
and the mocking mouth of the delighting Archer-goddess;
and she longed to know her husband, that she too
might butcher her son for her refusing consort,
herself both child-slayer and bedfellow, that someone might say:
"A new Procne, a child-killer, is ill-wed Aura."
And watching her, pregnant with new children,
Artemis came near with a laughing face,
and provoked the wretched one, and spoke with a loveless voice:

"I saw Sleep, the chamber-servant of the Paphian; I saw of the Loves
the deceiving streams of the yellow bridal spring,
where with a guileful drink young women loose their girdle
of like age, the robber of virginity, in a marriage-dream;
I saw the slope, I saw, where by a yoking rock
unawares a woman is wedded to deceiving sleep;
I saw the love-mountain of Cypris, where, stealing
the virginity of women, husbands slip away.
Tell me, bed-fleeing woman, why today do you walk gently?
You who were once storm-swift, why do you go heavy-kneed?
You were wedded unwilling, and you know not your husband;
you cannot hide your secret marriage; for swollen
your milk-new breasts proclaim your husband.
Tell me, heavy-sleeping boar-slayer, maiden, bride,
how do you wear your green, reddening form?
Who stained your bed? Who plundered your virginity?
Yellow Naiads, do not hide the bridegroom of Aura.
I know, heavy-laden woman, your secret husband;
your marriage does not escape me, even if you wish to hide it,
your husband does not escape me; weighed down in body by sleep,
unshaken, you were wedded as a consort to Dionysus.
But leave your bow; refusing the quiver,
celebrate the rites of your woman-mad Bacchus,
bearing the drums in your hand and the cry of the fair-horned pipes.
And by your marriage-fulfilling bed I beseech you,
what gifts did your husband Dionysus give you?
Surely he gave you a fawnskin, the herald of your bed?
Surely he gave you bronze rattles, the toys of your children?
I am persuaded that he gave you a thyrsus, the thrower against lions;
and perhaps he gave cymbals, which the nurses shake,
remedies for babes against tearful pains."

She spoke in mockery; and the goddess went back again,
shooting beasts a second time, and grieving
she gave her cares to the airy winds.
And the mountain-roaming girl, without witness, high on a rock,
handling the sharp arrow of her painful labor,
had the dreadful roaring of a lioness in childbed;
and the rocks cried back; and answering the loud-thundering
voice of the girl, ill-sounding Echo bellowed.
And clasping her hands, like a lid, over her travail,
she shut the swift birth-pang of the ripening labor,
and held back the new-finished birth; for she would not
call hated Artemis to her labor;
and she refused the daughters of Hera, lest ever, as children
of the stepmother of Bacchus, they bear down on her labor.
And the girl in distress broke out a downcast cry,
goaded by the stings of unknown necessity:

"So may I see the Archer-goddess and rushing Athena,
so may I behold both pregnant;
prove Artemis in labor, midwife Seasons,
by the witness of childbirth, and say to the Trito-born:
'Gray-eyed maiden, new-bearing mother, motherless.'
So may I see maiden-loving Echo suffering the same,
bedded by Pan or by Dionysus, author of evils.
Artemis, you too, bearing, will be Aura's comfort,
dripping female milk for the childbed from a male breast."

She spoke, lamenting the heavy stings of childbirth.
And the Archer-goddess held back the birth, and to the
child-bearing bride she gave the toil of a hindered labor.
And Nicaea, the helmswoman of the rite of Lyaeus,
watching the toil and the shames of raving Aura,
broke out such a secret, pitying voice:

"Aura, suffering the same, lament your virginity too;
and bearing in your belly the burden of a painful labor,
endure with me, after the bed, to have the stings of childbirth too,
endure to offer your unfamiliar breast to the babes.
And whence did you too drink wine, the plunderer of my girdle?
And whence did you too drink wine, until you became pregnant, Aura?
And you too have suffered, bed-fleeing one, what I suffered; but you too
blame the deceiving sleep of the bride-decking Loves.
One guile fitted marriage to us both; one husband of Aura
made the maiden Nicaea the mother of children;
no longer have I a beast-slaying bow, no longer a string,
as before, do I draw an arrow too; but I am a wretched
loom-toiling woman, and no longer a rushing Amazon."

She spoke, pitying the child-fulfilling toil of Aura,
as one who herself had made trial of a wretched birth.
And the daughter of Leto, hearing the cry of heavy-voiced Aura,
came a second time, proud, near the bride;
and she provoked the suffering one, and cried with a goading word:

"Maiden, who made you a mother of children in childbed?
You who know no marriage, whence got you milk in your breast?
I did not see, I did not hear, that a maiden bears a son.
Surely my father changed nature? Surely women
bear apart from marriage? For you, maiden-loving girl,
are in labor with new children, though you hate Aphrodite.
Surely the women in childbed do not call Artemis
the helmswoman of necessary birth, because you alone
in your bearing have no need of the rustic Archer-goddess?
Nor did Eileithyia, the deliverer of your race,
behold your Dionysus from a midwifeless womb;
but the thunderbolts brought him half-finished to birth.
Do not be angry that you bear children among the crags;
for Rhea, the queen of the crags, made trial of childbirth;
what envy is there ever in this? You bear children among the mountains,
like the mountain-roaming wife of mountain-haunting Dionysus."

She spoke; and angry, the bride in childbed grieved,
ashamed before Artemis even in her pains. Ah, most wretched,
she was near the birth and wished to be a maiden.
And the babe came swifter to the light; for while Artemis
was still speaking her arrow-shooting word of childbirth,
the double, self-summoned birth of Aura was brought to light,
her labor loosed, whence, from the twin children,
the high-headed mountain of Rhea was named Dindymon.
And the goddess, beholding the new, fair-childed offspring,
turning back spoke such a word with answering voice:

She spoke, and swift-sandalled entered the shady wood.
And calling Nicaea, his Cybeleid bride,
who still blamed her bed, Dionysus showed
Aura in childbed, smiling; and of the desert girl
he spoke, boasting of his newly-fulfilled marriage:

"Just now, Nicaea, hardly, you found comfort of the Loves;
just now again Dionysus has accomplished a stealthy bed,
and plundered the marriage of another maiden; and in the hills
she who once fled even the mere name of the Loves,
the mountain-girl Aura, saw a like fate to your chamber.
You alone did not receive sweet sleep, the escort of the Loves,
you alone did not drink the deceiving wine, the robber of the girdle;
but, unknown, from a new-opened spring,
the bride-decking wine welled up again, and Aura drank.
But she knows the arrow of necessary childbirth;
by your Telete, your dance-weaving daughter, I beseech you,
hasten to lift up my son, lest she destroy him
with bold hands, my ill-contriving Aura;
for I know that of the twin babes she will slay one child
in her ungovernable madness; but you, succor Iacchus;
be the guardian of the better birth, that your Telete
may be a handmaid both to the son and to the father."

So speaking, proud Bacchus withdrew again,
exulting over both his Phrygian marriages,
the elder wife and the younger bride.
And holding a heavy grief beside the birth-fulfilling rock,
lifting her children, the mother in childbed cried out:

. . . she set under the cave the childbed meal of a lioness;
but the new fair-childed offspring of Dionysus
the leopard, licking the body with flesh-devouring jaws,
with prudent heart tended at her wise breast;
and the marvelling serpents circled the childbed
with venom-shooting mouths, since, guarding the new children,
the bridegroom of Aura made even the beasts gentle.
And with roving foot the girl of Lelantos sprang up,
holding the wild temper of a shaggy-breasted lioness,
and unattainable she hurled into the airy storms
one of her children, snatched from the beasts' jaws;
and the newly-born child, in a whirl of dust,
slid down headlong from the air to the ground;
and snatching it up she buried it in her own throat,
feasting on a dear meal. And from the loveless mother
the maiden Archer-goddess, frightened, snatched the other child
of Aura in childbed, and walking through the thicket
lifted the boy in her unfamiliar child-tending arm.
And after the bed of Bromius, after the whirl of childbirth,
fleeing the reproach of marriage, rustic Aura,
keeping the maiden-loving reverence of her ancient modesty,
came near the Sangarius; and with her back-strained bow
into the streams she threw her uncared-for quiver,
and headlong she leaped into the deep current,
with ashamed eyes refusing the light of Eos,
and was hidden by the river's surges; and Cronos' son
changed her into a fountain; and of the mountain-poured spring
her breasts became the jet, her body the flow, her hair the flowers,
and her horn became the bow of the fair-horned river,
bull-formed, and the reed-cord became the string,
and the reeds, turned into arrows, whistled,
and rushing through the muddy depth of the river
the poured quiver gurgled into a hollow hiding-place.
And the Archer-goddess lulled her wrath; and about the thicket,
seeking the tracks of crag-loving Lyaeus,
she went, lifting the newly-born babe of Aura,
carrying the bastard burden on her arm; and ashamed
she gave the male child to her brother Dionysus.
And the father gave his son to Nicaea, the midwife bride;
and she lifted him, and from the topmost nipple
pressing the life-giving moisture of her child-nursing breasts
she reared the boy. And taking him high upon his chariot,
Bacchus the infant still, the son named after his father,
Bacchus laid beside mystic Attic Athena,
babbling 'Euoi'; and the goddess within her temple,
Pallas, received him in her unwedded, god-receiving bosom;
and to the child she offered the breast that Erechtheus alone had sucked,
dripping bastard milk of itself from her unripe breast.
And she laid him beside the Eleusinian Bacchants;
and about the boy Iacchus the ivy-bearing Marathonian
Nymphs circled in dance, and for the newborn
god they lifted the night-dancing Attic pine;
and they propitiated the god after the son of Persephone,
and after the child of Semele, and set up sacrifices
to late-born Lyaeus and to first-born Dionysus,
and to the third, Iacchus, they crashed out a new hymn.
And with the triple rites Athens were stirred into Bacchic frenzy;
and the citizens struck up a late-fulfilled dance,
glorifying Zagreus together with Bromius and Iacchus.

Nor did Bacchus forget the Cydonian Loves,
but even of his former, dead bride he was mindful;
and the circling Crown of departed Ariadne,
the witness of his love, he fixed in Olympus,
an unceasing herald of his garland-loving marriage.
And the vine-clad god, treading his father's air,
shared one table with his fair-laboring father,
and after the mortal feast, after the former pouring of wine,
he drank the heavenly nectar from better cups,
enthroned with Apollo, sharing the hearth of the son of Maia.
